Since the operator $E_{j}$ sends $(\bar{\mathbb{Z}}_{l})^{2g}$ to $\frac{1}{|\disc(f)|}v_{j}$ and $E_{\lambda_{g+j}}$ sends $(\bar{\mathbb{Z}}_{l})^{2g}$ to $\frac{1}{|\disc(f)|}w_{j}$ for $1\leq j\leq g$ , it follows from the fact that $\sum_{j=1}^{2g}E_{j}=\id$ that $\frac{1}{|\disc(f)|}(\bar{\mathbb{Z}}_{l})^{2g}\subseteq N$ . Hence

$$ |\det(N)|\geq|\disc(f)|^{2g}\implies\prod_{i=1}^{g}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}\geq|\disc(f)|^{2g}\implies|\alpha_{i}|\geq|\disc(f)|^{g}. $$

In particular, if we scale the $v_{i}$ by $\alpha_{i}^{-1}$ so that $P\in\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ , it follows that $1\leq||v_{i}||\leq|\disc(f)|^{g}$ .

We can now apply the argument in the $\operatorname{GL}_{g}$ case to conclude that $||P||,||P^{-1}||\leq|\disc(f)|^{-(g+1)}$ . Then if $A^{\prime}$ denotes the Jacobian matrix for $(dp_{1},\ldots,dp_{g})$ at $PMP^{-1}$ which uses the basis $PMP^{-1}X^{(-)}_{i,j}$ , the matrix $A^{\prime}=AB$ where $B$ is the $\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}\times\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ matrix corresponding to conjugation by $P$ for the basis $X^{(-)}_{i,j}$ at the identity. Since $||P||,||P^{-1}||\leq|\disc(f)|^{-(g+1)}$ , it follows that the singular values of $B$ and $B^{-1}$ are bounded above by $|\disc(f)|^{-(g+1)}$ . Thus

$$ |\det(AA^{T})|\geq|\det((A^{\prime})(A^{\prime})^{T}||\disc(f)|^{g(g+1)} $$

and we are now reduced to understanding the case where $M$ is a diagonal matrix.

In the diagonal case, it is easy to check that again, only the diagonal matrices $X_{i,i}^{(-)}$ matter. We thus again obtain $|\det(AA^{T})|=|\disc(f)|^{2}$ and hence we obtain our inequality as desired. ∎

Note that by the Cauchy–Binet formula, $\det(AA^{T})$ is the sum of squares of the determinants of the maximal minors of $A$ . In particular, there exists a maximal minor of $A$ whose determinant is $\geq|\disc(f)|^{e/2}$ .

Let $c$ be the exponent of $l$ in $\disc(f)^{e}$ , where $e$ is in Proposition 5.5. Fix a characteristic polynomial $f$ with $\mathbb{Z}$ -coefficients. We now turn our attention to studying lifts of $M\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k-c})$ , where $\Char(M)=f$ mod $l^{k-c}$ , to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k})$ with characteristic polynomial $f$ mod $l^{k}$ , where $k-c\geq 1$ .

#### Proposition 5.6.

Assume that $k>2c$ and that $M$ lifts to a matrix $\tilde{M}\in\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k})$ with $\Char(\tilde{M})=f$ mod $l^{k}$ . Then $M$ lifts to a matrix $\tilde{M}_{0}\in\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ with $\Char(\tilde{M}_{0})=f$ .

#### Proof.

We first fix some lift $M_{0}$ of $\tilde{M}$ to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ with characteristic polynomial $f_{0}$ which need not be equal $f$ . This exists because $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ is smooth over $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ . Then every lift of $M$ to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{2(k-c)})$ is given by

$$ M_{0}+M_{0}l^{k-c}\left(a_{i,j}X^{(A)}_{i,j}+b_{i,j}X^{(B)}_{i,j}+c_{i,j}X^{(C)}_{i,j}\right) $$

where $a_{i,j},b_{i,j},c_{i,j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ . Hence to obtain a lift $\tilde{M}_{0}$ of $M$ to mod $l^{2(k-c)}$ with $\Char(\tilde{M}_{0})=f$ is equivalent to solving $f_{k}(a_{i,j},b_{i,j},c_{i,j})=0$ for $1\leq k\leq g$ , where each $f_{k}$ is the equation corresponding to the coefficient of $x^{2g-i}$ being equal to that of $f$ .

Now observe that the Jacobian matrix for the tuple $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{g})$ agrees with $l^{k-c}A$ , where $A$ is the Jacobian of the differential $(dp_{1},\ldots,dp_{g})$ at $T_{M_{0}}\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ in our standard basis, after taking mod $l^{2(k-c)}$ as any degree two terms involving $a_{i,j},b_{i,j},c_{i,j}$ will be $0$ . Since $2(k-c)>k$ , we obtain that there is a maximal minor whose determinant has order $\leq k$ . Since $\tilde{M}$ gives us a lift whose characteristic polynomial agrees with that of $f$ mod $l^{k}$ , we can apply Proposition 5.1 with the starting tuple $a_{i,j}=b_{i,j}=c_{i,j}=0$ along with $e=0$ . This gives us a lift $\tilde{M}_{0}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{2(k-c)})$ with $a_{i,j}=b_{i,j}=c_{i,j}=0$ mod $l$ and hence a lift of $\tilde{M}$ to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{2(k-c)})$ with characteristic polynomial $f$ . We can now repeat the process with $2(k-c)$ replacing $k$ and using $\tilde{M}_{0}$ as our new $\tilde{M}$ and $\tilde{M}_{0}$ mod $l^{2(k-c)-c}$ as our new $M$ . Then as $2(k-c)>k$ , iterating this process will provide us a lift to $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ as desired. ∎

Now let $k$ be large enough so that $k-c\geq\frac{k+1}{2}$ . Fix a congruence class $M$ mod $l^{k-c}$ with $\Char(M)=f$ mod $l^{k-c}$ with $M\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k-c})$ . We want to show that the number of lifts of $M$ to $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ with characteristic polynomial being $f$ is proportional to the number of lifts to $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k+1}\mathbb{Z}$ .

#### Proposition 5.7.

If $k-c\geq\frac{k+1}{2}$ , then the number of lifts of $M$ to mod $l^{k+1}$ with characteristic polynomial $f$ is exactly $l^{\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}-g}$ times the number of lifts of $M$ to mod $l^{k}$ with characteristic polynomial $f$ .

#### Proof.

First, we may assume there exists one such lift to mod $l^{k}$ . Then by Proposition 5.6, there exists a lift $M_{0}$ in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ such that $\Char(M_{0})=f$ . We may then describe every lift of $M$ to $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k})$ as

$$ M=M_{0}+M_{0}l^{k-c}\left(a_{i,j}X^{(A)}_{i,j}+b_{i,j}X^{(B)}_{i,j}+c_{i,j}X^{(C)}_{i,j}\right). $$

We want to solve for $\Char(M)=f$ mod $l^{k}$ . Since $k-c\geq\frac{k}{2}$ , the expression for each coefficient of $\Char(M)$ is linear in $a_{i,j},b_{i,j},c_{i,j}$ . In fact, as $\Char(M_{0})=f$ mod $l^{k}$ , it is equivalent to solving the linear system of equations $Ax=0$ mod $l^{c}$ where $x=(a_{i,j},b_{i,j},c_{i,j})^{T}$ . Similarly if we want to lift to $l^{k+1}$ , it is equivalent to solving $Ax=0$ mod $l^{c+1}$ .

We now write $A$ in Smith normal form, i.e. write $A=UDV$ where $U,V$ are invertible matrices over $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ and $D$ is a $g\times\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ matrix with entries only on the diagonal. Then the linear system is equivalent to $Dx=0$ mod $l^{c}$ and mod $l^{c+1}$ . If the diagonal has entries $d_{1},\ldots,d_{g}$ , then note that the order of $l$ dividing $d_{i}$ is $\leq c$ . It is then straightforward to deduce that the number of solutions mod $l^{c+1}$ is exactly $l^{\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}-g}$ times that of the number of solutions mod $l^{c}$ as desired. ∎

Proposition 4.13 directly follows from the discussion above.

### 5.3. Bounding matrices with zero discriminant

Our next proposition will give an upper bound on the number of $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ points of the solutions for a polynomial $f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ . When $k=1$ , then Lang–Weil bound implies that we can obtain a bound of the form $O_{\deg f}(l^{n-1})$ . However as we see from the example of $f(x)=x^{2}$ , we obtain $l^{k/2}$ many solutions and so we cannot expect a bound of the form $O(l^{k(n-1)})$ . We will show that we can still get a power savings that scales linearly with $k$ . For a polynomial $P$ , define the $l$ -adic valuation $||P||_{l}$ as the maximum of the $l$ -adic valuations of the coefficients.

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})$ be a degree $e$ polynomial with integer coefficients with $||P||_{l}=1$ . Then there exist constants $C,\delta>0$ depending only on $d$ , such that for any prime number $l$ and a natural number $k$ , there are at most $Cel^{k(d-\frac{\delta}{Ce})}$ solutions to $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})=0$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})^{d}$ .

#### Proof.

We first handle the one variable case first. By [7, Lemma 7], since $||P||_{l}=1$ , for any integer $\mu>0$ there exists at most $\deg P=e$ many $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ -elements $(A_{i},B_{i})$ for which $A_{i}\mathbb{Z}_{l}+B_{i}$ are the solutions to $\ord_{l}(P(x))\geq\mu$ and we may assume that $A_{i}=l^{a_{i}}$ so we have $l^{\mu}\mid f(l^{a_{i}}x+B_{i})$ . Expanding out for the pair $(A_{m},B_{m})$ and looking at the coefficient of $x^{j}$ , we obtain

$$ l^{\mu}\mid l^{a_{m}j}\sum_{i=j}^{e}c_{i}\binom{i}{j}(B_{m})^{i-j} $$

for every $j$ where $P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{e}c_{i}x^{i}$ . Let $c_{j}$ be the largest $j$ for which $\ord_{l}(c_{j})=0$ . Then we have

$$ \ord_{l}\left(\sum_{i=j}^{e}c_{i}\binom{i}{j}(B_{m})^{i-j}\right)=\ord_{l}(c_{j})=0. $$

Thus we must have

$$ l^{\mu}\mid l^{a_{m}j}\implies a_{m}\geq\frac{\mu}{e}. $$

In particular taking $\mu=k$ , we can have at most $el^{k-\frac{k}{e}}$ many such solutions as desired.

We now move onto the general case. We write $P=Q_{e}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d-1})x_{d}^{e}+\cdots+Q_{0}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d-1})$ with $Q_{e}\not=0$ . Since $||P||_{l}=1$ , we must have $||Q_{j}||_{l}=1$ for some $j$ . Given $k$ , we first remove all the tuples $x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}$ mod $l^{k}$ such that $Q_{j}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d-1})\equiv 0$ mod $l^{k/2}$ . By induction on the number of variables, this removes

$$ C_{d-1}el^{k\left(d-\frac{\delta_{d-1}}{2C_{d-1}e}\right)} $$

many tuples. For each tuple $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d-1})$ for which $Q_{j}(\mathbf{x})$ is not divisible by $l^{k/2}$ , it follows that we obtain a polynomial $P_{\mathbf{x}}$ in $x_{d}$ for which $||P_{\mathbf{x}}||_{l}\geq l^{-k/2}$ . Factoring this common power of $l$ out, the remaining $x_{d}$ must satisfy $P_{\mathbf{x}}(x_{d})\equiv 0$ mod $l^{k/2}$ where now $||P_{\mathbf{x}}||_{l}=1$ . It follows from the one variable case that there are at most

$$ C_{1}el^{k\left(d-\frac{\delta_{1}}{2C_{1}e}\right)} $$

solutions. Adding these two up gives us $C_{d}$ and $\delta_{d}$ as desired. ∎

We would like to apply this to the discriminant polynomial on $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ . We will exploit the fact that $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ is locally étale over $\mathbb{A}^{\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}}$ . We first show that if $f:X\to Y$ is étale, then the number of $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ -points in a fiber of $f$ can be bounded.

#### Lemma 5.9.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a finite étale morphism of noetherian schemes over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Then there exists $d>0$ such that for every prime power $l^{k}$ , the size of a fiber of $f:X(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\to Y(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ is bounded by $d$ .

#### Proof.

We may cover $X$ with an open cover $\{U_{i}\}$ and $Y$ with $\{V_{i}\}$ such that $f(U_{i})\subseteq V_{i}$ and $\pi_{i}U_{i}\to V_{i}$ is standard étale, i.e. of the form $A\to A[x]_{g}/(h)$ where $g,h\in A[x]$ and $h$ monic with $h^{\prime}$ invertible. Then a $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ point $z$ of $A$ corresponds to a morphism $\varphi:A\to\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ and a $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ point in $\pi_{i}^{-1}(z)$ corresponds to an extension $\tilde{\varphi}:A[x]_{g}/(h)\to\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ .

Let $\bar{g},\bar{h}$ be the image of $g,h$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})[x]$ under $\varphi$ . Then an extension corresponds exactly to a solution $\alpha$ of $\bar{h}(\alpha)=0$ mod $l^{k}$ along with $\bar{g}(\alpha)$ being invertible. But $h^{\prime}$ being invertible in $A[x]_{g}/h$ implies that $h^{\prime}(\alpha)\not=0$ for each root $\alpha$ of $\bar{h}(x)$ mod $l$ . Hensel’s lemma then implies each root of $\bar{h}(x)$ mod $l$ lifts uniquely to a root of $\bar{h}(x)$ mod $l^{k}$ and in particular, we have $|\pi_{i}^{-1}(x)|\leq\deg h$ . As there are finitely many $U_{i}$ ’s, there is a uniform upper bound on $|\pi_{i}^{-1}(x)|$ as desired and this proves our upper bound. ∎

As $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ is smooth over $\mathbb{Z}$ , we may cover $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ locally with open sets $U_{i}$ such that there is a morphism $f_{i}:U_{i}\to\mathbb{A}^{m}$ , where $m=\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ , which is étale. The discriminant of the characteristic polynomial cuts out a codimension one subscheme $X$ of $U_{i}$ , and we may take its scheme-theoretic image $Y$ which is a codimension one subscheme of $\mathbb{A}^{m}$ . We can then apply Proposition 5.8 to bound $Y(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ and then apply Lemma 5.9 to bound $X(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ .

However, we would like to obtain a bound for the discriminant polynomial of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ that is uniform in $p$ . For each fixed $l$ , we have an isomorphism between $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ and $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p^{\prime}}$ over $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ , if $p/p^{\prime}$ is a nonzero quadratic residue mod $l$ , given by sending the matrix $M$ to $cM$ where $c^{2}=p/p^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ , which multiplies the discriminant by a power of $c$ . Hence, the number of matrices $M\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k})$ with $l^{k}\mid\disc(f_{M})$ is exactly the number of matrices $M^{\prime}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k})$ with $l^{k}\mid\disc(f_{M^{\prime}})$ . Thus, we effectively have two cases depending on whether $p$ is a quadratic residue or non-residue.

Now, we consider a different isomorphism between $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ and $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ given by multiplication by $\diag(p,\ldots,p,1,\ldots,1)$ . This isomorphism however does not respect the discriminant and instead we obtain a polynomial $P(M,p)=P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{4g^{2}},p)$ on $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ corresponding to $\disc(f_{M})$ on $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ . Here, $x_{1},\ldots,x_{4g^{2}}$ are the entries of the matrix in $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ .

In each chart $U_{i}\to\mathbb{A}^{m}$ , let $U_{i}=\Spec A_{i}$ . Then we have a polynomial expression $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{4g^{2}},p)$ where each $x_{i}\in A_{i}$ . Let $B=\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]$ so that $A_{i}$ is an étale $B$ -algebra. By shrinking $U_{i}$ , we may assume that $A_{i}$ is a standard étale algebra, i.e. $A_{i}\simeq B[x]_{g}/(h)$ where $g,h\in B[x]$ and $h$ is monic with $h^{\prime}$ invertible in $B[x]_{g}/(h)$ . We now show that there is a polynomial $R(x)\in B[x]$ such that $R(p)\in B$ is a multiple of $P(M,p)$ in $A_{i}$ . Since the subscheme $X$ is cut out by $P(M,p)$ , this means that $R(p)$ vanishes in the scheme-theoretic image $Y$ .

#### Lemma 5.10.

Let $B$ be a domain and let $A=B[x]_{g}/(h)$ be a standard étale algebra. Let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\in A$ and $y\in B$ . Consider the element $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y)$ where $P$ is a polynomial in $n+1$ variables with $\mathbb{Z}$ -coefficients. There is then a polynomial $R(x)\in B[x]$ , depending only on $P$ and $x_{i}$ ’s, such that $R(y)$ is a multiple of $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y)$ in $A$ .

#### Proof.

Note that $B[x]/h$ is integral over $B$ since $h$ is monic. Let $A^{\prime}$ be the integral closure of $B$ in $\Frac(B[x]/h)$ so that $A\subseteq A^{\prime}$ . Let $g^{\prime}$ be the norm of $g$ with respect to the finite extension $\Frac(A)$ over $\Frac(B)$ . Then for some sufficiently large $c$ , we have that $(g^{\prime})^{c}x_{i}$ is integral over $B$ . Now consider the product

$$ Q(y)=\prod_{(x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime})}P(x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime},y) $$

where we vary $x_{i}^{\prime}$ over all conjugates of $x_{i}$ over $B$ , of which there are only finitely many since $\Frac(A)$ is a finite extension of $\Frac(B)$ . This expands out to a symmetric polynomial in each of the $x_{i}^{\prime}$ ’s and since $(g^{\prime})^{c}x_{i}$ is integral, it follows that $Q(y)=\frac{R(y)}{(g^{\prime})^{c^{\prime}}}$ for some polynomial $R\in B[x]$ that depends only on $P$ and the $x_{i}$ ’s. Hence we have

$$ R(y)=(g^{\prime})^{c^{\prime}}\prod_{(x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime})}P(x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime},y). $$

Let $P^{\prime}$ be the product of $(g^{\prime})^{c^{\prime}}$ along with the terms $P(x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime}y)$ , where we vary all possible $(x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime})$ except our original tuple $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ . Then $P^{\prime}\in\Frac(B[x]_{g}/(h))$ and since $P^{\prime}$ is clearly integral over $B$ , it must lie in $A^{\prime}$ .

Now note that there is an element $f\in B$ so that $fA^{\prime}\subseteq A$ . Indeed, we know that $A^{\prime}$ is finitely generated as a $A$ -module, say by $a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}$ and for each $a_{i}$ , we can find a suitable $f_{i}\in A$ . Each $f_{i}$ has a multiple $b_{i}\in B$ and then we can take $f=\prod_{i=1}^{r}b_{i}$ . Thus $fP^{\prime}\in A$ with $f\in B$ and it follows that

$$ f\cdot R(y)=P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y)\cdot f\cdot P^{\prime} $$

with $fP^{\prime}\in A\implies fR(y)$ is a multiple of $P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y)$ as desired. ∎

Now we put everything together to show that most matrices in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ have nonzero discriminant modulo $l^{k}$ .

#### Proof of Proposition 4.14.

Recall our setup above where we cover $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ with finitely many opens so that we have a morphism $f_{i}:U_{i}\to\mathbb{A}^{m}$ that is standard étale with $U_{i}=\Spec A_{i}$ . On each chart $U_{i}$ , there is a polynomial $P_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{4g^{2}},p)$ where $x_{i}\in A_{i}$ , such that under the isomorphism $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}\simeq\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ it is equal to $\disc(f_{M})$ . Also recall that for each $l$ , we have two cases depending on whether $p$ is a quadratic or non-quadratic residue, and it suffices to give a bound for a specific choice of $p$ in each case.

Let $X_{i,p}=\Spec A_{i}/(P_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{4g^{2}},p))\subseteq U_{i}$ . It suffices to give an upper bound on $\#X_{i,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ , and so by Lemma 5.9 it suffices to bound $\#Y_{i,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ where $Y_{i,p}$ is the scheme theoretic image of $X_{i,p}$ under $f_{i}$ . By Lemma 5.10, we have a polynomial $R_{i}(x)\in B[x]$ with $B=\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]$ such that $R_{i}(p)$ is a multiple of $P_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{4g^{2}},p)$ in $A_{i}$ , which implies that $Y_{i,p}$ is a subscheme of $V(R_{i}(p))$ . Hence, it suffices to bound the number of solutions to $R_{i}(p)=0$ mod $l^{k}$ where $R_{i}(p)$ is viewed as a polynomial in $\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]$ .

Proposition 5.8 tells us that we can get this by giving a bound for $||R_{i}(p)||_{l}$ . For the case of quadratic residues we can simply choose $p=1$ which gives a constant bound. For non-quadratic residues, we need a little more work. The coefficient of $x_{1}^{i_{1}}\cdots x_{m}^{i_{m}}$ for $R_{i}(p)$ is a polynomial $R_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}(p)$ in $p$ . Pick one such polynomial which is not identically zero, then since this can have at most a finite number of zeroes, for sufficiently large $l$ we can choose a non-quadratic residue $p$ such that $l$ doesn’t divide $R_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}(p)$ . There are only a finite set of small $l$ so $l^{\ord_{l}(R_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}(p))}\leq C$ is uniformly bounded. Thus, by possibly dividing $R_{i}(p)$ by a small power of $l$ and applying Proposition 5.8, we have for some uniform constant $\delta>0$

$$ \#\{R_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m},p)=0\text{ mod }l^{k}\}\leq l^{k(m-\delta)}. $$

As we only have finitely many $i$ ’s, we may find a $p$ that works for every $i$ . Thus, taking the union across $U_{i}$ we obtain

$$ \#\left\{M\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\ \middle|\ l^{k}\mid\disc(f_{M})\right\}\leq l^{k(\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}-\delta)}. $$

We get the desired result after dividing by $\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})=\Theta(l^{k\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}})$ . ∎

## 6. Effective Chebotarev density theorem in families

As mentioned in the proof overview, our goal in this section is to use an effective Chebotarev density theorem in families of number fields to truncate the infinite product $\prod_{l}v_{l}(f_{A})$ appearing in Theorem 1.10.

We state the effective Chebotarev density theorem given in [41], which extends the work of [33] for more general Galois groups and does not rely on the strong Artin conjecture. Let $G$ be a nontrivial finite group and $L/\mathbb{Q}$ be a Galois extension of number fields with $\Gal(L/\mathbb{Q})\cong G$ . A rational prime $l$ is unramified when $l\nmid D_{L}$ , and in this case define the Artin symbol $\left[\frac{L/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]$ to be the conjugacy class of $\Frob_{l}$ in $G$ . We want an effective bound on how $\left[\frac{L/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]$ is equidistributed, so for a conjugacy class $C\subseteq G$ we define

$$ \pi_{C}(x,L/\mathbb{Q})\coloneqq\#\left\{l\text{ prime }\middle|\ l\leq x,\ l\nmid D_{K},\ \left[\frac{L/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]=C\right\}. $$

Then, the effective Chebotarev theorem bounds how far this is from the expected amount.

#### Theorem 6.1 ([41, Theorem 2.1]).

Fix a nontrivial finite group $G$ , and constants $\epsilon>0$ and $Q\geq 3$ . Let $\mathfrak{F}_{G}$ be a family of number fields $L$ that are Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\Gal(L/\mathbb{Q})\cong G$ . Define $\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)=\{L\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}\colon D_{L}\leq Q\}$ , and

$$ \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}\coloneqq\max_{L^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}\#\{L\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)\colon L\cap L^{\prime}\neq\mathbb{Q}\}. $$

For all except $O(\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}Q^{\epsilon})$ number fields $L\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)$ , the following statement is true. If $C\subseteq G$ is a conjugacy class, then

$$ \left|\pi_{C}(x,L/\mathbb{Q})-\frac{|C|}{|G|}\Li(x)\right|=O\left(x\exp\left(-\frac{1}{29}\left(\frac{\log(x)}{|G|}\right)^{1/2}\right)\right)\text{ for }x\geq(\log D_{L})^{10^{9}|G|^{3}/\epsilon}. $$

Call $L$ an $\epsilon$ -good number field if Equation (6.1) is true for the constant $\epsilon>0$ . In Section 6.1, we use Equation (6.1) in the case when $\widetilde{K}$ is $\epsilon$ -good to deduce that the tail end $\prod_{l>l_{0}}v_{l}(f_{A})$ is close to $1$ , allowing us to truncate the product as desired. In Section 6.3, we bound the number of exceptional fields which are not $\epsilon$ -good, showing that the truncation works generically.

### 6.1. Prime splitting and truncation

Let $A$ be a simple, ordinary abelian variety with generic Galois group $G=(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ , and $l$ be a good rational prime satisfying $l\nmid 2p\disc(f_{A})$ , so we have $v_{l}(f_{A})=\zeta_{K,l}(1)/\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)$ by Lemma 4.7. Furthermore, $l$ is unramified in $K\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/f_{A}(x)$ and thus also unramified in both $K^{+}$ and the Galois closure $\widetilde{K}$ . By definition, we have that

$$ \zeta_{K,l}(1)=\prod_{\text{prime }\mathfrak{l}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K},\,\mathfrak{l}\mid l}\frac{1}{1-N(\mathfrak{l})^{-1}}=1+\frac{\#\{\text{prime }\mathfrak{l}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}\mid N(\mathfrak{l})=l\}}{l}+O(l^{-2}). $$

The analogous statement applies for the totally real field $K^{+}$ , so combining them we get

$$ \frac{\zeta_{K,l}(1)}{\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)}=1+\frac{a_{K,l}}{l}+O(l^{-2}) $$

where we define

$$ a_{K,l}\coloneqq\#\{\text{prime }\mathfrak{l}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}\mid N(\mathfrak{l})=l\}-\#\{\text{prime }\mathfrak{l}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K^{+}}\mid N(\mathfrak{l})=l\}. $$

To determine $a_{K,l}$ , we need to know how $l$ splits in both $K$ and $K^{+}$ , and the following Proposition tells us that this information is determined by $\left[\frac{\widetilde{K}/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]$ .

#### Proposition 6.2 ([19, Proposition 2.8, Chapter III]).

Let $H$ be the subgroup of $G$ fixing $K$ , and suppose $\left[\frac{\widetilde{K}/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]$ has cycles of length $t_{1},\ldots,t_{s}$ when acting on the cosets of $H$ in $G$ . Then, the rational prime $l$ splits into primes $\mathfrak{l}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{l}_{s}$ in $K$ where $N(\mathfrak{l}_{i})=l^{t_{i}}$ . The same statement holds when we replace $K$ with $K^{+}$ and $H$ with $H^{+}$ .

Hence, for $\sigma\in G$ we define $a_{\sigma}=|(G/H)^{\sigma}|-|(G/H^{+})^{\sigma}|$ to be the difference in the number of cosets of $H$ and $H^{+}$ which are fixed by $\sigma$ . This is the same up to conjugacy, so for a conjugacy class $C\subseteq G$ we define $a_{C}=a_{\sigma}$ for $\sigma\in C$ . Hence, the above proposition tells that $a_{K,l}=a_{\left[\frac{\widetilde{K}/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]}$ .

#### Lemma 6.3.

The average of $a_{\sigma}$ among all $\sigma\in G$ is $0$ .

#### Proof.

We show that the average size of $(G/H)^{\sigma}$ is $1$ . Indeed, any coset $gH$ is a fixed point of $\sigma$ if and only if $\sigma gH=gH$ , i.e. $g^{-1}\sigma g\in H$ which happens with $|H|/|G|$ probability. There are $|G|/|H|$ possible cosets, so by linearity of expectation, we expect an average of $1$ coset of $H$ in $G$ to be fixed. The same argument shows that the average size of $(G/H^{+})^{\sigma}$ is also $1$ , so by taking the difference we have the desired result. In principle, this proof works because both $\zeta_{K}$ and $\zeta_{K^{+}}$ have simple poles at $s=1$ . ∎

Heuristically, Chebotarev’s density theorem tells us that $\left[\frac{\widetilde{K}/\mathbb{Q}}{l}\right]$ is equidistributed, so by the lemma above, $\zeta_{K,l}(1)/\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)$ should have an average of $1+O(l^{-2})$ across all primes $l$ . The factors greater than $1$ should cancel out with those that are smaller than $1$ , making the tail end of the infinite product equals to $1$ plus a small error. We make this rigorous starting from Equation (6.1), in a similar way to [28, Section 4].

#### Proposition 6.4.

Suppose $\widetilde{K}$ is an $\epsilon$ -good number field, i.e. it satisfies Equation (6.1) with the constant $\epsilon>0$ . Then, there exists constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ such that for $l_{0}\geq(\log D_{L})^{C_{1}/\epsilon}$ , we have

$$ \prod_{l>l_{0}}\frac{\zeta_{K,l}(1)}{\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)}=1+O\left(\exp\left(-C_{2}\log(l_{0})^{1/2}\right)\right). $$

#### Proof.

First, we note that the contribution from ramified primes are insignificant as each term is $1+O(l_{0}^{-1})$ and there are at most $\log(D_{L})$ many ramified primes. From now on we only consider the product over unramified primes, and by taking the logarithm, we have

$$ \sum_{l>l_{0}}\log\left(\frac{\zeta_{K,l}(1)}{\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)}\right)=\sum_{l>l_{0}}\left(\frac{a_{K,l}}{l}+O(l^{-2})\right)=\sum_{l>l_{0}}\frac{a_{K,l}}{l}+O(l_{0}^{-1}). $$

By partial summation,

$$ \sum_{l>l_{0}}\frac{a_{K,l}}{l}=\int_{l_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{s(x)}{x^{2}} $$

where

$$ \begin{split}s(x)&\coloneqq\sum_{l_{0}<l\leq x}a_{K,l}=\sum_{C}a_{C}\left(\pi_{C}(x,L/\mathbb{Q})-\pi_{C}(l_{0},L/\mathbb{Q})\right)\\
&=\sum_{C}a_{C}\frac{|C|}{|G|}(\Li(x)-\Li(l_{0}))+O\left(x\exp\left(-C_{3}\log(x)^{1/2}\right)\right)\end{split} $$

where the latter sum is over conjugacy classes $C\subseteq G$ and $C_{3}>0$ is some constant. By Lemma 6.3, the sum in the second line evaluates to zero and we are left with the error term. Substituting this back, we have

$$ \sum_{l>l_{0}}\log\left(\frac{\zeta_{K,l}(1)}{\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)}\right)=O\left(\int_{l_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{\exp(-C_{3}\log(x)^{1/2})}{x}+l_{0}^{-1}\right)=O\left(\exp\left(-C_{3}\log(l_{0})^{1/2}\right)\right) $$

which gives the desired result after exponentiating. ∎

### 6.2. Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem

In order for Proposition 6.4 to be useful, we need to show that most of the $\widetilde{K}$ are $\epsilon$ -good. The main input for this is an effective Hilbert irreducibility theorem. Most versions in the literature either do not give explicit dependence on the coefficients on the polynomial in question, or give a polynomial dependence, which is not strong enough for our purposes. We state the version in [32] which only has a $\log$ dependence on the coefficients of the polynomial which this was in turn proven by means of a Bombieri-Pila type of bound. Here, we simplify the statement in the case when the polynomial has coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$ . In [32], only the statement bounding the number of specializations such that $f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)$ has a root is given but it is straightforward to deduce the corresponding statement regarding irreducibility following [32, Lemma 4.2]. Here, we denote $[B]=\mathbb{Z}\cap[-B,B]$ , and the height $H(f)$ of an integer polynomial can be defined as the maximum absolute value of its coefficients divided by the gcd of them.

#### Theorem 6.5 ([32, Theorem 5.5]).

Fix $s\geq 1$ and let $f(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s},Y)\in\mathbb{Z}[T_{1},\ldots,T_{s},Y]$ be irreducible of degree $d_{Y}$ in the variable $Y$ and degree $d_{T}$ in the $T_{i}^{\prime}s$ . Then there are positive constants $\mu,\nu$ depending on $s,d_{T},d_{Y}$ such that

$$ \#\{(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})\in[B]^{s}\mid f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)\text{ has a solution }y\in\mathbb{Z}\}=O\left((\log H(f)+1)^{\mu}B^{s-\frac{1}{2}}(\log(B))^{\nu}\right). $$

#### Corollary 6.6.

Fix a positive integer $s$ and let $f(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s},Y)\in\mathbb{Z}[T_{1},\ldots,T_{s},Y]$ be irreducible of degree $d_{Y}$ in the variable $Y$ and $d_{T}$ in the $T_{i}$ ’s. Then there are positive constants $\mu,\nu$ depending on $s,d_{T},d_{Y}$ such that

$$ \#\{(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})\in[B]^{s}\mid f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)\text{ is reducible over }\mathbb{Z}\}=O\left((\log H(f)+1)^{\mu}B^{s-\frac{1}{2}}(\log B)^{\nu}\right). $$

#### Proof.

We follow the strategy of [32, Proposition 4.1], adapting it for multiple variables. We first assume that $f$ is monic in $Y$ . Let $\bar{\mathbb{Q}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s})}$ be the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s})$ and let $f(\mathbf{T},Y)=\prod_{i=1}^{d_{Y}}(y-y_{i})$ where each $y_{i}\in\bar{\mathbb{Q}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s})}$ . Each $y_{i}$ is integral over $\mathbb{Z}[T_{1},\ldots,T_{s}]$ and so for any $\omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d_{Y}\}$ and non-negative integer $j$ with $j\leq|\omega|$ , the element $\tau_{\omega,j}$ which is the $j^{th}$ symmetric sum of the $y_{i}$ ’s in $\omega$ is integral over $\mathbb{Z}[T_{1},\ldots,T_{s}]$ . Let $P_{\omega,j}(\mathbf{T},Y)$ be the minimal polynomial of $\tau_{\omega,j}$ . Then it is monic and has coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[T_{1},\ldots,T_{s}]$ .

Now suppose we have a specialization $t_{1},\ldots,t_{s}\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)$ is reducible over $\mathbb{Z}$ , so we obtain a factorization

$$ f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)=\prod_{i\in\omega}(Y-y_{i}(\mathbf{t}))\prod_{i\not\in\omega}(Y-y_{i}(\mathbf{t})) $$

for some $\omega\subseteq d_{Y}$ with $1\leq|\omega|\leq d_{Y}-1$ . Take $R(Y)=\prod_{i\in\omega}(Y-y_{i}(\mathbf{t}))$ . Then the coefficients of $R(Y)$ are $\tau_{\omega,j}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})$ up to a sign. At least one of the $\tau_{\omega,j}$ does not lie in $\mathbb{Q}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s})$ else $f(\mathbf{T},Y)$ would be reducible over $\mathbb{Q}(T_{1},\ldots,T_{s})$ . If we let $P_{\omega,j}$ be the minimal polynomial for this particular $\tau_{\omega,j}$ , then $2\leq\deg P_{\omega,j}\leq 2^{d_{Y}}$ and $P_{\omega,j}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)$ has $\tau_{\omega,j}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})$ as a root which lies in $\mathbb{Z}$ .

It now suffices to note that the number of such $P_{\omega,j}$ ’s are bounded in terms of $d_{Y},d_{T}$ , their degree is bounded in terms of $d_{Y}$ , and their log-height is bounded in terms of a multiple of $(\log H(P)+1)$ that depends only on $d_{Y}$ and $d_{T}$ , much like in [32, Lemma 4.2]. Thus by applying Theorem 6.5 on each of the $P_{\omega,j}$ ’s, we obtain our upper bound as desired when $f(\mathbf{T},Y)$ is monic in $Y$ .

In general, we write

$$ f(\mathbf{T},Y)=a_{0}(\mathbf{T})Y^{d_{Y}}+\cdots+a_{d_{Y}}(\mathbf{T}) $$

and consider

$$ g(\mathbf{T},Y)=a_{0}(T)^{d_{Y}-1}f\left(\mathbf{T},\frac{Y}{a_{0}(T)}\right)=Y^{d_{Y}}+a_{1}(T)Y^{d_{Y}-1}+\cdots+(a_{0}(T))^{d_{Y}-1}a_{d_{Y}}(T). $$

This expands to a monic polynomial in $Y$ with degree $d_{Y}$ in $Y$ and degree bounded in terms of $d_{T}$ in $T$ . It is clear that $\log(H(g)+1)$ is bounded by a constant, depending on $d_{T},d_{Y}$ and $s$ , times $\log(H(f)+1)$ and that $g$ is irreducible since $f$ is irreducible. Under a specialization such that $a_{0}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})\not=0$ , we have $g(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)$ is reducible if and only if $f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},Y)$ is. If we had a specialization such that $a_{0}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})=0$ , we are in a case where the degree drops and we can handle that by induction. Hence the general case follows from the monic case as desired. ∎

### 6.3. Bounding exceptional fields

Let $G=(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ and $\mathfrak{F}_{G}$ be the family of number fields $\widetilde{K}$ for $K\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/f_{A}(x)$ where $A$ ranges across all simple ordinary abelian varieties $A/\mathbb{F}_{p}$ of dimension $2g$ with generic Galois group $\Gal(\widetilde{K}/\mathbb{Q})\cong G$ . Recall from Proposition 2.5 that such a polynomial $f_{A}(x)$ can be written as $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ for some $\mathbf{a}\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ , so we denote the corresponding fields to be $K_{\mathbf{a}}$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ . Furthermore, note that $\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ is upper bounded by a polynomial in $p$ , and because $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is defined to be monic, we see that $\disc(K_{\mathbf{a}})$ and thus also $\disc(\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}})$ are also bounded polynomially in $p$ . Hence, we have $\mathfrak{F}_{G}=\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)$ where $Q=O(p^{A})$ for some constant $A$ .

Recall that our goal is to bound the proportion of $\mathbf{a}$ for which $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ is not $\epsilon$ -good, and we wish to do this by upper bounding $\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}=\max_{L^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}\#\{L\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)\colon L\cap L^{\prime}\neq\mathbb{Q}\}$ . Hence, for each $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ , we want to upper bound the number of fields $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ that intersect it nontrivially. Since $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ only has a bounded number of subfields $L\neq\mathbb{Q}$ , it suffices to show that for any such subfield that the proportion of $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ containing $L$ is small.

Our first step is to show that there is no field $L$ which is contained in every $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ .

#### Lemma 6.7.

For any number field $L\neq\mathbb{Q}$ , there exists $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ not necessarily in $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ where $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group and does not contain $L$ .

#### Proof.

We use a discriminant argument. Suppose that there exists such a field $L$ such that every $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ with generic Galois group contains it. Since every nontrivial extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is ramified, $L$ has to be ramified at some prime $l$ , so $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ must also be ramified at $l$ . This implies that $K_{\mathbf{a}}$ is ramified at $l$ because $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ is the compositum of the Galois conjugates of $K_{\mathbf{a}}$ . Thus, for each prime $l$ it suffices to find some $K_{\mathbf{a}}$ with generic Galois group where $l$ does not ramify.

We first deal with the case $l\neq p$ . Consider the polynomials $x^{2g}+p^{g}$ and $x^{2g}+px^{2g-2}+p^{2}x^{2g-4}+\cdots+p^{g}$ and it is easy to show using a root of unity argument that these have discriminants $(-1)^{g}(2g)^{2g}p^{g(2g-1)}$ and $(-1)^{g}2^{2g}(g+1)^{2g-2}p^{g(2g-1)}$ respectively. Furthermore, note that $x^{2g}+x^{2g-1}+\cdots+x^{g}+px^{g-1}+p^{2}x^{g-2}+\cdots+p^{g}$ is equal to $x^{2g}+x^{2g-1}+\cdots+1$ modulo $2$ which has odd discriminant. Noting that $g$ and $g+1$ are coprime, we see that for any prime $l\neq p$ at least one of the above polynomials of the form $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ have discriminant coprime to $l$ . Furthermore, this remains true under translate $\mathbf{a}$ by multiples of $l$ . The proof of Proposition 2.14 shows that a generic $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ has Galois group $G$ (here, we need to take larger boxes depending on $l$ , so $\mathbf{a}$ may not be in $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ ), which implies that there is some translate $\mathbf{a}$ for which $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group and $l$ does not ramify.

The case of $l=p$ is more difficult because by Lemma 4.9 we have that $p^{g(g-1)}\mid\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ for every $\mathbf{a}$ , so the above strategy does not work naively. We choose $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ with $\ord_{p}(a_{i})=0$ for all $i$ such that $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group and also satisfying $p^{g(g-1)}\mid\mid\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ by Lemma 4.9. Now let $\alpha$ be a root of $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ and consider an embedding $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}\xhookrightarrow{}\bar{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}$ . It suffices to show that under any such embedding, we must have $\mathbb{Q}_{p}(\alpha)$ being unramified over $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ .

First by Newton polygons, it follows that $g$ of the roots of $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ satisfy $|x|_{p}=1$ and the other $g$ satisfy $|x|_{p}=p^{-1}$ . Let $b_{1},\ldots,b_{g}$ be the roots satisfying $|b_{i}|_{p}=1$ and let $c_{1},\ldots,c_{g}$ be the other roots. Since the discriminant satisfy $|\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})|_{p}=p^{-g(g-1)}$ , it follows that $|b_{i}-b_{j}|_{p}=1$ and $|c_{i}-c_{j}|_{p}=0$ .

We now have two cases. The first case is when $\alpha$ is among the $b_{i}$ ’s, say $\alpha=b_{1}$ . We consider the conjugates of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ . Since conjugates have the same absolute value, they must be among the $b_{i}$ ’s, say $b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}$ . We may then form a basis of integral elements of $\mathbb{Q}_{p}(\alpha)$ by $1,\frac{\alpha}{p},\ldots,\frac{\alpha^{k-1}}{p^{k-1}}$ as $|\alpha|_{p}=1$ . Since $\frac{b_{i}}{p}$ are the conjugates of $\frac{\alpha}{p}$ over $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ , the discriminant of this basis has absolute value equivalent to

$$ \prod_{1\leq i\not=j\leq k}\left|\frac{b_{i}}{p}-\frac{b_{j}}{p}\right|_{p}=1 $$

as $|\frac{b_{i}}{p}-\frac{b_{j}}{p}|_{p}=1$ for each $i,j$ . It follows that $\mathbb{Q}_{p}(\alpha)$ is unramified over $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ . Similarly if $\alpha$ is among the $c_{i}$ ’s, the same argument goes through without dividing by $p$ as we already have $|c_{i}-c_{j}|_{p}=1$ . Hence $\mathbb{Q}_{p}(\alpha)$ is unramified over $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ for any embedding $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}\xhookrightarrow{}\bar{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}$ which implies that $p$ is unramified in $K_{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ as desired. ∎

Now, let $L$ be a minimal subfield (has no nontrivial subfields) of $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}^{\prime}}$ for some $\mathbf{a}^{\prime}\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ . We use the following method to detect whether $L$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ intersect. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be primitive roots of $L$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ respectively and consider $\alpha+\beta$ . In the case where the two fields intersect, $L$ must be contained in $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ so $\alpha+\beta$ is also contained inside $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ .

Otherwise, $\alpha+\beta$ must generate the compositum $L\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ . To see this, first note that the compositum has degree $[L:\mathbb{Q}][\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}:\mathbb{Q}]$ by [29, Corollary 3.19] as $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois. Then, suppose otherwise that $\alpha+\beta$ generates a proper subfield of $L\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , so there exists different embeddings $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\colon L\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ for which $\sigma_{1}(\alpha+\beta)=\sigma_{2}(\alpha+\beta)$ . This implies that $\sigma_{1}(\alpha)-\sigma_{2}(\alpha)=\sigma_{1}(\beta)-\sigma_{2}(\beta)$ , but this is contained in the intersection of the Galois closure of $L$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ which is $\mathbb{Q}$ . In fact, this must be zero because if we let $c=\sigma_{1}(\beta)-\sigma_{2}(\beta)$ , then $c=\beta-\sigma_{1}^{-1}\sigma_{2}(\beta)$ , but $\sigma_{1}^{-1}\sigma_{2}$ has finite order, say $m$ , in $\Gal(\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}/\mathbb{Q})$ , which means that $0=\beta-(\sigma_{1}^{-1}\sigma_{2})^{m}(\beta)=mc$ . This implies that $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ are the same embeddings for both $L$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , and hence also for $L\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , giving a contradiction.

Using the minimal polynomials of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ , we can construct a polynomial with root $\alpha+\beta$ of the expected degree, so the above argument says that this polynomial is irreducible if and only if the fields $L$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ don’t intersect. Then, this allows us to apply Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem.

Keeping this setting, we construct this polynomial in the following two lemmas, starting with the minimal polynomial for $L$ with root $\alpha$ .

#### Lemma 6.8.

There exists a monic polynomial $P_{L}(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ with coefficients at most polynomial in $p$ such that $L\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/P_{L}(x)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $L$ be the fixed field of the subgroup $H$ in $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ . By the proof of the primitive element theorem, we can construct a primitive element $\gamma=\sum_{i}c_{i}\gamma_{i}$ of $K_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ , where $c_{i}=O(1)$ are bounded integers and $\gamma_{i}$ are the roots of $f_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}(x)$ . Then, $\gamma$ is a root of the polynomial

$$ Q(x)=\prod_{\sigma_{h}\in H}(x-\sigma_{h}(\gamma)), $$

and also note that the coefficients are elementary symmetric polynomials $e_{1},\ldots,e_{|H|}$ with variables $\sigma_{h}(\gamma)$ .

We claim that $L=\mathbb{Q}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{|H|})$ . Indeed, the latter field is $H$ -invariant so $L$ contains it and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ is at most a degree $|H|$ extension of the field by $Q(x)$ so we must have equality. Again, we can find a primitive element $\delta=\sum_{i}d_{i}e_{i}$ of $L$ where $d_{i}$ are bounded integers, and we let

$$ P_{L}(x)=\prod_{\sigma_{g}\in G/H}(x-\sigma_{g}(\delta)) $$

which is well defined since $\delta$ is already $H$ -invariant. The coefficients of $P_{L}(x)$ are $G$ -invariant so they are in $\mathbb{Q}$ , and furthermore they are algebraic integers and hence in $\mathbb{Z}$ , so this is indeed a monic integer minimal polynomial of $L$ .

In fact, the coefficients of $P_{L}(x)$ are polynomials of the form $R(\gamma_{i})$ which are invariant when the indices are permuted according to $G=(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ . By pairing the roots into pairs $\{\gamma_{2i+1},\gamma_{2i+2}\}$ , the polynomial $R(\gamma_{i})$ is symmetric in each pair and thus can be expressed as elementary symmetric polynomials in each pair. However, recall that the pair $\{\gamma_{2i+1},\gamma_{2i+2}\}$ are the solutions to $x^{2}-\alpha_{i}x+p=0$ where $\alpha_{i}$ are the roots of $f^{+}_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ , so we can write $R(\gamma_{i})=R^{\prime}(\alpha_{i},p)$ . But now the expression in terms of $\alpha_{i}$ is $S_{g}$ invariant, so it can be expressed as the coefficients of $f^{+}_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ which in turn can be expressed as the coefficients of $f_{\mathbf{a^{\prime}}}$ , which have size at most polynomial in $p$ . Tracing back, because $c_{i}$ and $d_{i}$ were bounded, we have the desired result. ∎

Now, we construct the polynomial for $\alpha+\beta$ as discussed previously.

#### Lemma 6.9.

There exists an polynomial $R(x,\mathbf{a})\in\mathbb{Z}[x,a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}]$ irreducible in the variable $x$ with coefficients bounded polynomially in $p$ , such that for any $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ , if $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ is irreducible as a polynomial in $x$ then $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group and does not intersect $L$ .

#### Proof.

For now, we fix $\mathbf{a}$ so that $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ is the field obtained in Lemma 6.7 and choose bounded $c_{i}$ such that $\beta=\sum_{i}c_{i}\gamma_{i}$ is a primitive root of $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , where here $\gamma_{i}$ are the roots of $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ . Let $Q(x)=\prod_{\sigma\in G}(x-\sigma(\beta))$ , this has degree $|G|$ and just like the proof of Lemma 6.8 we can write each coefficient of $Q(x)$ as a polynomial in $\mathbf{a}$ with coefficients bounded polynomially in $p$ , so we can rewrite this as $Q(x,\mathbf{a})$ .

The polynomials $P_{L}(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ which are primitive roots of $L$ and $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ respectively. We want a polynomial $R(x)$ with root $\alpha+\beta$ , so we consider the elements $(\alpha+\beta)^{i}$ for $0\leq i\leq|G|[L:\mathbb{Q}]$ . Using the monic polynomials $P_{L}(x)$ as well as $Q(x)$ we can express each of these as a linear combination of monomials $\alpha^{j}\beta^{k}$ for $0\leq j<[L:\mathbb{Q}]$ and $0\leq k<|G|$ . By a simple Gaussian elimination argument, there is a linear dependence between $(\alpha+\beta)^{i}$ which gives rise to a not necessarily monic polynomial $R(x)$ of degree $[L\colon\mathbb{Q}]|G|$ with $\alpha+\beta$ as a root. Furthermore, $R(x)$ is irreducible because its root generates $L\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ which is a number field of the same degree. Since the coefficients of $R(x)$ can be written as a polynomial in $\mathbf{a}$ with coefficients bounded polynomially in $p$ , we write it in the form of $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ . The irreducibility of $R(x)$ then implies the irreducibility of $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ in the variable $x$ .

Now we allow $\mathbf{a}$ to vary, and suppose for some new choice of $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ that $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ is irreducible in $x$ . Then, we can define the $\gamma_{i}$ to be the roots of the polynomial $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ and $\beta=\sum_{i}c_{i}\gamma_{i}$ , which value is now dependent on $\mathbf{a}$ . However, since our construction is completely algebraic, it is still true that the new $\alpha+\beta$ is still a root of $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ . Since it is irreducible, $\alpha+\beta$ generate a field of degree $[L\colon\mathbb{Q}]|G|$ . At the same time, it lies in the compositum of $L\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , which forces this to be of degree $[L\colon\mathbb{Q}]|G|$ . In particular, this implies that $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group and does not intersect $L$ . ∎

Then, we can apply Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem as stated in Corollary 6.6 to bound the number of fields intersecting $L$ .

#### Lemma 6.10.

There exists some constant $C>0$ independent of $L$ such that there are at most $O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}}(\log p)^{C})$ many $\mathbf{a}\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ where $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group and also intersects $L$ .

#### Proof.

Cover $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ with hypercubes of length $p^{1/2}$ using Proposition 2.10, and there are $O(p^{g(g-1)/4})$ such hypercubes in the cover. Apply Corollary 6.6 to the polynomial $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ in Lemma 6.9, noting that we can shift the origin of the box $[B]$ while keeping the coefficients and thus the height $H(f)$ bounded by a polynomial in $p$ . This shows that there are at most $O(p^{g/2-1/4}(\log p)^{C})$ vectors $\mathbf{a}$ in each box where $R(x,\mathbf{a})$ is reducible, and thus $O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}}(\log p)^{C})$ such $\mathbf{a}$ in total. ∎

Finally, we bound the proportion of $\mathbf{a}$ for which the corresponding $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ are not $\epsilon$ -good. A naive argument would be to say that $\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}=O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}}(\log p)^{C})$ by Lemma 6.10 and thus Theorem 6.1 implies that $O(m_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}Q^{\epsilon})$ many number fields that are not $\epsilon$ -good. However, it is possible that there are many $\mathbf{a}$ such that $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ are isomorphic to the same number field, and one can show that this is in fact the case. Nevertheless, we are able to prove it with a small trick.

#### Proposition 6.11.

There exists a constant $A>0$ such that for any $\epsilon>0$ , there are at most $O(p^{-1/4+A\epsilon})$ proportion of irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials with generic Galois group that are not $\epsilon$ -good.

#### Proof.

Enumerate the number fields up to isomorphism in $\mathfrak{F}_{G}$ as $K_{1},K_{2},\ldots$ where for each $K_{i}$ there are exactly $n_{i}$ vectors $\mathbf{a}$ where $K_{i}\cong\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ . Note that $\sum n_{i}=\Theta(p^{g(g+1)/4})$ by Corollary 2.11. Split $\mathfrak{F}_{G}$ into disjoint subsets indexed by $j$ , where the $j$ -th set $\mathfrak{F}_{G}^{j}$ contains the $K_{i}$ for which $n_{i}\in[2^{j},2^{j+1})$ , and note that there are $O(\log p)$ such subsets.

For each $j$ , consider any $K_{i}\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}^{j}$ and let $\mathbf{a^{\prime}}$ be such that $K_{i}\cong\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}^{\prime}}$ . By looking at the minimal subfields and applying Lemma 6.10, there are at most $O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}}(\log p)^{C})$ many $\mathbf{a}$ where $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ intersects $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}^{\prime}}$ . However, each field in $\mathfrak{F}_{G}^{j}$ is isomorphic to at least $2^{j}$ many $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , so there are at most $O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}}(\log p)^{C}2^{-j})$ many $K\in\mathfrak{F}_{G}^{j}$ that intersect $K_{i}$ , giving a bound for $m_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}^{j}(Q)}$ . Then, applying Theorem 6.1 and recalling that $Q$ is polynomial in $p$ , there are $O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}+A\epsilon}2^{-j})$ many number fields in $\mathfrak{F}^{j}_{G}$ that are not $\epsilon$ -good. But for each one of these fields there are at most $2^{j+1}$ occurrences of it as some $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , so there are at most $O(p^{\frac{g(g+1)-1}{4}+A\epsilon})$ many $\mathbf{a}$ such that $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ is not $\epsilon$ -good that come from $\mathfrak{F}_{G}^{j}$ . Summing over all $j$ gives the desired answer. ∎

## 7. Summing Euler products

In this section, we prove a lemma which allows us to average a finite product of Euler factors in a box, and we combine this with our results in the previous sections to prove Theorem 1.7.

### 7.1. Averaging products of periodic factors

After truncating the sum using the effective Chebotarev theorem, we need to take a sum over $\mathbf{a}$ of $\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ . We present the following lemma which helps us average a finite product of Euler factors. This is a generalization of [28, Proposition 6.4] and in a similar spirit to [24], [9, Section 4].

#### Proposition 7.1.

Let $m\geq 1$ and for $0\leq i\leq m$ , let the functions $h_{i}\colon\mathbb{Z}^{g}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be $w_{i}$ -periodic in every variable, have average value $z_{i}$ , and also assume that the $w_{i}$ are pairwise coprime. Let $T=\max_{0\leq i\leq m}w_{i}$ be an upper bound for the periods. Let $m_{0}=\max_{\mathbf{a}}(h_{0}(\mathbf{a}))$ and $m_{i}=\max_{\mathbf{a}}(|\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))|)$ for $1\leq i\leq m$ . Let $C=\max_{0\leq i\leq m}m_{i}$ and choose $D\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}m_{i}$ . Then, the average of the product in a box of side length $N$ is approximately equal product of the averages:

$$ \frac{1}{N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}\prod_{i=0}^{m}h_{i}(\mathbf{a})=\prod_{i=0}^{m}z_{i}+O\left(\frac{D(mCT)^{6D+1}}{N}+C2^{-6D}\right). $$

Here, we denote $[1,N]=\{1,2,\ldots,N\}$ .

#### Proof.

By Taylor expansion, the term on the left is

$$ \begin{split}\frac{1}{N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}\prod_{i=0}^{m}h_{i}(\mathbf{a})&=\frac{1}{N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))\right)\\
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))\right)^{n}\\
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{1}+\cdots+b_{m}=n,\\
b_{i}\geq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\prod_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))^{b_{i}}.\end{split} $$

On the other hand, define the independent random variables $H_{i}$ with the distribution of $h_{i}(\mathbf{a})$ where $\mathbf{a}$ is chosen randomly, this is well defined by the periodicity of $h_{i}$ . Then, by independence and linearity of expectation applied to the Taylor expansion, the term on the right is

$$ \begin{split}\prod_{i=0}^{m}z_{i}&=z_{0}\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{m}H_{i}\right]=z_{0}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(H_{i})\right)^{n}\right]=z_{0}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{1}+\cdots+b_{m}=n,\\
b_{i}\geq 0\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\log(H_{i})^{b_{i}}\right]\\
&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{1}+\cdots+b_{m}=n,\\
b_{i}\geq 0\end{subarray}}z_{0}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\log(H_{i})^{b_{i}}\right].\end{split} $$

It suffices to bound the difference between the inner terms for each $n$ . For $n>6D$ , using Stirling’s formula we conclude that both terms

$$ \frac{1}{n!N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))\right)^{n}\text{ and }z_{0}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n!}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(H_{i})\right)^{n}\right] $$

are $O(CD^{n}/n!)=O(C2^{-n})$ . so summing over $n\geq 6D$ we get an error contribution of $O(C2^{-6D})$ .

Next, suppose $n\leq 6D$ , then consider the term $h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\prod_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))^{b_{i}}$ where $\sum b_{i}=n$ . This is periodic in each variable with period dividing $P=w_{0}\prod_{i\colon b_{i}>0}w_{i}\leq T^{n+1}$ by condition (a). By Chinese Remainder Theorem, since $w_{i}$ are coprime, we have in a box $B$ of side length $P$ that

$$ \frac{1}{P^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in B}h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\prod_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))^{b_{i}}=z_{0}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\log(H_{i})^{b_{i}}\right]. $$

By subdividing the $[1,N]^{g}$ into boxes of side length $P$ , we have $O(N^{g-1}T^{n+1})$ terms leftover, and after accounting for these terms we have

$$ \frac{1}{N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[1,N]^{g}}h_{0}(\mathbf{a})\prod_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_{i}(\mathbf{a}))^{b_{i}}=z_{0}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\log(H_{i})^{b_{i}}\right]+O\left(\frac{(CT)^{n+1}}{N}\right). $$

Summing this for $n\leq 6D$ over the tuples $b_{1}+\cdots+b_{m}=n$ of which there are less than $m^{n}$ many, which gives a error contribution of $O\left(D(mCT)^{6D+1}/N\right)$ .

∎

### 7.2. Proof of Theorem 1.7

Our overall strategy is to first give a lower bound $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)$ for each $t$ , and then turn this into an $L^{1}$ -bound by showing this lower bound accounts for most of the PPAVs in $\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ . We divide the proof into several parts for clarity.

#### 7.2.1. Part I: Applying Theorem 1.10

Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{g}\cap[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ be the subset of $\mathbf{a}$ satisfying the following conditions:

- (1) $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is an irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial (so $f_{\mathbf{a}}=f_{A}$ for a simple ordinary abelian variety $A$ ).

- (2) $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ has generic Galois group $G=(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ .

- (3) $\ord_{p}(\disc(f))=g(g-1)$ .

- (4) The corresponding $\widetilde{K}_{\mathbf{a}}$ , which we recall to be the Galois closure of $\mathbb{Q}[x]/f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ , is $\epsilon_{1}$ -good, where we choose a sufficiently small constant $\epsilon_{1}>0$ .

By Lemma 2.12, Proposition 2.14, Lemma 4.9 and Corollary 6.11, there are at most $O(p^{-1/5})$ proportion of ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials which do not satisfy at least one of the conditions above. For each trace $t$ , define $\mathcal{F}_{t}=\mathcal{F}\cap\{a_{1}=t\}$ .

Applying Theorem 1.10, we have

$$ \#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)=\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{\mathbb{Z}}^{g}\cap[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})}\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},f_{\mathbf{a}})\geq\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}_{t}}\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},f_{\mathbf{a}})=p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}_{t}}v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\prod_{l}v_{l}(f_{\mathbf{a}}). $$

#### 7.2.2. Part II: Truncating to a finite product

By Lemma 4.7 and 4.8 we have that for $l\nmid 2p\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ and $l=p$ that $v_{l}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=\zeta_{K,l}(1)/\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)$ . There are at most $O(\log(p))$ remaining bad primes and Proposition 4.11 tells us for $l\neq p$ that $v_{l}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\geq 1-C_{1}/l$ for some constant $C_{1}$ . Choose $l_{0}=\exp(C_{2}\log\log(p)^{2})$ for some sufficiently large constant $C_{2}$ . Then, combining these with Proposition 6.4, we lower bound the tail by

$$ \prod_{l>l_{0}}v_{l}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\geq 1-O\left(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon}\right). $$

#### 7.2.3. Part III: Lower bounding by the auxiliary factor $v_{l}^{\prime}(f)$

The point of introducing this auxiliary factor is two-fold: (1) to make the local factors periodic and (2) being able to upper bound the local factors. This is a complication that arises because of our imperfect results in Section 4.3.2. For each prime $l\leq l_{0}$ , we choose an integer $k=k(l)$ depending on $l$ as follows. Let $l_{1}=\log(p)^{1-\epsilon}$ , then for $l\leq l_{1}$ define $k$ to be the largest integer such that $l^{k}\leq l_{0}$ which implies that $l^{k}>\sqrt{l_{0}}$ , and for $l_{1}<l\leq l_{0}$ set $k=1$ . Define the auxiliary factor

$$ v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=\begin{cases}v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})&\text{if }\ord_{l}(\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}}))\leq k/C_{3}\\
\max(1-C_{1}/l,0)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

where we pick $C_{3}>1$ to be the constant in Proposition 4.13 so that we have $v_{l}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\geq v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ . Furthermore $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ is $l^{k}$ -periodic in each of the variables $\mathbf{a}$ . Recall that by Proposition 4.11 we have a lower bound $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\geq 1-C_{1}/l$ , but now we also have an upper bound $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\leq l^{k(g+1)}\leq l_{0}^{g+1}$ simply by the definition of $v_{l,k}$ .

Furthermore, if $l>l_{1}$ we can show that $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=1+O(l^{-1})$ . Indeed, in this case, we defined $k=1$ , so $\ord_{l}(\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}}))\leq k/C_{3}$ implies that $l\nmid\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ so $l$ is a good prime and $v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=1+O(l^{-1})$ as it is a ratio of local zeta functions by Lemma 4.7.

Combining the above, we have

$$ \#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)\geq\left(1-O\left(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon}\right)\right)p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}_{t}}v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}}). $$

#### 7.2.4. Part IV: Making the region a disjoint union of boxes

Consider a subdivision of $\mathbb{R}^{g}$ into boxes $B$ of side length $N=p^{1/4}$ , and let $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g}^{-})=\bigsqcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}}B$ be the union of those boxes which are contained inside $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ . Define $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\mathbb{Z}^{g}\cap[p](\mathcal{R}_{g}^{-})=\bigsqcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}}B\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ and $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{t}=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\cap\{a_{1}=t\}=\bigsqcup_{B_{t}\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}B_{t}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ , where the family $\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{B_{t}=B\cap\{t\leq a_{1}<t+1\}\mid B\in\mathcal{B},B_{t}\neq\emptyset\}$ consists of the nonempty slices of boxes at trace $t$ . Then, to convert the sum from being over $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ to $\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\prime}$ , note that for any $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}$ , we upper bound

$$ v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\leq O(1)\cdot\prod_{l_{1}<l\leq l_{0}}(1+O(l^{-1}))\cdot\prod_{l\leq l_{1}}l_{0}^{g+1}=O(p^{1/6}) $$

Hence, adding the terms with $\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{t}$ we obtain

$$ \begin{split}\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)\geq&\left(1-O\left(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon}\right)\right)p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\prime}}v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})-|\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{t}|O(p^{1/6})\right).\end{split} $$

#### 7.2.5. Part V: Averaging out the Euler product in boxes

We wish to apply Proposition 7.1 to average out the product in the boxes of side length $N$ . In the notation of the proposition, take $h_{0}(\mathbf{a})=\prod_{l\leq 2C_{1}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ which has period $\leq l_{0}^{2C_{1}}$ and $m_{0}=\max(h_{0})=l_{0}^{2(g+1)C_{1}}$ . Then, for each prime $2C_{1}<l\leq l_{0}$ assign some $h_{i}(\mathbf{a})=v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ , which has period $\leq l_{0}$ . Then, we have $m_{i}=O(\log(l_{0}))$ where we crucially used that $1-C_{1}/l>1/2$ so that it is okay to take the log on the lower bound. In addition, recall that if $l>l_{1}$ then $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=1+O(l^{-1})$ so $m_{i}=O(l^{-1})$ . All in all, this yields the constants $m,C,T\leq l_{0}^{O(1)}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{m}m_{i}=O(l_{1}\log(l_{0}))$ so we can choose $D=\Theta(\log(p)^{1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}})$ . Then for any $g$ -dimensional box $B$ of side length $N$ , Proposition 7.1 gives

$$ \frac{1}{N^{g}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in B\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}}\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l}+O(\log(p)^{-1}) $$

where $z_{l}$ is the average of $v_{l}^{\prime}$ . We can also apply this to a slice $B_{t}$ by fixing $a_{1}=t$ and let $a_{2},\ldots,a_{g}$ vary in a $(g-1)$ -dimensional box, to get

$$ \frac{1}{N^{g-1}}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in B_{t}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}}\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l,t}+O(\log(p)^{-1}), $$

where $z_{l,t}$ is the average of $v_{l}^{\prime}$ subject to $a_{1}=t$ . Combining the two tells us that

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t\in[t_{0}+1,t_{0}+N]}\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l,t}=\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l}+O(\log(p)^{-1}). $$

#### 7.2.6. Part VI: Separating the archimedean and non-archimedean terms

By Proposition 4.1, recall that $v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ is the density function of $\mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}$ at $[p]^{-1}(\mathbf{a})$ . Since the density function is continuous on a compact set, it is uniformly continuous and thus within each slice $B_{t}$ , $v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ varies by at most $O(p^{-1/4})$ . For all $B_{t}$ choose some vector $\mathbf{a}_{B_{t}}\in B_{t}$ , then we decouple the archimedean and non-archimedean factors by applying the equation above:

$$ \begin{split}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\prime}}v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})&=\sum_{B_{t}\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}(v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}_{B_{t}}})+O(p^{-1/4}))\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in B_{t}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{g}}\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\\
&=\left(\sum_{B_{t}\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}N^{g-1}\left(v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}_{B_{t}}})+O(p^{-1/4})\right)\right)\left(\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l,t}+O(\log(p)^{-1})\right).\end{split} $$

It is clear that we can approximate the first term using an integral

$$ \int_{[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})\cap\{t\leq a_{1}<t+1\}}v_{\infty}(f_{\mathbf{a}})da_{1}\cdots da_{g}+O(p^{-1/4})\Vol([p](\mathcal{R}_{g}^{+})), $$

and changing variables to $\mathbf{b}=[p]^{-1}(\mathbf{a})$ and applying Proposition 4.1 gives

$$ p^{g(g+1)/2}\left(\int_{\mathcal{R}_{g}\cap\left\{\frac{t}{\sqrt{p}}\leq a_{1}<\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{p}}\right\}}\mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}+O(p^{-1/4})\right)=p^{(g(g+1)-1)/2}\left(\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})+O(p^{-1/4})\right). $$

#### 7.2.7. Part VII: Finding a common lower bound

In order to get to an $L^{1}$ -bound between the two distributions $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)/\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)$ , we give a distribution that lower bounds both of them. Substituting Equation (7.4) into Equation (7.2) and dividing by $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})=(1+O(p^{-1/2}))p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})}$ , we get that $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)/\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\geq M(t)$ where $M(t)$ is given by

$$ \begin{split}\frac{1-O(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon})}{\sqrt{p}}\left(\left(\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})-O(p^{-1/4})\right)\left(\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l,t}-O(\log(p)^{-1})\right)-\frac{|\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{t}|}{p^{g(g+1)/2}}O(p^{1/6})\right).\end{split} $$

We want to show that $M(t)$ also lower bounds $\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)$ , and for that we need to compare $z_{l,t}$ to $v_{l}(t)$ . By definition of $v_{l}^{\prime}$ and Proposition 4.11, we have $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\leq v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ , so $z_{l,t}\leq v_{l,k}(t)$ as the latter is the average of $v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ across $a_{1}=t$ . Furthermore, by Proposition 4.4 and 4.5, we have $v_{l}(t)=1+O(l^{-2})$ and $v_{l,k}(t)=v_{l}(t)(1+O(l^{-\max(2,k)}))$ . Combining these, we have

$$ \begin{split}\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l,t}&\leq\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\cdot\prod_{l\leq l_{1}}\left(1+O(l_{0}^{-1/2})\right)\prod_{l>l_{1}}(1+O(l^{-2}))=(1+O((\log p)^{-1+\epsilon}))\prod_{l}v_{l}(t).\end{split} $$

Absorbing the error factor, we see that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\geq M(t)$ .

#### 7.2.8. Part VIII: Bounding losses from lower bound

Because $M(t)$ lower bounds $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)/\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , the $L^{1}$ -distance between these two distributions is simply the difference in both sums. It is clear that $\sum_{t}\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)/\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})=1$ . Now we lower bound the sum over $M(t)$ . First note that

$$ \sum_{t}\frac{|\mathcal{F}^{\prime}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{t}|}{p^{g(g+1)/2}}=\frac{|\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\setminus\mathcal{F}|}{p^{g(g+1)/2}}=O(p^{-1/5}) $$

because from Part I of the proof there are at most $O(p^{-1/5})$ proportion of vectors which do not satisfy some given condition. Then, we repeat the method in Part IV, breaking the sum into intervals of length $N$ , separating the archimedean and non-archimedean factors, changing the sum into an integral as in Part IV, and then applying Equation (7.3) to get

$$ \begin{split}&\sum_{|t|\leq 2g\sqrt{p}}\left(\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})-O(p^{-1/4})\right)\left(\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l,t}-O(\log(p)^{-1})\right)\\
&=\sqrt{p}\left(\int_{[-2g\sqrt{p},2g\sqrt{p}]}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t)dt-O(p^{-1/4})\right)\left(\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l}+O(\log(p)^{-1})\right).\end{split} $$

The integral is simply $1$ so we are left to lower bound $\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l}$ . The definition of $v_{l}^{\prime}$ is such that all matrices $\gamma$ with $\ord_{l}(\disc(f_{\gamma}))\leq k/C_{3}$ are included which is exactly the condition of Proposition 4.13, so

$$ z_{l}\geq\frac{\#\{\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid\mult(\gamma)=p,l^{k/C_{3}}\nmid\disc(\gamma)\}}{\#\{\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid\mult(\gamma)=p\}}\geq 1-O(l^{-k\delta}) $$

for some constant $\delta>0$ , where we used Proposition 4.14 in the last inequality.

We can also prove a uniform bound $z_{l}\geq 1-O(l^{-2})$ as follows. First, note that $l\neq p$ since our range is $l\leq l_{0}<p$ , and we can assume $l\neq 2$ as we are only concerned with asymptotics. If $l\nmid\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ , then $l$ is a good prime for $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ and so $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})=1+O(l^{-1})$ by Lemma 4.7. Also note that if we just averaged $v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ we would get $1$ by definition. Hence, the error comes when $l\mid\disc(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ , and note that by Lemma 4.9, there are $O(l^{-1})$ proportion of characteristic polynomials satisfying this. Furthermore, for each of them, by definition, $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\geq 1-C_{1}/l$ , so it differs from $v_{l,k}(f_{\mathbf{a}})$ by at most $O(l^{-1})$ , giving the desired result.

Hence, combining the two lower bounds for appropriate intervals, we have

$$ \prod_{l\leq l_{0}}z_{l}\geq\prod_{l\leq l_{1}}(1-O(l_{0}^{-\delta/2}))\prod_{l_{1}<l\leq l_{0}}(1-O(l^{-2}))=1-O((\log p)^{-1+\epsilon}), $$

and substituting our results back into the sum over $M(t)$ gives

$$ \sum_{|t|\leq 2g\sqrt{p}}M(t)\geq 1-O((\log p)^{-1+\epsilon}). $$

Hence, the $L^{1}$ distance between $M(t)$ and $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)/\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ is $O((\log p)^{-1+\epsilon})$ .

#### 7.2.9. Part IX: Upper bounding sum of expected distribution

We are left with showing that the $L^{1}$ distance between $\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)$ and $M(t)$ is small, so it suffices to upper bound the sum $\sum_{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)$ . We basically repeat our method: truncate the infinite product, make each local factor periodic, apply Proposition 7.1, and split into archimedean and non-archimedean parts. However, this time it is a lot easier because of the concrete bounds given in Proposition 4.4 and 4.5. It is pretty clear that because we start with better bounds for $v_{l}(t)$ then $v_{l}(f)$ , the error term here would definitely be smaller than the error incurred in the previous part of the proof. Nevertheless, for completeness we give as best a bound as we can. Since this part is independent of the previous part of the proof, we choose to reuse some variables for notational simplicity.

Take $l_{0}=p^{\epsilon}$ for a sufficiently small $\epsilon$ , and let $k=k(l)$ be the largest integer such that $l^{k}\leq p^{4\epsilon}$ , which implies that $l^{k}>p^{2\epsilon}$ . Applying Proposition 4.4 and 4.5, we approximate the infinite product with a finite product of periodic local factors:

$$ \prod_{l}v_{l}(t)=\prod_{l>l_{0}}(1+O(l^{-2}))\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}(1+O(l^{-k}))v_{l,k}(t)=(1+O(p^{-\epsilon}))\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l,k}(t). $$

Suppose $v_{l,k}(t)\geq 1/2$ when $l>C$ for some constant $C$ , then apply Proposition 7.1 with $h_{0}(t)=\prod_{l\leq C}v_{l,k}(t)$ , and assign $h_{i}(t)$ to each $v_{l,k}(t)$ with $C<l\leq l_{0}$ . We see that $m\leq p^{\epsilon}$ , $T=\max(l^{k})\leq p^{4\epsilon}$ , $C=O(1)$ , $D=O(1)+\sum_{l}l^{-2}=O(1)$ . Picking $N=p^{1/2-\epsilon}$ , if $\epsilon$ is sufficiently small then

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t\in[t_{0}+1,t_{0}+N]}\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l,k}(t)=1+O(p^{-\epsilon}) $$

where we used the fact that $v_{l,k}(t)$ average to $1$ by definition.

Applying the method in Part VI with the above equation like in Equation (7.5), we have

$$ \sum_{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l,k}(t)=\left(\int_{[-2g\sqrt{p},2g\sqrt{p}]}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t)dt+O(p^{-\epsilon})\right)(1+O(p^{-\epsilon}))=1+O(p^{-\epsilon}) $$

so combining this with the first equation simply gives

$$ \sum_{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)=1+O(p^{-\epsilon}). $$

In conclusion, summing both $L^{1}$ distances, we get an error of $O((\log p)^{-1+\epsilon})$ . However, the computation here seems to imply that it could be strengthened to $O(p^{-\epsilon})$ . The current barrier to improving our bound is that we are forced to pick $l_{1}=(\log p)^{1-\epsilon}$ because of Equation (7.1). This in turn stems from having a loose upper bound of $v_{l}^{\prime}(f_{\mathbf{a}})\leq l_{0}^{g+1}$ because we were not able to prove an upper bound of $1+O(l^{-1})$ for $v_{l}(f)$ as in Conjecture 4.10.

## Appendix A Stable orbital integrals as Gekeler ratios (by Jeff Achter and Julia Gordon)

Let $G=\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ , thought of as a smooth group scheme over $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ , and suppose $\gamma_{0}\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ has generic fiber which is regular and semisimple (as an element of $G({\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ ). Below we will recall the definition of a certain measure, the geometric measure, on the stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ , and use it to define an orbital integral on the stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ (it also defines the measure on the rational orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ , but this is not relevant for the present paper).

On one hand, as in (3.3), define a renormalized orbital integral

$$ \nu_{l}(\gamma_{0})=\frac{l^{d(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}({\mathbb{F}}_{l})}\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0},l}(\mathbf{1}_{G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})}), $$

where for a smooth scheme $X\to\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ , $d(X)$ denotes it relative dimension.

On the other hand, as in (3.4), for a polynomial $f(T)\in\mathbb{Z}_{l}[T]$ with nonzero discriminant, we define the stable Gekeler ratio as follows:

#### Definition A.1.

For a polynomial $f(T)\in\mathbb{Z}_{l}[T]$ with nonzero discriminant,

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{l,n}(f) \displaystyle=\frac{\#\left\{\gamma\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})\mid f_{\gamma}\equiv f\bmod l^{n}\right\}}{\#G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})/(\#{\mathbb{A}}^{g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})\#\mathbb{G}_{m}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n}))} \displaystyle\nu_{l}(f) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\nu_{l,n}(f). $$

Let $f_{\gamma_{0}}$ be the characteristic polynomial of $\gamma_{0}$ . The goal of this appendix is to give an essentially self-contained proof of Proposition A.2:

#### Proposition A.2.

For $\gamma_{0}\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ , the stable orbital integral with respect to the geometric measure (the RHS of the equality below) can be expressed as a limit of Gekeler ratios:

$$ \nu_{l}(f_{\gamma_{0}})=\sum_{\gamma\in S_{\gamma_{0}}}\nu_{l}(\gamma), $$

where $\gamma$ ranges over a set $S_{\gamma_{0}}$ of representatives for the rational conjugacy classes inside the stable conjugacy class of $\gamma_{0}$ .

We also prove a similar result (with a different test function) for $l=p$ in §A.3 below.

#### Remark A.3.

In [1], the authors purported to give an explicit formula for each rational orbital integral $\nu_{l}(\gamma_{[A,\lambda]})$ in terms of matrix counts; it needs a modification. A detailed explanation and erratum will appear elsewhere.

#### Remark A.4.

While we prove this lemma for the purposes of the present paper only for $G=\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ , the argument works much more generally. A similar statement in full generality will appear elsewhere.

### A.1. Measures

#### A.1.1. Counting measure

Let $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ be a discrete valuation ring with fraction field $K$ , with residue field $\kappa$ of finite cardinality $l$ , and with normalized absolute value ${\left|\cdot\right|}=l^{-\operatorname{val}_{p}(\cdot)}$ . Let $R_{n}=R/\mathfrak{m}^{n}$ , and let $\pi_{n}:R\to R_{n}$ be the truncation map.

For any $R$ -scheme $X$ , we denote by $\pi_{n}^{X}$ the corresponding map $\pi_{n}^{X}:X(R)\to X(R_{n})$ induced by $\pi_{n}$ . If $X$ is flat (in particular, if $X$ is smooth), we let $d(X)$ be the relative dimension of $X$ over $R$ .

Once and for all, fix the Haar measure $dx$ on $\mathbb{A}^{1}(K)$ such that the volume of ${\mathbb{A}}^{1}(R)=R$ is $1$ . With this normalization, the fibres of the standard projection $\pi_{n}^{\mathbb{A}^{d}}:\mathbb{A}^{d}(R)\to\mathbb{A}^{d}(R_{n})$ have volume $l^{-nd}$ .

Now suppose $X$ is smooth over $R$ , with a non-vanishing top degree differential form $\omega_{X}$ . Integrating $\omega_{X}$ defines a Borel measure ${\left|d\omega_{X}\right|}$ on $X(R)$ (well-defined since, if $\omega_{X}$ exists, it is unique up to multiplication by a unit), and

$$ \vol_{{\left|d\omega_{X}\right|}}(X(R))=\frac{\#X_{\kappa}(\kappa)}{l^{d(X)}} $$

[42]. Indeed, if $X$ is smooth of relative dimension $d$ , then $X(K)$ is an analytic manifold, locally isomorphic to ${\mathbb{A}}^{d}(K)$ ; the Jacobian of any such isomorphism is a non-vanishing top degree differential, and thus has to agree with $\omega_{X}$ up to a unit. Therefore, by the Jacobian transformation rule, ${\left|d\omega_{X}\right|}$ is the pullback of the Haar measure defined by $\omega_{{\mathbb{A}}^{d}}$ as above, under any such local isomorphism.

#### Lemma A.5.

If $X$ is smooth over $R$ and if $A\subset X(R_{n})$ , then

$$ \vol_{{\left|d\omega_{X}\right|}}(\pi_{n}^{X})^{-1}(A)=\frac{\#A}{l^{nd(X)}}. $$

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove this in the case where $A$ consists of a single point. Since (as reviewed above) $X$ is analytically locally isomorphic to ${\mathbb{A}}^{d(X)}$ , the result follows from the corresponding calculation on affine space. ∎

#### A.1.2. Geometric measure

Continue to let $G=\gsp_{2g}$ . As in [1, §2.3], let ${\mathbb{A}}_{G}={\mathbb{A}}^{g}\times{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ be the space of characteristic polynomials of elements of $G$ , and let $\mathfrak{c}:G\to{\mathbb{A}}_{G}$ be the morphism which takes an element to the coefficients of its characteristic polynomial, except the last coordinate is the multiplier $\eta$ rather than the determinant $\det$ . For $\gamma_{0}\in G(R)$ , let

$$ Y_{\gamma_{0}}=\mathfrak{c}^{-1}(\mathfrak{c}(\gamma_{0})). $$

Then for any $R$ -algebra $\alpha:R\to S$ , we have

$$ Y_{\gamma_{0}}(S)=\left\{\gamma\in G(S):\alpha(f_{\gamma})=\alpha(f_{\gamma_{0}})\right\}. $$

Now suppose $\gamma_{0}$ has regular semisimple generic fibre in $G(K)$ . Since the stable orbit of a regular semisimple element of $G(K)$ is determined by its characteristic polynomial, we have

$$ Y_{\gamma_{0}}(K)=\left\{\gamma\in G(K)|f_{\gamma}=f_{\gamma_{0}}\right\}=\left\{\gamma\in G(K)\mid\exists g\in G(\bar{K}):g^{-1}\gamma g=\gamma_{0}\right\}. $$

On ${\mathbb{A}}_{G}$ , let $\omega_{{\mathbb{A}}_{G}}=dx_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx_{g}\times\frac{d\eta}{\eta}$ . Now, $\omega_{G}$ is a generator of the top exterior power of the cotangent bundle of $G$ . For each $a\in\mathbb{A}_{G}(K)$ , there is a unique generator $\omega^{\mathrm{geom}}_{a}$ of the top exterior power of the cotangent bundle of the fibre ${\mathfrak{c}}^{-1}(a)$ such that

$$ \omega_{G}=\omega^{\mathrm{geom}}_{a}\wedge\omega_{{\mathbb{A}}_{G}}. $$

Since the stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ coincides with the fibre ${\mathfrak{c}}^{-1}({\mathfrak{c}}(\gamma_{0}))$ , we obtain a measure $\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}=\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\mathfrak{c}(\gamma_{0})}$ associated to $\omega^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\mathfrak{c}(\gamma_{0})}$ on $Y_{\gamma_{0}}(K)$ .

Then for any $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(G(K))$ ,

$$ \int_{G(K)}\phi(g)\,{\left|d\omega_{G}\right|}=\int_{\mathbb{A}_{G}(K)}\int_{{\mathfrak{c}}^{-1}(a)}\phi(g)\,d\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{a}\,{\left|d\omega_{\mathbb{A}_{G}}(a)\right|}. $$

This measure also appears in [14].

The stable orbital integral of $\phi$ with respect to the geometric measure is then

$$ \mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom},\mathrm{stable}}_{\gamma_{0}}(\phi)=\int_{Y_{\gamma_{0}}(K)}\phi(g)d\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}. $$

Let $S_{\gamma_{0}}$ be a set of representatives for the conjugacy classes inside the stable conjugacy class of $\gamma_{0}$ . Then we may equivalently write

$$ \mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom},\mathrm{stable}}_{\gamma_{0}}(\phi)=\sum_{\gamma\in S_{\gamma_{0}}}\int_{O(\gamma)}\phi(g^{-1}\gamma g)d\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}, $$

where $O(\gamma)$ stands for the rational orbit of $\gamma$ . The stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ is the disjoint union of $O(\gamma)$ as $\gamma$ runs over $S_{\gamma_{0}}$ ; and each orbit $O(\gamma)$ is open in the stable orbit; and $d\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}$ restricts to an invariant measure on each $O(\gamma)$ for $\gamma\in S_{\gamma_{0}}$ .

### A.2. Gekeler numbers and volumes, for $l$ not equal to $p$

We specialize to the case $R=\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ . Let $\gamma_{0}\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ be regular semisimple, with characteristic polynomial $f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)$ . For each positive integer $n$ , consider the subset $V_{n}(\gamma_{0})$ of $G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ defined as

$$ \displaystyle V_{n}=V_{n}(\gamma_{0}) \displaystyle\coloneqq\left\{\gamma\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})\mid f_{\gamma}(T)\equiv f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)\bmod l^{n}\right\} \displaystyle=\left\{\gamma\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})\mid\pi_{n}^{\mathbb{A}_{G}}({\mathfrak{c}}(\gamma))=\pi_{n}^{\mathbb{A}_{G}}({\mathfrak{c}}(\gamma_{0}))\right\} \displaystyle=(\pi_{n}^{G})^{-1}(Y_{\gamma_{0}}(R_{n}))\text{ (by \hyperref@@ii[E:ygammapoints]{{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{E:ygammapoints}\/)}}})} \displaystyle V(\gamma_{0}) \displaystyle\coloneqq\cap_{n\geq 1}V_{n}(\gamma_{0}). $$

We define an auxiliary ratio:
