$$ v_{n}(\gamma_{0})\coloneqq\frac{\vol_{{\left|d\omega_{G}\right|}}(V_{n}(\gamma_{0}))}{l^{-(g+1)n}}. $$

Now we would like to relate the limit of these ratios $v_{n}(\gamma_{0})$ both to the limit of Gekeler ratios $\nu_{l,n}(\gamma_{0})$ and to a stable orbital integral.

Let $\phi_{0}=\mathds{1}_{G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})}$ be the characteristic function of the maximal compact subgroup $G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ in $G(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ .

#### Proposition A.6.

We have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}v_{n}(\gamma_{0})=\mathcal{O}_{\gamma_{0}}^{\mathrm{geom},\mathrm{stable}}(\phi_{0}). $$

#### Proof.

Because for regular semisimple elements equality of characteristic polynomials is equivalent to stable conjugacy in $G({\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ , $V(\gamma_{0})$ is the intersection of $G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ with the stable orbit $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{stable}}(\gamma_{0})$ of $\gamma_{0}$ in $G(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ . Then the stable orbital integral $\mathcal{O}_{\gamma_{0}}^{\mathrm{geom},\mathrm{stable}}(\phi_{0})$ is nothing but the volume of the set $V(\gamma_{0})$ , as a subset of $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{stable}}(\gamma_{0})=Y_{\gamma_{0}}({\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ , with respect to the measure $d\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}$ .

Let $a_{0}={\mathfrak{c}}(\gamma_{0})=(\underline{a}_{0},q)\in(\mathbb{A}^{g}\times{\mathbb{G}}_{m})(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ , and let $U_{n}(a_{0})$ be its neighbourhood of radius $l^{-n}$ in every coordinate. Its volume (with respect to the usual measure on the affine space) is $\vol_{\mu_{\mathbb{A}_{G}}}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))=l^{-(g+1)n}$ . (Since $l\nmid q$ , ${\left|\eta(\gamma_{0})\right|}={\left|q\right|}=1$ ; and so if $\pi_{1}(\gamma)=\pi_{1}(\gamma_{0})$ , then ${\left|\eta(\gamma)\right|}=1$ . Therefore, for such $\gamma$ , the factor $\frac{1}{|\eta(\gamma)|}$ in the definition of $\mu_{\mathbb{A}_{G}}$ is just $1$ .)

Moreover, by definition, $V_{n}(\gamma_{0})={\mathfrak{c}}^{-1}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))\cap G(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ . Consequently,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}v_{n}(\gamma_{0})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\vol_{|d\omega_{G}|}({\mathfrak{c}}^{-1}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))\cap G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}))}{\vol_{|d\omega_{{\mathbb{A}}_{G}}|}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))}=\vol_{\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}}(V(\gamma_{0})), $$

by definition of the geometric measure. ∎

#### Lemma A.7.

We have the following relation between these auxiliary ratios and our stable Gekeler ratios:

$$ v_{n}(\gamma_{0})=\frac{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}{l^{d(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}\nu_{l,n}(f_{\gamma_{0}}). $$

#### Proof.

Continue to let $Y_{\gamma_{0}}=\mathfrak{c}^{-1}(\mathfrak{c}(\gamma_{0}))\subset G$ be the stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ . Recall (A.2) that $V_{n}(\gamma_{0})=(\pi_{n}^{G})^{-1}(Y_{\gamma_{0}}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n}))$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle v_{n}(\gamma_{0}) \displaystyle=\frac{\vol_{{\left|d\omega_{G}\right|}}(V_{n}(\gamma_{0}))}{l^{-(g+1)n}} \displaystyle=\frac{\#Y_{\gamma_{0}}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}{l^{d(G)n}\cdot l^{-(g+1)n}}\quad\text{(Lemma \ref{L:subofsmooth})} \displaystyle=\frac{\#Y_{\gamma_{0}}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})/(\#G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})/\#{\mathbb{A}}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n}))}{l^{d(G)n}\cdot l^{-(g+1)n}/(\#G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})/\#{\mathbb{A}}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n}))} \displaystyle=\frac{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})\#{\mathbb{G}}_{m}({\mathbb{Z}}/l^{n})}{l^{(d(G)-1-g)n}\#{\mathbb{A}}^{g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})\#{\mathbb{G}}_{m}({\mathbb{Z}}/l^{n})}\frac{\#Y_{\gamma_{0}}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}{\#G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})/\#{\mathbb{A}}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})} \displaystyle=\frac{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}{l^{d(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}\frac{\#Y_{\gamma_{0}}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}{\#G(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})/\#{\mathbb{A}}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}. $$

∎

We finally come to the point of this appendix in the $l\neq p$ case.

#### Proof of Proposition A.2.

We now compute (with $O(\gamma)$ denoting the rational orbit of $\gamma$ , which is an open subset of $O^{\mathrm{stable}}(\gamma_{0})$ and thus inherits the geometric measure):

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\gamma\in S_{\gamma_{0}}}\nu_{l}(\gamma) \displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in S_{\gamma_{0}}}\frac{l^{d(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}({\mathbb{F}}_{l})}\int_{O(\gamma)}\phi_{0}(g^{-1}\gamma g)d\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}} \displaystyle=\frac{l^{d(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}({\mathbb{F}}_{l})}\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom},\mathrm{stable}}_{\gamma_{0}}(\phi_{0}) \displaystyle=\frac{l^{d(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}({\mathbb{F}}_{l})}\lim_{n\to\infty}\nu_{n}(\gamma_{0}) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\nu_{l,n}(f_{\gamma_{0}}). $$

∎

### A.3. The case $l=p$

In all the arguments above, the support of the test function of interest was contained in $G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , which made it possible to do all the calculations with the Haar measure on $G$ . When $l=p$ , we are dealing with an integral matrix that does not have an integral inverse; thus we need to create a geometric framework for such matrices. As far as we understand, there is no canonical $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ -scheme on which to do this calculation.

We make one choice of such a scheme, suitable for the present purposes but likely not optimal, namely, we define a $\mathbb{Z}$ -scheme $\mathcal{M}$ such that $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})=\gsp_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})\cap\mat(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ . (This construction works for all primes $l$ , though it is needed here only for $l=p$ .)

Over ${\mathbb{Z}}$ , we have the scheme $\mat_{2g}$ of $2g\times 2g$ matrices with coefficients in ${\mathbb{Z}}$ .

Let $J\in\mat_{2g}({\mathbb{Z}})$ be the block diagonal matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{g}\\ -I_{g}&0\end{pmatrix}$ .

Let $\mathcal{M}\subset\mat_{2g}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}$ be the closed subscheme which, on $S$ -points, is given by

$$ \mathcal{M}(S)=\left\{(A,m)\in\mat_{2g}(S)\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}(S):A^{T}JA=m\cdot J\right\}. $$

(The point is that $\mathcal{M}$ is defined by equations in $m$ and the entries of $A$ .) If $(A,m)\in\mathcal{M}(S)$ , then $m$ is completely determined by $A$ . Consequently, we often abuse notation and view an element of $\mathcal{M}(S)$ as an element of $\mat_{2g}(S)$ .

The open subscheme $\mathcal{M}^{*}\coloneqq\mathcal{M}\times_{\mat_{2g}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}}(\mat_{2g}\times\mathbb{G}_{m})$ is isomorphic to $G$ , and in particular is smooth. Therefore, the singular locus of $\mathcal{M}$ is supported in the locus $m=0$ .

The mistake in the original paper was in requiring the existence of a lift of a solution to the congruence condition on characteristic polynomials $\mod p^{n}$ to a point in $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ congruent to some conjugate of $\gamma_{0}$ $\mod p^{n}$ . That condition is too stringent; the only lifting condition we should require is that an approximate solution lift to a symplectic similitude matrix. Now we can define the (‘stable’) Gekeler ratio at $l=p$ as well. This definition extends the definition given above for $l\neq p$ , since the condition of lifting to $\mathcal{M}$ is automatically satisfied when $l$ does not divide the determinant of $\gamma$ .

#### Definition A.8.

For each rational prime $l$ , let

$$ \nu_{l}(f_{\gamma_{0}})=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\left\{\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n}):f_{\gamma}\equiv f_{\gamma_{0}}\bmod l^{n}\text{\ and there exists \ }\tilde{\gamma}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}):\tilde{\gamma}\equiv\gamma\mod l^{n}\right\}}{\#\gsp_{2g}({\mathbb{Z}}/l^{n})/\#\mathbb{A}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}. $$

This definition initially seems very inconvenient for computation, since it refers to $l$ -adic points. Fortunately, the ‘lifting to a symplectic similitude’ condition is satisfied automatically when $\gamma_{0}$ comes from an ordinary $X$ , and can be checked at a finite level for general $X$ (see Lemma A.11 below).

Thus, for $X$ ordinary, A.9 simplifies to the following formulation.

#### Definition A.9.

If $X$ is ordinary, for each rational prime $l$ , let

$$ \nu_{l}(f_{\gamma_{0}})=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\left\{\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n}):f_{\gamma}\equiv f_{\gamma_{0}}\bmod l^{n}\right\}}{\#\gsp_{2g}({\mathbb{Z}}/l^{n})/\#\mathbb{A}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{n})}. $$

We recall the setup of [1]. We start with $q=p^{e}$ and fix a principally polarized abelian variety $(X,\lambda)/{\mathbb{F}}_{q}$ where $1/2$ is not a slope of the $p$ -divisible group $X[p^{\infty}]$ . From this, we derived data $\delta_{0}\in G({\mathbb{Q}}_{q})$ and $\gamma_{0}\in G({\mathbb{Q}}_{p})$ . Let $R=\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ and let $f(T)=f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)\in R[T]$ be the characteristic polynomial of $\gamma_{0}$ . Let $s=s_{X}$ be the largest slope of $X[p^{\infty}]$ which is less than $1/2$ . (Note that $X$ is ordinary if and only if $s_{X}=0$ .) The following factorization exists precisely because $X[p^{\infty}]$ is assumed to have no component of slope $1/2$ .

#### Lemma A.10.

There is a factorization $f(T)=h(T)h^{+}(T)$ over $R[T]$ , where $h$ is a polynomial of degree $g$ all of whose roots $\alpha_{i}$ have $p$ -adic valuation $e_{i}:=\ord_{p}(\alpha_{i})$ satisfying $0\leq e_{i}\leq s_{X}e<\frac{e}{2}$ , and where $h^{+}(T)=T^{g}h(q/T)$ (and thus all roots of $h^{+}$ have $p$ -adic valuation $\frac{e}{2}<(1-s_{X})e\leq\ord_{p}(q/\alpha_{i})\leq e$ ).

#### Proof.

Because $\gamma_{0}=N_{{\mathbb{Q}}_{q}/{\mathbb{Q}}_{p}}(\delta_{0})$ , the Newton polygon of the polynomial $f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)$ is equal to the Newton polygon of the $p$ -divisible group $X[p^{\infty}]$ scaled by $e$ . Let $\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{g}$ be the roots of $f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)$ in $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{p}$ with $p$ -adic valuation at most $es_{X}$ . Because $\gal({\mathbb{Q}}_{p})$ preserves the valuation on $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{p}$ , $\left\{\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{g}\right\}$ is stable under $\gal({\mathbb{Q}}_{p})$ , and thus $h(T)\coloneqq\prod_{1\leq i\leq g}(T-\alpha_{i})$ and $h^{*}(T):=\prod(T-q/\alpha_{i})$ lie in ${\mathbb{Q}}_{p}[T]$ ; by Gauss’s lemma, they are elements of $R[T]$ . ∎

In the following statement, note that $e^{*}\leq\lfloor 2s_{X}e\rfloor\leq e$ ; and that if $X$ is ordinary, then $e^{*}=0$ and the liftability hypothesis is vacuous.

#### Lemma A.11.

Suppose $n>e$ and $\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(R_{n})$ satisfies

$$ f_{\gamma}(T)=\pi_{n}(f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)). $$

Let $e^{*}=\max_{i,j}(\min(e,e_{i}+e_{j}))$ . If $\gamma$ lifts to $\mathcal{M}(R_{n+e^{*}})$ , then it lifts to $\mathcal{M}(R)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $V_{n}=V\otimes R_{n}$ . The multiplier $\mu(\gamma)$ can be read off from $f_{\gamma}(T)$ , and thus coincides with $\pi_{n}(\mu(\gamma_{0}))$ . Consequently, for all $x$ and $y$ in $V_{n}$ we have

$$ \langle\gamma x,\gamma y\rangle=q\langle x,y\rangle. $$

The $R$ -factorization of $f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)$ induces a factorization

$$ f_{\gamma}(T)=h(T)h^{+}(T) $$

in $R_{n}[T]$ .

Let $V_{n}=V\otimes R_{n}$ , and let $U$ be the maximal saturated submodule of $\ker h(\gamma)$ . Then $U$ is a $\gamma$ -stable summand of $V_{n}$ . (One way to see this is by constructing $U$ as follows. Let $\tilde{\gamma}$ be a lift of $\gamma$ to $\mat_{2g}(R)$ with characteristic polynomial $f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)$ – this is possible because $\mat_{2g}$ , unlike $\mathcal{M}$ , is smooth. Let $\tilde{U}=\ker h(\tilde{\gamma})$ , and and then let $U=\tilde{U}\otimes_{R}R_{n}$ .)

We verify that $U$ is isotropic. It suffices to see this after an extension of scalars. Consequently, possibly after replacing $R$ with the integral closure of ${\mathbb{Z}}_{p}$ in the splitting field of $f_{\gamma_{0}}(T)$ , we may and do assume that $h(T)$ has a (nonunique!) factorization $h(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{g}(T-\alpha_{i})$ , where $\ord_{p}(\alpha_{i})\leq es_{X}$ . Use this to produce a basis for $U$ in which $\gamma$ is upper-triangular. Specifically, choose an $R_{n}$ -basis $x_{1},\dots,x_{g}$ for $U$ such that

$$ \gamma(x_{j})=\alpha_{j}x_{j}+\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}x_{i}. $$

On one hand, we have

$$ \displaystyle\langle\gamma x_{1},\gamma x_{2}\rangle \displaystyle=q\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle=p^{e}\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle. \displaystyle\langle\gamma x_{1},\gamma x_{2}\rangle \displaystyle=\langle\alpha_{1}x_{1},\alpha_{2}x_{2}+a_{12}x_{1}\rangle \displaystyle=\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle \displaystyle p^{e_{12}^{*}}\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle \displaystyle=0\text{ in }R_{n} e_{12}^{*}=\min(e,e_{1}+e_{2})\leq e^{*} \displaystyle\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle \displaystyle\in p^{n-e_{12}^{*}}R_{n}. $$

Suppose $\gamma$ admits a lift $\tilde{\gamma}\in\mathcal{M}(R_{n+e^{*}})$ ; let $\tilde{x_{i}}$ be a compatible choice of lift of $x_{i}$ . Then the same calculation shows that

$$ \displaystyle p^{e_{12}^{*}}\langle\tilde{x_{1}},\tilde{x_{2}}\rangle \displaystyle=0\text{ in }R_{n+e^{*}} \displaystyle\langle\tilde{x_{1}},\tilde{x_{2}}\rangle \displaystyle\in p^{n+e^{*}-e_{12}^{*}}R_{n+e^{*}}; \displaystyle\pi_{n}(\langle\tilde{x_{1}},\tilde{x_{2}}\rangle) \displaystyle=\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle=0\text{ in }R_{n}. $$

Inductively, the same argument shows that $\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle=0$ for all $1\leq i\leq j\leq g$ . We conclude that $U$ is a maximal isotropic summand of $V_{n}$ .

Similarly, let $W$ be the maximal saturated submodule of $\ker(h^{*}(\gamma))$ . It, too, is a $\gamma$ -stable maximal isotropic subspace. Moreover, because $h$ and $h^{*}$ share no common roots in $R_{n}$ , $W$ is isomorphic, via $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ , to the dual of $U$ .

Choose an $R_{n}$ -basis for $U$ , and choose the dual basis for $W$ . Then $\gamma|_{U}$ is specified by a matrix $A\in\mat_{g}(R_{n})$ ; $\gamma|_{W}$ is specified by a matrix $D\in\mat_{g}(R_{n})$ ; and because $\gamma\in G(R_{n})$ , we have $A^{T}D=qI_{g}$ . Because the symplectic group acts transitively on symplectic bases for $V$ , $\gamma$ is $G(R_{n})$ -conjugate to the block-diagonal matrix $\beta:=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ 0&D\end{pmatrix}$ .

Let $\tilde{U}$ and $\tilde{W}$ be lifts of $U$ and $W$ , respectively, to maximal isotropic summands of $V$ . Let $\tilde{A}$ be a lift of $A$ to $\End(\tilde{U})\cong\mat_{g}(R)$ , and choose $\tilde{D}$ so that $\tilde{A}^{T}\tilde{D}=qI_{g}$ ; then each of $\tilde{A}$ and $\tilde{D}$ lies in $\mat_{g}(R)\cap\gl_{g}({\mathbb{Q}}_{p})$ . Finally, let $\tilde{\beta}$ be the block-diagonal matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{A}&0\\ 0&\tilde{D}\end{pmatrix}$ ; then $\tilde{\beta}\in\mathcal{M}(R)$ is $G(R)$ -conjugate to a lift of $\gamma$ .

∎

#### A.3.1. Finishing the calculation at $l=p$

With the new definitions of the Gekeler ratio, we can now complete the proof of the equality between the Gekeler ratio and the orbital integral in the case $l=p$ , along the lines of [1, Section 4.3]. Lemma 3.7 in [1] holds, and almost everything in Section 4.3 there holds without change as well: Lemmas 4.8, 4.9 do not mention the ratios at all, and Lemma 4.10 is a statement about geometric orbital integrals, which does not involve the erroneously defined ratios. Lemma 4.11 concerns the Serre-Oesterlé measure on $\gsp_{2g}$ , which coincides with the measure $|d\omega_{G}|$ , and also is not affected by the error. Only Corollary 4.12 uses the incorrect definition of the ratio $\nu_{p}$ , and thus needs to change. However, its proof is correct as long as we use the correct definition of $\nu_{p}$ . We include the corrected version for completeness.

#### Proposition A.12.

Suppose that either $X$ is ordinary or that $q=p$ . For $l=p$ , the Gekeler ratio (A.6) is related to the geometric orbital integral by

$$ \nu_{p}([X,\lambda])=q^{-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}}\frac{p^{\dim(G^{\textrm{der}})}}{\#G^{\textrm{der}}({\mathbb{Z}}_{p}/p)}O^{\mathrm{geom},\mathrm{stable}}_{\gamma_{0}}(\phi_{q,p}), $$

where $\phi_{q,p}$ is the characteristic function of the same double coset as in [1, §4C].

#### Proof.

First observe that $\vol_{{\left|d\omega_{A}\right|}}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))=qp^{-n\mathrm{rank}(G)}=qp^{-(g+1)n}$ , since we are using the invariant measure on the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -factor of $\mathbb{A}_{G}=\mathbb{A}^{\mathrm{rank}(G)-1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ , and for $\gamma_{0}$ (and therefore, for all points in $U_{n}$ ), the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -coordinate is the multiplier, with absolute value $q^{-1}$ . To give a proof which works uniformly in the cases $X$ ordinary and $q=p$ , we maintain the condition on lifting (and just remember that this condition is vacuous in the ordinary case). Thus, by Definition A.9 we can rewrite $\nu_{p}([X,\lambda])$ (with $G=\gsp_{2g}$ ) as

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{p}([X,\lambda])=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\#\left\{\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n}):f_{\gamma}\equiv f_{\gamma_{0}}\bmod p^{n},\exists\tilde{\gamma}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}):\tilde{\gamma}\equiv\gamma\mod p^{n}\right\}}{\#\gsp_{2g}({\mathbb{Z}}/p^{n})/\#\mathbb{A}_{G}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})} \displaystyle=\frac{p^{\dim(G^{\textrm{der}})}}{\#G^{\textrm{der}}({\mathbb{Z}}_{p}/p)}\cdot \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\#\left\{\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n}):f_{\gamma}\equiv f_{\gamma_{0}}\bmod p^{n},\ \exists\tilde{\gamma}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}):\tilde{\gamma}\equiv\gamma\mod p^{n}\right\}p^{-n(\dim(G)-\rk(G))}}{\vol_{|d\omega_{A}|}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))q^{-1}}, $$

whereas the geometric orbital integral is, by definition,

$$ \vol_{\mu^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{0}}}(V(\gamma_{0}))=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\vol_{|d\omega_{G}|}({\mathfrak{c}}^{-1}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))\cap\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}))}{\vol_{|d\omega_{A}|}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))}. $$

Thus all we need to do now is compare the numerators of (A.7) and (A.8). We present a somewhat ad hoc argument on point counts that follows the lines of the argument in [1, Lemma 4.11]. We recall that the Cartan decomposition for $G$ gives us $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})=\sqcup_{\lambda\in A^{+}}D_{\lambda,p}$ , where $A^{+}$ is the set of dominant co-characters, and $D_{\lambda,p}$ is the double coset $G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\lambda(p)G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . Instead of Lemma 4.11 of that paper, we prove the following.

#### Lemma A.13.

For $n$ sufficiently large:

- (1) The neighbourhood of the identity in $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ of valuative radius $n$ is contained in $G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ .

- (2) If $x\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ , then all lifts of $x$ to $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ lie in the same double coset of $G(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ .

- (3) If $x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ lift to elements of the same double coset of the Cartan decomposition for $G(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ , then the fibres of the map $\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}$ over $x$ and $x^{\prime}$ have the same volume with respect to the Haar measure $|d\omega_{G}|$ on $G(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ .

- (4) For each $x\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}/p^{n})\cap\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}(D_{e\mu_{0},p})$ , the fibre $\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}(x)$ has volume $q^{-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}+1}p^{-n\dim(G)}$ with respect to the measure $|d\omega_{G}|$ .

#### Proof.

1. A matrix sufficiently close to the identity has determinant $1$ ; it is in $G(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ by definition of $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , and is integrally invertible since the determinant is a unit.

2. Let $\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}$ be arbitrary lifts of $x$ to $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . We have $\gamma^{\prime}-\gamma$ is of the form $\gamma^{\prime}-\gamma=p^{n}X$ , where $X\in\mat_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . We can write $\gamma^{-1}\in G(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ as $\gamma^{-1}=p^{-\operatorname{val}_{p}(\det\gamma)}A$ , where $A\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ is a matrix of minors of $\gamma$ . Indeed, the entries of $A$ are minors of an integral matrix, thus integral; and since $\gamma^{-1}$ is a symplectic similitude, $A$ is also a symplectic similitude, and therefore $A\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . Multiplying by $\gamma^{-1}$ , we get: $\gamma^{-1}\gamma^{\prime}-I=p^{n-\operatorname{val}_{p}(\det(\gamma))}AX$ . The matrix $AX$ is integral; thus for $n\gg\operatorname{val}_{p}(\det(\gamma))$ , the matrix $\gamma^{-1}\gamma^{\prime}$ is integral and congruent to the identity modulo at least $p^{n-val_{p}(\det\gamma)}$ . Therefore, $\gamma^{-1}\gamma^{\prime}\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ by the previous item.

3. First, by assumption, the fibres of $\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}$ over $x$ and $x^{\prime}$ are non-empty, and then both fibres are contained in the same double coset of the Cartan decomposition for $G(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ by the previous point. Let $\gamma\in\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}(x)$ , $\gamma^{\prime}\in\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}(x^{\prime})$ . Then by assumption, there exist elements $k_{1},k_{2}\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ such that $\gamma^{\prime}=k_{1}\gamma k_{2}$ . Then if $\gamma^{\prime\prime}\equiv\gamma\mod p^{n}$ , we have $k_{1}\gamma^{\prime\prime}k_{2}\equiv\gamma^{\prime}\mod p^{n}$ , i.e.

$$ k_{1}\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}(\gamma)k_{2}\subset\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}(\gamma^{\prime}). $$

Since the roles of $\gamma$ and $\gamma^{\prime}$ in this argument could have been switched, we see that the fibre over $x^{\prime}$ is a translate of the fibre over $x$ by $\gamma^{-1}\gamma^{\prime}$ , and hence has the same volume with respect to the Haar measure on $G$ .

4. This is essentially proved in Lemma 4.11 of [1]. We modify the proof to fit the present statement.

Given the previous point, we just need to prove the statement for one element of the double coset $D_{e\mu_{0},p}$ . We take $g_{0}=e\mu_{0}(p)=\diag(q,\dots,q,1\dots,1)\in D_{e\mu_{0},p}$ , and let $x_{0}=\pi_{n}(\gamma_{0})\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ be the truncation of $g_{0}$ modulo $p^{n}$ . We know that each fibre of the map $\pi_{G,n}$ has volume $p^{-n\dim(G)}$ . Consider the left translation by $g_{0}$ map $L_{g_{0}}:G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\to\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , given explicitly by:

$$ \textstyle{L_{g_{0}}:G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})} \textstyle{{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\
C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}qA&qB\\
C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right].}} $$

It induces a map of truncated matrices

$$ \textstyle{L_{g_{0}}^{n}:G(\mathbb{Z}/p^{n})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})} \textstyle{{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\
C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}qA&qB\\
C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right];}} $$

unlike $L_{g_{0}}$ , this map is not injective.

We observe that $L_{g_{0}}$ takes each fibre of the truncation $\pi_{G,n}$ to a subset of a fibre of $\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}$ : for any $x\in G(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ , we have that $L_{g_{0}}(\pi_{G,n}^{-1}(x))\subset\pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(L_{g_{0}}^{n}(x))$ is an open subset. Since the measure $|d\omega_{G}|$ is invariant under $L_{g_{0}}$ , we just need to find the index of $L_{g_{0}}(\pi_{G,n}^{-1}(x))$ in $\pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(L_{g_{0}}^{n}(x))$ .

Note that if $\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\equiv g_{0}\mod p^{n}$ then $g_{0}^{-1}\gamma\equiv I\mod p^{n-e}$ , where $e=\operatorname{val}_{p}(q)$ ; in particular, $\gamma$ is in the image of a neighbourhood of $I$ under the map $L_{g_{0}}$ (when $n$ is large).

For simplicity, we move the calculation to the Lie algebra ${\mathfrak{g}}$ . Let $n\gg e$ . We can write the truncated exponential approximation: $g_{0}^{-1}\gamma=I+X+\frac{1}{2}X^{2}+\dots$ for some $X\in{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ ; in particular, there exists $X\in{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ such that $g_{0}^{-1}\gamma\equiv I+X\mod p^{2(n-e)}$ , and thus, since the exponential is bijective on a small neighbourhood of zero in ${\mathfrak{g}}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , our set $\pi_{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(L_{g_{0}}^{n}(x))/L_{g_{0}}(\pi_{G,n}^{-1}(x))$ is in bijection with the set

$$ \left\{X\in{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\mid X\equiv 0\mod p^{n}\right\}/\left\{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}qI_{g}&0\\
0&I_{g}\end{smallmatrix}\right]X:X\equiv 0\mod p^{n}\right\}. $$

This set is a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , so we just need to find its dimension, which equals the dimension of the kernel of the multiplication by $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}qI_{g}&0\\ 0&I_{g}\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ on ${\mathfrak{g}}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ .

We have ${\mathfrak{g}}=\mathfrak{sp}_{2g}\oplus\mathfrak{z}$ , where $\mathfrak{z}$ is the $1$ -dimensional Lie algebra of the centre. It will be convenient to decompose it further: let $\mathfrak{h}$ be the Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sp}_{2g}$ consisting of diagonal matrices, and let $V$ consist of matrices whose diagonal entries are all zero; then

$$ {\mathfrak{g}}=(\mathfrak{z}\oplus\mathfrak{h})\oplus V. $$

Consider the action of multiplication by $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}qI_{g}&0\\ 0&I_{g}\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ on each term of this direct sum decomposition.

On the term $\mathfrak{z}\oplus\mathfrak{h}$ it acts by $\diag(a_{1},\dots,a_{2g})\mapsto\diag(qa_{1},\dots,qa_{g},a_{g+1},\dots,a_{2g})$ , which in the $\mathfrak{z}\oplus\mathfrak{h}$ -coordinates can be written as (recalling that $a_{i}+a_{g+i}=z$ is independent of $i$ ):

$$ \displaystyle\frac{z}{2}\oplus\left(\frac{z}{2}-a_{g+1},\dots\frac{z}{2}-a_{2g},-\frac{z}{2}+a_{g+1},\dots-\frac{z}{2}+a_{2g}\right) \displaystyle\mapsto\frac{qz}{2}\oplus\left(\frac{qz}{2}-\frac{(q+1)a_{g+1}}{2},\dots\frac{qz}{2}-\frac{(q+1)a_{2g}}{2},-\frac{qz}{2}+\frac{(q+1)a_{g+1}}{2},\dots-\frac{qz}{2}+\frac{(q+1)a_{2g}}{2}\right). $$

The only points $(z,a_{g+1},\dots,a_{2g})$ that are killed $(\bmod p^{n})$ by this map are of the form $(z^{\prime},0,\dots,0)$ with $qz^{\prime}=0$ ; there are $q$ of them.

Next consider an element $X=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\ C&D\end{smallmatrix}\right]\in V$ . Then $A$ is determined by $D$ , and $B$ is skew-symmetric (up to a permutation of rows and columns). Multiplication by $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}qI_{g}&0\\ 0&I_{g}\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ scales each entry of $A$ and $B$ by a factor of $q$ , and does not change $C$ and $D$ . Since $A$ is determined by $D$ , the elements $X$ killed by this map are in bijection with symmetric matrices $B$ with entries in $\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n}$ that are killed by multiplication by $q$ . Since the space of such matrices is a $g(g+1)/2$ -dimensional linear space, the number of such matrices $B$ is $q^{g(g+1)/2}$ .

Therefore, every fibre of $\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}$ over a point of $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ is a disjoint union of $q^{g(g+1)/2+1}$ translates of the fibres of the map $\pi_{G,n}$ , and hence its volume is $q^{g(g+1)/2+1}p^{n\dim(G)}$ . ∎

Given the Lemma, it is easy to finish the proof of the Proposition. First, recall that

- (1) The stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ coincides with the rational orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ .

- (2) The intersection of the orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ with $\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ is contained in the single double coset $D_{e\mu_{0},p}$ [1, Lemma 4.8].

By definition, (in the case $X$ not ordinary) we only count the $x\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n})$ that have a lift $\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ . By the congruence of characteristic polynomials, such a lift would have to be in a $p^{n^{\prime}}$ -neighbourhood of the stable orbit of $\gamma_{0}$ (with possibly $n^{\prime}<n$ ), which coincides with the rational orbit in this case; and then by the statement (2) mentioned above, $\gamma$ would have to be congruent modulo $p^{n^{\prime}}$ to an element of, and therefore contained in, the double coset $D_{e\mu_{0}}$ . Then by the last point of Lemma A.13, the fibre $\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}(x)$ has volume $q^{g(g+1)/2+1}p^{-n\dim(G)}$ with respect to $|d\omega_{G}|$ . Therefore,

$$ \vol_{|d\omega_{G}|}(\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}({\mathfrak{c}}(\gamma_{0})))=q^{g(g+1)/2+1}p^{-n\dim(G)}\#\{\gamma\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}/p^{n})|\exists\tilde{\gamma}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}):\tilde{\gamma}\equiv\gamma\mod p^{n}\}. $$

We obtain, from (A.7) and (A.8):

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{p}([X,\lambda]) \displaystyle=q^{-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}-1}\frac{p^{\dim(G^{\textrm{der}})}}{\#G^{\textrm{der}}({\mathbb{Z}}_{p}/p)}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\vol_{|d\omega_{G}|}(\pi_{\mathcal{M},n}^{-1}({\mathfrak{c}}(\gamma_{0}))p^{-n\dim(G)}}{\vol_{|d\omega_{A}|}(U_{n}(\gamma_{0}))q^{-1}} \displaystyle=q^{-\frac{g(g+1)}{2}}\frac{p^{\dim(G^{\textrm{der}})}}{\#G^{\textrm{der}}({\mathbb{Z}}_{p}/p)}O^{\mathrm{geom}}(\gamma_{0}), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

# Uniform boundedness of small points on abelian varieties over function fields

**Authors:** Nicole Looper and Jit Wu Yap

## Abstract

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $K=k(B)$ be the function field of a geometrically irreducible projective curve $B$ over $k$ . Let $A/K$ be a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety with $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(A)=0$ . We prove that any $K$ -rational torsion point $x$ of $A$ has order uniformly bounded in terms of $g$ and the gonality of $B$ . We also prove a uniform lower bound on the Néron–Tate height $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)$ in terms of the stable Faltings height $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ for any $K$ -rational point $x$ whose forward orbit is Zariski dense, proving the Lang–Silverman conjecture over function fields of characteristic $0$ .

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction 1.1 Proof Strategy 1.2 Higher Dimensional Arakelov-Green’s Functions 1.3 Degeneration by Ultrafilters 1.4 Acknowledgements

- 2 Background 2.1 Heights over Function Fields 2.2 Abelian Varieties and Schemes 2.3 Moduli Space of Curves

- 3 Lower Bound on Arakelov-Green’s functions 3.1 A General Lower Bound 3.2 A Positive Lower Bound for Abelian Varieties

- 4 Degenerations of Sequences of Points 4.1 Degeneration via Ultrafilters 4.2 Application to Moduli of Abelian Varieties

- 5 Uniform Positivity for Arakelov-Green’s Functions

- 6 Uniform Bounds for Semistable Principally Polarized Abelian Varieties

- 7 Néron Models for Potential Good Reduction

- 8 Uniform Bounds for Principally Polarized Abelian Varieties

- 9 The case of Everywhere Good Reduction

- 10 Reducing to the Principally Polarized Case

- References

## 1. Introduction

In his landmark work [85, 86], Mazur proved a uniform bound on the order of a $\mathbb{Q}$ -rational torsion point on any elliptic curve $E/\mathbb{Q}$ . In fact, Mazur even gave an exact list of all of the possible torsion subgroups of $E(\mathbb{Q})$ . This uniform boundedness result was generalized to number fields $K$ by Kamienny [66], Kamienny–Mazur [65] and Merel [87], who proved the existence of an upper bound on the order of a $K$ -rational torsion point on any elliptic curve over $K$ depending only on $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ . This bound was later made effective by Parent [93].

There are analogous statements over function fields. For $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ the function field of a smooth projective curve $B/\mathbb{C}$ , an upper bound on the order of a $K$ -torsion point for a non-isotrivial elliptic curve $E/K$ was given in terms of the genus $g(B)$ by Levin [73]. Upper bounds depending only on the gonality $\operatorname{gon}(B)$ were obtained by Abramovich [1] and Nguyen–Saito [91].

For elliptic curves over function fields of arbitrary characteristic, an upper bound depending only on the genus was given by Cojocaru and Hall [24]. Poonen [100] subsequently proved an upper bound depending only on the gonality.

For higher dimensional abelian varieties over number fields, results over one-parameter families were obtained by Cadoret–Tamagawa [19] and Ellenberg–Hall–Kolwaski [36]. Statistical results were also shown by Laga–Thorne [71].

Our first main result is a uniform boundedness statement for abelian varieties $A/K$ , where $K=k(B)$ is a function field of a curve $B$ over a field $k$ of characteristic $0$ . By a curve $B$ , we mean a smooth geometrically integral projective variety of dimension $1$ . We say that an abelian variety $A/K$ has no $K$ -isotrivial part if its $K/k$ -trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(A)$ is $0$ . We write $\operatorname{gon}(B)$ for the gonality of $B$ .

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $K=k(B)$ be the function field of a curve $B/k$ , where $\operatorname{char}k=0$ . There exists an integer $N=N(g,\operatorname{gon}(B))$ , depending only on $g$ and $\operatorname{gon}(B)$ , such that for any abelian variety $A/K$ of dimension $g$ with no $K$ -isotrivial part, any torsion point $x\in A(K)$ has order at most $N$ .

Our methods also yield a uniform lower bound on the canonical height of a non-torsion $K$ -rational point. A conjecture of Lang [72, Page 92] predicts for any number field $K$ , there is a uniform constant $c=c(K)>0$ such that if $E/K$ is an elliptic curve and $x\in E(K)$ is non-torsion, then

$$ \widehat{h}_{E}(x)\geq c(K)\cdot\log\left|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\cal{D}_{E/K})\right| $$

where $\cal{D}_{E/K}$ is the minimal discriminant of $E/K$ and $\widehat{h}_{E}$ is the Néron–Tate height for $E$ .

Silverman obtained partial results on Lang’s conjecture in [104] and the analogous statement for function fields $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ was proven by Hindry and Silverman [61], where $c$ only depends on the genus $g(B)$ of the base curve. Silverman also extended the conjecture to abelian varieties in [105], where we require the orbit $\mathbb{Z}\cdot x$ to be Zariski dense (see also [94]).

Our second main result is a Lang–Silverman type result for abelian varieties over $K=k(B)$ , with a lower bound proportional to the stable Faltings height. Given an abelian variety $A/K$ , let $K^{\prime}=k^{\prime}(B^{\prime})$ be a finite extension over which $A/K^{\prime}$ has semistable reduction. Let $\cal{N}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}$ be the Néron model of $A/K^{\prime}$ . Then we define the stable Faltings height to be

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A):=\frac{1}{[K^{\prime}:K]}\deg(e^{*}\Omega^{g}_{\cal{N}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}}) $$

where $e:B^{\prime}\to\cal{N}^{\prime}$ is the identity section and $\Omega_{\cal{N}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}}^{g}$ is the $g$ th exterior power of the relative cotangent bundle for $\cal{N}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}$ . This quantity is independent of the choice of $K^{\prime}$ .

#### Theorem 1.2.

Let $K=k(B)$ be the function field of a curve $B/k$ , where $\operatorname{char}k=0$ . There exists a $c=c(g,\operatorname{gon}(B))>0$ , depending only on $g$ and $\operatorname{gon}(B)$ , such that if $A/K$ is a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety with no $K$ -isotrivial part, $L$ is a symmetric ample line bundle on $A$ , and $x\in A(K)$ is a point such that $\mathbb{Z}\cdot x$ is Zariski dense in $A$ , then

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)\geq c\max\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A),1\}. $$

For Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, it is easy to reduce to the case of $k=\mathbb{C}$ . There have been many partial results toward Theorem 1.1. Bakker and Tsimerman [10] prove it for abelian varieties with real multiplication. Over function fields of characteristic $0$ , uniform bounds on the maximal $n$ for which a level $n$ -structure exists over $K$ , i.e., for which all $n^{2g}$ -torsion points are $K$ -rational, have been proven by Nadel [89] when the genus $g(B)$ equals $0$ or $1$ , and by Hwang–To [62] for general $B$ . The methods used in these articles rely on studying the hyperbolicity of the moduli space that parametrizes abelian varieties with an $n$ -torsion point/level $n$ structure and thus do not carry over to the arithmetic setting.

Our approach is different from the ones above. Its underlying philosophy is the same as that used in Hindry–Silverman’s proof of Theorem 1.2 for elliptic curves [61]. These methods largely transfer to the number field setting. The only place where we use that $K$ is a function field in a crucial way is in invoking the Arakelov inequality. The Arakelov inequality was first proven by Faltings [39] and then refined by Deligne [32].

#### Theorem 1.3.

(Arakelov Inequality) Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be the function field of a curve $B/\mathbb{C}$ and let $A/K$ be a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety with semistable reduction. Let $S$ be the set of places of bad reduction of $A/K$ . If $2g(B)-2+|S|\geq 0$ , then

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)\leq\frac{g}{2}(2g(B)-2+|S|). $$

One might conjecture that an analogue of Theorem 1.3 should hold over number fields. For $g=1$ , this is Szpiro’s conjecture [110] which is equivalent to the $abc$ conjecture. The fact that Szpiro’s conjecture would imply Theorem 1.1 for elliptic curves over number fields was already observed by Frey [45]. Hindry–Silverman [61] further show that Szpiro’s conjecture implies (1). Some partial results in this direction in higher dimensions were also obtained by Clark and Xarles [23].

In [59, 60], Hindry and Pacheco conjectured that a positive characteristic version of Theorem 1.3 holds under some suitable hypotheses, generalizing a prior result of Szpiro [110]. It should be possible to obtain analogous results in positive characteristic if their conjecture is true.

#### Conjecture 1.4 (Hindry–Pacheco [59, 60]).

Let $K=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}(B)$ be the function field of a curve $B$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ and let $A/K$ be a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety with semistable reduction and nonzero Kodaira-Spencer map for which $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}(A)=0$ . Let $S$ be the set of places of bad reduction of $A$ . Then there are constants $c_{1}(g),c_{2}(g,K)>0$ such that if $p\geq c_{1}$ , then

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)\leq c_{2}(|S|+1). $$

When $K$ is a number field, there have been many results toward bounding the number of $K$ -torsion points or the Néron–Tate height of a non-torsion $K$ -rational point in terms of the Faltings height $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ [83, 29, 95, 48]. We note that both [29] and [95] have bounds that are uniform over certain families of abelian varieties, proving special cases of Theorem 1.1 and 1.2 for number fields.

### 1.1. Proof Strategy

As mentioned earlier, our proof strategy for Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 follows that of Hindry and Silverman. This argument has been generalized and applied to arithmetic dynamics in various uniformity settings [11, 63, 75, 76, 77, 116] and we will follow this more modern viewpoint. First, we may reduce to the case where $k=\mathbb{C}$ ; see Section 10. Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ . Given a place $v\in M_{K}$ , we let $A_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ denote the Berkovich analytification of $A$ over $\mathbb{C}_{v}$ the completion of $\overline{K_{v}}$ . Let $\cal{N}_{v}/R_{v}$ be the Néron model of $A$ over the valuation ring $R_{v}$ of $K_{v}$ , and let $\cal{N}_{v,s}$ denote its special fiber. Our argument exploits the following two properties regarding points on $A(K)$ with small Néron–Tate height.

- (i) If $v\in M_{K}$ is a place of stable bad reduction and the number of components of $\cal{N}_{v,s}$ is small, then any point $x\in A(K)$ is subject to strong restrictions on where it lives in $A_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

- (ii) Any generic sequence of $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -stable finite sets of points $F_{n}\subseteq A(\overline{K})$ with Néron–Tate heights tending to $0$ and $|F_{n}|\to\infty$ equidistributes to the Haar measure on the skeleton of $A_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

If $F$ is a large set of $K$ -rational points, these two properties are in tension with each other. If one has some uniform control on this tension as $A$ varies, then this yields a uniform upper bound on $|F|$ .

We first restrict to the case of elliptic curves. For simplicity, let us assume that our elliptic curve $E/K$ has semistable reduction and that $E$ has at least one place of bad reduction. Hindry and Silverman first apply the Arakelov inequality (or Szpiro’s conjecture if one is working over a number field) to conclude that there is a subset $T\subseteq M_{K}$ with $|T|\geq\frac{h(E)}{M}$ for some uniform $M=M(g(B))>0$ , such that $(i)$ holds for all $v\in T$ . By “small” in (i) we mean that the number of components is uniformly bounded by some integer $D$ . Then replacing our small points $x$ with $[D!]x$ , we may assume that for all $v\in T$ , the reductions of our points lie in the identity component of the Néron model.

To exploit (ii), given $N$ distinct points $x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\in E(K)$ , Hindry and Silverman look at the averaged quantity

$$ \frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\not=j}\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x_{i}-x_{j}) $$

where $\hat{\lambda}_{v}$ is the local Néron–Tate height for the place $v$ . The two main properties of this average are that if $E_{N}$ is a sequence of sets in $E(\overline{K})$ with $|E_{N}|=N$ , then

$$ \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\not=j}\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x_{i}-x_{j})\geq 0, $$

and if equality holds, then the sets $E_{N}$ must equidistribute to the Haar measure $\mu_{E,v}$ on $E_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ [7]. However, for $v\in T$ , equidistribution cannot happen as our points all retract to a finite set of points on $E_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ . This leads to a positive average: indeed, by a direct computation, Hindry and Silverman show that when $E_{N}$ consists solely of points reducing to the identity component of the Néron model at $v$ , we must have

$$ \frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\not=j}\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x_{i}-x_{j})\geq\frac{1}{12}\log^{+}|j(E)|_{v}. $$

On the other hand, for any nonarchimedean $v\not\in T$ , we have the so called Elkies lower bound [41, 5]

$$ \frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\not=j}\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x_{i}-x_{j})\geq-\frac{C}{N}\log^{+}|j(E)|_{v} $$

where $C>0$ is independent of $E$ . As $|T|\geq\frac{h(E)}{M}$ , this leads to a contradiction after summing over all $v\in M_{K}$ for $N$ sufficiently large; indeed, for any set $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}$ of distinct $K$ -rational points of $E$ ,

$$ \frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{v\in M_{K}}\sum_{i\not=j}\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x_{i}-x_{j})=\frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\not=j}\widehat{h}_{E}(x_{i}-x_{j}), $$

and this quantity is small if $\widehat{h}_{E}(x_{i})$ is small for all $i$ .

To generalize this argument to higher dimensions, there are three main obstacles. The first is to find a suitable analogue of $\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x-y)$ for higher dimensional abelian varieties. The second is to establish the Elkies lower bound (3) in terms of this analogue. The third is to prove a corresponding uniform positive lower bound analogous to (2) when the points $x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}$ reduce to the identity component of the Néron model that is independent of $A$ and $v$ . The greatest challenge lies in finding analogues of these three that are mutually compatible.

### 1.2. Higher Dimensional Arakelov-Green’s Functions

The first two obstacles have been overcome by the first author in her recent preprint [78]. Given an abelian variety $A/K$ and a very ample line bundle $L$ by which $A$ is embedded into $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , we assume we have an endomorphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ that extends multiplication by $[m]$ for some $m\geq 2$ . Let $\dim H^{0}(A,L^{n})=c(n)$ . Given a basis $\cal{B}_{n}\subseteq H^{0}(A,L^{n})$ , we may define a higher-dimensional Arakelov-Green’s function

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}:(A^{\operatorname{an}}_{v})^{c(n)}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} $$

which generalizes the averaged quantity $\sum_{i\not=j}\hat{\lambda}_{v}(x_{i}-x_{j})$ . The value

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)}) $$

will be a real number unless there is a nonzero $s\in H^{0}(A,L^{n})$ for which $x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)}$ all lie on $\operatorname{div}(s)$ , in which case it will be $+\infty$ . If a different basis $\cal{B}^{\prime}_{n}$ is used, then $g_{\cal{B}^{\prime}_{n},v}$ differs from $g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}$ by a constant.

In [78], inspired by earlier work of Baker [9] for the case of endomorphisms on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , the first named author constructed a sequence of special bases $\{\cal{B}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , depending on the data of a homogeneous lift $F:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}^{N+1}$ of $f$ , such that for every place $v\in M_{K}$ , we have the inequality

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)})\geq-C_{f,v}\frac{\log n}{n}+r(F) $$

where $C_{f,v}$ is a constant depending on $f$ and $v$ that can be made explicit. Here, $r(F)$ is a negative multiple of $\log|\operatorname{Res}(F)|$ where $\operatorname{Res}$ is the Macaulay resultant, chosen so that $g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}$ itself does not depend on the lift $F$ . Equation (4) may be viewed as an analogue of Elkies lower bound (3). This construction has also been recently used by the second author [115] to prove a quantitative version of Yuan’s equidistribution theorem [118] for polarized dynamical systems over archimedean places.

Using results of Boucksom and Eriksson [17] and their extensions by Boucksom–Gubler–Martin [18], the first author showed that if one has a sequence of $c(n)$ -tuples $\{\vec{P}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , and if

$$ \liminf_{n\to\infty}g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}(\vec{P}_{n})=r(F) $$

for the special bases $\cal{B}_{n}$ , then the tuples $\vec{P}_{n}$ must equidistribute to the non-archimedean canonical measure $\mu_{A,v}$ on $A_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

We now give some background on the equidistribution of small points. Equidistribution of points with small Néron–Tate height towards the Haar measure was first observed and proven by Szpiro–Ullmo–Zhang [109] over archimedean places, and was then used to prove the Bogomolov conjecture by Ullmo [111] and Zhang [123]. For elliptic curves $E$ , a non-archimedean equidistribution theorem was established by Baker–Petsche [7], and analogous results for dynamical systems on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ were proven by Baker–Rumely [6], Autissier–Chambert-Loir [4, 22] and Favre–Rivera-Letelier [44]. For higher-dimensional abelian varieties (and more generally polarized dynamical systems), Chambert-Loir [22] defined a probability measure $\mu_{A,v}$ that lives on the Berkovich analytification $A_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ and plays the role of the Haar measure at archimedean places.

In [55, 54, 56], Gubler uses convex and tropical geometry to study $\mu_{A,v}$ and establishes an equidistribution theorem for small points over function fields. We note that Yuan and Zhang have extended the equidistribution theorem to the more general setting of adelic line bundles on quasi-projective varieties [118, 117] (see also [49]). Gubler uses his equidistribution result to prove the geometric Bogomolov conjecture for abelian varieties with totally degenerate reduction [54]. The geometric Bogomolov conjecture was subsequently proven in full by Xie–Yuan [113], building on the work of Yamaki [114]. For function fields over $\mathbb{C}$ , there is a different approach by Gao–Habegger [47] and Cantat–Gao–Habegger–Xie [20].

In another direction, Berman, Boucksom and Witt Nystrom [13] used the variational approach of Szpiro–Ullmo–Zhang to prove an equidistribution result for Fekete points on complex manifolds. Given a complex manifold $X$ and a hermitian line bundle $L$ , one can define a notion of an $n$ -transfinite diameter with respect to a basis $\cal{B}_{n}$ of $H^{0}(X,L^{n})$ . Our Arakelov-Green’s function $g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}$ is essentially $-\log$ of this transfinite diameter. A $c(n)$ -tuple is said to be $n$ -Fekete if the value of the Arakelov-Green’s function evaluated on that tuple realizes the ( $-\log$ of the) $n$ -transfinite diameter. Any sequence of $n$ -Fekete points equidistributes to the equilibrium measure associated to $(X,L)$ as $n\to\infty$ . This was extended to the non-archimedean setting by Boucksom–Eriksson [17] and Boucksom–Gubler–Martin [18]. We note that Rumely [103] and Rumely–Lau–Varley [102] had previously studied the relation between Arakelov theory and transfinite diameters.

Going back to Gubler’s work, he shows that if $A$ has stable bad reduction at $v$ , then one can define a continuous retraction map $r:A_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ where $\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ is a real torus with $k\geq 1$ . The dimension $k$ of the real torus is exactly the toric rank of the semiabelian variety corresponding to the special fiber of the Néron model of $A$ . The pushforward of $\mu_{A,v}$ under $r$ is the Haar measure on $\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ . On the other hand, if $x\in A(K)$ reduces to the identity component of the special fiber at $v$ , then $r(x)=0\in\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ . In particular, if $\vec{P}_{n}$ is a tuple with $r(\vec{P}_{n})=0$ , then there exist $N,\delta>0$ depending on $A$ and $v$ such that if $n\geq N$ , then

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}(\vec{P}_{n})\geq\delta+r(F). $$

The main challenge in using (5) for the purposes of this paper is to find a uniform $(N,\delta)$ that makes (5) hold for all $g$ -dimensional abelian varieties $A$ over a non-archimedean field $K$ .

### 1.3. Degeneration by Ultrafilters

To achieve this, we will use a degeneration argument to show a weaker statement that suffices for our paper. Degeneration arguments have shown to be very useful in proving uniformity results in both arithmetic dynamics and Diophantine geometry. DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [33] and Yuan [119] both use degeneration arguments to prove results toward the uniform Bogomolov conjecture, and Poineau [97, 98] uses degenerations to prove the Bogomolov–Fu–Tschinkel conjecture. The approach by degenerations differs from the breakthroughs on the uniform Mordell–Lang conjecture by Dimitrov–Gao–Habbeger [34], Kühne [69] and Gao–Ge–Kühne [46], which rely on studying the non-degeneracy of families of subvarieties.

We will use a method developed by Luo [81, 82], who uses ultrafilters to construct rescaling limits for sequences of rational maps $f_{n}:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of degree $d$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . This was formalized using Berkovich spaces by Favre–Gong [43, 50], and it is thus readily adapted to the setting of abelian varieties. The second author has also applied it to prove some uniform boundedness statements in arithmetic dynamics [116]. We remark that there are related constructions by Amini–Nicolussi for the moduli space of curves [2, 3] and also by Poineau [99] and Song [107].

We briefly describe the construction here. Let $X=\cal{A}_{g,3}$ be the fine moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties with level $3$ structure over $\mathbb{C}$ , and fix a compactification $\overline{X}$ of $X$ . Following Silverman [106], for any valued field $K$ containing $\mathbb{C}$ , we can define a local height function $\lambda_{\partial X}$ with respect to the boundary $\partial X$ . This function behaves like $-\log\mathrm{dist}(\cdot,\partial X)$ .

Now let $(A_{n}/K_{n})$ be a sequence of principally polarized abelian varieties with level $3$ structure over algebraically closed complete non-archimedean valued fields $(K_{n},|\cdot|_{n})$ contaning $\mathbb{C}$ as a trivially valued subfield, such that each $A_{n}$ has bad reduction over $K_{n}$ . Then $\lambda_{\partial X}(A_{n})>0$ and we can thus define $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial X}(A_{n})^{-1}$ . For $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_{n})$ , we let

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}=\left\{(x_{n})\in\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}K_{n}:\sup_{n}|x_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}<\infty\right\}, $$

which can be viewed as the product of the rescaled valued fields $(K_{n},|\cdot|^{\varepsilon_{n}})$ in the category of Banach rings. Then by Proposition 4.3, there is a unique morphism $x:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to X$ such that the precomposition of $x$ with the inclusion $\iota_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ yields the morphism defined by $A_{n}/K_{n}$ .

It was already known to Berkovich [12, Proposition 1.2.3] that the Berkovich spectrum $\cal{M}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})$ of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ under the norm $||(x_{n})||=\sup_{n}|x_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}_{n}$ is in bijection with the set of ultrafilters $\beta\mathbb{N}$ under the map

$$ \omega\to\left((x_{n})\mapsto\lim_{\omega}|x_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}\right); $$

see also [43, Theorem 3.8]. If $\cal{H}(\omega)$ is the residue field of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ for a non-principal ultrafilter $\omega$ , we obtain an induced morphism $x_{\omega}:\operatorname{Spec}\cal{H}(\omega)\to X$ which gives us an abelian variety $A_{\omega}$ over $\cal{H}(\omega)$ . The field $\cal{H}(\omega)$ is algebraically closed and is a non-archimedean field under $|\cdot|_{\omega}$ . One shows that $A_{\omega}$ has bad reduction over $\cal{H}(\omega)$ . Observe that $A_{\omega}$ might not be defined over a discretely valued subfield of $\cal{H}(\omega)$ , so we require an extension of Gubler’s results to general non-archimedean fields. This was achieved by Gubler and Stadloder [53].

Now let $U$ be a Zariski open of $X$ such that we have a closed embedding $\cal{A}_{U}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ , where $\cal{A}_{U}$ is the universal abelian scheme over $U$ . Assume that we have an endomorphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ that lifts multiplication by $[m]$ for some $m\geq 2$ . Then after fixing a homogeneous lift $F:\mathbb{A}_{U}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}_{U}^{N+1}$ of $f$ , the first author’s Arakelov-Green’s function construction may be carried out in a relative way over $U$ , and we may speak of a consistent choice of a special basis $\cal{B}_{k}$ for any abelian variety $A/K$ whose associated point in $X$ lies in $U(K)$ .

For any $C>0$ , we say that an abelian variety $A/K_{v}$ whose associated point in $X$ lies in $U(K_{v})$ is $C$ -centered if $\lambda_{\partial U}(A)\leq C\lambda_{\partial X}(A)$ . The key uniformity result, which serves as the higher-dimensional version of (2), is the following theorem (see Theorem 5.2). It is proven by degeneration via ultrafilters. Fix an increasing function $h:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $h(n)=c(k_{n})$ for some $k_{n}$ depending on $n$ . (Recall that $c(n):=\dim H^{0}(A,L^{n})$ .) For $v\in M_{K}$ a place of stable bad reduction, we say that $A_{v}:=A\times_{K}K_{v}$ is $n$ -good if given $x_{1},\ldots,x_{h(n)}\in A(K)$ that reduce to the identity component of the Néron model at $v$ , we have

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{k_{n}},v}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(k_{n})})\geq\frac{1}{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(A)+r(F_{K}). $$

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $U$ be a Zariski open of $X=\cal{A}_{g,3}$ . For any increasing function $h:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ where for each $n$ , we have $h(n)=c(k_{n})$ for some $k_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ , and any $C>0$ , there exists a nonempty finite list of integers $\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{m}\}$ such that for any non-archimedean complete algebraically closed field $K$ containing $\mathbb{C}$ as a trivially valued subfield, and for any principally polarized abelian variety $A/K$ of dimension $g$ with bad reduction which is $C$ -centered with respect to $U$ , we have that

$$ A/K\text{ is }n_{i}\text{-good for some }i\text{ with }1\leq i\leq m. $$

The set $\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{m}\}$ can depend on the open set $U$ along with the above-constructed rational map $f$ and homogeneous lift $F$ . However, it is independent of $K$ and the dimension $g$ principally polarized abelian variety $A/K$ which is $C$ -centered with respect to $U$ .

Theorem 1.5 is certainly weaker than asking for a uniform $N$ and $\delta$ such that (5) holds uniformly for all $n\geq N$ and all $g$ -dimensional abelian varieties, but it is enough for our purposes, as $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ can be covered with finitely many such $U$ . Using this, we prove Theorem 1.1 for semistable abelian varieties with at least one place of bad reduction in Section 6.

To extend our argument to the non-semistable case, we obtain positive lower bounds on $g_{\cal{B}_{n},v}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)})$ under the assumption that $A$ has bad reduction at $v$ , but good reduction after a finite extension. This is handled in Sections 7 and 8. We address the case of everywhere good reduction in Section 9, and then use Zarhin’s trick and reduction to the principally polarized case to prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, with the additional restriction of dependence on the genus $g(B)$ . We finally upgrade the bound to depend only on the gonality via Weil restrictions, using the case of $gd$ -dimensional abelian varieties to deduce the case of $g$ -dimensional abelian varieties over $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ with $\operatorname{gon}(B)=d$ .

## 2. Background

In this section, we go through some preliminary background. We first review the theory of global and local heights for closed subschemes over quasi-projective varieties over function fields. This was set forth by Silverman [106]; see also the exposition by Matsuzawa [84]. We then recall some facts about abelian varieties and schemes, in particular about the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ with level $3$ structure and its compactifications. We finally end with some facts regarding the Hodge bundle on the moduli space of curves.

### 2.1. Heights over Function Fields

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . We let $M_{K}$ be the following set of inequivalent nontrivial absolute values: for each $v\in B(\mathbb{C})$ , we may define an absolute value $|\cdot|_{v}:K^{\times}\to\mathbb{R}$ via

$$ |f|_{z}:=e^{-\operatorname{ord}_{z}(f)}\text{ for }f\in K^{\times}, $$

where $\operatorname{ord}_{z}(f)$ is the order of vanishing of $f$ at $z$ . The set $M_{K}$ satisfies the product formula; that is to say, for any $f\in K^{\times}$ we have

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}}\log|f|_{v}=0. $$

This allows us to define a global height function on $h:\mathbb{P}^{n}(K)\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ by letting

$$ h([x_{0}:\cdots:x_{n}])=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}\log\max\{|x_{0}|_{v},\ldots,|x_{n}|_{v}\}, $$

where the product formula ensures that this is well-defined independent of our choice of $x_{i}$ . Under suitable normalizations [14, Remark 1.5.22], we may extend this to a well-defined function $h:\mathbb{P}^{n}(\overline{K})\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ , which we will call the standard Weil height. Unlike the case of number fields where every number field is canonically realized as an extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ , there is no canonical realization of the function field $K$ as an extension of $\mathbb{C}(t)$ , and hence our height function depends on a choice of reference field. If $K^{\prime}/K$ is a finite extension and we take $K^{\prime}$ to be our reference field, we have $h_{K^{\prime}}(x)=[K^{\prime}:K]h_{K}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{P}^{n}(K^{\prime})$ .

In general, given a projective variety $X$ over $K$ and an line bundle $L$ , we may define a height function $h_{L}:X(\overline{K})\to\mathbb{R}$ . However, this height function is only well-defined up to an $O(1)$ term and depends on some choice of the data of $L$ . However, if both $X$ and $L$ are defined over $\mathbb{C}$ , then one has a canonical choice of $h_{L}$ . The same holds for height functions $h_{Z}$ associated to closed subscehemes $Z$ of $X$ [106], as we now explain.

Let $X$ be a projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and $D$ a Cartier divisor on $X$ . Let $L,M$ be basepoint free line bundles on $X$ for which $\mathcal{O}(D)\simeq L\otimes M^{-1}$ . Fix a meromorphic section $s_{D}$ of $\mathcal{O}(D)$ . Picking bases of the spaces of global sections $s=\{s_{0},\ldots,s_{n}\}$ of $L$ and $t=\{t_{0},\ldots,t_{m}\}$ of $M$ , we may define the local height for any valued field $K\supseteq\mathbb{C}$ relative to the presentation $\cal{D}=(s_{D},L,s,M,t)$ to be

$$ \lambda_{\cal{D}}(p)=\max_{k}\min_{l}\log\left|\frac{s_{k}}{t_{l}s_{D}}(p)\right| $$

for all $p\in(X\setminus D)(K)$ , where $\frac{s_{k}}{t_{l}s_{D}}$ is a rational function on $X$ . A priori, this depends on the presentation $\cal{D}$ . In the usual setting of heights over global fields, one shows that the local heights for two different presentations differ by an $O(1)$ term. However if we assume that $\mathbb{C}$ is trivially valued in $K$ , they turn out to be equal.

#### Proposition 2.1.

Let $\cal{D},\cal{D}^{\prime}$ be two presentations that are defined over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $K$ be a non-archimedean field containing $\mathbb{C}$ as a trivially valued subfield. Then $\lambda_{\cal{D}}=\lambda_{\cal{D}^{\prime}}$ on $(X\setminus D)(K)$ .

#### Proof.

By [14, Remark 2.2.13], there exists a finite list of elements $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$ such that

$$ |\lambda_{\cal{D}}-\lambda_{\cal{D}^{\prime}}|\leq\log^{+}\max\{|p_{1}|,\ldots,|p_{m}|\} $$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value from $K$ . Since $\mathbb{C}$ is trivially valued, it follows that $\lambda_{\cal{D}}=\lambda_{\cal{D}^{\prime}}$ . ∎

Now pick a local affine chart $U$ over $\mathbb{C}$ with affine coordinates $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})$ , where our Cartier divisor $D$ is given locally by the function $f\in\mathcal{O}(U)$ . Then we have a simple formula for $\lambda_{\cal{D}}$ when evaluated on points $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})$ with $|a_{i}|\leq 1$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

Let $U\subseteq X$ be an affine open over $\mathbb{C}$ with affine coordinates $a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}$ such that our Cartier divisor $D$ is given by $f\in\mathcal{O}(U)$ . If $x\in U(K)$ has coordinates $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N})$ with $|x_{i}|\leq 1$ , then

$$ \lambda_{\cal{D}}(x)=\log|f(x)|^{-1}. $$

#### Proof.

First assume that the line bundles $L$ and $M$ are trivialized by $U$ . Let $B$ be the bounded set $B=\{x\in U:|x_{1}|,\ldots,|x_{N}|\leq 1\}$ , and let $C_{B}(f)=\sup_{x\in B}\{|f(x)|\}$ . Since $\mathbb{C}$ is trivially valued, we have $C_{B}(f)\leq 1$ . By the proof of [84, Lemma 4.24], we obtain

$$ \lambda_{\cal{D}}(x)=\log|f(x)|^{-1} $$

for all $x\in B$ as desired.

We now remove the assumption that $L$ and $M$ are trivial on all of $U$ . Because $L$ and $M$ are locally free of rank $1$ , we may cover $U$ by finitely many distinguished affines $D(g_{1}),\ldots,D(g_{n})$ , $g_{i}\in\mathcal{O}(U)$ such that both $L$ and $M$ are trivial on each $D(g_{i})$ . Since $\{D(g_{i})\}$ covers $U$ , the functions $g_{i}$ generate the unit ideal in $\mathcal{O}(U)$ , so there exist coefficients $c_{i}\in\mathbb{C}$ with

$$ \sum_{i}c_{i}g_{i}=1\quad\text{in }\mathcal{O}(U). $$

Let

$$ B=\{x\in U(K)\mid|x_{j}|\leq 1\text{ for all affine coordinates }x_{j}\text{ on }U\}, $$

and fix $x\in B$ . Evaluating the identity $\sum c_{i}g_{i}=1$ at $x$ , and using that $\mathbb{C}$ is trivially valued, yields

$$ 1=\left|\sum_{i}c_{i}g_{i}(x)\right|=\max_{i}|c_{i}g_{i}(x)|=\max_{i}|g_{i}(x)|. $$

Hence at least one $g_{i_{0}}$ satisfies $|g_{i_{0}}(x)|=1$ . Thus $x\in D(g_{i_{0}})(K)$ , and in this affine chart both $L$ and $M$ are trivial by hypothesis. On the distinguished affine $D(g_{i_{0}})$ , the coordinate ring is $\mathcal{O}(U)[g_{i_{0}}^{-1}]$ , so the coordinates on $D(g_{i_{0}})$ are the original affine coordinates $x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}$ on $U$ , together with the function $g_{i_{0}}^{-1}$ . For our specific point $x$ , we have $|x_{j}|\leq 1$ by definition of $B$ , and $|g_{i_{0}}(x)^{-1}|=1$ because $|g_{i_{0}}(x)|=1$ . Thus all coordinates of $x$ on $D(g_{i_{0}})$ have norm $\leq 1$ . Since $L$ and $M$ are trivial on this distinguished affine, the conclusion of the first paragraph applies to $x$ , yielding

$$ \lambda_{\mathcal{D}}(x)=\log|f(x)|^{-1}. $$

This completes the proof.∎

We now move on to local heights associated to closed subschemes. Let $Y$ be a closed subscheme of $X$ defined over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $Y=D_{1}\cap\cdots\cap D_{r}$ be the scheme-theoretic intersection of $D_{1},\dots,D_{r}$ , where each $D_{i}$ is a Cartier divisor defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Choose a collection $\cal{Y}=(\cal{D}_{1},\ldots,\cal{D}_{r})$ of presentations of the $D_{i}$ , so that we obtain local height functions $\lambda_{\cal{D}_{i}}$ . We then define

$$ \lambda_{\cal{Y}}=\min\{\lambda_{\cal{D}_{1}},\lambda_{\cal{D}_{2}},\ldots,\lambda_{\cal{D}_{r}}\}. $$

#### Proposition 2.3.

For any two presentations $\cal{Y}$ and $\cal{Y}^{\prime}$ , the local height functions $\lambda_{\cal{Y}}$ and $\lambda_{\cal{Y}^{\prime}}$ are equal.

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove the case where $\cal{Y}^{\prime}=\cal{Y}\cup\{\cal{E}\}$ for $\cal{E}$ a presentation of some Cartier divisor $E$ . Let $U$ be an affine open for which the presentations $\cal{D}_{i},\cal{E}$ are trivialized. By [84, Claim 4.26], on the bounded subset $B$ of $U(K)$ (points whose affine coordinates have norm $\leq 1$ ), we have

$$ \lambda_{\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}(x)\geq\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}(x)-\gamma(U,B;\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{E}) $$

for some constant $\gamma(U,B;\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{E})$ depending on $U,B,\mathcal{Y}$ , and $\mathcal{E}$ . By Proposition 2.2, the correction terms appearing in $\gamma(U,B;\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{E})$ vanish, so $\gamma(U,B;\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{E})=0$ and hence $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}\geq\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}$ on $B$ .

The reverse inequality is immediate from the definitions of $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}$ , so $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}=\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}$ on $B$ . By the proof of [14, Theorem 2.2.11], we may find a cover $\{U_{i}\}$ of $X$ such that the union of the bounded subsets $B_{i}$ of each $U_{i}$ contains all points of $X$ . Hence we have $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}=\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}$ globally as desired. ∎

As a result, we obtain the following description of the local height functions of a closed subscheme when restricted to an affine open.

#### Proposition 2.4.

Let $U\subseteq X$ be an affine open over $\mathbb{C}$ with affine coordinates $a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}$ such that on $U$ , the closed subscheme $Y=D_{1}\cap\cdots\cap D_{r}$ is cut out by the functions $f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in\mathcal{O}(U)$ . If $x\in U(K)$ has coordinates $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N})$ with $|x_{i}|\leq 1$ , then we have

$$ \lambda_{\cal{Y}}(x)=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\log|f_{i}(x)|^{-1}\} $$

for any presentation $\mathcal{Y}$ of the Cartier divisors $D_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

For $\mathcal{Y}=(\mathcal{D}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{D}_{r})$ , we have $\lambda_{\cal{Y}}=\min\lambda_{\mathcal{D}_{i}}$ , and by Proposition 2.3, $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}$ is independent of the choice of presentation. Restricting to the affine open $U$ , we know by Proposition 2.2 that if $D_{i}$ is given by $g_{i}$ , we have $\lambda_{\mathcal{D}_{i}}=\log|g_{i}(x)|^{-1}$ if $x\in U(K)$ has affine coordinates satisfying $|x_{i}|\leq 1$ for all $i$ . It thus suffices to show that

$$ \min_{1\leq i\leq r}\{\log|g_{i}(x)|^{-1}\}=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\log|f_{i}(x)|^{-1}\}. $$

Since, on $U$ , the closed subscheme $Y$ is cut out by $\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\}$ and also by $\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\}$ , it follows that the ideals of $\mathcal{O}(U)$ generated by $\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\}$ and $\{g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\}$ are equal. Thus for any $f_{i}$ , there exist $c_{j}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $f_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}c_{j}g_{j}$ . Since $|c_{j}|=1$ for all $j$ , it follows that

$$ |f_{i}(x)|\leq\max_{1\leq j\leq r}|g_{j}(x)|\implies\log|f_{i}(x)|^{-1}\geq\min_{1\leq j\leq r}\log|g_{j}(x)|^{-1}. $$

Thus

$$ \min_{1\leq i\leq m}\log|f_{i}(x)|^{-1}\geq\min_{1\leq j\leq r}\log|g_{j}(x)|^{-1}. $$

The reverse inequality follows similarly and we get equality as desired. ∎

We now list some basic properties that these local heights associated to closed subschemes satisfy. These can all be found in [106], but the main thing we want to emphasize as per Proposition 2.3 is that our local height functions are canonical. We thus drop the presentations in our notation and simply write $\lambda_{Y}$ in lieu of $\lambda_{\mathcal{Y}}$ , etc. Furthermore, the constants appearing in the bounds only depend on the geometry of $X$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and not on the non-archimedean field $K$ .

#### Proposition 2.5.

Let $X$ be a projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $Y,Z$ closed subschemes of $X$ . Then for any non-archimedean field $K$ with $\mathbb{C}$ a trivially valued subfield, we have functions

$$ \lambda_{Y},\lambda_{Z}:X(K)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} $$

satisfying the following properties:

- (i) If $Z\subseteq Y$ then $\lambda_{Z}\leq\lambda_{Y}$ .

- (ii) If $\operatorname{Supp}Z\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}Y$ , then there is a constant $c>0$ , independent of $K$ , such that $\lambda_{Z}\leq c\lambda_{Y}$ .

- (iii) Let $\varphi:X\to X^{\prime}$ be a morphism of projective varieties over $\mathbb{C}$ . Let $Y^{\prime}$ be a closed subscheme of $X^{\prime}$ . Then $\lambda_{\varphi^{*}Y}=\lambda_{Y^{\prime}}.$

- (iv) Let $U\subseteq X$ be an open set and let $W\subseteq X$ be the complement of $U$ . If $Z|_{U}\subseteq Y|_{U}$ , then there exists a constant $c>0$ , independent of $K$ , such that $\lambda_{Z}\leq\lambda_{Y}+c\lambda_{W}$ .

#### Proof.

The first claim is clear as given any presentation $\cal{Y}$ of $Y$ , we may add $\cal{Y}$ to any presentation $\cal{Z}$ of $Z$ and this does not change $\lambda_{Z}$ . As the local heights $\lambda_{Z}$ and $\lambda_{Y}$ are defined by taking minima as in (6), it follows that $\lambda_{Z}\leq\lambda_{Y}$ .

The second claim follows similarly. Since $\operatorname{Supp}Z\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}Y$ , the Nullstellensatz implies that $nZ\subseteq Y$ for some positive integer $n>0$ . As $\lambda_{nY}=n\lambda_{Y}$ , we obtain $\lambda_{Z}\leq n\lambda_{Y}$ as desired.

The third claim follows immediately from definitions. For the fourth claim, it suffices to find $n$ such that $Z\subseteq Y+nW$ , which is done in [106, Theorem 2.1(g)]. ∎

We now state Lemma 5.1 of [106].

#### Proposition 2.6.

Let $\varphi:X\to X^{\prime}$ be a dominant rational map of projective varieties. Let $U\subseteq X$ be an open for which $\varphi|_{U}$ is a morphism. Let $Z$ be the reduced closed subscheme for $X\setminus U$ . For a closed subscheme $Y$ of $X^{\prime}$ , let $\varphi^{*}Y$ be the Zariski closure of the preimage of $Y$ under $\varphi|_{U}$ . Then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for all non-archimedean fields $K$ with $\mathbb{C}$ a trivially valued subfield, we have

$$ |\lambda_{Y}\circ\varphi-\lambda_{\varphi^{*}Y}|\leq c\lambda_{Z} $$

on $U$ .

#### Proof.

There is a sequence of blowups of $X$ with centers contained in $Z$ yielding a birational map $\pi:\widetilde{X}\dashrightarrow X$ such that the composite $\varphi\circ\pi:\widetilde{X}\dashrightarrow X^{\prime}$ extends to a morphism $\widetilde{\varphi}:\widetilde{X}\to X^{\prime}.$ Moreover, $\pi$ is an isomorphism over $U$ and on $U^{\prime}:=\pi^{-1}(U)$ we have $\widetilde{\varphi}=\varphi\circ\pi$ . Let $Z^{\prime}=(\tilde{X}\setminus U^{\prime})_{\mathrm{red}}$ be the reduced closed subscheme of $\tilde{X}\setminus U^{\prime}$ . Then we have

$$ |\lambda_{(\varphi\circ\pi)^{*}Y}-\lambda_{\tilde{\varphi}^{*}Y}|\leq c\lambda_{Z^{\prime}} $$

for some $c>0$ by (iv) of Proposition 2.5, as $(\varphi\circ\pi)^{*}Y$ and $\tilde{\varphi}^{*}Y$ are both equal on $U^{\prime}$ . Since $\operatorname{Supp}Z^{\prime}=\operatorname{Supp}\pi^{*}Z$ , we have

$$ c^{\prime}\lambda_{Z}\circ\pi=c^{\prime}\lambda_{\pi^{*}Z}\geq\lambda_{Z^{\prime}} $$

for some $c^{\prime}>0$ . Thus

$$ \lambda_{(\varphi\circ\pi)^{*}Y}-\lambda_{\tilde{\varphi}^{*}Y}\leq(cc^{\prime})\lambda_{Z}\circ\pi. $$

Pushing forward along the isomorphism $\pi:U^{\prime}\to U$ gives, for $u\in U$ ,

$$ \lambda_{\widetilde{\varphi}^{*}Y}(\pi^{-1}(u))=\lambda_{\varphi^{*}Y}(u), $$

because on $U^{\prime}$ the divisor $\widetilde{\varphi}^{*}Y$ is the pullback of $\varphi^{*}Y$ via $\pi$ . Similarly,

$$ \lambda_{(\varphi\circ\pi)^{*}Y}(\pi^{-1}(u))=\lambda_{Y}(\varphi(u)), $$

because on $U^{\prime}$ we have $\lambda_{(\varphi\circ\pi)^{*}Y}=\lambda_{Y}\circ(\varphi\circ\pi)$ . Combining with (7) gives

$$ |\lambda_{Y}\circ\varphi-\lambda_{\varphi^{*}Y}|\leq(cc^{\prime})\lambda_{Z} $$

as desired. ∎

Now let $X$ be a quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $\overline{X}$ be a compactification of $X$ , that is to say, a proper variety containing $X$ as an open dense subscheme. Letting $\partial X$ be the reduced closed subscheme whose support is $\overline{X}\setminus X$ , we obtain a local height function $\lambda_{\partial X}$ that depends on our compactification. It turns out that any two such local height functions are commensurate.

#### Proposition 2.7.

Let $\lambda_{\partial X},\lambda^{\prime}_{\partial X}$ be two such local height functions associated to two different compactifications. Then there exists a $c\geq 1$ such that

$$ c^{-1}\lambda_{\partial X}\leq\lambda^{\prime}_{\partial X}\leq c\lambda_{\partial X} $$

for all non-archimedean fields $K$ with $\mathbb{C}$ a trivially valued subfield.

#### Proof.

Let $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{X}^{\prime}$ be the two compactifications yielding $\lambda_{\partial X}$ and $\lambda^{\prime}_{\partial X}$ respectively. We apply Proposition 2.6 to the rational map $\varphi:\overline{X}\to\overline{X}^{\prime}$ which is the identity on $X$ . Letting $Y=\overline{X}^{\prime}\setminus X$ , we see that since $\varphi^{*}Y=\emptyset$ , the local height function $\lambda_{\varphi^{*}Y}$ associated to it is $0$ . Hence taking $Z=\overline{X}\setminus X$ and applying Proposition 2.6, we obtain

$$ |\lambda_{Y}\circ\varphi|\leq c\lambda_{Z}. $$

But $\lambda_{Y}\circ\varphi$ is simply $\lambda_{Z^{\prime}}$ on $X$ , where $Z^{\prime}=\overline{X}^{\prime}\setminus X$ , and so we obtain $\lambda_{Z^{\prime}}\leq c\lambda_{Z}$ . The other inequality follows from reversing the roles of $Z$ and $Z^{\prime}$ . ∎

Given a product formula field $K$ , $X$ quasi-projective over $K$ , and $Z\subseteq X$ a closed subscheme, we may associate to it a global height function $h_{Z}$ , which for all $x\in(X\setminus Z)(K)$ is given by

$$ h_{Z}(x)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}\lambda_{Z,v}(x), $$

where $\lambda_{Z,v}$ is the local height function $\lambda_{Z}$ for the field $K_{v}$ . In general, $h_{Z}(x)$ is only canonical up to a constant term, but in the special case where $K_{v}$ contains $\mathbb{C}$ as a trivially valued subfield for all $v\in M_{K}$ and $X,Z$ are defined over $\mathbb{C}$ , we have seen that each $\lambda_{Z,v}$ is independent of the underlying presentation of $Z$ , and hence so is $h_{Z}$ . The right-hand side of (8) is a priori only defined for $x\in(X\setminus Z)(K)$ , but if $Z$ is a Cartier divisor, then one may choose a linearly equivalent divisor $D^{\prime}$ whose support does not meet the given $x$ . It turns out that $h_{D}=h_{D^{\prime}}$ and so for Cartier divisors, we obtain a well-defined height function on $X(K)$ . We still have the following inequality relating heights associated to ample divisors with those associated to closed subschemes.

#### Proposition 2.8.

Let $D$ be an ample divisor and $Z\subseteq X$ a closed subscheme defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any product formula field $K$ with $\mathbb{C}$ a trivially valued subfield of $K_{v}$ for all $v\in M_{K}$ , we have

$$ h_{Z}\leq ch_{D} $$

for all $x\in(X\setminus Z)(K).$

#### Proof.

We write $Z=\cap_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}$ as an intersection of Cartier divisors $E_{i}$ . As $\lambda_{Z}\leq\lambda_{E_{i}}$ on $(X\setminus E_{i})(K)$ , it follows that $h_{Z}\leq h_{E_{i}}$ on $(X\setminus E_{i})(K)$ . On the other hand, for each $i$ , there exists a constant $c_{i}$ such that $h_{E_{i}}\leq c_{i}h_{D}$ ; for example, we may choose $c_{i}$ such that $c_{i}D-E_{i}$ is very ample. Thus taking $c=\max\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\}$ , we obtain

$$ h_{Z}\leq ch_{D} $$

on $(X\setminus E_{i})(K)$ for each $E_{i}$ . As $\cap_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}=Z$ , it follows that $h_{Z}\leq ch_{D}$ on $(X\setminus Z)(K)$ as desired. ∎

Another comparison theorem that we need is the following.

#### Proposition 2.9.

Let $X,Y$ be quasi-projective varieties over $\mathbb{C}$ and $\varphi:X\to Y$ a morphism. Let $\overline{X},\overline{Y}$ be compactifications of $X,Y$ respectively and let $L,M$ be ample line bundles on $\overline{X},\overline{Y}$ . Then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any product formula field $K$ for which $\mathbb{C}$ is a trivially valued subfield of $K_{v}$ for all $v\in M_{K}$ , we have

$$ h_{M}\circ\varphi\leq ch_{L} $$

for all $x\in X(K)$ .

#### Proof.

By the linearity relation $h_{M^{\otimes\ell}}=\ell h_{M}$ for $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ , we may assume without loss that $M$ is very ample. Let $D_{1},\ldots,D_{n}$ be effective Cartier divisors such that $\mathcal{O}(D_{i})$ is isomorphic to $M$ for all $i$ and $\cap D_{i}=\emptyset$ . For each $D_{i}$ , we may consider the local height function $\lambda_{D_{i}}$ . By Proposition 2.6, we know that

$$ |\lambda_{D_{i}}\circ\varphi-\lambda_{\varphi^{*}D_{i}}|\leq c_{i}\lambda_{Z} $$

for some $c_{i}>0$ , where $\varphi^{*}D_{i}$ denotes the Zariski closure in $\overline{X}$ of the preimage of $D_{i}$ under $\varphi$ and $Z=\overline{X}\setminus X$ . Summing over $v\in M_{K}$ , we obtain

$$ |h_{D_{i}}\circ\varphi-h_{\varphi^{*}D_{i}}|\leq c_{i}h_{Z} $$

for all $x\in(X\setminus\varphi^{*}D_{i})(K)$ . As Proposition 2.8 implies the existence of a constant $c$ such that $\max\{h_{Z},h_{\varphi^{*}D_{i}}\}\leq ch_{L}$ for all $i$ , we may let $c^{\prime}=\max\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\}$ in order to conclude from (9) that

$$ h_{D_{i}}\circ\varphi\leq(c^{\prime}+1)ch_{L} $$

for all $x\in(X\setminus\varphi^{*}D_{i})(K)$ . Since $\cap D_{i}=\emptyset$ , it follows that $(\cap\varphi^{*}D_{i})\cap X=\emptyset$ , and so by our choice of $D_{i}$ , we have

$$ h_{M}\circ\varphi\leq(c^{\prime}+1)ch_{L} $$

for all $x\in X(K)$ as desired. ∎

Note that if $L$ is a very ample line bundle on a projective variety $X$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ where $B$ is a smooth projective curve, then any $x\in X(K)$ spreads to a morphism $x:B\to X$ and $h(x)$ is equivalent to $\deg_{B}(x^{*}L)$ , i.e., the degree of the pullback $x^{*}L$ as a line bundle on $B$ [14, Example 2.4.11].

### 2.2. Abelian Varieties and Schemes

Let $K$ be a field and $A/K$ be an abelian variety. We let $A^{t}$ denote the dual abelian variety of $A$ over $K$ . It can be identified with the connected component $\operatorname{Pic}^{0}(A/K)$ of the identity of the Picard variety of $A$ . Given a line bundle $L$ of $A$ , we may define a morphism

$$ \lambda(L):A\to A^{t} $$

given by sending $a\mapsto t_{a}^{*}L\otimes L^{-1}$ where $t_{a}:A\to A$ is the translation by $a$ map. If $L$ is ample, then $\lambda(L)$ is an isogeny, i.e., a surjective homomorphism with finite kernel.

A polarization $\lambda$ of $A$ is a homomorphism $\lambda:A\to A^{t}$ such that over $\overline{K}$ , it is of the form $\lambda(L)$ for some ample line bundle $L$ on $A_{\overline{K}}$ . We say that the polarization is principal if $\lambda$ is an isomorphism.

In general for an abelian scheme $A/S$ where $S$ is an artbirary scheme, it is a theorem of Raynaud [21, I.1.9] that the dual $A^{t}$ exists and is also an abelian scheme. We may define a polarization of $A/S$ to again be a homomorphism $\lambda:A\to A^{t}$ such that for each geometric point $\overline{s}$ of $S$ , we have an equality $\lambda_{\overline{s}}=\lambda(\cal{L}_{\overline{s}})$ for some ample line bundle $\cal{L}_{\overline{s}}$ on $A_{\overline{s}}$ . For any polarization $\lambda:A\to A^{t}$ , there exists a symmetric ample invertible sheaf $\cal{L}$ on $A$ such that $\lambda(\cal{L})=2\lambda$ [88, Proposition 6.10], i.e., such that $\cal{L}$ induces the polarization $2\lambda_{\overline{s}}$ on each geometric point $A_{\overline{s}}$ .

For an abelian scheme $A/S$ , let $A[n]=\ker[n]$ denote the $n$ -torsion subgroup. A principal polarization $\lambda$ on $A/S$ induces a non-degenerate skew-symmetric pairing $A[n]\times A[n]\to\mu_{n}$ [21, I.1.7]. A level $n$ structure for an abelian scheme $A/S$ of relative dimension $g$ is an isomorphism of group schemes between $A[n]$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{2g}$ , where $A[n]=\ker[n]$ . For a level $n$ structure to exist, it is necessary for $n$ to be invertible in $O_{S}$ , so that $S$ is a $\mathbb{Z}[1/n]$ -scheme.
