For $n\geq 1$ , we let $\cal{A}_{g,n}$ denote the fine moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties (ppavs) with level $n$ structure over $\mathbb{C}$ . We will let $\cal{A}_{g}$ denote the moduli space of ppavs over $\mathbb{C}$ . For $n\geq 3$ , this is a quasi-projective scheme over $\mathbb{C}$ by Mumford [88, Theorem 7.10]. We now fix $n=3$ . There is a universal abelian scheme $\cal{A}$ over $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ with a principal polarization $\lambda:\cal{A}\to\cal{A}^{t}$ . Then there is a universal invertible sheaf $\cal{L}$ on $\cal{A}$ such that if $(A,\lambda)$ is a principally polarized abelian variety over $K$ with level $3$ structure, then the pullback of $\cal{L}$ to $A$ induces $2\lambda$ .

We are interested in two different compactifications of $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ . The first is known as the minimal (Satake or Bailly–Borel) compactification, and we will denote it by $\cal{A}^{*}_{g,3}$ . This is a projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ which contains $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ as an open dense subvariety. Furthermore, there is an ample line bundle $\omega$ on $\cal{A}_{g,3}^{*}$ known as the Hodge bundle. On $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ , it is equivalent to $\bigwedge^{g}e^{*}\Omega^{1}_{\cal{A}}$ , where $\Omega^{1}_{\cal{A}}$ is the relative cotangent bundle of the universal abelian scheme $\cal{A}$ over $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ and $e:\cal{A}_{g,3}\to\cal{A}$ is the identity section. The line bundle $\omega$ can be used to compute the Faltings height [39] of a semistable principally polarized abelian variety $A/K$ where $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ is the function field of a smooth projective curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ as follows: passing to a finite extension $K^{\prime}=\mathbb{C}(B^{\prime})$ , we may assume that $A/K^{\prime}$ has level $3$ structure, and so we obtain a $K^{\prime}$ -point on $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ . Since $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}^{*}$ is projective (hence proper), this $K^{\prime}$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ defined by $A/K^{\prime}$ extends from the generic point $\operatorname{Spec}K^{\prime}$ of $B^{\prime}$ to all of $B^{\prime}$ . In other words, by the valuative criterion for properness, any rational map $B^{\prime}\dashrightarrow\mathcal{A}_{g,3}^{*}$ coming from the moduli point of $A/K^{\prime}$ extends uniquely to a regular morphism $p_{A}:B^{\prime}\to\mathcal{A}_{g,3}^{*}$ . We may then define the stable Faltings height $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ as

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)=\frac{1}{[K^{\prime}:K]}\deg_{B^{\prime}}(p_{A}^{*}\omega). $$

By [39, Section 2], this agrees with the usual definition via Néron models.

The second compactification of $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ that we are interested in is the arithmetic toroidal compactifications which were constructed by Faltings–Chai [21]. Over $\mathbb{C}$ , these compactifications were known before Faltings–Chai [37] but it was known that there was a semiabelian scheme over the compactification. By [21, V.5.8], there exists a compactification $\overline{\cal{A}}_{g,3}$ of $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ which is a projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ . More importantly for us, there exists a universal semiabelian scheme $G\to\overline{\cal{A}}_{g,3}$ extending the universal abelian scheme $\cal{A}\to\cal{A}_{g,3}$ . Note that Faltings and Chai only compactify the moduli space of ppavs with symplectic level $n$ structure. However, $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ consists of a union of disjoint copies of the moduli space with symplectic level $n$ structure [21, IV.6.2(b)] and hence we can simply compactify each copy individually.

We now turn to the setting of abelian varieties $A$ over a function field $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ where $B$ is a smooth projective curve over $\mathbb{C}$ . Given a symmetric ample line bundle $L$ , we may define the Néron–Tate height $\widehat{h}_{A,L}$ as

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}h_{L}([n]x)\text{ for }x\in A(\overline{K}) $$

where $h_{L}$ is a Weil height for the line bundle $L$ . In general, we will omit the dependence on $L$ and simply write $\widehat{h}_{A}$ . By [46, Lemma 2.3], two such line bundles $L,L^{\prime}$ induce the same Néron–Tate height function if $c_{1}(L)=c_{1}(L^{\prime})$ where $c_{1}$ is the first Chern class. Furthermore by [46, Lemma 2.1], two ample line bundles $L,L^{\prime}$ have the same first Chern class if and only if they induce the same polarization on $A$ .

On the other hand, there is a universal polarization $\lambda_{\mathrm{univ}}$ on $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ , characterized by the property that pulling it back along any moduli point $(A,\lambda)$ gives the polarization $\lambda$ on $A$ . The universal symmetric ample line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on the universal abelian scheme is normalized so that its first Chern class represents $2\lambda_{\mathrm{univ}}$ , and therefore pulling back $\mathcal{L}$ along $(A,\lambda)$ produces a symmetric ample line bundle on $A$ whose first Chern class is $2\lambda$ . It follows that every $K$ -point $(A,\lambda)$ of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ determines a unique Néron–Tate height on $A(\overline{K})$ via the pullback of the universal symmetric ample line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ .

### 2.3. Moduli Space of Curves

We now recall some properties of the moduli space of curves following [119, Section 3.1]. Let $M_{g}$ be the coarse moduli space of smooth, projective, connected curves of genus $g$ over $\mathbb{C}$ , and let $\overline{M}_{g}$ be the coarse moduli space of stable curves of genus $g$ . Then $\overline{M}_{g}$ is a proper variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and carries with it a $\mathbb{Q}$ -line bundle $\lambda$ , which we will call the Hodge bundle. The line bundle $\lambda$ has the following characterization [27, Section 4]: given any family $f:X\to S$ of stable curves, we obtain a morphism $p:S\to\overline{M}_{g}$ where $p$ maps $s$ to the point on $\overline{M}_{g}$ corresponding to the stable curve $f^{-1}(s)$ . Then $p^{*}\lambda$ is the line bundle given by $\det(f_{*}\omega_{X/S})$ , where $\omega_{X/S}$ is the relative dualizing sheaf.

Now let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $C/K$ be a smooth curve of genus $g\geq 2$ . Let $K^{\prime}=\mathbb{C}(B^{\prime})$ be an extension for which $C/K^{\prime}$ has semistable reduction. Then there exists a stable model $\cal{C}/B^{\prime}$ and hence we obtain a morphism $p:B^{\prime}\to\overline{M}_{g}$ . We can define the stable Faltings height of our curve as

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(C)=\frac{1}{[K^{\prime}:K]}\deg_{B^{\prime}}(p^{*}\lambda). $$

This is also equal to $h_{\lambda}(C)$ , the height on $C$ arising via pullback of the Hodge bundle $\lambda$ to the point of $\overline{M}_{g}(K)$ corresponding to $C/K$ . Let $\cal{C}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}$ be the minimal regular model of $C/K^{\prime}$ . Let $\pi:\mathcal{C}\to B^{\prime}$ and $\pi^{\prime}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\to B^{\prime}$ denote the respective structure morphisms of $\cal{C}$ and $\cal{C}^{\prime}$ . We have an equality

$$ \deg(\pi^{\prime}_{*}\omega_{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}})=\deg(\pi_{*}\omega_{\mathcal{C}/B^{\prime}}). $$

Noether’s formula [41, Section 6] gives

$$ \deg(\pi^{\prime}_{*}\omega_{\cal{C}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}})=\frac{1}{12}(\omega^{2}_{\cal{C^{\prime}}/B^{\prime}}+N) $$

where $N$ is the total number of nodes on $\cal{C}^{\prime}$ .

By construction, $p^{*}\lambda\cong\det(\pi_{*}\omega_{\mathcal{C}/B^{\prime}})$ , and since $\det(\pi_{*}\omega_{\mathcal{C}/B^{\prime}})$ is a line bundle on $B^{\prime}$ whose degree equals the degree of the vector bundle $\pi_{*}\omega_{\mathcal{C}/B^{\prime}}$ on $B^{\prime}$ , we obtain $\deg_{B^{\prime}}(p^{*}\lambda)=\deg_{B^{\prime}}(\pi_{*}\omega_{\mathcal{C}/B^{\prime}})$ . Moreover, as the generic fiber of $\cal{C}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}$ is of genus $g\geq 2$ , we have the inequality $\omega^{2}_{\cal{C^{\prime}}/B^{\prime}}\geq 0$ [110, Proposition 1]. Combining these facts with (10) and (11), we conclude that

$$ [K^{\prime}:K]h_{\lambda}(C)=[K^{\prime}:K]h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(C)=\deg(\pi^{\prime}_{*}\omega_{\cal{C}^{\prime}/B^{\prime}})\geq\frac{N}{12}. $$

## 3. Lower Bound on Arakelov-Green’s functions

In this section, we introduce a higher-dimensional version of the Arakelov-Green’s functions due to the first author [78] along with some of the main results in [78], which appear here as Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 3.2. Theorem 3.1 gives us an explicit lower bound on the values of the Arakelov-Green’s functions while Proposition 3.2 gives us a criterion to obtain a positive lower bound for the Arakelov-Green’s function on an abelian variety with bad reduction.

To be specific, for an abelian variety $A/K$ with bad reduction where $K$ is a non-archimedean field, the theory of Gubler [56] provides a retraction map $r:A^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}/\Lambda$ where $\mathbb{R}^{m}/\Lambda$ is a real torus and $m\geq 1$ . If we have a collection of points that retract to $0$ , then we can obtain a positive lower bound on our Arakelov-Green’s functions. We then further study when can we say that a point $x\in A(K)$ lies in $r^{-1}(0)$ .

### 3.1. A General Lower Bound

Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be a valued field, with $|\cdot|$ extended to the algebraic closure $\overline{k}$ of $k$ . Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be a projective variety over $k$ , and let $f:X\to X$ be a degree $d\geq 2$ endomorphism of $X$ . Assume that $f$ extends to a morphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , which by abuse of notation we also denote by $f$ . Let $F:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}^{N+1}$ be a homogeneous lift of $f$ . We write $F=[F_{0}:\cdots;F_{n}]$ . If $P\in\mathbb{A}^{N+1}(k)$ , we write

$$ ||F(P)||=\max\{|F_{0}(P)|,\dots,|F_{N}(P)|\}. $$

We define the homogeneous filled Julia set of $F$ to be the set

$$ \mathcal{K}=\{P\in\mathbb{A}^{N+1}(\overline{k}):||F^{n}(P)||\not\to\infty\text{ as }n\to\infty\}. $$

Throughout, we will let

$$ \pi:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\setminus\{(0,\dots,0)\}\to\mathbb{P}^{N} $$

denote the natural projection.

We now build Arakelov-Green’s functions associated to this dynamical system. For each $n\geq 1$ , let $c(n)=\dim H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ , where $\mathcal{O}(1)$ is the pullback bundle on $X$ induced by the embedding $X\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}$ . We will assume that $X$ is normally embedded in $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , i.e., that $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},\mathcal{O}(n))\to H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ is surjective for all $n\geq 1$ . Given a choice of bases $\{\mathcal{B}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of $H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ respectively, there is a naturally induced such function

$$ g_{n}:X^{c(n)}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} $$

for each $n$ , constructed as follows. For a homogeneous lift $F:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}^{N+1}$ of $f$ , let $\widehat{H}_{F}:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\setminus\{0,\dots,0\}$ be given by

$$ \widehat{H}_{F}(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log||F^{n}(P)||. $$

(That this limit exists is shown in [67, proof of Theorem 9].) Write

$$ r(F)=\frac{1}{d^{N}(N+1)(d-1)}\log|\operatorname{Res}(F)|^{-1}, $$

where $\operatorname{Res}(F)$ denotes the Macaulay resultant of $(F_{0},\ldots,F_{N})$ . For $P\in X(k)$ , write $\widetilde{P}$ for a lift of $P$ to $\mathbb{A}^{N+1}(k)$ , with coordinates in $k$ . The Arakelov-Green’s function $g_{n}:X^{c(n)}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ associated to the basis $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ of $A_{n}$ is given by

$$ g_{n}\left(P_{1},\dots,P_{c(n)}\right)=\frac{1}{c(n)}\sum_{i=1}^{c(n)}\widehat{H}_{F}(\widetilde{P_{i}})-\frac{1}{n\cdot c(n)}\log\left|\mathrm{det}\left(\eta_{j}(\widetilde{P_{i}})\right)_{\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}}\right|+r(F). $$

It is readily verified that for a fixed $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ , this function is independent of the choice of lifts $\widetilde{P_{i}}$ and $F$ . Moreover, if $\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\prime}$ is another basis for $A_{n}$ , then its associated Arakelov-Green’s function differs by a constant from that associated to $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ . In the special case of $X=\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ the standard monomial basis of $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(n))=A_{n}$ , this $g_{n}$ coincides (up to replacing $r(F)$ by $\mathrm{Res}(F)$ ) with the function $\mathscr{E}(g):(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ given by

$$ \mathscr{E}(g)(P_{1},\dots,P_{n+1})=\frac{1}{n(n+1)}\sum_{i\neq j}g(P_{i},P_{j}) $$

for $g$ the dynamical Arakelov-Green’s functions introduced by Baker and Rumely (see [6, §3.4] and [8, §10.2]).

#### Definition 3.1.

Given a basis $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ of $H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ of order $c(n)$ , let

$$ d_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(\mathcal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(X))=\exp\left(\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\left(\widetilde{P_{1}},\dots,\widetilde{P}_{c(n)}\right)\\
\in(\mathcal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(X(\overline{k}))^{c(n)}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n\cdot c(n)}\log\left|\mathrm{det}\left(\eta_{j}(\widetilde{P_{i}})\right)_{\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}}\right|\right). $$

From here on out, we normalize $F$ so that $r(F)=0$ (by passing to an extension of $k$ if necessary), and consider the collection $\mathcal{G}$ of polynomials of the form $\left(F_{i}^{(\ell)}\right)^{j}$ , where $0\leq i\leq N$ , $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ , and $1\leq j\leq d-1$ . Let

$$ \mathcal{F}=\bigcup_{j=\lfloor t_{1}\rfloor}^{\lfloor t_{2}\rfloor}\left\{\eta_{i}G_{i}:G_{i}\in\mathcal{G}^{j}\textup{ and }\eta_{i}\textup{ is a standard monomial of deg.}<d(N+1)\right\} $$

where

$$ \mathcal{G}^{j}=\left\{G_{1}G_{2}\cdots G_{j}:G_{\ell}\in\mathcal{G}\textup{ for all }1\leq\ell\leq j\right\}. $$

#### Definition 3.2.

We will denote by $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ any basis of $H^{0}(X,O(n))$ consisting of vectors of the form (15) whenever $n\geq d(N+1)$ , and consisting of the standard monomial basis otherwise. We will denote by $c(n)$ the quantity $\dim_{k}H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ , even though this quantity clearly depends on $X$ and its embedding into $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ in addition to $n$ . When there is potential ambiguity as to the underlying dynamical system or the lift $F$ used in defining $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ , we will refer to $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ and $c(n)$ as being with respect to $(X,f)$ (as well as the lift $F$ ). The notation

$$ \left(\eta_{j}(P_{1},\dots,P_{c(n)})\right)_{\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}} $$

will denote the $c(n)\times c(n)$ matrix whose $i$ -th row corresponds to $P_{i}$ and whose $j$ -th column corresponds to $\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}$ .

We will call the above bases $\cal{B}_{n}$ good. Note that this notion depends on the polarized dynamical system $(X,f)$ along with its lift $F$ . Also note that for a good basis to be known to exist by definition, we must have a surjection $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},\mathcal{O}(n))\to H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ . For any fixed embedding $X\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , this is true for all sufficiently large $n$ . Conversely if we have a surjection $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},\mathcal{O}(n))\to H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}(n))$ , then a good basis always exists since $\cal{F}$ is a spanning set for $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},\mathcal{O}(n))$ [78, Section 2.2].

We have the following theorem [78, Theorem 3.1].

#### Theorem 3.1.

Let $k$ be a valued field with absolute value $|\cdot|$ , and let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be a projective variety Let $f:X\to X$ be a morphism of degree $d\geq 2$ which extends to $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ and let $F:\mathbb{A}_{k}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}_{k}^{N+1}$ be a homogeneous lift of $f$ . Let $\mathcal{K}$ be the homogeneous filled Julia set of $F$ . For this triple $(X,f,F)$ , and for $n\geq 1$ , let $c(n)$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n}$ be as in Definition 3.2. Let

$$ \pi:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\setminus\{(0,\dots,0)\}\to\mathbb{P}^{N} $$

be the natural projection. Let $R$ be the diameter of $\mathcal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(X)$ with respect to the distance defined by the supnorm. There is a constant $C=C(d,N)$ with the following property. For any $c(n)$ -tuple $\vec{P}=\left(P_{1},\dots,P_{c(n)}\right)$ of points in $\mathcal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(X)$ and any $n\geq 2$ , we have

$$ \log\left|\textup{det}\left(\eta_{j}(\vec{P})\right)_{\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}}\right|\leq C\max\{\log R,1\}(\log n)\cdot c(n). $$

(Here we define $\log(0)=-\infty$ .)

Note that Theorem 3.1 gives a lower bound on $g_{n}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{c(n)})$ . Indeed as we may choose any lifts $\tilde{P}_{i}$ of $P_{i}$ , we choose lifts (possibly after passing to an extension of $k$ ) such that the $\widehat{H}_{F}(\tilde{P}_{i})$ are arbitrarily close to $0$ . Thus we have the lower bound

$$ g_{n}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{c(n)})\geq-C\max\{\log R,1\}\frac{\log n}{n}+r(F). $$

In particular, we have

$$ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf g_{n}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{c(n)})\geq r(F). $$

Given an endomorphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ along with a lift $F:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}^{N+1}$ , we would like to bound the supnorm diameter $R$ of the homogeneous filled Julia set $\mathcal{K}$ of $F$ explicitly. This can be done by using [64, Lemma 6]. For simplicity, let’s assume that $|\cdot|$ is non-archimedean as that will be the only case we use. Letting

$$ \lambda(f)=-\log|\operatorname{Res}(F)|+(N+1)(d^{2})^{N}\log||F|| $$

be a local height function for the hypersurface $\{\operatorname{Res}(F)=0\}$ inside $\operatorname{Rat}_{d^{2}}^{N}$ , we have

$$ \frac{-\lambda(f)}{d-1}\leq\widehat{H}_{F}(P)-\log||P||-\frac{1}{d-1}\log||F||\leq 0 $$

for all $P\in\mathbb{A}^{N+1}$ . Inside $\mathcal{K}$ , we have $\widehat{H}_{F}(P)\leq 0$ and so

$$ \log||P||\leq\frac{\lambda(f)}{d-1}+\frac{1}{d-1}\log||F||. $$

Note that $\lambda(f)\geq 0$ since $|\cdot|$ is non-archimedean. Hence we may take

$$ R=O(\lambda(f)+\log||F||) $$

where our constant only depends on $d$ and $N$ .

Now suppose $K$ is a product formula field and assume further that $F$ has a coefficient that is $1$ , so that $\log||F||_{v}\geq 0$ for all $v\in M_{K}$ . This allows us to assume that for any $M_{K}^{\prime}\subseteq M_{K}$ ,

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}^{\prime}}N_{v}\log||F||_{v}\leq\sum_{v\in M_{K}}N_{v}\log||F||_{v}=h(f). $$

Thus, by the non-negativity of $\lambda_{v}$ at all $v\in M_{K}$ ,

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}^{\prime}}(\lambda_{v}(f)+\log||F|_{v})\leq\sum_{v\in M_{K}}(\lambda_{v}(f)+\log||F||_{v})=O(h(f)). $$

In particular, for any $M_{K}^{\prime}\subseteq M_{K}$ , combining this with (17) and (18) gives

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}^{\prime}}g_{\cal{B}_{k}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(k)})\geq\left(\sum_{v\in M_{K}^{\prime}}r(F)_{v}\right)-\frac{C\log k}{k}O(h(f)). $$

### 3.2. A Positive Lower Bound for Abelian Varieties

Let $K$ be a complete nonarchimedean valued field, and let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ embedded into $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ along with an endomorphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree $d^{2}$ that extends multiplication by $[d]$ on $A$ . We assume without loss that $A$ is normally embedded into $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , so that $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},\mathcal{O}(n))$ surjects onto $H^{0}(A,\mathcal{O}(n))$ . Pick a homogeneous lift $F:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}^{N+1}$ . Let $\{\mathcal{B}_{n}\}$ be a choice of basis for $H^{0}(A,\mathcal{O}(n))$ of the form given in Definition 3.2. For each $n$ , let $g_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{c(n)})$ be the associated Arakelov-Green’s function. By Theorem 3.1, if $\mathcal{K}$ is the homogeneous filled Julia set of $F$ , $\pi:\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ is the natural projection, and $\cal{B}_{n}$ is a sequence of good bases for $H^{0}(A,\mathcal{O}(n))$ , we obtain

$$ \limsup_{n}d_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\cal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(A))\leq\exp(-r(F)). $$

Given a $c(n)$ -tuple $\vec{P}\in A^{\operatorname{an}}$ , we say that $\vec{P}$ is Fekete if

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P})=\log d_{B_{n}}(\cal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(A)). $$

Given a sequence $(\vec{P}_{n})$ of $c(n)$ -tuples of points $P_{i}\in A^{\operatorname{an}}$ , along with a sequence of bases $(\cal{B}_{n})$ , not necessarily a sequence of good bases, we say that the sequence is asymptotically Fekete if

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(g_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P}_{n})+\log d_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\cal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(A))\right)=0. $$

Note that the notions of Fekete and asymptotically Fekete are independent of our choice of sequence of bases $\{\cal{B}_{n}\}$ .

By [78, Theorem 3.5], using the results of [18], it follows that there exists a unique probability measure $\mu_{A}$ , supported on $A^{\operatorname{an}}$ , such that for any sequence $(\vec{P}_{n})$ that is asymptotically Fekete, we have

$$ \frac{1}{c(n)}\sum_{x\in\vec{P}_{n}}\delta_{x}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}\mu_{A}. $$

In fact, we can describe $\mu_{A}$ . On $A^{\operatorname{an}}$ , as our line bundle $L=\mathcal{O}(1)$ is symmetric and ample, we have an isomorphism $\varphi:L^{n^{2}}\simeq[n]^{*}L$ for any $n\geq 1$ . Fix some $n\geq 2$ . There is then a canonical metric $|\cdot|$ by [122, Theorem 2.2] or [14, Theorem 9.5.3], unique up to a multiplicative constant, such that $(\varphi^{*}\circ[n]^{*}|\cdot|)^{1/n^{2}}=|\cdot|$ for our $n$ . Our metric is a limit of model metrics and hence semipositive, or psh in the sense of [18]. By [18, Corollary D], the measure $\mu_{A}$ coincides with the canonical measure $c_{1}(L,|\cdot|)^{\wedge g}$ where $g=\dim A$ , see [55] for more details on the definition of $c_{1}(L,|\cdot|)^{\wedge g}$ . Note that Chambert–Loir’s original definition [22] of the Monge–Ampère measures assumed that the valuation on $K$ comes from the algebraic closure of a field with discrete valuation but this assumption was subsequently removed by Gubler. There is a continuous retraction map [56, 53]

$$ r:A\to S(A)\simeq\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda $$

where $S(A)$ is the skeleton of $A$ , with dimension $0\leq k\leq g$ , and $\Lambda$ is a lattice in $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ .

We now assume that $A$ has bad reduction over $K$ , so that $k\geq 1$ . Let $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_{A}$ . Then [53, Theorem 1.2] tells us that $r(S)=\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ , i.e., the measure is supported on the entire skeleton. Suppose we are given a sequence of $c(n)$ -tuples $\vec{P}_{n}$ such that $r(\vec{P}_{n})=0$ . Define

$$ \mathfrak{d}_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P}_{n})=\exp(-g_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P}_{n})-\log d_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(\mathcal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(A))). $$

We claim that $\log\mathfrak{d}_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P}_{n})$ is bounded away from $0$ .

#### Proposition 3.2.

Let $\cal{B}_{n}$ be a sequence of good bases and $(\vec{P}_{n})$ a sequence of $c(n)$ -tuples of points such that $r(\vec{P}_{n})=0$ . Then there exists a $\delta>0$ such that

$$ \limsup\log\mathfrak{d}_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P}_{n})\leq-\delta. $$

In other words, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$ ,

$$ \log\mathfrak{d}_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P}_{n})\leq-\delta. $$

#### Proof.

Assume otherwise. Then there exists a sequence $n_{1}<n_{2}<\cdots$ such that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\log\mathfrak{d}_{\cal{B}_{n_{i}}}(\vec{P}_{n_{i}})=0. $$

We now replace our sequence of tuples so that for $n=n_{i}$ , we keep the original tuple but for each $n\not=n_{i}$ , we replace $\vec{P}_{n}$ with a Fekete tuple. Let $(\vec{Q}_{n})$ be this new sequence. Then since we have the upper bound

$$ \limsup_{i\to\infty}\log\mathfrak{d}_{\cal{B}_{n_{i}}}(\vec{P}_{n_{i}})\leq 0, $$

it follows that $(\vec{Q}_{n})$ is an asymptotically Fekete sequence of tuples. Applying (22), we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{c(n)}\sum_{x\in\vec{Q}_{n}}\delta_{x}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}\mu_{A} $$

and hence passing to the subsequence $\{n_{i}\}$ yields

$$ \frac{1}{c(n_{k})}\sum_{x\in\vec{P}_{n_{k}}}\delta_{x}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}\mu_{A} $$

too. However, for all $k$ and for all $x\in\vec{P}_{n_{k}}$ , we have $r(x)=0$ . As $r$ is continuous, $r^{-1}(0)$ is a closed set. It follows that we must have $\operatorname{supp}\mu_{A}\subseteq r^{-1}(0)$ . But this is impossible as $r(\operatorname{supp}\mu_{A})$ surjects onto $\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ , which is positive-dimensional as $k\geq 1$ by hypothesis. ∎

In the setting of Section 3.1, if we pick our lift $F$ so that $r(F)=0$ , by (21) we have

$$ \limsup_{n}\log d_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\cal{K}\cap\pi^{-1}(A))\leq 0. $$

In particular, Proposition 3.2 implies that there is some $\delta>0$ for which

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n}}(\vec{P})\geq\delta>0. $$

We want to understand the kernel $r^{-1}(0)$ . We recall the construction of the retraction map by Gubler [56, Section 4]. Let $R$ be the valuation ring of $K$ . Following [56, Section 4], by [16, Theorem 8.2], there is a unique connected formal group scheme $\cal{A}_{1}$ over $R$ with generic fiber $A_{1}$ (in the sense of Raynaud) such that $\cal{A}_{1}$ has semiabelian reduction and $A_{1}$ is isomorphic to an open analytic subgroup of $A^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

The semistable reduction theorem says that there is a short exact sequence

$$ 1\to T_{1}\xrightarrow{\iota_{1}}A_{1}\xrightarrow{q_{1}}B\to 1 $$

where $T_{1}$ is the maximal formal affinoid subtorus of $A_{1}$ and $B$ is the generic fiber of a formal abelian scheme $\cal{B}$ . We may identify $T_{1}$ with the subset $\{|x_{1}|=\cdots=|x_{n}|=1\}$ of the usual torus $T=(\mathbb{G}^{n}_{m})^{\operatorname{an}}$ . The uniformization $E$ of $A$ is given by an analytic group $E=(A_{1}\times T)/T_{1}$ , where $T_{1}$ acts by

$$ t_{1}\cdot(a,t)=(\iota_{1}(t_{1})+a,t_{1}^{-1}\cdot t). $$

This gives us an exact sequence

$$ 1\to T\to E\to B\to 1 $$

The closed immersion $T_{1}\to A_{1}$ extends to $T\xrightarrow{\iota}A^{\operatorname{an}}$ and hence, from the map $A_{1}\times T\to A^{\operatorname{an}}$ given by $(a_{1},t)\mapsto a+\iota(t)$ (whose kernel contains $T_{1}$ ), we obtain a homomorphism $\pi:E\to A^{\operatorname{an}}$ . This turns out to be a surjection and the kernel $\ker(\pi)=M$ is a discrete subgroup of $E$ .

Let $q_{1}:A_{1}\to B$ be the quotient map from $A_{1}$ to $B$ . We may find a chart of formal affinoids $\{V_{i}\}$ with respect to $\cal{B}$ covering $B$ such that $q_{1}^{-1}(V_{i})\simeq V_{i}\times T_{1}$ . We may choose sections $s_{i}:V_{i}\to A_{1}$ such that on each chart $V_{i}\times T_{1}$ of $A_{1}$ , we have $s_{i}:v\mapsto(v,1)\in V_{i}\times T_{1}$ . Then the transition maps $g_{i,j}=s_{i}-s_{j}$ are maps from $V_{i}\cap V_{j}$ to $T_{1}$ . Note also that the $V_{i}\times T$ form an atlas for $E$ since $E=(A_{1}\times T)/T_{1}$ . Fix coordinates $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ on $T=(\mathbb{G}^{n}_{m})^{\operatorname{an}}$ . Then we obtain coordinates on $V_{i}\times T$ just by looking at the $T$ -component. These depend on our choice of chart, but the function $|x_{i}|$ does not as the transition maps $g_{i,j}$ are valued in $T_{1}$ . We hence obtain a well-defined continuous map

$$ \begin{array}[]{llll}\operatorname{val}:&E&\to&\mathbb{R}^{n}\\
&p&\mapsto&(-\log|x_{1}|(p),\ldots,-\log|x_{n}|(p)).\end{array} $$

The discrete subgroup $M$ maps to a lattice $\Lambda$ and thus we get a map

$$ r:A^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}/\Lambda $$

that forms a retraction of $A^{\operatorname{an}}\cong E/M$ . This construction is independent of the choice of formal charts $\{V_{i}\}$ covering $B$ .

#### Proposition 3.3.

Under the retraction map $r$ , we have $r(A_{1})=0$ .

#### Proof.

The retraction map $r:A^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}/\Lambda$ is induced by the valuation map $\operatorname{val}:E\to\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Recall that we have an atlas of formal affinoid charts $\{V_{i}\}$ covering $B$ satisfying $q^{-1}(V_{i})\simeq V_{i}\times T_{1}$ . Then as noted previously, $E$ has an atlas given by the $V_{i}\times T$ and the functions $|x_{1}|,\ldots,|x_{n}|$ are defined by looking at the $T$ -coordinates under any chart of this atlas. But in this atlas, we have $A_{1}\simeq V_{i}\times T_{1}$ , and so clearly $\operatorname{val}(A_{1})=0$ . Hence we must have $r(\pi(A_{1}))=0$ . But by construction of $E$ , $A_{1}\subseteq A^{\operatorname{an}}$ is contained in $\pi(A_{1})$ , and hence $r(A_{1})=0$ as desired.∎

We now give a criterion for a point $x\in A(K)$ to lie in $A_{1}$ . Recall that $A_{1}$ is the generic fiber of a unique connected formal group scheme $\cal{A}_{1}$ over $R$ such that $\cal{A}_{1}$ has semiabelian reduction and that $A_{1}$ is isomorphic to an open analytic subgroup of $A^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

#### Proposition 3.4.

Let $G$ be a semiabelian scheme over $R$ with generic fiber $A$ . If $x\in A(K)$ lifts to $\tilde{x}\in G(R)$ , then $x\in A_{1}$ . In particular, $r(x)=0\in S(A)$ .

#### Proof.

Since $G$ is finitely presented over $R$ , we may take its formal completion $\cal{G}$ , which is a formal group scheme over $R$ . By [25, Theorem 5.3.1], its generic fiber $\cal{G}^{\operatorname{an}}$ is an open analytic subgroup of $A^{\operatorname{an}}$ . As by construction $\cal{G}$ has the same special fiber as $G$ , we see that $\cal{G}$ clearly has semi-abelian reduction. By uniqueness of $\cal{A}_{1}$ and connectedness of $\cal{G}$ , we thus must have $A_{1}=\cal{G}^{\operatorname{an}}$ . Now since $x$ lifts to an $R$ -point of $G$ , it lifts to an $R$ -point of $\cal{G}$ too and hence is a $K$ -point of $\cal{G}^{\operatorname{an}}$ as $\cal{G}^{\operatorname{an}}(K)=\cal{G}(R)$ . In particular, $x\in A_{1}$ .∎

When $A$ is defined over a discretely valued field $K^{\prime}\subseteq K$ , the existence of such a semiabelian scheme $G$ follows from the existence of Néron models. In general we may not have a Néron model but we can use the Faltings–Chai compactification to obtain a semiabelian model. Recall that we have a compactification $\overline{\cal{A}}_{g,3}$ of $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ such that the universal abelian scheme $\cal{A}$ over $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ extends to a semiabelian scheme $\cal{G}$ . Then after choosing level $3$ structure, $A$ defines a $K$ -point on $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ and hence by properness, we obtain an $R$ -point of $\overline{\cal{A}}_{g,3}$ . This gives us a semiabelian scheme $G/R$ with generic fiber $A/K$ . Note that [21, I.2.7] proves the uniqueness of such a semiabelian model $G$ if $R$ is noetherian and normal. We can also obtain uniqueness for general non-noetherian valuation rings by descending $G$ to a noetherian base, but this will not be necessary for us.

## 4. Degenerations of Sequences of Points

We now introduce the theory of degenerations of sequences of objects using ultrafilters. This was introduced in complex dynamics for rational maps on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ by Luo [81, 82] and then formalized using Berkovich spaces by Favre and Gong [43]. As the approach of Favre–Gong is algebraic, it is easy to extend their method to objects with a fine moduli space and in particular to abelian varieties. This will be useful to us as quantities coming from Arakelov theory are usually continuous with respect to degenerations [31, 33, 42, 98, 112, 119, 117]. We first review the general construction of degenerations on a general quasi-projective variety $X$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and then specialize this to the case of $X=\cal{A}_{g,3}$ later.

### 4.1. Degeneration via Ultrafilters

Let $X$ be a quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ . We will assume that all our varieties are irreducible unless stated otherwise. Let $(K_{n})$ be a sequence of complete algebraically closed non-archimedean fields containing $\mathbb{C}$ such that $\mathbb{C}$ is trivially valued. Let $(\varepsilon_{n})$ be a sequence of positive reals. We define

$$ \mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}=\{(x_{n})\in\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}K_{n}\mid|x_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}\text{ is bounded}.\}. $$

This is a Banach ring under the supremum norm $|(x_{n})|=\sup_{n}|x_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ . We have natural projection maps $\pi_{n}:\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ which induce projections $\pi_{n}:X(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})\to X(K_{n})$ .

#### Definition 4.1.

Let $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ be a sequence of points. An $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ is a point $x\in X(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})$ such that $\pi_{n}(x)=x_{n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ .

If an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration exists, it is necessarily unique.

#### Proposition 4.1.

There exists at most one $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $Y=\bigsqcup_{n\geq 1}\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}$ . Each projection $\pi_{n}\colon\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ induces

$$ \operatorname{Spec}(\pi_{n})\colon\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}, $$

and these glue to a single morphism

$$ f\colon Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}. $$

We claim that $f$ is an epimorphism in the category of separated, reduced schemes. Indeed, given $g,h:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to X$ such that $g\circ f=h\circ f$ , we can consider the diagonal embedding $\Delta:X\to X\times X$ , which is a closed immersion by separatedness of $X$ . Pulling back $\Delta(X)$ via $(g,h):\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to X\times X$ gives us a closed subscheme $Z$ of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ and the map $f:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ must factor through $Z$ since $g\circ f=h\circ f$ .

We claim that $f$ is dominant. Indeed, the image of $f$ consists of the kernels of the projection maps $\pi_{n}:\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ . Given any nonzero $a\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ with $a=(a_{n})$ , there must exist some $a_{n}\not=0$ and so $\pi_{n}(a)\not=0$ , which implies that $\ker(\pi_{n})\in D(a)$ . Since distinguished opens form a basis, it follows that $f(Y)$ is dense and hence $f$ is dominant as desired.

Since $f$ is dominant and factors through $Z$ , $Z$ must be dense in $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ . As $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ is reduced, it follows that $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ and hence $g=h$ as desired.

We now go back to our proposition. the points $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ define maps $\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to X$ which glue to

$$ f^{\prime}\colon Y\to X, $$

and $f^{\prime}$ is clearly unique. By definition an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration is a morphism

$$ \tilde{x}\colon\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to X $$

with $\tilde{x}\circ f=f^{\prime}$ . Given two such morphisms $\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2}$ , we have $\tilde{x}_{1}\circ f=\tilde{x}_{2}\circ f$ as maps from $Y$ to $X$ . Since $f$ is an epimorphism of reduced, separated schemes, pre-composition with $f$ is injective on morphisms. It follows that $\tilde{x}_{1}=\tilde{x}_{2}$ , proving uniqueness. ∎

Clearly an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration need not always exist. For example if $\varepsilon_{n}=1$ and $X=\mathbb{A}^{1}$ , then $x_{n}$ corresponds to an element of $K_{n}$ and an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration exists if and only if $|x_{n}|$ is bounded from above. However if $X$ is a projective variety, then an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration always exists.

#### Proposition 4.2.

Assume that $X$ is a projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ . Let $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ for all $n$ . Then an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ always exists.

#### Proof.

Let $\{U_{1},\ldots,U_{n}\}$ be an affine open cover for $X$ and let $Y=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}$ . Then we have a natural morphism $\pi:Y\to X$ and $Y$ is affine. Let $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ . Then since $X$ is projective, $x_{n}$ lifts to $\tilde{x}_{n}\in X(R_{n})$ where $R_{n}$ is the valuation ring of $K_{n}$ . Hence we have an induced morphism $\tilde{x}_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to X$ . Since $\{U_{i}\}$ is an open cover and $R_{n}$ is a valuation ring, if $\tilde{x}_{n}^{-1}(U_{i})$ contains the maximal ideal of $R_{n}$ then it contains all of $\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}$ . Thus $\tilde{x}_{n}\in U_{i}(R_{n})\subseteq Y(R_{n})$ .

Since $Y$ is affine, we may let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}$ be affine coordinates for $Y$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . Then $\tilde{x}_{n}$ has affine coordinates $a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}$ with $a_{n,i}\in R_{n}$ and $|a_{n,i}|\leq 1$ for all $1\leq i\leq N$ . Hence if we set $a_{i}=(a_{n,i})$ , we have $a_{i}\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ . We thus obtain an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point $(a_{i})_{i=1}^{N}$ of $Y$ that commutes with the projection map $\pi_{n}:\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ . Projecting it down to $X$ , we obtain our $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration as desired. ∎

#### Remark 4.1.

Observe that in Proposition 4.2, the resulting $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration is actually a $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $X$ for

$$ \mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}R_{n}, $$

where $R_{n}$ is the valuation ring of $K_{n}$ .

Now if $X$ is only quasi-projective, we may embed it into some projective compactification $\overline{X}$ . Then the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration exists on $\overline{X}$ and we can ask whether our $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point lies on $X$ . Recall that for each non-archimedean field $K$ having $\mathbb{C}$ as a trivially valued subfield, we have a local distance function $\lambda_{\partial X}$ depending on the compactification $\overline{X}$ . On an affine open $U_{i}\subseteq\overline{X}$ such that the reduced closed subscheme $(\overline{X}\setminus X)\cap U_{i}$ is given by $\{f_{1}=f_{2}=\cdots=f_{m}=0\}$ for $f_{j}\in\mathcal{O}(U_{i})$ , Proposition 2.4 implies that for $x\in U_{i}(K)$ whose affine coordinates in $U_{i}$ have norm $\leq 1$ , we have

$$ \lambda_{\partial X}(x)=\min_{1\leq i\leq n}-\log|f_{i}(x)|. $$

The function $\lambda_{\partial X}$ depends on the choice of compactification, but $\frac{\lambda_{\partial X}}{\lambda^{\prime}_{\partial X}}$ is bounded from above and below for any two compactifications.

#### Proposition 4.3.

Let $X$ be a quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ . Let $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ and let $(\varepsilon_{n})$ be a sequence of reals. Then an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ exists on $X$ if and only if $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})$ is uniformly bounded from above.

#### Proof.

Pick any projective compactification $\overline{X}$ of $X$ and let $\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ be a finite affine open cover of $\overline{X}$ . Let $Y=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{k}U_{i}$ be the disjoint union of the $U_{i}$ and let $\pi:Y\to\overline{X}$ be the natural projection. Then each $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ lifts to an $R_{n}$ -point of $\overline{X}$ and hence to an $R_{n}$ -point $\tilde{x}_{n}$ of $Y$ . We thus obtain a $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ -point $\tilde{x}$ of $Y$ which is an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(\tilde{x}_{n})$ , and so $\pi(\tilde{x})$ is an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ . Our proposition is then equivalent to verifying whether $\tilde{x}$ lies on $\pi^{-1}(X)$ .

Since $Y$ is affine, we may let $Y\simeq\mathbb{C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}]/I$ for some ideal $I$ . Then each $\tilde{x}_{n}$ has affine coordinates $a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}$ with $|a_{n,i}|\leq 1$ as it is an $R_{n}$ -point. Let $f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in\cal{O}(Y)$ be regular functions that cut out $Y\setminus\pi^{-1}(X)$ . Then we have

$$ \lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})=\lambda_{Y\setminus\pi^{-1}(X)}(\tilde{x}_{n})=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}-\log|f_{i}(\tilde{x}_{n})| $$

where the first equality follows from $\pi^{-1}(\partial X)=\pi^{-1}(\overline{X}\setminus X)=Y\setminus\pi^{-1}(X)$ and the second from (23). The affine coordinates of our $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point $\tilde{x}$ is given by $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})$ where each $a_{i}=(a_{n,i})$ . We wish to check whether our $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point lies on $\pi^{-1}(X)$ . This is equivalent to checking whether the pullback of the affine opens $D(f_{i})$ by $\tilde{x}$ cover $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ , which is equivalent to checking if

$$ J=(f_{1}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}),\ldots,f_{m}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})) $$

generate the unit ideal in $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ as $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ is reduced.

Now, an element $b=(b_{n})$ in $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ is in $(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})^{\times}$ if and only if $(|b_{n}|^{-1})^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ is uniformly bounded from above [43, Remark 3.7]. Hence if $J$ generates the unit ideal, then there exists $c_{i}$ with $c_{i}=(c_{n,i})^{\infty}_{n=1}$ with

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}f_{i}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})\in(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})^{\times}. $$

As $|c_{i,n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ is bounded from above as $n$ varies, (24) implies that

$$ \max_{1\leq i\leq m}|f_{i}(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N})|^{\varepsilon_{n}} $$

is uniformly bounded away from $0$ and so $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})$ is uniformly bounded from above. Conversely suppose that $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})\leq C$ for some $C>0$ . For each $n$ , let $i_{n}$ be an index such that

$$ -\log|f_{i_{n}}(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N})|=\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n}). $$

We define $c_{i}\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ as $c_{i}=(c_{1,i},\ldots,c_{n,j},\ldots)$ where $c_{n,j}=1$ if $i_{n}=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Then

$$ \left|\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}f_{i}(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N})\right|^{\varepsilon_{n}}=e^{-\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})\varepsilon_{n}} $$

and hence the left-hand side is uniformly bounded away from $0$ as $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})$ is uniformly bounded from above. Thus $\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{i}f_{i}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})\in(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})^{\times}$ and so our $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point lies in $X$ as desired. ∎

Hence if $\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})>0$ for all $n$ , then $\varepsilon_{n}=(\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n}))^{-1}$ is the smallest rescaling parameter (up to commensurability) that we can degenerate so that our $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point still lies on $X$ . Following Favre–Gong’s suggestion, we will call this the fundamental rescaling parameter.

#### Definition 4.2.

We will call such a sequence $(\varepsilon_{n})$ a fundamental rescaling parameter for the sequence $(x_{n})$ . Any two fundamental rescaling parameters have their ratios uniformly bounded from above or below.

In principle, we are free to pick any sequence that is much smaller than $(\varepsilon_{n})$ , but it will turn out that the fundamental rescaling parameter will be the more useful sequence, based on Proposition 4.5.

Recall that the Berkovich spectrum of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ is in bijection with the set of ultrafilters $\omega$ on $\mathbb{N}$ [12, Proposition 1.2.3], where the bijection [43, Theorem 3.8] sends

$$ \omega\mapsto\left((a_{n})\mapsto\lim_{\omega}|a_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}\right). $$

As $|a_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ is bounded from above, this sequence lies in a compact interval and hence its $\omega$ -limit exists as a real number. For non-principal ultrafilters, we will let $|\cdot|_{\omega}$ denote the norm associated to $\omega$ . There is an associated maximal ideal $\ker(\omega)=\{a\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\mid|a|_{\omega}=0\}$ and the quotient $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}/\ker(\omega)$ gives a residue field $\cal{H}(\omega)$ which is complete with respect to $|\cdot|_{\omega}$ and algebraically closed.

Given an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ with $(\varepsilon_{n})$ being a fundamental rescaling parameter, we obtain an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $X$ and hence an $\cal{H}(\omega)$ point $x_{\omega}$ of $X$ . Let $\cal{R}(\omega)$ be the valuation ring of $\cal{H}(\omega)$ . One might ask whether it is possible to lift $x_{\omega}$ to an $\cal{R}(\omega)$ point of $X$ . This turns out to never be the case if each $x_{n}$ cannot be lifted to an $R_{n}$ -point, i.e., if $\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})>0$ for all $n$ . We first need the following basic proposition.

#### Proposition 4.4.

Let $X$ be a variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $x\in X(K)$ where $K$ is a complete non-archimedean field with $\mathbb{C}$ a trivially valued subfield and with valuation ring $R$ . Then $x$ lifts to an $R$ -point of $X$ if and only if $\lambda_{\partial X}(x)=0$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\overline{X}$ be a projective compactification and let $U_{i}$ be an affine cover. Since $\overline{X}$ is projective, $x$ lifts to an $R$ -point $\tilde{x}$ on $\overline{X}$ . Let $U_{i}$ be an affine chart containing this $R$ -point. Then on $U_{i}$ , $x$ has affine coordinates $\leq 1$ . If $f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in\cal{O}(U_{i})$ cut out $(\overline{X}\setminus X)\cap U_{i}$ , then $\tilde{x}\in X(R)$ if and only if $\tilde{x}$ has empty intersection with $\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}V(f_{i})$ . Since $R$ is a valuation ring, this is equivalent to saying at least one of the $f_{i}(x)$ is invertible, which is equivalent to

$$ \lambda_{\partial X}(x)=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}\{-\log|f_{i}(x)|\}=0 $$

as desired.∎

#### Proposition 4.5.

Let $X$ be a variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and $(K_{n})$ a sequence of complete non-archimedean fields with $\mathbb{C}\subseteq K_{n}$ trivially valued. Let $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ be a sequence of points. Assume that $\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})>0$ for all $n$ and let $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})^{-1}$ . Let $x$ be an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ and let $x_{\omega}$ be the induced $\cal{H}(\omega)$ -point on $X$ . Then $x_{\omega}$ does not lift to an $\cal{R}(\omega)$ -point on $X$ .

#### Proof.

Note that the degeneration $x$ of $(x_{n})$ exists by Proposition 4.3. The point $x_{\omega}$ lifts to an $\cal{R}(\omega)$ -point if and only if $\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{\omega})=0$ . As in the previous Proposition, we can let $U_{1},\ldots,U_{m}$ be an affine open cover of $\overline{X}$ . For each $x_{n}$ , there exists a $U_{i_{n}}$ such that the affine coordinates of $x_{n}$ satisfy $|\cdot|\leq 1$ by properness of $\overline{X}$ . Since there are only finitely many possibilities for $i_{n}$ , we can find a $j$ such that the set $E=\{n\mid i_{n}=j\}$ is $\omega$ -large.

Let $f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in\cal{O}(U_{j})$ cut out $U_{j}\cap(\overline{X}\setminus X)$ . Then for $n\in E$ , we know that

$$ \lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}-\log|f_{i}(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N})| $$

where the affine coordinates of $x_{n}$ in $U_{j}$ are $a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}$ . Clearly $x_{\omega}$ has absolute value $\leq 1$ in the coordinates of $U_{j}$ because $E$ is $\omega$ -large. Hence

$$ \lambda_{\partial X}(x_{\omega})=-\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\min_{1\leq i\leq m}-\log|f_{i}(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N})|=-\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})=1 $$

and so $x_{\omega}$ does not lift to an $\cal{R}(\omega)$ -point.∎

### 4.2. Application to Moduli of Abelian Varieties

We now apply the above construction to the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties. We would like to work with $\cal{A}_{g}$ directly, but since it is an algebraic stack and not a variety, we will instead work with $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ , the fine moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties of dimension $g$ with level $3$ structure. We will work over $\mathbb{C}$ , in which case $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ is a quasi-projective irreducible variety over $\mathbb{C}$ by [21, IV.6.8].

For an abelian variety $A/K$ where $K$ is a non-archimedean algebraically closed field, we say that $A$ has bad reduction if $A$ does not extend to an abelian scheme $\cal{A}$ over $R$ where $R$ is the valuation ring of $K$ . We first show that $\cal{A}_{g,3}$ is able to capture the notion of bad reduction.

#### Proposition 4.6.

Let $A/K$ be a principally polarized abelian variety of dimension $g$ , where $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ for a discrete valuation ring $R$ . Suppose that $A$ has good reduction. Then any $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ whose underlying abelian variety is $A$ extends to an $R$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ . Equivalently, if a $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ does not extend to $R$ , then its underlying abelian variety has bad reduction.

#### Proof.

The natural morphism

$$ \mathcal{A}_{g,3}\longrightarrow\mathcal{A}_{g} $$

is finite étale, hence proper. Therefore a $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ extends to an $R$ -point if and only if its image in $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ does. Thus it suffices to show that if $A$ has good reduction, then the $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ corresponding to $(A,\lambda)$ extends to $R$ .

By assumption, there exists an abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}/R$ whose generic fiber is $A$ . Extending the $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ amounts to extending the given principal polarization $\lambda$ on $A$ to a principal polarization on $\mathcal{A}$ .

By [52, Proposition 8.9.1], since $\mathcal{A}$ is of finite presentation and smooth over $R$ , there exists a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}$ -subalgebra $R^{\prime}\subseteq R$ with fraction field $K^{\prime}$ and an abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}/R^{\prime}$ whose base change to $R$ is $\mathcal{A}$ , and whose generic fiber $A^{\prime}/K^{\prime}$ pulls back to $A/K$ . Moreover, after replacing $R^{\prime}$ by its integral closure in $K^{\prime}$ , we may assume that $R^{\prime}$ is a normal domain and that the given principal polarization $\lambda$ descends to a polarization $\lambda^{\prime}$ on $A^{\prime}/K^{\prime}$ .

By the proof of [21, Theorem 1.9], the polarization $\lambda^{\prime}$ extends to a polarization $\lambda^{\prime}_{R^{\prime}}$ on $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}/R^{\prime}$ . Since the degree of a polarization is locally constant in families and the generic fiber is principally polarized, the extended polarization on $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}/R^{\prime}$ is again principal.

For $f:\mathrm{Spec}(R)\to\mathrm{Spec}(R^{\prime})$ , form the base changes

$$ \mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}(R^{\prime})}\operatorname{Spec}(R),\qquad\mathcal{A}^{\vee}=(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})^{\vee}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}(R^{\prime})}\operatorname{Spec}(R), $$

and let

$$ p:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\qquad q:\mathcal{A}\to\operatorname{Spec}(R), $$

be the projections associated to $\mathcal{A}$ . Consider the morphisms

$$ u_{1}:=\lambda^{\prime}_{R^{\prime}}\circ p:\mathcal{A}\to(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})^{\vee},\qquad u_{2}:=q:\mathcal{A}\to\operatorname{Spec}(R). $$

These satisfy the compatibility condition

$$ \pi^{\vee}\circ u_{1}=f\circ u_{2}, $$

where $\pi^{\vee}:(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})^{\vee}\to\operatorname{Spec}(R^{\prime})$ is the structure morphism. Therefore, by the universal property of $(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})^{\vee}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}(R^{\prime})}\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ , the pair $(u_{1},u_{2})$ determines a unique morphism $f^{*}\lambda^{\prime}:\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow\mathcal{A}^{\vee}$ . This is a polarization on $\mathcal{A}$ . Since the degree of a polarization is preserved under base change, the morphism $f^{*}\lambda^{\prime}$ is again principal, and it extends the given polarization on the generic fiber. Thus the $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ defined by $(A,\lambda)$ extends to an $R$ -point, and by properness so does the original $K$ -point of $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ . ∎

Let $X=\cal{A}_{g,3}$ and in what follows let $(A_{n})$ be a sequence of principally polarized abelian varieties over $K_{n}$ such that each $A_{n}$ has bad reduction. After choosing some level $3$ structure, we let $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ represent $A_{n}$ . Since $A_{n}$ has bad reduction, Proposition 4.6 tells us that $\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})>0$ . Let $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})^{-1}$ . By Proposition 4.3, an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ exists and we obtain a $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $X$ . Since $X$ is a fine moduli space, this corresponds to a principally polarized abelian scheme $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ over $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ . Furthermore by Propositions 4.4 and 4.6, if $\omega$ is some non-principal ultrafilter, the induced abelian variety $A_{\mathcal{H}(\omega)}$ over $\cal{H}(\omega)$ has bad reduction.

We now define the $\omega$ -limit of a sequence of points $x_{n}\in A_{n}(K_{n})$ . In general, one can define it as the $\omega$ -limit of $(x_{n})$ inside the Berkovich analytification of $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . As this is a compact Hausdorff space, the $\omega$ -limit will exist. However, we give a simpler ad hoc definition that is enough for our applications.

We first put ourselves in a situation where we have an embedding of $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ into projective space $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . Choose an affine open subset $U\subseteq X$ and a closed immersion of $U$ -schemes $\iota_{U}:\mathcal{A}_{U}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ for the universal abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}_{U}\to U$ . (This is possible after shrinking $U$ , since $\mathcal{A}_{U}\to U$ is a projective morphism.) Suppose that each point $x_{n}$ lies in $U$ , and that there is some constant $c>0$ such that $\lambda_{\partial U}(x_{n})\leq c\,\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})$ for all $n$ . We claim that the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ constructed above yields an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $U$ , i.e., a morphism $\phi:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow U$ . Indeed, since each $x_{n}$ lies in $U$ , we may view $(x_{n})$ as a sequence of $U(K_{n})$ -points. By assumption there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $\lambda_{\partial U}(x_{n})\leq c\,\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})$ for all $n$ . Recall that we have chosen $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})^{-1}$ , so that $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})=1$ . Hence

$$ \varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial U}(x_{n})\leq c\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})=c $$

and the sequence $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial U}(x_{n})$ is uniformly bounded from above. Since $U$ is quasi-projective, Proposition 4.3 applied with $X=U$ implies that $(x_{n})$ admits an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration with values in $U$ . Thus the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration constructed above gives a morphism $\phi:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow U.$

Pulling back the universal abelian scheme on $U$ along $\phi$ gives an abelian scheme

$$ A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}:=\mathcal{A}_{U}\times_{U}\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}. $$

Since closed immersions are stable under base change, the base change of $\iota_{U}$ along $\phi$ is a closed immersion

$$ \iota_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}:A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}=\mathcal{A}_{U}\times_{U}\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}\times_{U}\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\simeq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}. $$

Thus we obtain an embedding $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ .

We now turn to a general description of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -points of $\mathbb{P}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . Note that an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ corresponds to $[a_{0}:\cdots:a_{N}]$ , where each $a_{i}\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ and $(a_{0},\ldots,a_{N})$ generates the unit ideal of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ . These are identified up to scalar multiplication by an element of $(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})^{\times}$ .

#### Proposition 4.7.

Let $P_{n}=[a_{n,0}:\cdots:a_{n,N}]$ be a point of $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{K_{n}}$ , where we normalize the $a_{n,i}$ so that $\max\{|a_{n,i}|\}=1$ . If we let $a_{i}=(a_{n,i})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , then $[a_{0}:\cdots:a_{N}]$ defines an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point on $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ that is independent of our choice of lifts of $P_{n}$ satisfying $\max\{|a_{n,i}|\}=1$ .

#### Proof.

Since $|a_{n,i}|\leq 1$ for all $n,i$ , each $a_{i}$ lies in $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ . For each $n$ , choose an index $i_{n}$ with $|a_{n,i_{n}}|=1$ . Define $c_{i}=(c_{n,i})_{n=1}^{\infty}\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ by $c_{n,i}=1$ if $i=i_{n}$ and $0$ otherwise. Then

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{N}c_{n,i}a_{n,i}=a_{n,i_{n}}, $$

so $\left|\sum_{i}c_{n,i}a_{n,i}\right|=1$ for every $n$ . Thus the element

$$ u:=\sum_{i=0}^{N}c_{i}a_{i}\in\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon} $$

satisfies $|u_{n}|=1$ for all $n$ , and therefore $u\in(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})^{\times}$ . Hence $(a_{0},\ldots,a_{N})$ generates the unit ideal in $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ , and so defines a point of $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ .

If $(a_{n,i}^{\prime})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is another choice of homogeneous coordinates with $\max_{i}|a_{n,i}^{\prime}|=1$ , then for each $n$ the two tuples differ by a scalar $\lambda_{n}\in K_{n}^{\times}$ with $|\lambda_{n}|=1$ . Hence $\lambda=(\lambda_{n})\in(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})^{\times}$ , and $a_{i}^{\prime}=\lambda a_{i}$ . Therefore $[a_{0}^{\prime}:\cdots:a_{N}^{\prime}]=[a_{0}:\cdots:a_{N}]$ in $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})$ .∎

Hence given $x_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{N}(K_{n})$ , we obtain a well-defined $x\in\mathbb{P}^{N}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})$ , which we call the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ . Note that this is the unique section $x:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ that induces $x_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}_{K_{n}}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , where uniqueness follows from Proposition 4.1. We claim that if the $x_{n}$ are chosen to be in $A_{n}(K_{n})$ , then $x\in A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})$ .

#### Proposition 4.8.

Let $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ be the closed subscheme obtained by base change from the projective embedding $A_{U}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ as described above. Suppose that for each $n$ , the point $x_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{N}(K_{n})$ lies in $A_{n}(K_{n})$ . Let $x:\operatorname{Spec}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})\to\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ be the $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $\mathbb{P}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}^{N}$ induced by the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of the sequence $(x_{n})$ , obtained via Proposition 4.7. Then $x$ factors through $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ ; equivalently, $x\in A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $I\subseteq\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}[T_{0},\ldots,T_{N}]$ be the homogeneous ideal defining the closed subscheme $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . Choose homogeneous coordinates

$$ [a_{0}:\cdots:a_{N}]\in\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}) $$

representing the morphism $x:\operatorname{Spec}(\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon})\to\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . Then $x$ factors through $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ if and only if

$$ f(a_{0},\ldots,a_{N})=0\quad\text{in }\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon} $$

for every homogeneous polynomial $f\in I$ .

For each $n$ , the specialization map $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ sends $a_{i}$ to the corresponding coordinate $a_{n,i}$ of $x_{n}$ , and the specialization of $x$ is $x_{n}$ . Since $x_{n}$ lies in $A_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{K_{n}}$ , we have

$$ f_{n}(a_{n,0},\ldots,a_{n,N})=0\quad\text{in }K_{n} $$

for every generator $f=(f_{n})\in I$ and every $n$ , where $f_{n}\in K_{n}[T_{0},\ldots,T_{N}]$ denotes the specialization of $f$ . Hence

$$ f(a_{0},\ldots,a_{N})=(f_{n}(a_{n,0},\ldots,a_{n,N}))_{n=1}^{\infty}=(0)_{n=1}^{\infty}=0 $$

as an element of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ .

Thus every polynomial in $I$ vanishes on $(a_{0},\ldots,a_{N})$ , so $x$ annihilates the defining ideal of $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . It follows that $x$ factors through the closed immersion $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ .∎

Hence for any ultrafilter $\omega$ , we obtain a well-defined point $x_{\omega}\in A_{\omega}(\mathcal{H}(\omega))$ . We shall call $x_{\omega}$ the $\omega$ -limit of the sequence $(x_{n})$ . Observe that if $x:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ is the section arising from the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ , then the point $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{H}(\omega)\to A_{\omega}$ given by the base change of $x$ along $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ equals $x_{\omega}$ .

The main property that the $\omega$ -limit satisfies is the following. For any homogeneous degree $d$ polynomial $F$ on $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ with $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -coefficients, we may define a function on $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\cal{H}(\omega)}$ by

$$ \psi_{F}=\frac{|F_{\omega}(x_{0},\ldots,x_{N})|_{\omega}}{\max\{|x_{0}|_{\omega},\ldots,|x_{N}|_{\omega}\}^{d}}, $$

where $F_{\omega}$ is the induced homogeneous degree $d$ polynomial over $\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ and $(x_{0},\ldots,x_{N})$ is any homogeneous lift of our point in $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\cal{H}(\omega)}$ . Let $F_{n}$ be degree $d$ polynomial on $K_{n}$ induced by $F$ , and let $\psi_{F_{n}}$ be the corresponding function on $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{K_{n}}$ . Then

$$ \psi_{F}(x_{\omega})=\lim_{\omega}\psi_{F_{n}}(x_{n})^{\varepsilon_{n}}\implies\log\psi_{F}(x_{\omega})=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\log\psi_{F_{n}}(x_{n}) $$

where we take the $\omega$ -limit on the extended real line $[-\infty,\infty]$ .

We now recall the relevant compactification of $X=\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ . Faltings–Chai [21] constructed, given some choice of auxiliary data, a compactification $\overline{X}=\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ of $X$ , which is a proper algebraic stack over $\mathbb{C}$ . Different choices of this auxiliary data generally give rise to non-isomorphic compactifications. Moreover, there exist choices of compactification for which $\overline{X}$ is in fact a projective algebraic variety over $\mathbb{C}$ [21, Theorem 5.8]. We will let $\overline{X}=\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ denote such a choice. The compactification $\overline{X}$ carries a universal semiabelian variety $G\to\overline{X}$ extending the universal abelian variety over $X$ [21, Theorem IV.6.7].

For each abelian variety $A_{n}/K_{n}$ with associated point $x_{n}\in X(K_{n})$ , and $R_{n}$ the valuation ring of $K_{n}$ , the properness of the compactification $\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ guarantees that $x_{n}$ extends to a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}(R_{n})\to\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ , and pulling back the universal semiabelian scheme $G\to\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ along this morphism yields a semiabelian scheme $G_{n}/R_{n}$ . Now let $x_{n}\in A_{n}(K_{n})$ be a sequence of points such that each $x_{n}$ lifts to a point in $G_{n}(R_{n})$ . We will show that in this case, the resulting $\omega$ -limit point $x_{\omega}\in A_{\omega}(\mathcal{H}(\omega))$ extends to an $\mathcal{R}(\omega)$ -point of the semiabelian model $G_{\omega}$ , where $\mathcal{R}(\omega)$ is the valuation ring of $\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ , and $G_{\omega}$ is defined by the base change

$$ G_{\omega}:=G\times_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}}\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{R}(\omega)). $$

We do so in order to further show the following fact about the retraction of $x_{\omega}$ (still assuming that $x_{n}$ lifts to an $R_{n}$ -point of $G_{n}$ for all $n$ ). Since $A_{\omega}$ has bad reduction, it has a canonical skeleton $S(A_{\omega})$ , which is isomorphic to a real torus $\mathbb{R}^{k}/\Lambda$ , and a retraction map $r:A_{\omega}^{\operatorname{an}}\to S(A_{\omega})$ . We will prove that $r(x_{\omega})=0$ . By Proposition 3.4, it suffices to show that $x_{\omega}$ lifts to an $R(\omega)$ -point of $G_{\omega}$ .

To do this, set

$$ \mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}:=\{(x_{n})\in\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}K_{n}\mid|x_{n}|\leq 1\}. $$

Then $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ is a subring of $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ , and for every ultrafilter $\omega$ the induced homomorphism $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ restricts to a homomorphism $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow\mathcal{R}(\omega)$ , since elements of $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ have $\omega$ -norm $\leq 1$ . We will construct a semiabelian scheme $\mathcal{G}/\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ whose base change to $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ is $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ , and whose base change to $\mathcal{R}(\omega)$ is $G_{\omega}$ . We begin with the following proposition.

#### Proposition 4.9.

Let $(x_{n})\in\mathcal{A}_{g,3}(K_{n})$ be a sequence of points and let $(\varepsilon_{n})$ be a fundamental rescaling parameter. If $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ is the abelian scheme corresponding to our $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration, then there exists a semiabelian scheme $G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$ whose base change to $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ is $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $X=\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ and let $(x_{n})$ be the given sequence. By assumption, $(\varepsilon_{n})$ is a fundamental rescaling parameter, so $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})^{-1}$ , and therefore $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}(x_{n})=1$ is uniformly bounded. Thus by Proposition 4.3, the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ exists on $X$ itself; in other words, the degeneration defines a morphism $x:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow X\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ . By Remark 4.1, this morphism extends to a morphism $\tilde{x}:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ . Let $G\longrightarrow\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ denote the universal semiabelian scheme on the Faltings–Chai compactification. Define

$$ G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}:=G\times_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}, $$

which is a semiabelian scheme over $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ . Base changing along $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ gives

$$ G_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}:=G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\times_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}=G\times_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}. $$

Since $x$ factors through the open subvariety $X=\mathcal{A}_{g,3}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{A}}_{g,3}$ , and since the restriction of $G$ to $X$ is the universal abelian scheme, it follows that $G_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ is obtained by pulling back the universal abelian scheme along $x$ . By definition, this pullback is precisely the degeneration family $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . Hence there is a canonical isomorphism $G_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\cong A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ . ∎

Now suppose we have a sequence of points $(x_{n})$ of $A_{n}(K_{n})$ such that $x_{n}$ lifts to an $R_{n}$ -point of $G_{n}$ for all $n$ . We wish to show that we may glue these points together to obtain a $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ -section of $G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$

#### Proposition 4.10.

Let $G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$ be as in Proposition 4.9. There exists a section $x:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\to G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$ such that for each $n$ , the base change of $x$ along the natural map $\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ agrees with the given morphism $x_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to G_{n}$ .

#### Proof.

For each $n$ , the given point $x_{n}\in G_{n}(R_{n})$ corresponds to a morphism

$$ x_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\longrightarrow G_{n}=G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}. $$

Equivalently, by composing with the projection $G_{n}\to G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$ , we may view $x_{n}$ as a morphism

$$ x_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\longrightarrow G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}} $$

whose composition with $G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ is induced by the natural projection $\pi_{n}:\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\to R_{n}$ .

Since $G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$ is a scheme of finite type over $\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ , it admits a finite affine open cover $\{W_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}$ with each $W_{i}=\operatorname{Spec}C_{i}$ . Because each $R_{n}$ is a valuation ring, the image of $\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}$ under $x_{n}$ must be contained in a single affine open $W_{i_{n}}$ . On each $W_{i_{n}}=\operatorname{Spec}(C_{i_{n}})$ , the morphism $x_{n}$ is given by a ring homomorphism $C_{i_{n}}\to R_{n}$ . Taking these homomorphisms coordinatewise defines a ring homomorphism

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}\to\prod_{n}R_{n}=\mathscr{B^{\varepsilon}} $$

as follows. For each $n$ , we first project $\prod_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}$ down to $C_{i_{n}}$ and then compose with $x_{n}:C_{i_{n}}\to R_{n}$ to obtain a morphism $\prod_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}\to R_{n}$ . Taking the product gives us a ring morphism $\prod_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}\to\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ .

Thus we obtain a $\mathscr{B^{\varepsilon}}$ -point of $\prod_{i=1}^{m}W_{i}$ which naturally defines a $\mathscr{B^{\varepsilon}}$ -point $x:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\to G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}$ . By construction, for each $n$ the base change of $x$ along $\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}$ induces the original morphism $x_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to G_{n}$ , since both are defined by the same coordinate ring homomorphism $\Gamma(W_{i_{n}},\mathcal{O})\to R_{n}$ .∎

Recall that the $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration of $(x_{n})$ determines a section

$$ x_{\mathscr{A}}:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}. $$

For any ultrafilter $\omega$ , base change along $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{H}(\omega)\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ defines a point

$$ x_{\omega}\in A_{\omega}(\mathcal{H}(\omega)),\qquad A_{\omega}:=A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{H}(\omega), $$

which by definition is the $\omega$ -limit of the sequence $(x_{n})$ . On the other hand, by Proposition 4.10 (note that we are making the standing assumption that $x_{n}$ lifts to an $R_{n}$ -point of $G_{n}$ for all $n$ ), there exists a section

$$ x_{\mathscr{B}}:\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}} $$

whose base change to $\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}$ recovers each $x_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to G_{n}$ . Base changing this section along

$$ \operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{R}(\omega)\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon} $$

produces a section

$$ x_{\omega}^{G}\in G_{\omega}(\mathcal{R}(\omega)),\qquad G_{\omega}:=G_{\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{B}^{\varepsilon}}\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{R}(\omega). $$

Passing to the generic fiber identifies the induced $\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ -point of $G_{\omega}$ with a point of

$$ A_{\omega}=G_{\omega}\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{R}(\omega)}\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{H}(\omega), $$

using the canonical identification $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\cong G_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ from Proposition 4.9. By construction, this $\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ -point of $A_{\omega}$ , induced from $x_{\omega}^{G}$ , and the $\omega$ -limit point $x_{\omega}$ defined via $x_{\mathscr{A}}$ both specialize to the same $x_{n}$ for every $n$ . Since $\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ is the ultraproduct residue field of the $K_{n}$ with respect to $\omega$ , so that a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{H}(\omega)\to A_{\omega}$ is uniquely determined by its compositions with the projections to the $A_{n}$ , it follows that these two $\mathcal{H}(\omega)$ -points coincide, and hence that the $\omega$ -limit point $x_{\omega}\in A_{\omega}(\mathcal{H}(\omega))$ lifts to an $\mathcal{R}(\omega)$ -point of $G_{\omega}$ (namely $x_{\omega}^{G}$ ). By Proposition 3.4, this implies that the retraction of $x_{\omega}$ to the skeleton vanishes.

#### Corollary 4.11.

Assume each $x_{n}$ lifts to an $R_{n}$ -point of $G_{n}$ . Then the $\omega$ -limit $x_{\omega}$ lifts to an $\cal{R}(\omega)$ -point of $G_{\omega}$ . In particular, $r(x_{\omega})=0$ in $S(A_{\omega})$ .

## 5. Uniform Positivity for Arakelov-Green’s Functions

We now combine the results in Sections 3.2 and 4.2 to obtain a uniform positive lower bound on $g_{\cal{B}_{n}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)})$ under suitable hypotheses. This will be a key input in obtaining uniform bounds on the number of small points on abelian varieties.

Let $U\subseteq\cal{A}_{g,3}$ be an open irreducible affine chart such that for the universal abelian scheme $A_{U}$ on $U$ , we have an embedding $A_{U}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ and furthermore, for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the multiplication by $[n]$ morphism on $A_{U}$ extends to a morphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ of degree $d=n^{2}$ . Fixing a homogeneous lift $F=(F_{0},\ldots,F_{N})$ of $f$ , this means that the homogeneous resultant $\operatorname{Res}(F)$ is an invertible element of $\mathcal{O}(U)$ .

This allows us to perform the first author’s construction of good bases and dynamical Arakelov-Green’s functions in a relative setting over $U$ . If we let $F^{k}=(F^{(k)}_{0},\ldots,F^{(k)}_{N})$ , then [64, Lemma 4] that any homogeneous polynomial $G$ with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}(U)$ of degree at least $(N+1)(d^{k}-1)+1$ can be written as

$$ G=\sum P_{i}F^{(k)}_{i} $$

for appropriate homogeneous polynomials $P_{i}$ over $\mathcal{O}(U)$ . In particular if we let $\cal{G}$ be the collection of polynomials of the form $(F_{i}^{(k)})^{j}$ for $1\leq j\leq d$ , then the set

$$ \cal{F}=\bigcup_{j=\lfloor t_{1}\rfloor}^{\lfloor t_{2}\rfloor}\{\eta_{i}G_{i}\mid G_{i}\in\cal{G}^{j}\text{ and }\eta_{i}\text{ monomial of degree }\leq d(N+1)\} $$

is a spanning set for the space of degree $n$ polynomials, where we may take $t_{1},t_{2}=O(\log n)$ .

Let $L$ be the ample line bundle on $\cal{A}_{U}$ corresponding to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ . By replacing $L$ by $L^{4}$ , we know that for each $s\in U$ , $L$ gives a projectively normal embedding of $\cal{A}_{s}$ into $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{s}$ [68] and hence we have a surjection $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}_{U}^{N},\mathcal{O}(n))\to H^{0}(\cal{A}_{U},L^{n})$ For any $K$ -point of $U$ , pulling back via the $K$ -point gives us an embedding $A_{K}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}_{K}$ and also a surjection

$$ H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N}_{K},\mathcal{O}(n))\to H^{0}(A_{K},L^{n}). $$

By [88, Proposition 6.13], we have $\dim H^{0}(A_{K},L^{n})=c(n)$ for some constant $c(n)$ that is independent of our $K$ -point on $U$ , as $\pi_{*}(L^{n})$ is a locally free sheaf on $U$ .

As the multiplication by $n$ map extends to a morphism $f$ on $\mathbb{P}^{N}_{U}$ and we have fixed a homogeneous lift $F:\mathbb{A}_{U}^{N+1}\to\mathbb{A}_{U}^{N+1}$ , pulling back by the $K$ -point gives us a consistent choice of a polarized dynamical system $(A_{K},f_{K})$ and homogeneous lift $F_{K}$ . We define the notion of good basis pointwise on $\cal{A}_{U}$ , where a good basis $\cal{B}_{n}$ for $A_{K}$ is defined as in Definition 3.2 with respect to the lift $F_{K}$ of $f_{K}$ . Observe that any good basis is the pullback of a subset of sections of $\cal{F}$ by the $K$ -point.

Now assume that $(K,|\cdot|)$ is a complete valued field. Given any set of sections $\cal{B}_{n}\subseteq H^{0}(A_{K},L_{K}^{n})$ of size $c(n)$ , recall from §3 that we may define an Arakelov-Green’s function $g_{\cal{B}_{n}}:A_{K}^{c(n)}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ by setting

$$ g_{\cal{B}_{n}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)})=\frac{1}{c(n)}\sum_{i=1}^{c(n)}\widehat{H}_{F_{k}}(\tilde{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{n\cdot c(n)}\log\left|\det\big((\eta_{j}(\tilde{x}_{i}))_{\eta\in\cal{B}}\big)\right|+r(F_{K}) $$

where $(f_{K},F_{K})$ is the pullback of $(f,F)$ by $\operatorname{Spec}K\to U$ and

$$ r(F_{K})=\frac{1}{d^{N}(N+1)(d-1)}\log|\operatorname{Res}(F_{K})|^{-1}. $$

Here, the $\tilde{x}_{i}$ are lifts of $x_{i}$ to $\mathbb{A}^{N+1}(K)$ . Recall that $g_{\cal{B},n}$ is independent of the choice of lifts of the $x_{i}$ . Note that this definition makes sense even if $\cal{B}_{n}$ is not a basis, in which case we have $g_{\cal{B},n}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(n)})=+\infty$ for all $x_{i}$ .

We first prove the following basic continuity property. Fix a sequence $(\varepsilon_{n})$ of positive real numbers and assume that we have an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $U$ . Then pulling back $A_{U}/U$ along $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}\to U$ , we obtain an abelian scheme $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ along with an embedding $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ and a morphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ extending $[n]$ on $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ with homogeneous lift $F$ . Then for a set of sections $\cal{B}_{k}\subseteq H^{0}(\mathbb{P}_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}^{N},\mathcal{O}(k))$ of size $c(k)$ , pulling back via $K_{n}\to\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ and $\cal{H}(\omega)\to\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ , we get induced sets of sections $\cal{B}_{k,n}$ and $\cal{B}_{k,\omega}$ for $H^{0}(A_{n},L^{k}_{n})$ and $H^{0}(A_{\omega},L_{\omega}^{k})$ respectively. We thus get Arakelov-Green’s functions $g_{\cal{B}_{k},n}$ and $g_{\cal{B}_{k},\omega}$ .

#### Proposition 5.1.

Let $A_{\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}}$ be the abelian scheme constructed above and for each $n$ , let $x_{n,1},\ldots,x_{n,c(k)}$ be points on $A_{n}(K_{n})$ . Let $x_{i}$ be the $\omega$ -limit of $(x_{1,i},x_{2,i},\ldots)$ for any non-principal ultrafilter $\omega$ . Then we have

$$ \lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}g_{\cal{B}_{k},n}(x_{n,1},\ldots,x_{n,c(k)})=g_{\cal{B}_{k},\omega}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c(k)}), $$

where we take the $\omega$ -limit in the extended reals $[-\infty,\infty]$ .

#### Proof.

By assumption, the sequence $(f_{n})$ of rational maps admits an $(\varepsilon_{n})$ -degeneration in $\operatorname{Rat}^{N}_{d}$ . Equivalently, the associated points of $\operatorname{Rat}^{N}_{d}(K_{n})$ define an $\mathscr{A}^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $\operatorname{Rat}^{N}_{d}$ . Under the standard compactification $\operatorname{Rat}^{N}_{d}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N^{\prime}}$ with boundary $\{\operatorname{Res}=0\}$ , Proposition 4.3 implies that the sequence $(\varepsilon_{n}\log|\operatorname{Res}(f_{n})|^{-1})$ is uniformly bounded from above.

Now choose lifts $F_{n}$ of $f_{n}$ such that $||F_{n}||_{n}=1$ . Then $F_{\omega}=\lim_{\omega}F_{n}$ is a lift of $f_{\omega}$ satisfying $||F_{\omega}||_{\omega}=1$ . We clearly have

$$ \lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}r(F_{n})=r(F_{\omega}) $$

and

$$ \lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\log|\det(\eta_{j}(\tilde{x}_{i,n}))_{\eta\in\cal{B}}|_{n}=\log|\det(\eta_{j}(\tilde{x}))_{\eta\in\cal{B}}|_{\omega} $$

by direct computation. It suffices to show that

$$ \widehat{H}_{F_{\omega}}(\tilde{x})=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\widehat{H}_{F_{n}}(\tilde{x}_{n}). $$

By definition, for all $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ we have

$$ \widehat{H}_{F_{\omega}}=\varepsilon_{\omega}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log||F_{\omega}^{n}||_{n} $$

where we set $\varepsilon_{\omega}=1$ for $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathbb{N}$ . We have the telescoping sum

$$ \varepsilon_{\omega}\left(\widehat{H}_{F_{\omega}}(\tilde{x}_{\omega})-\frac{1}{d^{k}}\log|F_{\omega}^{(k)}(\tilde{x}_{\omega})|_{\omega}\right) $$

$$ =\varepsilon_{\omega}\sum_{n\geq k}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\left(\frac{1}{d}\log|F_{\omega}^{({n+1})}(\tilde{x}_{\omega})|_{\omega}-\log|F_{\omega}^{n}(\tilde{x}_{\omega})|_{\omega}\right), $$

and by [64, Lemma5], we may bound

$$ \varepsilon_{\omega}\left|\frac{1}{d}\log|F^{({n+1})}(\tilde{x}_{\omega})|_{\omega}-\log|F^{n}(\tilde{x}_{\omega})|_{\omega}\right| $$

in terms of $\varepsilon_{\omega}|\operatorname{Res}(f)|_{\omega}^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon_{\omega}||F||_{\omega}$ . As $\varepsilon_{\omega}|\operatorname{Res}(f)|^{-1}_{\omega}$ is uniformly bounded and $||F||_{\omega}=1$ , there exists a uniform constant $C>0$ such that
