$$ (\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}\times B)\times_{B}\eta\;\cong\;\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{K},\quad K=\mathbb{C}(B). $$

Restricting $\tilde{A}$ to this fiber yields $\tilde{A}_{\eta}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{K}$ . Since $f$ is a unit in $K^{\times}$ , the equations $fF_{i}=0$ cut out the same subscheme as $F_{i}=0$ , namely $A\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{K}$ . As $B$ has degree $M^{\prime}+c_{2}M$ in $\mathbb{P}^{m}$ , the subvariety $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}\times B\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}\times\mathbb{P}^{m}$ has bidegree $(1,M^{\prime}+c_{2}M)$ . Using the Segre embedding to embed $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}\times\mathbb{P}^{m}$ into projective space $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ for $N=(N_{1}+1)(m+1)-1$ completes the proof.∎

Now given any $x\in A(K)$ with $\widehat{h}_{A}(x)\leq\delta$ , we obtain an extension $\tilde{x}:B\to\tilde{A}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}$ where we use the embedding from Proposition 9.6. We wish to bound the degree of the image $\tilde{x}(B)$ .

#### Proposition 9.7.

There exists a constant $C_{2}>0$ , depending only on $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ , such that the degree of $\tilde{x}(B)$ in $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ is at most $C_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

We first bound the degree of $\tilde{x}(B)$ in $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{\mathbb{C}}\times B$ , where we use the line bundle $p_{1}^{*}\mathcal{O}(1)$ for $\mathcal{O}(1)$ on $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{\mathbb{C}}$ . Here, $p_{1}$ is the projection to the first coordinate. In this case, this is exactly the standard Weil height $h(x)$ when $x$ is viewed as a point of $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}(K)$ . Recall from the discussion before Proposition 9.4 that we have an embedding $A\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}_{K}^{N_{1}}$ and an endomorphism $F:\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{K}\to\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}_{K}$ of degree $n_{1}^{2}$ that extends multiplication-by- $[n_{1}]$ . By [64, Lemma 6], there exists a $c>0$ , depending only on $N_{1}$ and $n_{1}$ , such that

$$ |\widehat{h}_{F}(x)-h(x)|\leq ch(F) $$

for all $x\in\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}(K)$ . Since $\widehat{h}_{F}(x)$ is a multiple of $\widehat{h}_{A}(x)$ that depends only on $g$ , it follows that $\widehat{h}_{F}(x)$ is bounded solely in terms of $g$ and $\delta$ . By Proposition 9.3, we have $h(F)\leq c_{1}h_{\omega}(A)$ and so there is a constant $c^{\prime}>0$ depending only on $g$ and $\delta$ for which $h(x)\leq c^{\prime}(h_{\omega}(A)+1)$ .

Now the embedding $B\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{m}$ is induced by a line bundle $L$ on $B$ of degree at most $M^{\prime}+c_{2}M$ . Under the Segre embedding for $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}\times\mathbb{P}^{m}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ induces some power of $L$ multiplied by some power of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for $\mathbb{P}^{N_{1}}$ on our curve $\tilde{x}(B)$ , where the powers can be bounded in terms of $N_{1}$ and $m$ . Thus the degree of $\tilde{x}(B)$ in $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ can be bounded in terms of only $M^{\prime}+c_{2}M,cc^{\prime}h_{\omega}(A),N_{1}$ and $m$ , all of which are bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ .∎

This finishes our first step. We proceed with the next step where we reduce our problem to bounding the number of irreducible components of the Hilbert scheme on $\tilde{A}$ .

For any positive integer $\beta$ , consider the Hom scheme $H_{\beta}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ that represents morphisms $\tilde{x}:B\to\tilde{A}$ satisfying the following two conditions:

- (i) The image curve $\tilde{x}(B)\subset\tilde{A}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{N}$ has degree at most $\beta$ ;

- (ii) The composition $\pi_{2}\circ\tilde{x}:B\to B$ is the identity map, so that $\tilde{x}$ is a section of the fibration $\pi_{2}:\tilde{A}\to B$ .

The $\operatorname{Hom}$ scheme $H_{\beta}$ is of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$ (see the discussion after Lemma 7.5 of [26]). Hence it has only finitely many irreducible components. As explained before, any point $x\in A(K)$ lifts to a section $\tilde{x}:B\to\tilde{A}$ , which by Proposition 9.7 has bounded degree. Hence for a suitable $\beta$ , this gives us an element of $H_{\beta}$ . Conversely, given a section $s:B\to\tilde{A}$ , we may take the generic fiber to obtain a $K$ -point of $A$ . The following rigidity phenomena reduces Theorem 9.1 to bounding the number of irreducible components of $H_{\beta}$ for a suitable $\beta$ .

#### Proposition 9.8.

Any two elements of $H_{\beta}(\mathbb{C})$ that lie on the same irreducible component correspond to the same equivalence class $x\in A(K)/\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)(\mathbb{C})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\tilde{x},\tilde{y}\in H_{\beta}(\mathbb{C})$ lie on the same irreducible component of dimension at least $1$ (the case of $0$ -dimensional components is trivial). Then there exists an irreducible curve $X\subseteq H_{\beta}$ containing both $\tilde{x}$ and $\tilde{y}$ . Since $H_{\beta}$ represents a Hom functor, the curve $X\subseteq H_{\beta}$ corresponds to a morphism

$$ \mathcal{P}:X\times B\to\tilde{A} $$

over $B$ , which defines a family of sections of $\tilde{A}\to B$ parametrized by $X$ . For each $t\in X(\mathbb{C})$ , the restriction $\mathcal{P}_{t}:=\mathcal{P}|_{\{t\}\times B}$ is a section $\tilde{x}_{t}:B\to\tilde{A}$ , and in particular $\mathcal{P}_{\tilde{x}}=\tilde{x}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\tilde{y}}=\tilde{y}$ .

Let $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}(B))$ denote the generic point of $B$ . To study the behavior of the family on the generic fiber, we form the fiber product

$$ (X\times B)\times_{B}\eta\cong X\times_{\mathbb{C}}\eta=:X_{K}, $$

where $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ . Pulling back $\mathcal{P}$ along this map yields a morphism

$$ \mathcal{P}_{K}:X_{K}\to\tilde{A}_{\eta}=A, $$

which we interpret as a $K$ -morphism $P:X_{K}\to A$ .

Let $\overline{X}$ be a smooth projective compactification of $X$ , and set $\overline{X}_{K}=\overline{X}\times_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Spec}(K)$ . Then $P$ extends to a morphism

$$ P:\overline{X}_{K}\to A. $$

Since $\overline{X}_{K}$ is a smooth proper curve over $K$ , after fixing some basepoint $x_{0}\in\overline{X}(\mathbb{C})$ , the morphism $P$ factors through its Albanese variety $\mathrm{Alb}(\overline{X}_{K})$ , which is an abelian variety over $K$ defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Let $\iota_{K}:\overline{X}_{K}\to\mathrm{Alb}(\overline{X})_{K}$ be our embedding sending $\iota_{K}(x_{0})$ to $0$ and $\eta:\mathrm{Alb}(\overline{X})_{K}\to A$ be the morphism so that $P=\iota_{K}\circ\eta$ . Then $\eta-P(x_{0})$ is a map of abelian varieties between $\mathrm{Alb}(\overline{X})_{K}$ and $A$ .

By the universal property of the trace

$$ \tau:\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)_{K}\to A, $$

there is a map of abelian varieties $f:\mathrm{Alb}(\overline{X}_{K})\to\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)$ so that $\eta-P(x_{0})=f\circ\tau$ . Hence $P=P(x_{0})+(f\circ\iota)_{K}$ and for any element $x\in\overline{X}$ . This implies that $P_{x}$ and $P_{y}$ agree as elements of $A(K)/\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)(\mathbb{C})$ .∎

With Propositions 9.7 and 9.8, it suffices to bound the number of irreducible components of $H_{C_{2}}$ for $C_{2}$ in Proposition 9.7. Consider the larger Hom scheme $H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ which consists of all morphisms $\tilde{x}:B\to\tilde{A}$ with $\tilde{x}(B)\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}$ having degree at most $C_{2}$ . We first state a preliminary lemma.

#### Proposition 9.9.

The number of irreducible components of $H_{C_{2}}$ is bounded above by the number of irreducible components of $H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\Phi:H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)$ denote the morphism of schemes given by post-composition with $\pi_{2}:\tilde{A}\to B$ . Then $H_{C_{2}}\subseteq H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ is the fiber $\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{B})$ , representing those morphisms $f:B\to\tilde{A}$ of degree at most $C_{2}$ such that $\pi_{2}\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{B}$ .

Case 1: $g(B)\geq 2$ . In this case, $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)$ is a union of $B(\mathbb{C})$ with a finite discrete scheme, since a smooth projective curve of genus $\geq 2$ admits only finitely many non-trivial morphisms to itself. In particular, the identity morphism $\mathrm{id}_{B}$ is an isolated point. The fiber $H_{C_{2}}=\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{B})$ is then clopen in $H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ , being the fiber over an isolated point. Since clopen subsets are always unions of connected components, it follows that $H_{C_{2}}$ is a union of connected components of $H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ , and in particular

$$ \#\{\text{irreducible components of }H_{C_{2}}\}\leq\#\{\text{irreducible components of }H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}\}. $$

Case 2: $g(B)=1$ . Fix a basepoint $x_{0}\in B(\mathbb{C})$ to identify $B$ with an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{C}$ . For each $x\in B(\mathbb{C})$ , let $\tau_{x}:B\to B$ denote the translation-by- $x$ automorphism. Define the subgroup

$$ T:=\{\tau_{x}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)\mid x\in B(\mathbb{C})\}, $$

which is isomorphic to $B$ as a group scheme. In particular, $T$ is an irreducible, clopen subset of $\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ . Since $\Phi$ is a morphism of schemes and $T\subseteq\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ is clopen, the preimage $\Phi^{-1}(T)\subseteq H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ is clopen as well, and hence a union of connected components. The identity morphism $\mathrm{id}_{B}\in T$ , so the fiber $H_{C_{2}}:=\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{id}_{B})$ lies in $\Phi^{-1}(T)$ .

Now define a morphism $\varphi:T\times H_{C_{2}}\to\Phi^{-1}(T)$ by $(\tau_{x},f)\mapsto f\circ\tau_{x}$ . This is well-defined because

$$ \Phi(f\circ\tau_{x})=\pi_{2}\circ f\circ\tau_{x}=(\pi_{2}\circ f)\circ\tau_{x}=\mathrm{id}_{B}\circ\tau_{x}=\tau_{x}. $$

We define the inverse morphism $\psi:\Phi^{-1}(T)\to T\times H_{C_{2}}$ by $\tilde{f}\mapsto(\pi_{2}\circ\tilde{f},\tilde{f}\circ(\pi_{2}\circ\tilde{f})^{-1})$ . Since $\pi_{2}\circ\tilde{f}\in T$ is invertible, this map is well-defined and inverse to $\varphi$ , giving an isomorphism $\Phi^{-1}(T)\cong T\times H_{C_{2}}$ .

As $T\cong B$ is irreducible, the irreducible components of $\Phi^{-1}(T)$ correspond bijectively to those of $H_{C_{2}}$ , and we conclude

$$ \displaystyle\#\{\text{irreducible components of }H_{C_{2}}\} \displaystyle=\#\{\text{irreducible components of }\Phi^{-1}(T)\} \displaystyle\leq\#\{\text{irreducible components of }H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}\}. $$

Case 3: $g(B)=0$ . In this case, $B\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , and the scheme $\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ is stratified by degree:

$$ \mathrm{Hom}(B,B)=\bigsqcup_{d\geq 0}\mathrm{Hom}_{d}(B,B). $$

The degree 1 component corresponds to $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^{1})\cong\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ , which we again denote by $T\subseteq\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ . This is a connected algebraic group, and a clopen subset of $\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ . As before, the preimage $\Phi^{-1}(T)\subseteq H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ is thus clopen, and hence a union of connected components. Define the morphism $\varphi:T\times H_{C_{2}}\to\Phi^{-1}(T)$ by $(\alpha,f)\mapsto f\circ\alpha$ , which is well-defined (i.e., does in fact map to $\Phi^{-1}(T)$ ) because

$$ \Phi(f\circ\alpha)=\pi_{2}\circ f\circ\alpha=(\pi_{2}\circ f)\circ\alpha=\mathrm{id}_{B}\circ\alpha=\alpha. $$

The inverse is given by $\psi:\Phi^{-1}(T)\to T\times H_{C_{2}}$ , $h\mapsto(\Phi(h),h\circ\Phi(h)^{-1})$ , and defines an isomorphism $\Phi^{-1}(T)\cong T\times H_{C_{2}}$ . Since $T\cong\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ is irreducible, we again obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\#\{\text{irreducible components of }H_{C_{2}}\} \displaystyle=\#\{\text{irreducible components of }\Phi^{-1}(T)\} \displaystyle\leq\#\{\text{irreducible components of }H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}\}. $$

∎

Next, we have an embedding $H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}\xhookrightarrow{}\operatorname{Hilb}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ , by sending $\tilde{x}:B\to\tilde{A}$ to its graph $\Gamma_{\tilde{x}}$ . In fact this embedding is an open immersion [92, Theorem 6.6] .

Furthermore there is a finite set of polynomials $\{Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{E}\}$ such that any $\tilde{x}\in H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ , the graph $\Gamma_{\tilde{x}}$ has Hilbert polynomial $Q_{i}$ for some $i$ . As the graph $\Gamma(\tilde{x})$ is isomorphic to $B$ , it is a smooth projective curve of genus $g(B)$ . Hence its Hilbert polynomial must be of degree one with constant coefficient $g(B)$ . Its leading coefficient is given by its degree and so the $Q_{i}$ ’s are of the form $it+g(B)$ , where we let $i$ vary from $1$ to $C_{2}$ .

Let $\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ be the components corresponding to the Hilbert polynomial $Q_{i}$ . Then $H^{\prime}_{C_{2}}$ embeds into $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{C_{2}}\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ as an open subscheme. By the Proposition 9.10 below, it suffices to now bound the number of irreducible components of each $\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ .

#### Proposition 9.10.

Let $X,Y$ be noetherian schemes and assume $Y$ is an open subscheme of $X$ . Then the number of irreducible components of $Y$ is bounded above by that of $X$ .

#### Proof.

Write $X=\bigcup_{i\in I}X_{i}$ for $\{X_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ the set of irreducible components of $X$ . Then $Y=\bigcup_{i\in I}(X_{i}\cap Y)$ . Each nonempty $X_{i}\cap Y$ is irreducible as $Y$ is a Zariski open in $X_{i}$ , and since $X_{i}$ is closed in $X$ , the intersection $X_{i}\cap Y$ is also closed in $Y$ and hence must be an irreducible component. Therefore the set of irreducible components of $Y$ consists exactly of those $X_{i}\cap Y$ which are nonempty, yielding our desired bound.∎

It now suffices to bound the number of irreducible components of each $\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ . To do this, we will use the work of Gotzmann. Recall that a coherent sheaf $F$ on $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ is $m$ -regular if and only if

$$ H^{i}(\mathbb{P}^{r},F(m-i))=0 $$

for every integer $i>0$ . The smallest such $m$ is the Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity of $F$ . Let $P$ be the Hilbert polynomial of a homogeneous ideal $I\subset k[x_{0},\ldots,x_{r}]$ . We define the Gotzmann number $\varphi(P)$ of $P$ as the infimum of all $m$ for which the ideal sheaf $I_{Z}$ is $m$ -regular for all closed subvarieties $Z\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{r}$ with Hilbert polynomial $P$ . We will let $\varphi(Z)$ be the Gotzmann number of the Hilbert polynomial of $I_{Z}$ . Note that

$$ \operatorname{Hilb}_{I_{Z}}(n)=\binom{n+r}{r}-\operatorname{Hilb}_{Z}(n). $$

We now state [70, Theorem 5.8]. In Section 5 of [70], the variety $X$ is assumed to be smooth but this is not necessary. Note that $\operatorname{Hilb}^{P}$ in our notation is $\operatorname{Hilb}^{\binom{n+r}{r}-P}$ in Kweon’s notation. Let $R_{n}=\mathbb{C}[x_{0},\ldots,x_{r}]_{n}$ be the $n$ th graded piece.

#### Theorem 9.11.

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{r}$ be a closed subvariety defined by polynomials of degree at most $d$ . Fix a Hilbert polynomial $P(n)$ and let $t\geq\max\{\varphi(P),d\}$ . Then there is an embedding

$$ \operatorname{Hilb}^{\binom{n+r}{r}-P(n)}X\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}(\wedge^{\binom{t+r}{r}-P(t)}R_{t}) $$

such that the image is cut out by equations of degree at most $\binom{t+r+1}{r}-P(t+1)+1$ .

The following proposition allows us to bound the number of irreducible components of the image in terms of the degree of the equations cutting it out.

#### Proposition 9.12.

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}$ be a closed subscheme that is cut out by equations of degree $\leq d$ . Then the number of irreducible components of $X$ is bounded in terms of $d$ and $n$ .

#### Proof.

Since the number of irreducible components remain invariant when passing to the reduced scheme, we may assume that we are working in the category of varieties. We induct on the stronger claim that given any irreducible subvariety $Y\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{n}$ of dimension $r$ and degree $e$ , any subvariety $X\subseteq Y$ that is set theoretically cut out by equations of degree $\leq d$ has its number of irreducible components bounded in terms of $r,e$ and $d$ . We will induct on the dimension $r$ , where the case of $r=0$ is clear.

Assuming we have proven the claim for all dimension $\leq r$ irreducible subvarieties, let $Y$ be an irreducible subvariety of dimension $r+1$ and degree $e$ . Let $H$ be a hypersurface of degree $\leq d$ and consider the subvariety $Y\cap H$ where $H$ does not contain $Y$ . Then $\dim(Y\cap H)\leq r$ and as $\deg(Y\cap H)\leq ed$ , there are at most $ed$ many irreducible components $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}$ . For each component $Z_{i}$ , the degree is bounded above by $ed$ and hence by induction, if $X$ is a subvariety of that irreducible component which is cut out by equations of degree $\leq d$ , the number of irreducible components of $X$ will be bounded in terms of $e,d$ and $r$ . Then the number of irreducible components of a subvariety $X$ of $Y\cap H$ cut out by equations of degree $\leq d$ may be bounded by taking its sum of the irreducible components of $X\cap Z_{i}$ , which gives us a bound in terms of $e,d$ and $r$ as desired. ∎

By Theorem 9.11 and Proposition 9.12, it suffices to now obtain an upper bound on the Gotzmann number $\varphi(Q_{i})$ and the degree of equations that cut out $B\times\tilde{A}$ . We know that $\tilde{A}$ is cut out by equations of at most degree $C_{2}$ , but this might not cut out $\tilde{A}$ scheme-theoretically. We remedy this through the following propositions.

#### Proposition 9.13.

[74, Corollary 3.3] Let $S=K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]$ and let $I$ be a homogeneous ideal of $S$ . Let $I$ be a homogeneous ideal in $S$ of dimension $r\geq 1$ and generated by forms of degree at most $d$ . Then

$$ \operatorname{reg}(\sqrt{I})\leq d^{(n-1)2^{r-1}} $$

where $\operatorname{reg}$ denotes the Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity.

Recall that $\operatorname{reg}(J)$ of a homogeneous ideal $J$ is an upper bound on the minimal $D$ such that $J$ may be defined by equations of degree at most $D$ . Hence there is some $C_{3}>0$ , depending only on $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ , such that $\tilde{A}$ is scheme-theoretically cut out by equations of at most degree $C_{3}$ . By Proposition 9.6, we may embed $B\times\tilde{A}$ into some large projective space $\mathbb{P}^{N^{\prime}}$ so that it is cut out by equations of degree at most $d$ , with $d$ and $N^{\prime}$ depending only on $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ . We are now ready to complete the last step of this section.

#### Proposition 9.14.

There exists a constant $C_{4}>0$ , depending only on $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ , such that the number of irreducible components of $\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ is at most $C_{4}$ for $1\leq i\leq C_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $Q^{\prime}_{i}(n)=\binom{n+N^{\prime}}{N^{\prime}}-Q_{i}(n)$ . Then clearly there is an upper bound on $\varphi(Q^{\prime}_{i})$ for $0\leq i\leq C_{2}$ that depends only on $C_{2},g(B)$ and $N^{\prime}$ by simply taking the maximum of $\varphi(Q^{\prime}_{i})$ , which again depends only on $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ . By Theorem 9.11, we obtain an upper bound on the degree of equations cutting out $\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q^{\prime}_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ inside some $\mathbb{P}^{N^{\prime\prime}}$ with $N^{\prime\prime}$ bounded from above by $(g,g(B),M,\delta)$ . Proposition 9.12 gives us an upper bound on the number of irreducible components as desired.

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 9.1.

By Propositions 9.8, 9.9 and 9.10, it suffices to bound the number of irreducible components of $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{C_{2}}\operatorname{Hilb}^{Q_{i}}_{B\times\tilde{A}}$ . By Proposition 9.14, the number of irreducible components is bounded in terms of $g,g(B),M$ , and $\delta$ . ∎

We obtain the following corollary for abelian varieties with everywhere good reduction immediately, using (42). Recall that for a ppav $(A,\lambda)$ , we let $L$ be a symmetric ample line bundle inducing $\lambda$ and let $\widehat{h}_{A}$ denote the Néron–Tate height with respect to $L$ .

#### Theorem 9.15.

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ for a smooth projective curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $\delta>0$ be a constant. Then there exists a natural number $N\geq 1$ , depending only on $(g,g(B),\delta)$ , such that for any principally polarized abelian variety $A/K$ of dimension $g$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)=0$ having everywhere good reduction, we have

$$ \left\{x\in A(K)\mid\widehat{h}_{A}(x)\leq\delta\right\}\leq N. $$

## 10. Reducing to the Principally Polarized Case

We finally handle the case of general abelian varieties by reducing to the case of principally polarized abelian varieties using Zarhin’s trick [120]. This is a standard trick and has been used in various theorems to extend the ppav case to the case of general abelian varieties, for example in Falting’s proof of the Mordell conjecture [40].

Combining Theorems 8.4 and 9.1, we have proven the following theorem.

#### Theorem 10.1.

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be a function field over $\mathbb{C}$ where $B$ is a smooth projective curve over $\mathbb{C}$ . Let $(A,\lambda)$ be a principally polarized abelian variety of dimension $g$ over $K$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)=0$ . Then there exist constants $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ depending on $g,g(B)$ such that the set

$$ \{x\in A(K)\mid\widehat{h}_{A}(x)\leq c_{2}\max\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A),1\}\} $$

lies on $\operatorname{div}(s)$ for some nonzero $s\in H^{0}(A,L^{c_{1}})$ where $L$ induces $2\lambda$ on $A$ .

Here, we let $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ be the stable Faltings height; in other words, if $K^{\prime}/K$ is an extension for which $A$ has semistable reduction, then

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)=\frac{1}{[K^{\prime}:K]}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A/K^{\prime}), $$

where $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A/K^{\prime})$ is the usual Faltings height of $A$ over $K^{\prime}$ . Before we continue, we will state a result of Nakamayae [90] which will allow us to pass from points lying on $\operatorname{div}(s)$ to points lying on a proper abelian subvariety. For a finite set $\Gamma\subseteq A(\overline{K})$ , let

$$ \Gamma(k)=\{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}\mid x_{i}\in\Gamma\}. $$

Set

$$ \overline{\Gamma}(k)=\bigcup_{i=0}^{k}\Gamma(k) $$

where by convention we define $\Gamma(0)=\{0\}$ .

#### Theorem 10.2.

[90, Theorem 1] Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ . Let $A$ be a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety over $K$ and $L$ an ample line bundle on $A$ . Let $s\in H^{0}(A,L)$ be a nonzero section. Suppose $s$ vanishes on $\overline{\Gamma}(g)$ where $\Gamma$ and $\overline{\Gamma}(g)$ is as above. Then there exists a proper abelian subvariety $H\subseteq A$ such that

$$ |(\Gamma+H)/H|\cdot\deg_{L}(H)\leq\deg_{L}(A). $$

One obstacle in utilizing Theorem 10.2 is that $H$ is only defined over the algebraic closure. We circumvent this in the following proposition.

#### Proposition 10.3.

Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ . Let $L$ be an ample line bundle. Let $H\subsetneq A_{\overline{K}}$ be a proper algebraic subgroup of $A_{\overline{K}}$ and let $x\in A(K)$ lie on $H$ . Then there exist integers $N,D>0$ , depending only on $\deg_{L}(H)$ , such that $[N]x$ lies on a proper abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}/K$ with $\deg_{L}(B^{\prime})\leq D$ .

#### Proof.

We may replace $L$ with $L^{3}$ and hence assume that $L$ is very ample. Then the number of connected components of $H$ is bounded above by $\deg_{L}(H)$ . Replacing $x$ with $[\deg_{L}(H)!]x$ , we may assume that $x$ lies on the identity component of $H$ and thus assume that $H$ is an abelian subvariety.

Next, let $H_{1}=H,H_{2},\ldots,H_{k}$ be the $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -conjugates of $H$ . Note that as $H$ is an abelian subvariety, $k$ is uniformly bounded in terms of $g$ by [101, Theorem 1.1] (cf. [96, Introduction]). As $x$ is a $K$ -point of $H$ , it must lie in the intersection $\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}H^{\prime}_{i}$ .

Note that $\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}H^{\prime}_{i}$ is an algebraic subgroup defined over $K$ as it is $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -stable. Hence the connected component of the identity is also defined over $K$ and is geometrically irreducible [108, Tag 0B7R]. Let $B^{\prime}$ be this connected component. Then $\deg_{L}(B^{\prime})\leq\deg_{L}(\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}H^{\prime}_{i})$ and $B^{\prime}$ is necessarily a proper abelian subvariety of $A$ defined over $K$ .

The number of connected components of $\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}H^{\prime}_{i}$ is clearly bounded from above by its degree with respect to $L$ . It follows that we may find an $N$ , depending only on $\deg_{L}(H)$ , so that $[N]x$ lies on $B^{\prime}$ , as desired.∎

We next recall Zarhin’s trick [121, Section 4]. Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ with a polarization $\lambda:A\to A^{t}$ of degree $d$ . We wish to construct a principal polarization on $A^{4}\times(A^{t})^{4}$ over $K$ . Fix some $s\geq 1$ such that $s\equiv-1\pmod{d}$ and write $s=\sum_{i=1}^{4}a_{i}^{2}$ as a sum of four squares, with the $a_{i}$ being non-negative integers. Let

$$ I=\left(\begin{matrix}a_{1}&-a_{2}&-a_{3}&-a_{4}\\
a_{2}&a_{1}&a_{4}&-a_{3}\\
a_{3}&-a_{4}&a_{1}&a_{2}\\
a_{4}&a_{3}&-a_{2}&-a_{1}\end{matrix}\right)\in M_{4\times 4}(\mathbb{Z}). $$

This may naturally be viewed as an element of $\operatorname{End}(A^{4})$ . Consider the isogeny

$$ \pi:A^{8}=A^{4}\times A^{4}\to(A^{t})^{4}\times A^{4},(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},y)\mapsto(\lambda(x_{1}),\ldots,\lambda(x_{4}),I(x)-y). $$

Then there exists a principal polarization $\mu$ on $X=(A^{t})^{4}\times A^{4}$ over $K$ that pulls back to $\lambda_{A^{8}}$ under $\pi$ . One important fact we need is that if $L_{X}$ is the line bundle inducing $2\mu$ , then $\deg_{L_{X}}(A)$ and $\deg_{L_{X}}(A^{t})$ are bounded in terms of $d$ and $g$ .

#### Proposition 10.4.

Let $A^{\prime}$ be any of the four coordinate copies of $A$ inside $X=(A^{t})^{4}\times A^{4}$ . Then $\deg_{L_{X}}(A^{\prime})=2d(g!)$ . Similarly if $(A^{\prime})^{t}$ denotes any of the four coordinate copies of $A^{t}$ inside $X$ , then $\deg_{L_{X}}((A^{\prime})^{t})$ can be bounded solely in terms of $d$ and $g$ .

#### Proof.

Let $L_{A}$ be a line bundle inducing $2\lambda_{A}$ on $A$ and $L_{A^{8}}$ a line bundle inducing $2\lambda_{A^{8}}$ on $A^{8}$ . Since $\mu$ pulls back to $\lambda_{A^{8}}$ under $\pi$ , it follows that $\pi^{*}L_{X}=L_{A^{8}}$ . Let $A_{1}$ denote the first coordinate in $(A^{t})^{4}\times A^{4}$ . It follows from the projection formula that if $A^{\prime}\subseteq A^{8}$ is such that $\pi(A^{\prime})=A_{1}$ and $\pi$ is a finite morphism when restricted to $A^{\prime}$ , then

$$ \deg(\pi:A^{\prime}\to A_{1})\deg_{L_{X}}(A_{1})=\deg_{L_{A^{8}}}(A^{\prime}). $$

We may take the fifth copy of $A$ inside $A^{8}$ as such an $A^{\prime}$ , as $\pi$ maps $A^{\prime}$ isomorphically to $A_{1}$ . Since $\lambda_{A}^{8}$ restricts to $\lambda_{A}$ on $A^{\prime}$ , equation (48) then gives

$$ \deg_{L_{X}}(A_{1})=\deg_{L_{A^{8}}}(A^{\prime})=\deg_{2\lambda_{A}}(A)=2d(g!), $$

where the last equality is due to the fact that $\lambda_{A}$ is a degree $d$ polarization. Similarly if $A_{1}^{t}$ denotes the first copy of $A^{t}$ in $X$ , then the abelian subvariety $A^{\prime\prime}$ given by

$$ A^{\prime\prime}=\{(x,0,0,0,I(x))\text{ for }x\in A\}\subseteq A^{8} $$

maps surjectively to $A_{1}^{t}$ under $\pi$ with some finite degree. We now calculate $\deg_{L_{A^{8}}}(A^{\prime\prime})$ . We first view $A^{\prime\prime}$ as the image of $A_{1}$ under $f=(\operatorname{id},0,0,0,I)\in\operatorname{End}(A^{8})$ and we identify $A_{1}$ with $A$ . We now write $f=\sum_{i=1}^{8}f_{i}$ , where $f_{i}$ is the $i$ th coordinate. Then $f_{1}^{*}L_{A^{8}}=L_{A}$ and $f_{i}^{*}L_{A^{8}}=0$ for $i=2,3,4$ . For $5\leq i\leq 8$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i=5}^{8}f_{i}^{*}L_{A^{8}}=(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+a_{3}^{2}+a_{4}^{2})L_{A}=sL_{A}. $$

Hence $f^{*}\lambda_{A}^{8}=(s+1)\lambda_{A}$ , and so

$$ \deg_{f^{*}L_{A^{8}}}(A_{1})=(s+1)2d(g!) $$

which implies that $\deg_{L_{A^{8}}}(A^{\prime\prime})$ is bounded in terms of $(d,g)$ , as desired.∎

We are now ready to show that Theorem 10.1 will imply the following uniform statement for abelian varieties which are polarizable of degree $d\geq 1$ .

#### Theorem 10.5.

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be a function field, where $B/\mathbb{C}$ is a smooth projective curve. Let $A/K$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)=0$ and with polarization $\lambda:A\to A^{t}$ of degree $d$ . Then there exist constants $c_{2}$ and $c_{3}$ , depending only on $(g,g(B),d)$ , such that for any torsion $x\in A(K)$ , there exists an $m\leq c_{2}$ such that either $[m]x$ or $\lambda([m]x)$ lies in a proper abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ of either $A$ or $A^{t}$ respectively that is defined over $K$ and polarizable of degree $\leq c_{3}$ .

#### Proof.

We first apply Zarhin’s trick and embed $A$ into $X=(A\times A^{t})^{4}=A^{4}\times(A^{t})^{4}$ . The latter is a principally polarized abelian variety over $K$ with dimension $8g$ . Furthermore, the $K/\mathbb{C}$ -trace of $X$ is $0$ as this is true for $A$ and $A^{t}$ .

Let $x$ be our $K$ -torsion point and let $y=\lambda(x)\in A^{t}$ . Let $N$ be a positive integer to be chosen later. We consider the set of all points of the form

$$ ([a_{1}]x,[a_{2}]x,[a_{3}]x,[a_{4}]x,[a_{5}]y,[a_{6}]y,[a_{7}]y,[a_{8}]y)\in X $$

where $0\leq a_{i}\leq N$ for all $i$ . Let $\lambda_{X}$ be the principal polarization and let $L$ be the line bundle inducing $2\lambda_{X}$ . By Theorem 10.1, we know that all $K$ -torsion points of $X$ lie on $\operatorname{div}(s)$ for $s\in H^{0}(A,L^{c_{1}})$ , with $c_{1}$ depending only on $(g,g(B))$ . Observe that $\deg_{L^{c_{1}}}(X)$ is $2c_{1}(g!)$ . We now apply Theorem 10.2, with $\Gamma$ taken to be the set of all points of the form (49). It follows that there is an abelian subvariety $C$ of $X$ over $\overline{K}$ along with $N^{\prime}\leq\deg_{L^{c_{1}}}(X)$ points $g_{1},\ldots,g_{N^{\prime}}$ of $X(\overline{K})$ so that $\Gamma$ is contained in $\bigcup_{i=1}^{N^{\prime}}(g_{i}+C)$ . We now take $N=N^{\prime}+1$ . We also have the inequality

$$ \deg_{L^{c_{1}}}(C)\leq\deg_{L^{c_{1}}}(X). $$

Since $\deg_{L^{c_{1}}}(X)$ is bounded in terms of $c_{1}$ only, it is bounded in terms of $g$ and $g(B)$ .

Since $C$ is a proper abelian subvariety, if we let $A_{1},\ldots,A_{4}$ and $A^{t}_{1},\ldots,A^{t}_{4}$ denote the four copies of $A$ and $A^{t}$ inside $X$ , then either $C\cap A_{i}$ is a proper subvariety for some $i$ or $C\cap A_{j}^{t}$ is a proper subvariety for some $j$ . WLOG suppose that

$$ C\cap A_{4}^{t}\text{ is a proper subvariety.} $$

Recall that $y=\lambda(x)$ . Identifying $[i]y$ with $(0,\dots,0,[i]y)\in X$ , since $N\geq N^{\prime}+1$ , we see that for two distinct $1\leq i<j\leq N$ , we must have $[i]y,[j]y$ lying in the same coset $g_{m}+C$ , and so $[j-i]y$ lies in $C$ . Hence we have $[M]y\in C\cap A_{4}^{t}$ where $M$ is bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ . Furthermore, $\deg_{L}(C\cap A_{4}^{t})$ is bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ by Proposition 10.4 and (50).

We now apply Proposition 10.3 and hence obtain an abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ defined over $K$ with $\deg_{L}(B^{\prime})$ bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ and with $[N]y$ lying in $B^{\prime}$ and $N$ bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ , as desired.∎

#### Theorem 10.6.

Let $g,d$ be positive integers and let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be a function field over $\mathbb{C}$ . Then there exists a constant $N=N(g,g(B),d)$ such that for any abelian variety $A/K$ of dimension $g$ and polarizable of degree $d$ with no $K$ -isotrivial part, any $K$ -torsion point has order at most $N$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction on $g$ . If $A$ is polarizable of degree $d$ , note that its dual $A^{t}$ is also polarizable of degree $d$ . Let $x\in A(K)$ be a torsion point. Now applying Theorem 10.5, we know there exists an $m\leq c_{2}$ where $c_{2}=c_{2}(g,g(B),d)$ such that $[m]x$ or $\lambda([m]x)$ lies on a proper abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ defined over $K$ of dimension $\leq g-1$ and polarizable of degree $\leq c_{3}=c_{3}(g,g(B),d)$ . This abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ also satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(B^{\prime})=0$ . By induction, we obtain that $[m]x$ or $\lambda([m]x)$ has order at most $N^{\prime}(g,c_{3})$ , from which it follows that $x$ has order at most $N^{\prime}(g,c_{3})\cdot(c_{2}d)$ , i.e., order at most a constant depending only on $(g,g(B),d)$ .∎

We can now remove the dependence on $d$ by Zarhin’s trick.

#### Theorem 10.7.

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be a function field of a curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . There exists a constant $N=N(g,g(B))$ such that for any abelian variety $A/K$ of dimension $g$ with no $K$ -isotrivial part, any torsion point $x\in A(K)$ has order at most $N$ .

#### Proof.

By Theorem 10.6, such a constant exists for $8g$ -dimensional principally polarized abelian varieties. But by Zarhin’s trick, any abelian variety $A$ of dimension $g$ over $K$ may be embedded into an $8g$ -dimensional principally polarized abelian variety, also defined over $K$ . We then use that constant as our $N$ . ∎

We now prove the analogous statement for the Lang–Silverman conjecture.

#### Theorem 10.8.

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $g,d\geq 1$ be positive integers. There exist $c,m>0$ depending on $(g,g(B),d)$ such that if $A/K$ is a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety with no $K$ -isotrivial part, $L$ is a degree $d$ polarization on $A$ , and $x\in A(K)$ satisfies

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)\leq c\max\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A),1\}, $$

then $[m]x$ lies on an abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}/K$ such that $\deg_{L}(B^{\prime})$ is bounded only in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ .

#### Proof.

We first handle the case where $A$ is principally polarized. We briefly sketch the argument; it is similar to the proof of Theorem 10.5. Let $N$ be a positive integer to be determined momentarily, and let $c_{1},c_{2}$ be as in Theorem 10.1. If $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)\leq\frac{c_{2}}{(gN)^{2}}\max\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A),1\}$ , then Theorem 10.1 implies that $x,[2]x,\ldots,[gN]x$ all lie on $\operatorname{div}(s)$ for some $s\in H^{0}(A,L^{c_{1}})$ . Using Theorem 10.2 on $\Gamma=\{x,[2]x,\ldots,[N]x\}$ gives us some abelian subvariety $C\subseteq A_{\overline{K}}$ and a finite set of elements $g_{1},\ldots,g_{n}$ so that $x,[2]x,\ldots,[N]x$ all lie on $g_{i}+C$ for some $i$ . Here, $n$ is bounded in terms of $(g,g(B))$ . Then setting $N=n+1$ , there exist $1\leq i<j\leq N$ and $1\leq k\leq n$ such that $[j]x,[i]x$ lie on $g_{k}+C$ , so that $[j-i]x\in C$ . Proposition 10.3 gives us a multiple $[m]x$ lying on a proper abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ defined over $K$ , with $m$ bounded purely in terms of $g$ , $g(B)$ , and $\deg_{L}(B^{\prime})$ is bounded in terms of $g$ and $g(B)$ . This completes the proof in the case where $A$ is principally polarized.

We now move on to the general case where $A$ is polarized of degree $d$ . We apply Zarhin’s trick again to get

$$ \pi:A^{8}\to X=(A^{4})\times(A^{t})^{4} $$

along with line bundle $L_{X}$ on $X$ inducing twice of a principal polarization. Then we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{A^{8},L^{8}}(x)=\widehat{h}_{X,L_{X}}(\pi(x)). $$

Again, as in (49), we consider tuples

$$ ([a_{1}]x,\ldots,[a_{8}]x) $$

in $A^{8}$ where $0\leq a_{i}\leq N$ , for $N$ a positive integer to be determined later. Then if $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)\leq\frac{c_{2}}{N^{2}}\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A),1\}$ , we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{X,L_{X}}(\pi([a_{1}]x,\ldots,[a_{8}]x))\leq\frac{c_{2}}{\max}\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(X),1\} $$

since $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(X)=8h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ by [51]. Now apply Theorem 10.1 on $X$ . Then $\pi([a_{1}]x,\ldots,[a_{8}]x)$ all lie on $\operatorname{div}(s)$ for some $s\in H^{0}(X,L_{X}^{c_{1}})$ . Pulling back, we obtain that $[a_{1}]x,\ldots,[a_{8}]x$ lie on $\operatorname{div}(s^{\prime})$ for some $s^{\prime}\in H^{0}(A^{8},L^{c_{1}}_{A^{8}})$ . As in the ppav case, applying Theorem 10.2 with Proposition 10.3 and taking $N$ to be larger than the number of cosets gives us a proper abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ over $K$ with $\deg_{L}(B^{\prime})$ bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ and an $m>0$ bounded in terms of $(g,g(B),d)$ such that $[m]x$ lies in $B^{\prime}$ .∎

As an immediate corollary, we obtain the following.

#### Corollary 10.9.

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve $B$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $g\geq 1$ be a positive integer. There exists $c>0$ depending only on $g$ and $g(B)$ such that if $A/K$ is a $g$ -dimensional abelian variety with no $K$ -isotrivial part, $L$ is a symmetric ample line bundle on $A$ , and $x\in A(K)$ is such that $\mathbb{Z}\cdot x$ is Zariski dense in $A$ , then

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(x)\geq c\max\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A),1\}. $$

Here, $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ denotes the stable Faltings height of $A$ .

We will now prove that our uniform bounds only depend on the gonality of $B$ instead of the genus. This will follow from application of Weil restriction.

#### Proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 for $k=\mathbb{C}$ .

Let $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ and let $e$ be the gonality of $B$ . Then there exists a morphism $f:B\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of degree $e$ which realizes $K$ as a field extension of $\mathbb{C}(t)$ of degree $e$ . Let $A/K$ be our abelian variety with $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{C}}(A)=0$ . Consider $A^{\prime}=\operatorname{Res}_{K/\mathbb{C}(t)}(A)$ . This is an abelian variety over $\mathbb{C}(t)$ with dimension $eg$ , such that for any scheme $S$ over $\mathbb{C}(t)$ , we have a functorial bijection of sets

$$ A^{\prime}(S)=A(S\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}(t)}\operatorname{Spec}K). $$

In particular, we have the canonical equality of points $A^{\prime}(\mathbb{C}(t))=A(K)$ . If $B^{\prime}$ is an abelian variety over $\mathbb{C}$ , we have

$$ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}(t)}(B^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}(t)},A^{\prime})=\operatorname{Hom}_{K}(B^{\prime}_{K},A)=0 $$

and thus we must also have $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{C}(t)/\mathbb{C}}(A^{\prime})=0$ . We may now apply Theorem 10.7 and deduce a uniform bound on the number of torsion points in $A(K)$ that depends only on $\operatorname{gon}(B)$ and $g$ , as desired.

For Theorem 1.2, we apply the theory of Weil restriction of adelic line bundles by Loughran [80]. Given an ample line bundle $L$ on $A$ over $K$ , we obtain a line bundle $L^{\prime}=\operatorname{Res}_{K/\mathbb{C}(t)}(L)$ on $A^{\prime}$ over $\mathbb{C}(t)$ . Furthermore, given $x\in A(K)$ , if $y\in A^{\prime}(\mathbb{C}(t))$ is the point corresponding to $x$ , we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{A^{\prime},L^{\prime}}(y)=\widehat{h}_{A,L}(x). $$

Note that $A^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathbb{C}(t)}}$ is isomorphic to $A^{e}_{\overline{K}}$ . Let $x\in A(K)$ be such that $\mathbb{Z}\cdot x$ is Zariski dense in $A$ . Now let $A$ be polarizable of degree $d$ , so that $A^{\prime}$ is polarizable by some $L^{\prime}$ of degree $de$ . Theorem 10.8 tells us that there exist $c_{1},m_{1}>0$ depending only on $(g,d,e)$ such that if $\widehat{h}_{A^{\prime},L^{\prime}}(y)\leq c_{1}\max\{h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A^{\prime}),1\}$ , then $[m_{1}]y$ must lie in a proper abelian subvariety $C_{1}$ . Note that in applying Theorem 10.8, the base curve is isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and hence there is no dependence on the genus.

We now run an iterative process. Given a proper abelian subvariety $C_{n}$ of $A^{\prime}$ over $K$ with a positive integer $m_{n}$ such that $[m_{n}]y$ lies in $C_{n}$ , we obtain a constant $c_{n}>0$ depending only on $(\deg_{L^{\prime}}(C_{n}),m_{n},g,d,e)$ for which either:

- (i) $\widehat{h}_{A^{\prime},L^{\prime}}(y)\geq c_{n}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(C_{n})$ and we terminate the process;

- (ii) or there exists a proper abelian subvariety $C_{n+1}$ of $C_{n}$ defined over $K$ and positive integer $m_{n+1}$ for which $[m_{n+1}]y$ lies in $C_{n+1}$ and $\deg_{L^{\prime}}(C_{n+1}),m_{n+1}$ are bounded in terms of $(\deg_{L^{\prime}}(C_{n}),m_{n},g,d,e)$ .

Starting with our original $C_{1}$ , observe that our process must terminate in at most $eg$ many steps as $\dim C_{n+1}<\dim C_{n}$ . Let $C_{k}$ be the final abelian variety. Then $\widehat{h}_{A^{\prime},L^{\prime}}(y)\geq c_{k}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(C_{k})$ with $c_{k}$ depending only on $(g,d,e)$ since the constants for $C_{1}$ are bounded in terms of $(g,d,e)$ . It thus suffices to show that for any proper abelian subvariety $C$ of $A^{\prime}$ that contains $[N]y$ for some $N>0$ , we have $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(C)\geq h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ .

Passing to the algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{C}(t)}$ , we have an isomorphism

$$ \iota:A^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathbb{C}(t)}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_{\sigma:K\xhookrightarrow{}\overline{\mathbb{C}(t)}}A_{\overline{K}}^{\sigma}. $$

If we let $\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{e}$ be the different embeddings of $K$ into $\overline{\mathbb{C}(t)}$ , then the point $y$ corresponds to $(\sigma_{i}(x))_{i=1}^{e}$ under this isomorphism. If $C$ is a proper abelian subvariety of $A^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathbb{C}(t)}}$ containing $[N]y$ for some positive integer $N$ , then the projection of $\iota(C)$ to one of the copies of $A_{\overline{K}}$ must contain $A_{\overline{K}}$ , because $\mathbb{Z}\cdot x$ is Zariski dense in $A$ . Thus $A$ is an isogeny factor of $C$ and so we must have $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(C)\geq h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ as we are over a function field of characteristic $0$ . This proves Theorem 1.2 with an extra dependence on $d$ where $(A,L)$ is a polarization of degree $d$ . By using Zarhin’s trick as in the proof of Theorem 10.8, we can remove the dependency on $d$ . This completes the proof of Theorem 1.2. ∎

We now extend to the case where $k$ is an arbitrary field of characteristic $0$ . Let $k$ be such a field, let $B/k$ be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve with $K=k(B)$ , and let $A/K$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g$ . Choose a finitely generated subfield $k_{0}\subset k$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and models $B_{0}/k_{0}$ , $K_{0}=k_{0}(B_{0})$ , and $A_{0}/K_{0}$ with

$$ (A,B,K)\cong(A_{0},B_{0},K_{0})\otimes_{k_{0}}k. $$

Fix an embedding $k_{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ and set

$$ B_{\mathbb{C}}=B_{0}\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C},\qquad K_{\mathbb{C}}=\mathbb{C}(B_{\mathbb{C}}),\qquad A_{\mathbb{C}}=A_{0}\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}. $$

#### Lemma 10.10.

With notation as above, the following are equivalent:

- (i) $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(A)=0$

- (ii) $\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{0}/k_{0}}(A_{0})=0$

- (iii) $\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{\mathbb{C}}/\mathbb{C}}(A_{\mathbb{C}})=0$ .

In particular, $A$ has no $K$ -isotrivial part if and only if $A_{\mathbb{C}}$ has no $K_{\mathbb{C}}$ -isotrivial part.

#### Proof.

By definition, $A$ has no $K$ -isotrivial part iff its $K/k$ -trace vanishes:

$$ \operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(A)=0. $$

For any field extension $E\supset k_{0}$ there is a natural homomorphism

$$ I^{\prime}_{E/k_{0}}:\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{0}/k_{0}}(A_{0})\otimes_{k_{0}}E\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tr}_{EK_{0}/E}(A_{0}\otimes_{k_{0}}E) $$

which is an isogeny [26, Theorem 6.6]. Taking $E=k$ and $E=\mathbb{C}$ yields isogenies

$$ \operatorname{Tr}_{K_{0}/k_{0}}(A_{0})\otimes_{k_{0}}k\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(A),\qquad\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{0}/k_{0}}(A_{0})\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{\mathbb{C}}/\mathbb{C}}(A_{\mathbb{C}}). $$

In particular,

$$ \operatorname{Tr}_{K/k}(A)=0\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{0}/k_{0}}(A_{0})=0\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{Tr}_{K_{\mathbb{C}}/\mathbb{C}}(A_{\mathbb{C}})=0. $$

Hence $A_{\mathbb{C}}$ has no $K$ -isotrivial part.∎

#### Lemma 10.11.

Let $\pi:B_{\mathbb{C}}\to B_{0}$ be the base change of $B_{0}/k_{0}$ along an embedding $k_{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ . For any divisor $D$ on $B_{0}$ we have

$$ \deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}\big(\pi^{*}D\big)=\deg_{B_{0}}(D). $$

#### Proof.

Write $D=\sum_{c}n_{c}\,[c]$ over closed points $c$ of $B_{0}$ . Let $\pi:B_{\mathbb{C}}\to B_{0}$ be the projection from the base change $B_{\mathbb{C}}=B_{0}\times_{\mathrm{Spec}(k_{0})}\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C})$ . For each $c$ , the pullback divisor $\pi^{*}[c]$ is the closed subscheme $c\times_{\mathrm{Spec}(k_{0})}\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C})=\mathrm{Spec}(k(c)\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C})$ of $B_{\mathbb{C}}$ . Because $\mathrm{char}(k_{0})=0$ , the finite extension $k(c)/k_{0}$ is separable, so the $\mathbb{C}$ -algebra $k(c)\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}$ is isomorphic to a product of copies of $\mathbb{C}$ indexed by the $k_{0}$ -embeddings $k(c)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ . By the definition of degree on a curve over $\mathbb{C}$ , $\deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}(\pi^{*}[c])=\operatorname{length}_{\mathbb{C}}(k(c)\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C})=[k(c):k_{0}]=\deg_{B_{0}}([c])$ . Therefore

$$ \deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}(\pi^{*}D)=\sum_{c}n_{c}\,\deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}(\pi^{*}[c])=\sum_{c}n_{c}\,[k(c):k_{0}]=\deg_{B_{0}}(D). $$

∎

#### Lemma 10.12.

Let $L_{0}$ be a symmetric ample line bundle on $A_{0}$ , and let $L_{\mathbb{C}}:=L_{0}\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}$ . Let $x_{0}\in A_{0}(K_{0})$ , and let $x_{\mathbb{C}}:=x_{0}\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}$ . With notation as above,

$$ \widehat{h}_{A_{\mathbb{C}},L_{\mathbb{C}}}(x_{\mathbb{C}})=\widehat{h}_{A_{0},L_{0}}(x_{0}). $$

#### Proof.

We replace $K_{0}$ with a finite extension $K_{0}$ so that $A_{0}$ has semistable reduction. Let $\mathcal{N}_{0}\to B_{0}$ be the Néron model of $A_{0}$ . Then for some $n\geq 1$ , the symmetric ample line bundle $L_{0}^{n}$ on $A_{0}$ extends uniquely to a cubical line bundle $\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{0}$ on $\mathcal{N}_{0}$ , and the $K_{0}$ -point $x_{0}$ extends (by the Néron mapping property) to a section $s_{0}:B_{0}\to\mathcal{N}_{0}$ [30, Section 14.6]. The canonical height satisfies

$$ n\widehat{h}_{A_{0},L_{0}}(x_{0})=\deg_{B_{0}}\big(s_{0}^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\big). $$

Base change along $k_{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ gives the Néron model $\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}\to B_{\mathbb{C}}$ of $A_{\mathbb{C}}$ , the cubical extension $\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathbb{C}}$ of $L^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}$ , and the section $s_{\mathbb{C}}$ of $x_{\mathbb{C}}$ , with

$$ s_{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathbb{C}}=\pi^{*}\big(s_{0}^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\big), $$

where $\pi:B_{\mathbb{C}}\to B_{0}$ is the projection induced by base change. By Lemma 10.11,

$$ n\widehat{h}_{A_{\mathbb{C}},L_{\mathbb{C}}}(x_{\mathbb{C}})=\deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}\big(s_{\mathbb{C}}^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathbb{C}}\big)=\deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}\big(\pi^{*}(s_{0}^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{0})\big)=\deg_{B_{0}}\big(s_{0}^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}_{0}\big)=n\widehat{h}_{A_{0},L_{0}}(x_{0}). $$

∎

#### Lemma 10.13.

With notation as above, let $\omega=\bigwedge^{g}e^{*}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{A}}$ be the Hodge bundle on $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}$ . For $A_{0}/K_{0}$ as above, let $\lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}$ be the line bundle on $B_{0}$ obtained from $\omega$ via pullback, so that $h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{0}):=\deg_{B_{0}}\lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}$ . Then

$$ h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{\mathbb{C}})=\deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}\lambda_{A_{\mathbb{C}}/B_{\mathbb{C}}}=\deg_{B_{0}}\lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}=h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{0}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $\eta=\mathrm{Spec}K_{0}$ and $\eta_{\mathbb{C}}=\mathrm{Spec}K_{\mathbb{C}}$ with $K_{\mathbb{C}}=\mathbb{C}(B_{\mathbb{C}})$ , and let $[A_{0}]\in\mathcal{A}_{g,3}(K_{0})$ be the moduli point of $A_{0}$ , with base change $[A_{\mathbb{C}}]\in\mathcal{A}_{g,3}(K_{\mathbb{C}})$ . By definition,

$$ \lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}\big|_{\eta}=[A_{0}]^{*}\omega,\qquad\lambda_{A_{\mathbb{C}}/B_{\mathbb{C}}}\big|_{\eta_{\mathbb{C}}}=[A_{\mathbb{C}}]^{*}\omega_{\mathbb{C}}. $$

Base change along $k_{0}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ gives a canonical isomorphism of Hodge bundles on moduli,

$$ \omega_{\mathbb{C}}\cong\omega\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}, $$

hence on the generic fibers

$$ [A_{\mathbb{C}}]^{*}\omega_{\mathbb{C}}\cong\big([A_{0}]^{*}\omega\big)\otimes_{k_{0}}\mathbb{C}. $$

It follows that

$$ \lambda_{A_{\mathbb{C}}/B_{\mathbb{C}}}\cong\pi^{*}\lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}, $$

where $\pi:B_{\mathbb{C}}\to B_{0}$ is the projection induced by base change from $k_{0}$ to $\mathbb{C}$ . Applying Lemma 10.11 for $\pi$ , we get

$$ \deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}\lambda_{A_{\mathbb{C}}/B_{\mathbb{C}}}=\deg_{B_{\mathbb{C}}}\pi^{*}\lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}=\deg_{B_{0}}\lambda_{A_{0}/B_{0}}. $$

Thus $h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{\mathbb{C}})=h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{0})$ .∎

#### Corollary 10.14.

If

$$ \widehat{h}_{A_{\mathbb{C}},L_{\mathbb{C}}}(x_{\mathbb{C}})\geq c\max\{\,h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{\mathbb{C}}),1\} $$

holds for some $c>0$ , then

$$ \widehat{h}_{A_{0},L_{0}}(x_{0})\geq c\max\{\,h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A_{0}),1\}. $$

Finally, note that gonality is preserved under base change of constant fields. Applying this to the extensions $\mathbb{C}/k_{0}$ and $k/k_{0}$ proves that Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 hold when $\mathbb{C}$ is replaced by an arbitrary field $k$ of characteristic $0$ , and the $K/k$ -trace of $A$ is assumed to be $0$ .

# Non-Archimedean Rigidity and Uniformity for Common Preperiodic Points

**Authors:** Chen Gong and Jit Wu Yap

## Abstract

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed, complete non-Archimedean field of residue characteristic $0$ . Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ over $k$ which does not have potential good reduction. We prove that if $g$ is any other polynomial with the same Julia set, then $f$ and $g$ must be dynamically related.

As a consequence, we show that for any two complex polynomials $f,g$ of degree at least $2$ , either their sets of preperiodic points coincide, or the number of their common preperiodic points is uniformly bounded above by a constant depending only on the degrees, thereby answering a conjecture of DeMarco–Krieger–Ye for polynomials. We also establish relative results, allowing us to prove special cases of the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture.

## 1. Introduction

Standing assumptions. Throughout the paper, any metrized field $k$ will be assumed to be complete and non-trivially valued.

### 1.1. Non-Archimedean rigidity of Julia sets

Let $f:\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})$ be a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ . One of the central objects in complex dynamics is the Julia set of $f$ , denoted by $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ [84], which captures the locus of instability for the dynamics. The Julia set $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ carries with it an equilibrium measure $\mu_{f}$ [21, 81, 52], which is the unique Radon probability measure satisfying $\operatorname{supp}\mu_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ and

$$ f_{*}\mu_{f}=\mu_{f},\quad f^{*}\mu_{f}=d\cdot\mu_{f}. $$

It is an old problem, dating back to Julia [69], to determine when two rational maps $f,g$ share the same Julia set or even the same equilibrium measure. This problem has been extensively studied both in the polynomial setting [69, 2, 8, 7, 93] and also for general rational maps [38, 76, 77, 35, 101, 36, 66, 82]. These works reveal a rigidity phenomenon: two non-integrable11 1 We use the term “integrable” by analogy with the notion of integrable systems in Hamiltonian dynamics, see [97, 22]. (also called non-exceptional in [77]) rational maps share the same equilibrium measure if and only if they are dynamically related by an algebraic correspondence. These rigidity results, combined with arithmetic equidistribution [6, 23, 46, 104, 56, 103], play an important role in arithmetic dynamics; see for example [4, 5, 42, 65, 32, 82, 31].

Our first goal in this paper is to establish the corresponding rigidity results for Julia sets of polynomials over a non-Archimedean field $k$ with residue characteristic $0$ . The foundations of one-variable non-Archimedean dynamics were developed by Benedetto [9, 10, 11, 12] and Rivera-Letelier [92], leading to a theory of Fatou and Julia sets paralleling the complex case. Unlike their complex counterparts, however, these sets are not subsets of $\mathbb{P}^{1}(k)$ , but instead of the Berkovich analytification $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , a larger space introduced by Berkovich [14] to facilitate non-Archimedean geometry. The theory of non-Archimedean dynamics on $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ arises naturally from considering degenerations of families of rational maps over $\mathbb{C}$ [71, 27, 49, 79, 80, 43].

Similar to the complex case, to any rational map $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ over $k$ , one can associate an equilibrium measure $\mu_{f}$ , which is a Radon probability measure on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ supported on the Julia set $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ and satisfying (1.1). This measure was first constructed by Favre–Rivera-Letelier [45], and independently by Baker–Rumely [6] and Chambert-Loir–Thuillier [95, 23]. Its ergodic and entropy-theoretic properties were further investigated by Favre–Rivera-Letelier [47, 48].

We may now state our first main result. For a rational map $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ over $k$ , we say that $f$ does not have potential good reduction if its Julia set $\cal{J}_{f}$ is not a single point. For a Julia set $\cal{J}$ , we define $\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J})$ to be the set of affine linear transformations of $k$ that preserve $\cal{J}$ .

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed, complete non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0$ . Let $\mathcal{J}$ be the Julia set of a polynomial of degree at least $2$ which does not have potential good reduction. Let $g$ be a polynomial of minimal degree whose Julia set coincides with $\mathcal{J}$ .

For any polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ , the following conditions are equivalent:

- (1) There exist an integer $n\geq 1$ and $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g^{n}.$

- (2) The Julia sets coincide: $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}.$

- (3) The equilibrium measures coincide: $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}.$

- (4) The Green functions coincide: $G_{f}=G_{g}.$

- (5) The Böttcher coordinates at $\infty$ agree up to a root of unity: $\phi_{f}=\lambda\phi_{g}$ , where $\lambda$ is a root of unity.

As a corollary of Theorem 1.1, we are able to answer (Proposition 5.8) a question raised by Favre–Gauthier in [42, Remark 3.10]. We note that our assumption of $\cal{J}$ being not a single point is necessary: for any monic polynomial $f$ with coefficients all having norm $\leq 1$ , its Julia set $\cal{J}_{f}$ is always only the Gauss point $\{x_{g}\}$ and so we cannot possibly have rigidity.

We note that (1) easily implies (2) to (5). The equivalence of (3) and (4) follows from [46, Section 4] and the equivalence of (2) and (3) follows from [3, Theorem 10.91]. The main difficulty lies in showing that (2) implies (1). To overcome this, we construct a non-Archimedean analogue of DeMarco–McMullen’s simplicial tree [28], which serves as a combinatorial tool for studying the Julia set of a polynomial. The idea of using tree-like combinatorics to study dynamics of polynomials goes back to Branner–Hubbard [19, 20]. We show if $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ , then both $f$ and $g$ have the same associated tree, in particular having the same set of distinguished vertices, which allows us to study where the roots of $f^{n}(z)-\alpha$ and $g^{n}(z)-\alpha$ lie. We will explain this in detail in Section 1.3.

### 1.2. Uniform bound on common preperiodic points

The second goal of this paper is to demonstrate how non-Archimedean rigidity results, such as Theorem 1.1, can be applied to establish uniformity results for unlikely intersection problems. We thank Niki Myrto Mavraki for enlightening us with this perspective. Let $f,g$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . Then Baker–DeMarco [4] showed that either

$$ \operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g)\text{ or }|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)|<\infty $$

where $\operatorname{Prep}(f)$ denotes the set of preperiodic points for $f$ and similarly for $g$ . A higher-dimensional version was proven by Yuan–Zhang [102]. In [30], DeMarco–Krieger–Ye conjectured that there should exist a uniform constant $M=M(d)>0$ , depending only on $d$ , such that if $f,g$ are of degree $d\geq 2$ , then

$$ \operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g)\text{ or }|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)|\leq M. $$

Our second main result not only proves their conjecture for polynomials, but also extends it to the case of polynomials of different degrees, using Theorem 1.1.

#### Theorem 1.2.

Given any integers $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ , there exists a constant $M=M(d_{1},d_{2})$ , depending only on $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , such that for any two polynomials $f$ and $g$ of degrees $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ , one of the following holds:

$$ \operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g)\quad\text{or}\quad|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)|\leq M. $$

DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [29, 30] had previously shown their conjecture for rational maps belonging to either the quadratic unicritical family $\{z^{2}+c\}_{c\in\mathbb{C}}$ or to the Lattès family associated to the Legendre family of elliptic curves. Poineau [88, 89] subsequently proved their conjecture for any pair of Lattès maps $(f,g)$ , confirming a conjecture of Bogomolov–Fu–Tschinkel [16]. Mavraki–Schmidt [82] proved the conjecture for any one-parameter family of rational maps and DeMarco–Mavraki [32] showed the conjecture holds for a Zariski open $U\subset\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ where $\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ is the moduli space of all degree $d$ rational maps. The latter result was generalized by Gauthier [57] for rational maps with different degrees.

Mavraki–Schmidt [82] and DeMarco–Mavraki [32] both rely on the theory of non-degeneracy, which is the key ingredient in the recent breakthroughs on the uniform Mordell–Lang conjecture by Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger [34], Kühne [73] and Gao–Ge–Kühne [53]. Our approach follows DeMarco–Krieger–Ye’s [29, 30], Gauthier’s [57] and Poineau’s [88, 89], where we study an adelic energy pairing, introduced by Favre–Rivera-Letelier [46] and further studied by Fili [51], and prove uniform lower bounds. This is more in line with Yuan’s proof of the uniform Bogomolov conjecture for curves [105]. To obtain uniform lower bounds, we combine Theorem 1.1 with a degeneration argument by ultrafilters following Favre–Gong [43], which we will explain in detail later.

Combining our uniform lower bounds on the energy pairing with the powerful machinery of Yuan–Zhang [103, 105], we are able to establish relative versions of Theorem 1.2. Let $\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ and $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}$ denote the moduli space of polynomials of degree $d$ and the space of monic centered polynomials of degree $d$ respectively. Let $X\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ be an irreducible subvariety defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $\Delta\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ and consider the fibered power

$$ \Delta^{\dim X+1}\times X\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2(\dim X+1)}\times\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}. $$

#### Theorem 1.3.

Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always the monomial map $z^{d}$ and that $\operatorname{Prep}(f)\not=\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ for some $(f,g)\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ . Then the set

$$ \left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\dim X+1},f,g)\mid x_{i}\in\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)\right\}\subset(\Delta)^{\dim X+1}\times X $$

is not Zariski dense in $(\Delta)^{\dim X+1}\times X$ .

In fact, we prove a Bogomolov version of Theorem 1.3, which also handles points of small canonical height (Theorem 7.1). One may deduce Theorem 1.2 from Theorem 1.3, for example see [32, Lemma 5.4]. Theorem 1.3 can be viewed as a special case of the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture [33], as named by Noytaptim–Zhong [106, 86]. The DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture may be viewed as a vast dynamical generalization of the Relative Manin–Mumford conjecture proven by Gao–Habegger [54]. To state the conjecture, we have to introduce the notion of $\Phi$ -special subvarieties for a family of dynamical systems.

Let $S$ be a smooth and irreducible quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $\Phi:S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}\to S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be an algebraic family of endomorphisms of degree $d$ . Let $\mathbb{C}(S)$ be the function field of $S$ and let $\cal{X}\subseteq S\times\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be a closed irreducible subvariety that is flat over $S$ . We say that $\cal{X}$ is $\Phi$ -special if there exists a subvariety $\mathbf{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{\overline{\mathbb{C}(S)}}$ containing the generic fiber $\mathbf{X}$ of $\cal{X}$ and a polarizable endomorphism $\Psi:\mathbf{Y}\to\mathbf{Y}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{C}(S)}$ such that for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the following hold:

- (1) $\mathbf{\Psi}^{n}(\mathbf{Y})=\mathbf{Y};$

- (2) $\mathbf{\Psi}^{n}\circ\mathbf{\Phi}=\mathbf{\Phi}\circ\mathbf{\Psi}^{n}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ where $\mathbf{\Psi}$ is the generic fiber of $\Phi$ ;

- (3) $\mathbf{X}$ is preperiodic for $\mathbf{\Psi}$ .

We may now define the relative special dimension $r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}$ of $\cal{X}$ as

$$ r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}:=\min\{\dim\cal{Y}-\dim S\mid\cal{Y}\text{ is }\Phi-\text{special}\text{ and }\cal{X}\subset\cal{Y}\}. $$

Now let $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}$ be the dynamical Green $(1,1)$ -current associated to $\Phi$ [55, Section 2.2]. We can now state the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture.

#### Conjecture 1.4.

(DeMarco–Mavraki Conjecture) The following are equivalent:

- (1) $\cal{X}$ contains a Zariski dense set of $\Phi$ -preperiodic points;

- (2) $\widehat{T}_{\Phi}^{\wedge r_{\Phi,\cal{X}}}\wedge[\cal{X}]\not=0.$

DeMarco–Mavraki show the implication $(2)$ implies $(1)$ in their paper [33]. As a consequence of Theorem 1.3, we are able to show that the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture holds for all fibered powers $(\Delta)^{k}\times X\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2k}\times\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}.$ We only handle the case of equal degrees $d_{1}=d_{2}$ since the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture was stated for polarized endomorphisms only.

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $X\subseteq\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d}\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d}$ be an irreducible subvariety defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Assume that as $(f,g)$ varies over $X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , the map $f$ is not always $z^{d}$ . Fix a positive integer $k$ and let

$$ \cal{X}=(\Delta)^{k}\times X\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2k}\times X, $$

where we view $\cal{X}$ as a family over the base $X$ . Then the DeMarco–Mavraki conjecture is true for $\cal{X}$ .

### 1.3. Strategy of the proof

#### 1.3.1. Rigidity of Julia Sets

We first explain the proof of the implication (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1) in Theorem 1.1. We first reduce to the case where both $f,g$ have the same degree $d\geq 2$ , which we will assume for the rest of this section. Let us sketch the proof when $k=\mathbb{C}$ is Archimedean. The equality of Julia sets $J_{f}=J_{g}$ implies their dynamical Green’s functions $G_{f},G_{g}$ are equal. Let $\phi_{f},\phi_{g}:U\to D(0,1)$ be their associated Böttcher coordinates satisfying

$$ \phi_{f}(f(z))=\phi_{f}(z)^{d},\quad\phi_{g}(g(z))=\phi_{g}(z)^{d}, $$

where $U$ is some neighbourhood of $\infty$ . Then $G_{f}=G_{g}$ implies $\phi_{f}=c\phi_{g}$ for some explicit constant $c$ , using the fact that $G_{f}=\log|\phi_{f}|$ and similarly for $g$ . Baker–Eremenko [2] and Schmidt–Steinmetz [93] use the functional equations (1.2) to deduce that $f$ and $g$ must then be dynamically related.

When $k$ is non-Archimedean, the equality $J_{f}=J_{g}$ still implies that $G_{f}=G_{g}$ . We still have the non-Archimedean Böttcher coordinates $\phi_{f},\phi_{g}$ but it is no longer clear how to conclude that $\phi_{f}=c\phi_{g}$ . The main reason for this is that the norm function $|\cdot|:k\to\mathbb{R}$ contains less information for non-Archimedean fields than Archimedean fields because of the strong triangle inequality. As an example, if $\mathbb{L}$ denotes the completion of the field of Puiseux series $\bigcup_{n>0}\mathbb{C}((t^{1/n}))$ , then $|\cdot|$ maps $\mathbb{L}$ to $\exp(\mathbb{Q})$ , which is much smaller than $\mathbb{R}$ and hence captures less information. This is the reason why $G_{f}$ ’s are all equal if $f$ has good reduction.

We adopt a different approach to show that $f$ and $g$ must be dynamically related, exploiting the fact that $f$ has bad reduction which induces rich dynamics on $J_{f}$ . We first illustrate the argument for $f,g$ of the form $z^{2}+c$ , where $|c|>1$ . We first pick a large $\alpha>0$ so that $\{G_{f}<\alpha\}=\{G_{g}<\alpha\}$ is a disk $D(0,R)$ for some $R>0$ . Then

$$ \left\{G_{f}<\frac{\alpha}{2^{n}}\right\}=\left\{G_{g}<\frac{\alpha}{2^{n}}\right\}\implies f^{-n}(D(0,R))=g^{-n}(D(0,R)). $$

Now it is easy to show that for any $\varepsilon>0$ , we may find an $n$ large enough so that $f^{-n}(D(0,R))$ is the union of $2^{n}$ disjoint disks $\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{2^{n}}\}$ , each of radius $<\varepsilon$ . Hence the zeros of $f^{n}$ and $g^{n}$ can be paired up so that any pair $\{x,y\}$ satisfies $|x-y|<\varepsilon$ . Using Viète’s formulas and taking $\varepsilon\to 0$ allows us to deduce relations between the coefficients of $f$ and $g$ which lets us conclude.

In general, the dynamics of $f$ will be much more complicated than the quadratic case. To help describe the dynamics, we construct a non-Archimedean analogue of the DeMarco–McMullen tree [28], which is a simplicial tree associated to a polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . The set of ends of $T_{f}$ corresponds to the Julia set $\cal{J}_{f}$ . For a tame polynomial [39, 40, 96, 70] of degree $d\geq 2$ over a non-Archimedean field $k$ , we associate to it a subset

$$ T_{f}=\bigcup_{t>0}\partial\{G_{f}(z)<t\}\subseteq\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}, $$

whose closure in $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,an}$ is exactly the convex hull of $\mathcal{J}_{f}\cup\{\infty\}.$

We endow it with a distinguished set of vertices and edges so that $f$ acts on $T_{f}$ as a simplicial self-map. The assumption that $f$ has bad reduction ensures that $T_{f}$ has infinitely many vertices and edges and is hence interesting.

Given $f,g$ of degree $d\geq 2$ with $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ , one can show that $T_{f}=T_{g}$ as subsets of $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , and with the same set of vertices and edges. However, $f$ and $g$ may act differently. We show that for any $\varepsilon>0$ , we may find a finite subset $X\subseteq T_{f}$ such that

$$ f^{-1}(X)=g^{-1}(X)=Y\not=\emptyset $$

with every vertex of $Y$ representing a disk of radius $<\varepsilon$ (Proposition 5.2). This allows us to replicate the argument used in the case of $z^{2}+c$ and hence show that $f$ and $g$ must be dynamically related.

#### 1.3.2. Degenerations and Uniformity

We now explain how to deduce Theorem 1.2 from Theorem 1.1. By a specialization argument [30, Section 10.2], we may assume that $f,g$ are both defined over a number field $K$ . Following Favre–Rivera-Letelier [46] (see also Fili [51]), for each place $\nu\in M_{K}$ we may define a local energy pairing

$$ \langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}=-\iint_{\mathbb{P}_{\nu}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\times\mathbb{P}_{\nu}^{1,\mathrm{an}}}\log|x-y|_{\nu}d(\mu_{f,\nu}-\mu_{g,\nu})(x)d(\mu_{f,\nu}-\mu_{g,\nu})(y) $$

where $\mu_{f,\nu},\mu_{g,\nu}$ are the equilibrium measures of $f,g$ over $\mathbb{C}_{\nu}$ . We may then define a global adelic energy pairing by

$$ \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{\nu\in M_{K}}N_{\nu}\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu} $$

where $N_{\nu}=[K_{\nu}:\mathbb{Q}_{\nu}]/[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ . By the work of DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [29, 30], subsequently generalized by Gauthier [57] and Ang–Yap [1], proving Theorem 1.2 reduces to establishing uniform lower bounds on the global pairing $\langle f,g\rangle$ . More precisely, one needs the existence of a uniform constant $c=c(d_{1},d_{2})>0$ , depending only on $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ , such that if $\operatorname{Prep}(f)\not=\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ , then

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq c\max\{h(f)+h(g),1\} $$

where $h$ is a Weil height on polynomials.

To prove (1.3), we establish suitable uniform lower bounds on the local energy pairings $\langle f,g\rangle_{\nu}$ using a degeneration argument. This is the approach taken by DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [29] and Poineau [88] in the case of Lattes maps. We will sketch an example of such a uniform local lower bound and how to deduce it via degenerations.

Let $V$ be a positive-dimensional subvariety of $\mathrm{Poly}_{\mathrm{mc}}^{d_{1}}$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . There exists a maximal Zariski open $U\subseteq V$ such that for all $f\in U(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ , one has $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\mathbb{U}_{m}=\{\zeta^{m}=1\mid\zeta\in\mathbb{C}\}$ . Let $V^{\prime}=V\setminus U$ . One can verify that $V^{\prime}$ is defined by the vanishing of finitely many polynomials $\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{\ell}\}$ in the coefficients of $f$ .

Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be a non-trivially valued field of characteristic $0$ . If we write $f=\sum_{i=0}^{d_{1}}a_{i}z^{i}$ and $g=\sum_{i=0}^{d_{2}}b_{i}z^{i}$ , we define $|f|=\max\{|a_{i}|\}$ , $|(f,g)|=\max\{|a_{i}|,|b_{j}|,|b_{d_{2}}^{-1}|\}$ and

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime}}(f)=-\log\max\{|p_{1}(f)|,\ldots,|p_{\ell}(f)|\}. $$

The function $\lambda_{V^{\prime}}$ measures how close $f$ is to the subvariety $V^{\prime}$ . In particular, we have $\lambda_{V^{\prime}}(f)=+\infty$ if and only if $f\in V^{\prime}$ . We now state one of our uniform lower bounds.

#### Theorem 1.6.

Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be a field of characteristic $0$ equipped with a nontrivial absolute value, and fix $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ . Then there exist constants $C_{3},C_{4}>0$ depending only on $k$ , $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ such that the following holds:

Suppose that

$$ (f,g)\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})(k)\times\operatorname{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k) $$

satisfies

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime}}(f)\leq C_{1}\log|(f,g)|. $$

If positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ exist with $d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}$ , assume further that

$$ \log|f^{n_{1}}-\lambda g^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}\log|(f,g)|\quad\text{for all }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}. $$

Then

$$ \log|(f,g)|\geq C_{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle f,g\rangle\geq C_{4}\log|(f,g)|. $$

We also have the following variant of Theorem 1.6 where the condition of $|(f,g)|$ being sufficiently large is replaced by $k$ having sufficiently large residue characteristic.

#### Theorem 1.7.

For every $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ , there exist constants $C_{5},C_{6}>0$ depending only on $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ such that the following holds: Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be a non-Archimedean field whose residue characteristic is at least $C_{5}$ , and let

$$ (f,g)\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})\times\operatorname{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k) $$

satisfy

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime},k}(f)\leq C_{1}\log|(f,g)|. $$

Suppose moreover that whenever there exist positive integers $n_{1},n_{2}$ with

$$ d_{1}^{n_{1}}=d_{2}^{n_{2}}, $$

the following additional condition is imposed:

$$ \log|f^{n_{1}}-\lambda g^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}\log|(f,g)|\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}. $$

Then

$$ \langle f,g\rangle\geq C_{6}\log|(f,g)|. $$

Combining these two lower bounds gives us (1.3).

As mentioned earlier, Theorem 1.6 can be directly deduced from Theorem 1.1 using a degeneration argument. We follow the approach by Favre–Gong [43] which combines rescaling limits with ultrafilters. The idea of rescaling limits in complex dynamics was first introduced by Kiwi [71], where given a family of rational maps $(f_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{D}^{*}}$ parametrized by the punctured disk $\mathbb{D}^{*}$ , he constructs a rational map $f$ over the non-Archimedean field $\mathbb{C}((t))$ as a rescaled limit of the family. This has been expanded on by DeMarco–Faber [27] and Favre [49].

In his thesis, Luo [79, 80], using ultrafilters, generalizes Kiwi’s construction to any sequence of degree $d$ rational maps $(f_{n})$ over $\mathbb{C}$ . In particular, the sequence $(f_{n})$ need not be constrained in a one-parameter family and can vary in the entire moduli space $\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ . Favre–Gong then formalized Luo’s construction using the theory of Berkovich spaces, which allows each $f_{n}$ to be defined over possibly distinct metrized fields $k_{n}$ . The method of Favre–Gong has previously been applied by the second author to obtain uniformity results in both arithmetic dynamics [100] and Diophantine geometry with Looper [78].

We now sketch out the degeneration argument. Assume for contradiction that Theorem 1.6 is false. We obtain a sequence $(f_{n},g_{n})\in(V\setminus V^{\prime})(k)\times\mathrm{Poly}^{d_{2}}(k)$ such that

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime}}(f_{n})\leq C_{1}\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|,~\langle f_{n},g_{n}\rangle\leq\frac{1}{n}\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|; $$

$$ \log|(f_{n},g_{n})|\to\infty,~\text{and}~\log|f_{n}^{n_{1}}-\lambda g_{n}^{n_{2}}|\geq-C_{2}\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|\text{ for all }\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}. $$

We set $\varepsilon_{n}=(\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|)^{-1}\to 0$ . Fix a non-principal ultrafilter $\omega$ . Then we may associate to $(f_{n},g_{n})$ an $\omega$ -limit, which is a pair of degree $d$ polynomials $(f_{\omega},g_{\omega})$ defined over the metrized field

$$ \mathscr{H}(\omega)=\Bigl\{(z_{n})\in k^{\mathbb{N}}\ \bigm|\ \lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|^{\epsilon_{n}}<\infty\Bigr\}\Big/\Bigl\{(z_{n})\in k^{\mathbb{N}}\ \bigm|\ \lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|^{\epsilon_{n}}=0\Bigr\}. $$

The absolute value $|\cdot|_{\omega}$ on $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is given by $|(z_{n})|=\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ where $\lim_{\omega}$ denotes the $\omega$ -limit [43, Section 3]. The field $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is algebraically closed, non-Archimedean and of residue characteristic $0$ . By continuity, the pair $f_{\omega},g_{\omega}$ satisfies

$$ \langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle\leq\lim_{\omega}\frac{1}{n}\varepsilon_{n}\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|=0 $$

and furthermore, it is easy to reduce to the case where $f_{\omega}$ does not have potential good reduction. Since

$$ \lambda_{V^{\prime}}(f_{\omega})\leq\lim_{\omega}C_{1}\varepsilon_{n}\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|=C_{1}<+\infty, $$

we have $f_{\omega}\not\in V^{\prime}(\mathscr{H}(\omega))$ , which implies that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f_{\omega}})=\mathbb{U}_{m}$ . Applying Theorem 1.1, one obtains $f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}=\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}$ . But we also have

$$ \log|f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}-\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}}|\geq-\lim_{\omega}C_{2}\varepsilon_{n}\log|(f_{n},g_{n})|=-C_{2}, $$

and hence $f_{\omega}^{n_{1}}\not=\lambda g_{\omega}^{n_{2}}$ , giving us a contradiction.

Finally, we note that there is a theory of globally valued fields coming from the model theory point of view [99, 94, 98]. This is related to the theory of adelic curves by Chen–Moriwaki [24, 25] and also to the theory of Yuan–Zhang [103]. Globally valued fields can be viewed as a global analogue of valued fields, where one deals with fields equipped with a global height function, such as the Weil height on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Using ultrafilters [58] is a standard technique in model theory, allowing one to degenerate sequences of objects defined over globally metrized fields in a way analogous to degeneration over valued fields. The interested reader may consult Hultberg’s work [62] for applications to semiabelian varieties.

### 1.4. Further questions

We now raise a few further questions. The first question is whether an extension of Theorem 1.1 to rational maps exists. More generally, we can ask for a non-Archimedean rigidity statement for a pair of rational maps $(f,g)$ and a curve $C\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ . This will be addressed in a forthcoming work by Zhuchao Ji and the second author [67], with applications towards the uniform dynamical Manin–Mumford and Bogomolov conjecture on $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}$ .

Secondly, Theorem 1.1 only holds for residue characteristic $0$ and one may ask for analogues that hold for positive residue characteristic. Our proof relies crucially on residue characteristic being $0$ as we use the fact that $|n|=1$ for all positive integers $n$ . This leads us to formulate the following conjecture.

#### Conjecture 1.8.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed and complete non-Archimedean field, possibly of positive characteristic. Let $\cal{J}$ be the Julia set of a tame polynomial of degree at least $2$ which does not have potential good reduction. Let $g$ be a polynomial of minimal degree whose Julia set coincides with $\cal{J}$ . Then if $f$ is a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ with $\cal{J}_{f}=\cal{J}$ , there exists an integer $n\geq 1$ and $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g^{n}$ .

When $\cal{J}$ is not the Julia set of a tame polynomial, there are counterexamples. Let $p\geq 3$ be a prime number. Consider $f(z)=\frac{z^{p}-z}{p}$ and $g(z)=\frac{z^{p}-pz^{2}-z}{p}\in\mathbb{C}_{p}[z].$ Then the Julia set of both maps equals $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ ; see [13, Example 8.17] for an explanation in the case of $f$ , and the argument for $g$ is analogous. However, there do not exist affine transformations $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}$ such that $f\circ\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}\circ g.$ Observe that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ is infinite, which suggests that it should play a similar role as the circle $S^{1}$ in the Archimedean case. We make a more ambitious conjecture that if $\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J})$ is finite, then Conjecture 1.4 should be true.

#### Conjecture 1.9.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed and complete non-Archimedean field, possibly of positive characteristic. Let $\cal{J}$ be the Julia set of a polynomial of degree at least $2$ which does not have potential good reduction, such that $\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J})$ is finite. Let $g$ be a polynomial of minimal degree whose Julia set coincides with $\cal{J}$ . Then if $f$ is a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ with $\cal{J}_{f}=\cal{J}$ , there exists an integer $n\geq 1$ and $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g^{n}$ .

Conjecture 1.9 naturally leads to the question of classifying Julia sets $\cal{J}$ with $|\mathrm{Aut}(\cal{J})|=+\infty$ . We do not have a concrete conjecture for this question but we expect that over $\mathbb{C}_{p}$ , such a Julia set should be similar to $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ in nature.

Finally, it is interesting to ask whether one can deduce $\phi_{f}=c\phi_{g}$ directly from $G_{f}=G_{g}$ , in analogy with the case over $\mathbb{C}$ . At present, we do not know how to approach this problem.

## 2. Dynamics on the Berkovich projective line and potentials

### 2.1. Construction of the Berkovich projective line over a general Banach ring

We briefly recall the construction of the Berkovich projective line over a general Banach ring. We refer the reader to [75] for a detailed treatment.

A Banach ring $(B,\|\cdot\|)$ is, by convention, a commutative ring with unity endowed with a complete norm $\|\cdot\|\colon B\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ satisfying $\|a+b\|\leq\|a\|+\|b\|$ and $\|ab\|\leq K\|a\|\|b\|$ for some constant $K>0$ and for all $a,b\in B$ ; see [17, A.1.2.1].

The Berkovich spectrum $\mathcal{M}(B)$ is the set of all bounded multiplicative seminorms on $B$ , that is, maps $|\cdot|\colon B\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ satisfying $|a+b|\leq|a|+|b|$ , $|ab|=|a||b|$ , and $|\cdot|\leq C\|\cdot\|$ for some $C>0$ . For any $x\in\mathcal{M}(B)$ and $b\in B$ , we denote the value of $b$ at $x$ by $|b|_{x}$ or $|b(x)|$ .

The space $\mathcal{M}(B)$ is endowed with the weakest topology for which all functions of the form $x\longmapsto|b(x)|$ , $b\in B$ , are continuous. By [14, Theorem 1.2.1], the space $\mathcal{M}(B)$ is compact.

To define the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}_{B}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ over $B$ , we first define the Berkovich affine line $\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ .
