It is the set of all multiplicative seminorms on $B[T]$ whose restriction to $B$ belongs to $\mathcal{M}(B)$ . It is endowed with the weakest topology such that all functions $x\longmapsto|P(x)|$ , for some $P\in B[T]$ , are continuous.

For $x\in\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ , consider the prime ideal $\ker(x):=\{P\in B[T]\mid|P(x)|=0\}.$ The complete residue field $\mathscr{H}(x)$ is defined as the completion of the fraction field of $B[T]/\ker(x)$ with respect to the norm induced by $x$ .

The Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ is obtained by gluing two copies $X_{0}$ and $X_{1}$ of $\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ along $\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}\setminus\{0\}$ in the usual way. This construction yields homogeneous coordinates $[z_{0}:z_{1}]$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ . For simplicity, we write $z=z_{0}$ , $0=[0:1]$ , and $\infty=[1:0]$ , so that $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}=\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}\sqcup\{\infty\}.$ By construction, the space $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ is compact.

There is a canonical continuous map $\pi\colon\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(B),$ sending a point $x\in\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{B}$ to its restriction to $B$ . This map is proper, and for every $s\in\mathcal{M}(B)$ , the fiber $\pi^{-1}(s)$ is canonically identified with the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{\mathscr{H}(s)}$ .

### 2.2. Dynamics on $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$

We briefly recall some basic notions concerning the dynamics of rational maps on the Berkovich projective line. For the case $k=\mathbb{C}$ , see [84], and for the case $k\neq\mathbb{C}$ , see [68, 13].

#### 2.2.1. Berkovich projective line over a metrized field

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed complete metrized field, that is, a field endowed with a complete multiplicative norm $|\cdot|$ .

We say that $k$ is non-Archimedean if its norm satisfies the strong triangle inequality $|x+y|\leq\max\{|x|,|y|\}.$ By the Gelfand–Mazur theorem and Ostrowski’s theorem, if $k$ is Archimedean, then there exists $0<\varepsilon\leq 1$ such that $k$ is isometric to $\mathbb{C}_{\varepsilon}=(\mathbb{C},|\cdot|^{\varepsilon})$ , where $|\cdot|$ denotes the standard Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{C}$ . In this case, $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ is homeomorphic to the Riemann sphere $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$ .

If $k$ is non-Archimedean, then the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ carries the structure of a compact $\mathbb{R}$ -tree: for any $x,y\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , there exists a unique segment $[x,y]$ joining them.

There are exactly four types of points on $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ :

- (1) type I: There exists a rational function $R$ such that $|R(x)|=0$ . In this case, $x$ can be identified with a point of $\mathbb{P}^{1}(k)$ , and the associated seminorm is given by the evaluation map $P\mapsto|P(x)|$ ;

- (2) type II: There exist $a\in k$ and $r\in|k^{\times}|$ such that for every polynomial $P(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}(z-a)^{i}\in k[z]$ , one has

$$ |P(x)|=\max_{z\in\bar{D}(a,r)}|P(z)|=\max_{0\leq i\leq d}|a_{i}|r^{i}, $$

where $\bar{D}(a,r)$ denotes the closed ball of radius $r$ centered at $a$ ;

- (3) type III: There exist $a\in k$ and $r>0$ and $r\notin|k^{\times}|$ such that for every polynomial $P(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}(z-a)^{i}\in k[z]$ , one has

$$ |P(x)|=\sup_{z\in\bar{D}(a,r)}|P(z)|=\max_{0\leq i\leq d}|a_{i}|r^{i}. $$

- (4) type IV: There exists a sequence of decreasing closed balls $\bar{D}_{n}$ with $\bigcap\bar{D}_{n}=\emptyset$ , such that

$$ |P(x)|=\inf_{n}\max_{z\in\bar{D}_{n}}|P(z)| $$

for all $P\in k[z]$ .

The set of type I and type IV points forms the ends of the Berkovich tree. Type II points correspond to branch points of the tree, while type III points are regular points.

Moreover, if $k$ is spherically complete, i.e., every decreasing sequence of closed balls has nonempty intersection, then $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ has no type IV points. If $|k^{\times}|=\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , then $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ does not contain type III points.

We usually write $\zeta(a,r)$ for the type I, type II or III point associated with the closed ball $\bar{D}(a,r)$ , and we denote the Gauss point $\zeta(0,1)$ by $x_{g}$ . When $r=0$ , $\zeta(a,r)$ is the type I point defined by $a.$

#### 2.2.2. Dynamics of a rational map

Recall that a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ with coefficients in $k$ is given in homogeneous coordinates by

$$ f\colon[z_{0}:z_{1}]\longmapsto[P(z_{0},z_{1}):Q(z_{0},z_{1})], $$

where $P(z_{0},z_{1})=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}z_{0}^{i}z_{1}^{d-i}$ , and $Q(z_{0},z_{1})=\sum_{i=0}^{d}b_{i}z_{0}^{i}z_{1}^{d-i}$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $k[z_{0},z_{1}]$ without common factors. We denote by $\operatorname{Rat}_{d}(k)$ the set of rational maps of degree $d$ over $k$ . It can be viewed as an affine subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^{2d+1}$ defined by the nonvanishing locus of the normalized resultant

$$ |\operatorname{Res}(f)|\coloneqq\frac{|\operatorname{Res}(P,Q)|}{\max_{0\leq i,j\leq d}\{|a_{i}|,|b_{j}|\}^{2d}}\neq 0. $$

A rational map $f$ extends naturally to the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ by sending a point $x$ in the hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}_{k}=\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\setminus\mathbb{P}^{1}(k)$ to $f(x)$ , defined by the rule

$$ |h(f(x))|=|(h\circ f)(x)|\quad\text{for all }h\in k(z). $$

The induced endomorphism $f\colon\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ is continuous, finite, open, and surjective (see, for instance, [68, Proposition 4.3]). One can define a local degree $\deg_{x}(f)\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ at each point $x\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{f(y)=x}\deg_{y}(f)=d\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}. $$

The exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ of $f$ is the largest finite subset of $\mathbb{P}^{1}(k)$ that is totally invariant under $f$ . It contains at most two points. The Julia set $\mathcal{J}_{f}\subset\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ is the set of points $x$ such that, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ , $\bigcup_{n\geq 0}f^{n}(U)\supset\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\setminus\mathcal{E}.$ It is a closed and totally invariant subset of $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ . Its complement $\mathcal{F}(f)=\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\setminus\mathcal{J}_{f}$ is called the Fatou set. By [13, Theorem 8.7], the Julia set consists only of points of type I and type II.

A rational map $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ is said to have good reduction if its Julia set reduces to the Gauss point $x_{g}$ . By [47, Theorem C], this is equivalent to the condition that $f$ has zero entropy, or equivalently that $|\operatorname{Res}(f)|=1$ . We say that $f$ has potential good reduction if it is conjugate to a rational map with good reduction. Otherwise, we say $f$ does not have potential good reduction. When $k=\mathbb{C}$ , we adopt the convention that $f$ does not have good reduction.

#### 2.2.3. Tangent space and tangent map

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed non-Archimedean field.

Recall that the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ has a tree-like structure: for any two points $x,y\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , there is a unique segment $[x,y]$ joining them. A direction at a point $x\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ is an equivalence class in $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\setminus\{x\},$ where two points $y,y^{\prime}\neq x$ are equivalent if and only if $(x,y]\cap(x,y^{\prime}]\neq\varnothing.$

The set of directions at $x$ is called the tangent space at $x$ and is denoted by $T_{x}\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}.$ For $\vec{v}\in T_{x}\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , we denote by $U(\vec{v})$ the corresponding connected component of $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\setminus\{x\}$ . Thus, $U(\vec{v})$ is a connected open subset of $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ whose boundary is the singleton $\{x\}$ .

Every nonconstant rational map $f\in k(z)$ induces a map on tangent spaces,

$$ T_{x}f\colon T_{x}\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\longrightarrow T_{f(x)}\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}, $$

called the tangent map of $f$ at $x$ .

### 2.3. Potential theory

#### 2.3.1. Laplace operator

We briefly recall some notions from potential theory on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ . For the case $k=\mathbb{C}$ , see [60], and for the non-Archimedean setting, see [3, 44, 95].

Let $\sigma=\{P_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq l}$ be a finite collection of homogeneous polynomials of the same degree $l(\sigma)$ with no common zero. Define

$$ \psi_{\sigma}\coloneqq\frac{1}{l(\sigma)}\log\frac{\max\{|P_{1}|,\dots,|P_{l}|\}}{\max\{|z_{0}|,|z_{1}|\}^{l(\sigma)}}. $$

Then $\psi_{\sigma}\colon\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous.

Let $X$ be the closure of $\{\psi_{\sigma}\}$ in the space of continuous functions, endowed with the topology of uniform convergence. Denote by $\mathcal{M}^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k})$ the space of Radon probability measures on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ , endowed with the weakest topology such that, for every continuous function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ , the map $\mu\mapsto\int\varphi\,d\mu$ is a continuous function.

For each $u\in X$ , one can associate a signed measure $\Delta u$ such that $\mu_{\mathrm{can}}+\Delta u$ is a Radon probability measure, where $\mu_{\mathrm{can}}$ denotes the Haar probability measure on the unit circle when $k=\mathbb{C}$ , and the Dirac measure supported at the Gauss point when $k$ is non-Archimedean. This signed measure is called the Laplacian of $u$ .

The Laplace operator defines a continuous map: $\mu_{\mathrm{can}}+\Delta\colon X\to\mathcal{M}^{1}(\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k})$ , and satisfies $\Delta u_{1}=\Delta u_{2}$ if and only if $u_{1}-u_{2}$ is constant.

#### 2.3.2. Equilibrium measure

Let $f=[P:Q]$ be a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ . Given any rational map, one can associate an equilibrium measure $\mu_{f}$ whose support is the Julia set. We briefly recall its construction below.

For any function $\varphi\colon\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\to\mathbb{R}$ , define

$$ f_{*}\varphi(x)\coloneqq\sum_{y\in f^{-1}(x)}\deg_{y}(f)\,\varphi(y). $$

Equation (2.1) implies that if $\varphi$ is continuous, then $f_{*}\varphi$ is also continuous, and its sup-norm is bounded by $d$ times the sup-norm of $\varphi$ . Consequently, for any Radon measure $\rho$ , the pullback of $\rho$ by $f$ can be defined dually by $\int\varphi df^{*}\rho=\int f_{*}\varphi d\rho$ for any continuous function $\varphi.$

Set $\gamma_{f}\coloneqq\frac{1}{d}\log\frac{\max\{|P|,|Q|\}}{\max\{|z_{0}|^{d},|z_{1}|^{d}\}}.$ Iterating the identity for $f^{*}\mu_{\mathrm{can}}$ yields

$$ \frac{1}{d^{n}}(f^{n})^{*}\mu_{\mathrm{can}}=\mu_{\mathrm{can}}+\Delta\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{d^{k}}\,\gamma_{f}\circ f^{k}. $$

Since the series $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{d^{k}}\gamma_{f}\circ f^{k}$ converges uniformly in $X$ to $\varphi_{f}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{d^{k}}\,\gamma_{f}\circ f^{k},$ the limit of $\frac{1}{d^{n}}(f^{n})^{*}\mu_{\mathrm{can}}$ exists. We call this limit the equilibrium measure of $f$ , and denote it by $\mu_{f}$ . Thus,

$$ \mu_{f}=\mu_{\mathrm{can}}+\Delta\varphi_{f}. $$

This equilibrium measure satisfies the following equidistribution theorem. In the setting of complex polynomials, this result is due to Brolin [21], and for complex rational maps to Lyubich [81] and Freire-Lopes-Mañé [52]. In the non-Archimedean setting, it was established by Favre–Rivera-Letelier [45, 47].

#### Theorem 2.1.

Let $\rho$ be a Radon probability measure on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ . Then

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}(f^{n})^{*}\rho=\mu_{f}, $$

if and only if $\rho(\mathcal{E})=0$ . Moreover, $\frac{1}{d}f^{*}\mu_{f}=f_{*}\mu_{f}=\mu_{f}.$

#### 2.3.3. Energy pairing

Let $f$ and $g$ be two rational maps of degrees $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ , respectively. We define an energy pairing between $f$ and $g$ using the mutual energy introduced by Favre–Rivera-Letelier [46].

We define the Hsia kernel $H\colon\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\times\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\longrightarrow[-\infty,\infty)$ by

$$ H(x,y)=\begin{cases}|x-y|,&\text{if }k=\mathbb{C},\\[5.0pt]
\sup\{x,y\},&\text{if }k\text{ is non-Archimedean}.\end{cases} $$

In the non-Archimedean case, the quantity $\sup\{x,y\}$ is defined as follows: Let $x_{0}$ be the unique point satisfying $[x,\infty]\cap[y,\infty]=[x_{0},\infty].$ Then we set $\sup\{x,y\}\coloneqq\inf_{c\in k}|z-c|_{x_{0}}.$ In fact, when $x_{0}=\zeta(a,r)$ is of type I, II or III, then $\sup\{x,y\}$ is exactly the radius $r$ .

Since $\varphi_{f}$ and $\varphi_{g}$ are continuous functions, by [46, Lemma 2.4 and Lemma 4.3] the function $\log H(x,y)$ belongs to $L^{1}\bigl(|\mu_{f}-\mu_{g}|\times|\mu_{f}-\mu_{g}|\bigr)$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\times\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ . Therefore, one can define their energy pairing, denoted by $\langle f,g\rangle$ , by

$$ \langle f,g\rangle=-\iint\log H(x,y)\,d(\mu_{f}-\mu_{g})(x)\,d(\mu_{f}-\mu_{g})(y). $$

By [46, Proposition 2.6 and Proposition 4.5], one has $\langle f,g\rangle\geq 0$ , and moreover $\langle f,g\rangle=0$ if and only if $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

The energy pairing satisfies

$$ \langle f,g\rangle=-\int(\varphi_{f}-\varphi_{g})\,d(\mu_{f}-\mu_{g}). $$

#### Proof.

By Fubini’s theorem, we may write

$$ \langle f,g\rangle=-\int\Bigl(\int\log H(x,y)\,d(\mu_{f}-\mu_{g})(y)\Bigr)\,d(\mu_{f}-\mu_{g})(x). $$

By [46, §2.5 and §4.5], one has

$$ \int\log H(\cdot,y)\,d(\mu_{f}-\mu_{g})=\varphi_{f}-\varphi_{g}+C $$

for some constant $C\in\mathbb{R}$ . Since $\mu_{f}-\mu_{g}$ has total mass zero, the constant term integrates to zero, and the desired identity follows. ∎

## 3. Non-Archimedean degenerations by ultrafilters

### 3.1. Infinite product of Banach rings

#### 3.1.1. Ultrafilters and Stone–Čech compactification

We recall some basic notions concerning ultrafilters and the Stone–Čech compactification of the set $\mathbb{N}$ of natural numbers. We refer to [26] for a detailed account.

#### Definition 3.1.

A collection $\omega\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is called an ultrafilter if it satisfies the following properties:

- (1) $\emptyset\notin\omega$ ;

- (2) if $E,F\in\omega$ , then $E\cap F\in\omega$ ;

- (3) if $E\in\omega$ and $E\subseteq F$ , then $F\in\omega$ ;

- (4) for every $E\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ , either $E\in\omega$ or $E^{c}=\mathbb{N}\setminus E\in\omega$ .

Indeed, an ultrafilter $\omega$ may be viewed as a finitely additive $\{0,1\}$ -valued probability measure on $\mathbb{N}$ : a subset has measure $1$ if and only if it belongs to $\omega$ . Such sets are called $\omega$ -big. A property is said to hold $\omega$ -almost surely if it holds on an $\omega$ -big set.

For any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the family

$$ \omega_{n}=\{F\subseteq\mathbb{N}\mid n\in F\} $$

is an ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$ . Such an ultrafilter is called principal; it corresponds to the Dirac measure supported at $n$ . An ultrafilter that is not principal is said to be non-principal. The existence of non-principal ultrafilters is guaranteed by Zorn’s lemma.

We denote by $\beta\mathbb{N}$ the set of all ultrafilters on $\mathbb{N}$ . Identifying each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with the corresponding principal ultrafilter $\omega_{n}$ yields an injection $\mathbb{N}\hookrightarrow\beta\mathbb{N}$ .

For each subset $E\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ , we define $U_{E}=\{\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}\mid E\in\omega\}.$ For any $E,F\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ , one has $U_{E}\cap U_{F}=U_{E\cap F}$ . Hence the family $\{U_{E}\}_{E\subseteq\mathbb{N}}$ forms a basis for a topology on $\beta\mathbb{N}$ , whose open sets are precisely unions of such sets $U_{E}$ .

Equipped with this topology, the space $\beta\mathbb{N}$ , known as the Stone–Čech compactification of $\mathbb{N}$ , is compact and totally disconnected, and contains $\mathbb{N}$ as an open dense subset.

The notion of an ultrafilter allows one to define generalized limits of sequences in any compact Hausdorff space $X$ . Namely, for any ultrafilter $\omega$ on $\mathbb{N}$ and any sequence $(x_{n})\subset X$ , there exists a unique point $x\in X$ , called the $\omega$ -limit of $(x_{n})$ , and denoted by

$$ x=\lim_{\omega}x_{n}, $$

such that for every neighborhood $V$ of $x$ , one has $x_{n}\in V$ $\omega$ -almost surely.

Note that if $\omega=\omega_{m}$ is the principal ultrafilter associated with $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , then $\lim_{\omega}x_{n}=x_{m}.$ Thus, in most situations of interest, we shall restrict attention to non-principal ultrafilters.

#### 3.1.2. Product of Banach rings

Let $(k_{n})$ be a sequence of complete metrized fields which are algebraically closed, and denote by $|\cdot|_{n}$ the given absolute value on $k_{n}$ . A sequence of positive real numbers $(\epsilon_{n})$ is said to be adapted to $(k_{n})$ if, for each $n$ , one has $\epsilon_{n}\in(0,1]$ when $k_{n}$ is Archimedean and $\epsilon_{n}>0$ when $k_{n}$ is non-Archimedean. Then, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the function $|\cdot|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}\colon k_{n}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ again defines a complete multiplicative norm on $k_{n}$ .

Let $\epsilon=(\epsilon_{n})$ be a sequence adapted to $(k_{n})$ . We define the product Banach ring associated with $\epsilon$ as:

$$ A^{\epsilon}=\left\{(z_{n})\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}k_{n}\,\middle|\,\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}<+\infty\right\}. $$

Then $A^{\epsilon}$ , equipped with the norm $\|(z_{n})\|:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}},$ is a Banach ring.

By [14, Proposition 1.2.3], the Berkovich spectrum $\mathcal{M}(A^{\epsilon})$ is homeomorphic to the Stone–Čech compactification $\beta\mathbb{N}$ . The homeomorphism is given by the map $\beta\mathbb{N}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(A^{\epsilon}),$ which sends an ultrafilter $\omega$ to the multiplicative seminorm $|\cdot|_{\omega}$ defined by $|(z_{n})|_{\omega}=\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}.$

Note that the kernel of $|\cdot|_{\omega}$ : $\ker(\omega)\coloneqq\left\{(z_{n})\in\prod k_{n}\,\middle|\,\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}=0\right\}$ is a maximal closed ideal of $A^{\epsilon}$ . Therefore, the residue field of $A^{\epsilon}$ at $\omega$ is $\mathscr{H}(\omega)=A^{\epsilon}/\ker(\omega).$ Note that for any principal ultrafilter $\omega_{n}$ , the residue field $\mathscr{H}(\omega_{n})$ is canonically identified with $k_{n}$ endowed with the rescaled norm $|\cdot|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}$ .

When $\omega$ is a non-principal ultrafilter, the following proposition summarizes some main properties of the residue field $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ .

#### Proposition 3.2.

Fix a non-principal ultrafilter $\omega$ . Then the following statements hold:

- (1) $\mathscr{H}(\omega)=\mathbb{C}$ if and only if $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ $\omega$ -almost surely and $\lim_{\omega}\epsilon_{n}>0$ ;

- (2) the value group of $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is $\mathbb{R}_{+};$

- (3) $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is algebraically closed and spherically complete.

#### Remark 3.3.

When $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ and $\epsilon_{n}=1$ , we have $\mathscr{H}(\omega)=\mathbb{C}$ . By contrast, if $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}_{p}$ and $\epsilon_{n}=1$ , then $\mathscr{H}(\omega)\neq\mathbb{C}_{p}$ , since $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is spherically complete whereas $\mathbb{C}_{p}$ is not.

#### Proof.

If $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ $\omega$ -almost surely, the assertions follow from [43, Theorems 4.9 and 4.11]. We now assume that $k_{n}$ is non-Archimedean $\omega$ -almost surely.

In this case, $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is non-Archimedean, since for every $m\in\mathbb{N}$ one has $|m|_{\omega}=\lim_{\omega}|m|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}\leq 1.$ The fact that $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is algebraically closed follows from [100, Theorem 4.1]. The spherical completeness follows from [72, Lemma 1.14].

To prove that $|\mathscr{H}(\omega)|=\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , note first that $|k_{n}|_{n}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ since $k_{n}$ is algebraically closed. Hence, for any $r\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , one can choose $z_{n}\in k_{n}$ such that $\bigl||z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}-r\bigr|<\frac{1}{n}.$ The sequence $(z_{n})$ defines an element of $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ , and we have $|(z_{n})|_{\omega}=\lim_{\omega}|z_{n}|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}=r.$ ∎

### 3.2. Continuity of dynamics on the hybrid space

#### 3.2.1. Hybrid spaces

Hybrid spaces provide a framework that interpolates between complex and non-Archimedean geometries. The origin can be traced back to the compactification of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ -character varieties by Morgan–Shalen [85], and to later constructions using $\mathbb{R}$ -trees in the work of DeMarco–McMullen [28]. The notion of hybrid space was formalized by Berkovich [15], where the choice of Banach rings introduces substantial flexibility.

Hybrid spaces provide a natural framework for studying degenerations, particularly of measures. In holomorphic dynamics, this approach was introduced by Favre [49], building on a work of Boucksom–Jonsson [18]. He showed that the equilibrium measures associated with a meromorphic family converge, in a suitable sense, to a non-Archimedean one. This result was subsequently extended by Poineau [89] to more general Banach rings, and analogous statements were obtained by Favre–Gong [43] in the setting of product Banach rings arising from rescaled complex fields.

The hybrid space approach has since found applications in a variety of contexts, including character varieties [37, 32], automorphisms of algebraic varieties [63, 64], arithmetic dynamics [100] and Diophantine geometry [78].

We now construct hybrid spaces associated with product Banach rings over various base fields.

Let $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ be the Berkovich projective line over the product Banach ring $A^{\epsilon}$ . It is a compact Hausdorff space and there exists a canonical continuous projection

$$ \pi\colon\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(A^{\epsilon})\simeq\beta\mathbb{N}. $$

For any $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ , the fiber $\pi^{-1}(\omega)$ is canonically identified with $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{\mathscr{H}(\omega)}$ . In particular, for a principal ultrafilter $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the fiber $\pi^{-1}(n)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k_{n}}$ . Thus, $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ can be regarded as a fibration whose fibers are the spaces $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k_{n}}$ and their ultrafilter limits.

#### 3.2.2. Sequential hybridation

A rational map $f\colon\mathbb{P}^{1}_{A^{\epsilon}}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ defined over $A^{\epsilon}$ is given in homogeneous coordinates by a pair of homogeneous polynomials $P,Q$ of degree $d$ whose resultant is a unit in $A^{\epsilon}$ . When $A^{\epsilon}$ is a Banach ring, then $f$ induces a continuous map $f\colon\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}\to\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ over $\mathcal{M}(A^{\epsilon})\cong\beta\mathbb{N}$ , and for any $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ , we denote by $f_{\omega}$ the restriction of $f$ on the fiber $\pi^{-1}(\omega)$ . It is a rational map of degree $d$ defined over $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ .

We now provide a canonical way to encode a sequence of rational maps

$$ (f_{n})\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(k_{n}) $$

with bad reduction into a single dynamical system over the hybrid space.

To this end, we first associate to $(f_{n})$ the resultant sequence $\epsilon(f)=(\epsilon(f_{n}))$ , defined by

$$ \epsilon(f_{n})=\bigl(-\log(|\operatorname{Res}(f_{n})|/C_{d})\bigr)^{-1}, $$

where $C_{d}=e\,\sup_{\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(\mathbb{C})}|\operatorname{Res}|$ if $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ , and $C_{d}=1$ otherwise. This quantity is finite, since $|\operatorname{Res}|$ is continuous on $\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(\mathbb{C})$ and satisfies $\lim_{f\to\partial\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(\mathbb{C})}|\operatorname{Res}(f)|=0.$

By construction, the resultant sequence $\epsilon(f)$ is adapted to $(k_{n})$ .

#### Theorem 3.4.

Let $(f_{n})\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(k_{n})$ be a sequence of rational maps with bad reduction, and let $\epsilon=(\epsilon_{n})$ be a sequence adapted to $(k_{n})$ . Assume that there exists a constant $C>0$ , independent of $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , such that $\epsilon_{n}\leq C\,\epsilon(f_{n})$ for all $n$ . Then the following statements hold:

- (1) There exists a rational map $f\in\operatorname{Rat}_{d}(A^{\epsilon})$ inducing a continuous self-map

$$ f\colon\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}} $$

such that $\pi\circ f=\pi$ , and for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ one has $f|_{\pi^{-1}(n)}=f_{n}$ under the canonical identification $\pi^{-1}(n)\simeq\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k_{n}}$ ;

- (2) For a fixed ultrafilter $\omega$ , the following holds: (a) If $\lim_{\omega}\frac{\epsilon_{n}}{\epsilon(f_{n})}=0,$ then $f_{\omega}$ has good reduction; (b) If $\lim_{\omega}\frac{\epsilon_{n}}{\epsilon(f_{n})}\neq 0,$ then $f_{\omega}$ does not have good reduction.

#### Remark 3.5.

If $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ and we suppose $|\operatorname{Res}(f_{n})|=\sup_{M\in\mathrm{PGL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})}|\operatorname{Res}(M_{n}\cdot f_{n}\cdot M_{n}^{-1})|$ , then we get the sequential hybridation in [43, Theorem 1.1].

#### Remark 3.6.

Similar results were obtained by Luo [79, Remark after Theorem 1.2] for renormalized hyperbolic spaces, and by Looper–Yap [78, §4.1] for degenerations of abelian varieties.

#### Proof.

We write $f_{n}=[P_{n}\colon Q_{n}]$ , and normalize the coefficients of $P_{n}$ and $Q_{n}$ so that the maximum modulus of their coefficients is equal to $1$ . We may suppose $C>1.$ Note that

$$ \displaystyle|\operatorname{Res}(P_{n},Q_{n})|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}\in\left[e^{-(C+C|\log C_{d}|)},e^{(C+C|\log C_{d}|)}\right] $$

It follows that $P=(P_{n})$ and $Q=(Q_{n})$ are homogeneous polynomials with coefficients in $A^{\epsilon}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(P,Q)$ is a unit. Consequently, $f=(f_{n})$ defines an endomorphism of degree $d$ of $\mathbb{P}^{1}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ . By construction, (1) holds.

If $\mathscr{H}(\omega)=\mathbb{C}$ , then Proposition 3.2(1) implies that $\lim_{\omega}\epsilon_{n}>0.$ Hence only case (b) can occur, and by convention $f_{\omega}$ does not have good reduction. Now assume that $\mathscr{H}(\omega)$ is non-Archimedean. Note that

$$ |\operatorname{Res}(f_{\omega})|=\lim_{\omega}|\operatorname{Res}(f_{n})|_{n}^{\epsilon_{n}}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lim_{\omega}\frac{\epsilon_{n}}{\epsilon(f_{n})}=0. $$

Therefore, $f_{\omega}$ has good reduction if and only if $\lim_{\omega}\frac{\epsilon_{n}}{\epsilon(f_{n})}=0.$ ∎

#### 3.2.3. Continuity of energy pairings

Note that for any $f\in\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(A^{\epsilon})$ and any $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ , the equilibrium measure $\mu_{f_{\omega}}$ can be regarded as a Radon probability measure on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ supported on $\pi^{-1}(\omega)$ . One can show that the equilibrium measure depends continuously on $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ . The proof follows the same strategy as in [43, Theorem 6.8] in the case $k_{n}=\mathbb{C}$ .

#### Theorem 3.7.

Let $f\in\mathrm{Rat}_{d}(A^{\epsilon})$ for some $d\geq 2$ . The family of equilibrium measures $\bigl(\mu_{f_{\omega}}\bigr)_{\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}}$ defines a continuous family of positive measures on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ ; that is, for every continuous function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ , the map

$$ \omega\longmapsto\int\varphi\,d\mu_{f_{\omega}} $$

is continuous on $\beta\mathbb{N}$ .

The continuity of equilibrium measures implies the continuity of the rescaled energy pairings.

#### Theorem 3.8.

Let $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ be two integers. Let $f\in\operatorname{Rat}_{d_{1}}(A^{\varepsilon})$ and $g\in\operatorname{Rat}_{d_{2}}(A^{\varepsilon})$ . For each $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ , define

$$ \epsilon(\omega)=\begin{cases}\epsilon_{n},&\text{if }\omega\text{ is the principal ultrafilter }\omega_{n},\\
1,&\text{if }\omega\text{ is non-principal}.\end{cases} $$

Then the rescaled energy pairings

$$ \epsilon(\omega)\,\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle $$

depend continuously on $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $f=[P:Q]$ and $g=[U:V]$ be homogeneous representations of $f$ and $g$ , respectively. Define $\gamma_{f}\coloneqq\frac{1}{d_{1}}\log\frac{\max\{|P|,|Q|\}}{\max\{|z_{0}|^{d_{1}},|z_{1}|^{d_{1}}\}},$ and $\gamma_{g}\coloneqq\frac{1}{d_{2}}\log\frac{\max\{|U|,|V|\}}{\max\{|z_{0}|^{d_{2}},|z_{1}|^{d_{2}}\}}.$ Associated to these functions, set

$$ \varphi_{f}\coloneqq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{d_{1}^{k}}\,\gamma_{f}\circ f^{k},\qquad\varphi_{g}\coloneqq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{d_{2}^{k}}\,\gamma_{g}\circ g^{k}. $$

With these definitions, $\varphi_{f}$ and $\varphi_{g}$ are continuous functions on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{A^{\epsilon}}$ , and they satisfy

$$ \mu_{f_{\omega}}=\delta_{x_{g}}+\frac{1}{\epsilon(\omega)}\,\Delta\varphi_{f}\big|_{\pi^{-1}(\omega)},\qquad\mu_{g_{\omega}}=\delta_{x_{g}}+\frac{1}{\epsilon(\omega)}\,\Delta\varphi_{g}\big|_{\pi^{-1}(\omega)}. $$

Combining these identities with Proposition 2.2, we obtain

$$ \epsilon(\omega)\,\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle=-\int_{\pi^{-1}(\omega)}(\varphi_{f}-\varphi_{g})\,d(\mu_{f_{\omega}}-\mu_{g_{\omega}}). $$

On the other hand, by Theorem 3.7, the families of measures $(\mu_{f_{\omega}})$ and $(\mu_{g_{\omega}})$ depend continuously on $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ . Consequently, the quantity $\epsilon(\omega)\,\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle$ varies continuously with $\omega$ .∎

## 4. Polynomial Trees

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed, complete non-Archimedean field, possibly of positive characteristic. Given a polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ , we will construct a subset $T_{f}\subseteq\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , inspired by DeMarco–McMullen’s construction [28].

When $f$ is a tame polynomial (e.g. when the residue characteristic of $k$ is $0$ or at least $d+1$ ), we will endow $T_{f}$ with a distinguished set of vertices so that $f$ acts on $T_{f}$ simplicially.

### 4.1. Polynomial Dynamics

#### 4.1.1. Image of disks

We recall some basic facts concerning the images of disks under polynomial maps and refer the reader to [13] for a detailed discussion.

For $a\in k$ and $r>0$ , we define the open and closed disks in $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ as

$$ D(a,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\mid|z-a|_{x}<r\}\quad\text{and}\quad\bar{D}(a,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\mid|z-a|_{x}\leq r\}. $$

If $r\in|k^{\times}|$ , then $D(a,r)$ is said to be a rational open disk and $\bar{D}(a,r)$ is a rational closed disk. If $r\notin|k^{\times}|$ , we have $D(a,r)=\bar{D}(a,r)$ , and such a disk is called an irrational disk.

Let $D=D(a,r)$ or $\bar{D}(a,r)$ be a disk. We recall the notion of Weierstrass degree of $f$ on $D$ : Write the expansion of $f$ around $a$ as $f(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}(z-a)^{i}.$ If $D$ is a rational closed disk (resp. a rational open or irrational disk), the Weierstrass degree of $f$ on $D$ , denoted by $\mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f$ , is the largest (resp. the smallest) integer $0\leq\delta\leq d$ such that

$$ |a_{\delta}|r^{\delta}=\max_{0\leq i\leq d}\{|a_{i}|r^{i}\}. $$

By [13, Corollary 3.18], the image of a disk under $f$ is again a disk. More precisely, we have

$$ \displaystyle f\bigl(\bar{D}(a,r)\bigr)=\bar{D}\left(f(a),\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\{|a_{i}|r^{i}\}\right), \displaystyle f\bigl(D(a,r)\bigr)=D\left(f(a),\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\{|a_{i}|r^{i}\}\right). $$

In particular, $f$ maps a disk to a disk of the same type: it is open, rational closed, or irrational if and only if its image is of the same type. Moreover, by [13, Theorem 3.15], $f$ sends $D$ onto $f(D)$ with degree $\mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f$ , counted with multiplicities.

To each disk $D=D(a,r)$ or $\bar{D}(a,r)$ , one associates a type II or type III point $x=\zeta(a,r)$ , according to whether $r\in|k^{\times}|$ or not. By [13, Proposition 7.6], $f$ sends this type II or type III point to the point associated with the image disk, namely,

$$ \displaystyle f(x)=\zeta\left(f(a),\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\{|a_{i}|r^{i}\}\right). $$

If $D$ is open or irrational, then $x$ is the unique boundary point of $D$ . If $D$ is closed or irrational, the local degree $\deg_{x}f$ coincides with the Weierstrass degree of $f$ on $\bar{D}(a,r)$ , see [13, §7.4].

Let $D=D(a,r)$ or $\bar{D}(a,r)$ be a disk. Then $f^{-1}(D)$ is a disjoint union of disks. More precisely, we have the following proposition:

#### Proposition 4.1.

Let $x_{i}=\zeta(a_{i},r_{i})$ be the preimages of the point $\zeta(a,r)$ .

- (1) If $D=D(a,r)$ is open, let $D_{i,j}$ denote the connected components of $f^{-1}(D)$ with boundary point $x_{i}=\zeta(a_{i},r_{i})$ . Then, $D_{i,j}$ are disjoint disks and $\displaystyle f^{-1}(D)=\bigsqcup_{i,j}D_{i,j},\qquad\text{with }\sum_{j}\mathrm{wdeg}_{D_{i,j}}f=\deg_{x_{i}}f;$

- (2) If $D$ is a rational closed or an irrational disk $\bar{D}(a,r)$ , then

$$ f^{-1}(D)=\bigsqcup_{i}\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i}),\qquad\text{with }\mathrm{wdeg}_{\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i})}f=\deg_{x_{i}}f. $$

#### Lemma 4.2.

If $D_{1}\subsetneq D_{2}$ are two rational closed disks or two irrational disks, then $f(D_{1})\subsetneq f(D_{2})$ .

#### Proof.

Write $D_{i}=\bar{D}(a,r_{i})$ with $0<r_{1}<r_{2},$ and $f(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}(z-a)^{i}.$ Since $|k|$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ ,

$$ f(D_{1})=f(\bar{D}(a,r_{1}))=D(f(a),\max_{1\leq i\leq d}|a_{i}|r_{1}^{i})\subsetneq D(f(a),\max_{1\leq i\leq d}|a_{i}|r_{2}^{i})=f(D_{2}), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.1.

(1) Let $\vec{v}$ denote the tangent direction at $x$ represented by the disk $D$ . For each $x_{i}$ , let $\vec{v}_{i,j}$ be the tangent directions at $x_{i}$ such that $T_{x_{i}}f(\vec{v}_{i,j})=\vec{v},$ and let $D_{i,j}$ be the disk associated with $\vec{v}_{i,j}$ . By [3, Proposition 9.41], we have $f(D_{i,j})=D.$ Since $\partial D_{i,j}\subset f^{-1}(\partial D)$ , it follows that $D_{i,j}$ is a connected component of $f^{-1}(D)$ . Therefore, $f^{-1}(D)=\bigsqcup_{i,j}D_{i,j}.$

(2) Since $f(x_{i})=x$ , we have $f\bigl(\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i})\bigr)=\bar{D}(a,r).$ Hence, $f^{-1}(D)\supset\bigsqcup_{i}\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i}).$ By Lemma 4.2, since the disks $\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i})$ have the same image $\bar{D}(a,r)$ under $f$ , they are pairwise disjoint.

Note that $\deg_{x_{i}}f=\mathrm{wdeg}_{\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i})}f,$ and $\sum_{i}\deg_{x_{i}}f=d.$ Since any point admits $d$ preimages counted with multiplicity, we conclude $f^{-1}(D)=\bigsqcup_{i}\bar{D}(a_{i},r_{i}).$ ∎

#### 4.1.2. Dynamical Green’s function

We refer the reader to [42, §2.3] for a detailed discussion of the dynamical Green’s function. Here we briefly recall some basic notions.

Let $f(z)=a_{d}z^{d}+\cdots+a_{0}\in k[z]$ be a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ with $a_{d}\neq 0$ . It induces a continuous self-map $f:\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ on the Berkovich analytification of the affine line.

We define the filled-in Julia set of $f$ as

$$ \mathcal{K}_{f}=\left\{z\in\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\,\middle|\,|f^{n}(z)|\text{ remains bounded as }n\to\infty\right\}. $$

Set

$$ C_{f}=\max_{0\leq i<d}\Bigl\{1,\;\Bigl(\tfrac{|a_{i}|}{|a_{d}|}\Bigr)^{\!\frac{1}{d-i}},\;\Bigl(\tfrac{2}{|a_{d}|}\Bigr)^{\!\frac{1}{d-1}}\Bigr\}. $$

For any $|z|>C_{f}$ , one has $|a_{d}|\,|z|^{d}>|a_{i}|\,|z|^{i}$ for all $i<d$ . By the strong triangle inequality, this implies $|f(z)|=|a_{d}z^{d}|>2|z|.$ Iterating this estimate yields

$$ \displaystyle|f^{n}(z)|=|a_{d}|^{1+d+\cdots+d^{n-1}}|z|^{d^{n}}>2^{n}|z|\longrightarrow\infty. $$

It follows that the basin of attraction of infinity, defined as

$$ \Omega_{f}=\left\{z\in\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\,\middle|\,|f^{n}(z)|\to\infty\text{ as }n\to\infty\right\}, $$

is an open set whose complement is precisely $\cal{K}_{f}$ . Note that all periodic points in $k$ are contained in $\cal{K}_{f}$ . Consequently, $\cal{K}_{f}$ is a non-empty compact subset of $\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ contained in $\{|z|\leq C_{f}\}$ . Both $\cal{K}_{f}$ and $\Omega_{f}$ are totally invariant under $f$ , meaning $f^{-1}(\cal{K}_{f})=f(\cal{K}_{f})=\cal{K}_{f}$ and likewise for $\Omega_{f}$ . Moreover, the Julia set $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ is the boundary of $\mathcal{K}_{f}$ .

Observe that the function $\frac{1}{d}\log^{+}|f(z)|-\log^{+}|z|$ extends to a continuous function on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ . Consequently, there exists a constant $C\geq 0$ such that $\left|\frac{1}{d}\log^{+}|f(z)|-\log^{+}|z|\right|\leq C$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}.$ It follows that the sequence of functions $\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log^{+}|f^{n}(z)|$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}$ to a continuous function

$$ G_{f}(z)\coloneqq\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log^{+}|f^{n}(z)|, $$

called the Green function of $f$ .

We summarize some basic properties of the Green function in the following proposition.

#### Proposition 4.3.

Let $f(z)=a_{d}z^{d}+\cdots$ be a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ . Then:

- (1) $G_{f}\circ f=d\,G_{f}$ ;

- (2) if $|z|>C_{f}$ , one has $G_{f}(z)=\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}+\log|z|;$

- (3) $G_{f}(z)=0$ if and only if $z$ belongs to the filled-in Julia set $\cal{K}_{f}$ ;

- (4) for any affine map $L\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ , $G_{f}(L(z))=G_{L^{-1}\circ f\circ L}(z).$

#### Proof.

(1) By definition of the Green function,

$$ G_{f}(f(z))=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log^{+}|f^{n+1}(z)|=d\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n+1}}\log^{+}|f^{n+1}(z)|=d\,G_{f}(z). $$

(2) This follows directly from (4.3).

(3) If $z\in\cal{K}_{f}$ , then the sequence $|f^{n}(z)|$ is bounded, and hence $G_{f}(z)=0.$ Conversely, suppose $G_{f}(z)=0$ and $z\notin\cal{K}_{f}$ . Then $|f^{n}(z)|\to\infty$ , so for $n$ sufficiently large,

$$ |f^{n}(z)|>\max\!\left\{C_{f},\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}\right)\right\}. $$

By (1) and (2), this implies $d^{n}G_{f}(z)=G_{f}(f^{n}(z))>0,$ which leads to a contradiction.

(4) Let $L(z)=az+b$ . Note that $z$ belongs to the filled-in Julia set of $L^{-1}\circ f\circ L$ if and only if $L(z)$ belongs to the filled-in Julia set of $f$ . By (3), this yields $G_{L^{-1}\circ f\circ L}(z)=0$ iff $G_{f}(L(z))=0.$ Now assume $z\notin\cal{K}_{L^{-1}\circ f\circ L}$ , so that $|L^{-1}\circ f^{n}\circ L(z)|\to\infty.$ Note that $\log|L^{-1}(z)|=\log|z|+\log|a^{-1}|$ for $|z|$ large enough. Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle G_{L^{-1}\circ f\circ L}(z) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log|L^{-1}\circ f^{n}\circ L(z)| \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{d^{n}}\log|f^{n}(L(z))|=G_{f}(L(z)), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

#### 4.1.3. Sublevel set of the Green function

Now set $M_{f}=\max_{|z|\leq C_{f}+1}\{G_{f}(z),\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}+\log(C_{f}+1)\}$ . Then for any $t>M_{f}$ , Proposition 4.3(2) implies

$$ \displaystyle\{G_{f}<t\}=\Bigl\{\log|z|<t-\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}\Bigr\}, $$

which is an open disk. Moreover, we obtain the following proposition.

#### Proposition 4.4.

For any $t>0$ , the sublevel set $\{G_{f}<t\}$ is a finite disjoint union of open disks. Moreover, if $x$ is a boundary point of a connected component of $\{G_{f}<t\}$ , then $G_{f}(x)=t.$

#### Proof.

Choose an integer $n$ sufficiently large so that $td^{n}>M_{f}$ . By (4.4), we have

$$ \{G_{f}<td^{n}\}=\Bigl\{\log|z|<td^{n}-\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}\Bigr\}. $$

This set is an open disk whose boundary point is $x_{0}=\zeta\!\left(0,\exp\Bigl(td^{n}-\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}\Bigr)\right).$ By construction, $|x_{0}|=\exp\!\Bigl(td^{n}-\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}\Bigr)>C_{f},$ and it follows from Proposition 4.3(2) that $G_{f}(x_{0})=td^{n}.$

Since $\{G_{f}<t\}=f^{-n}\{G_{f}<td^{n}\},$ by Proposition 4.1, $\{G_{f}<t\}$ is a finite disjoint union of open disks, and $x$ belongs to $f^{-n}(x_{0})$ . Thus, we have

$$ G_{f}(x)=\frac{1}{d^{n}}G_{f}(f^{n}(x))=\frac{1}{d^{n}}G_{f}(x_{0})=t, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

### 4.2. Basic properties of the convex hull

#### 4.2.1. Convex hull of the Julia set with infinity

Fix a polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ over $k$ . Let $T_{f}$ denote the set of points in $\mathbb{A}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_{k}\setminus\mathcal{K}_{f}$ that belong to the convex hull of $\mathcal{J}_{f}\cup\{\infty\}$ . As a connected subset of $\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ , the set $T_{f}$ carries a natural $\mathbb{R}$ -tree structure.

The following proposition suggests that one can describe a point in $T_{f}$ using the Green function.

#### Proposition 4.5.

Let $x\in\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ . Then $x\in T_{f}$ if and only if $x$ is a boundary point of the sublevel set $\{G_{f}<t\}$ for some $t>0$ .

#### Lemma 4.6.

Let $x_{0}=\zeta(z_{0},r_{0})$ be a point in the Julia set of $f$ . Then the following statements hold:

- (1) $\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{0})$ is contained in the filled-in Julia set $\cal{K}_{f}$ ;

- (2) the Green function $G_{f}$ induces a strictly increasing, continuous, and surjective map

$$ [r_{0},\infty)\longrightarrow[0,\infty),\qquad r\longmapsto G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r)); $$

- (3) for every $r>r_{0}$ , $D(z_{0},r)$ is a connected component of $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r))\}.$

#### Proof.

We first prove that $G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r))$ is non-decreasing in $r$ . Let $x_{i}=\zeta(z_{0},r_{i})$ with $r_{1}<r_{2}$ . Then for every integer $n\geq 1$ , one has

$$ |f^{n}(x_{1})|=\sup_{z\in\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{1})}|f^{n}(z)|\leq\sup_{z\in\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{2})}|f^{n}(z)|=|f^{n}(x_{2})|. $$

Thus $G_{f}(x_{1})\leq G_{f}(x_{2})$ . Since $x_{0}\in\mathcal{J}_{f}$ , it follows that $x_{0}\in\mathcal{K}_{f}$ . By Proposition 4.3(3), we have $G_{f}(x_{0})=0$ . Consequently, for all $z\in\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{0})$ , it holds that $G_{f}(z)\leq G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r_{0}))=G_{f}(x_{0})=0$ , and hence $\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{0})\subset\mathcal{K}_{f}.$

To prove the second statement, we claim that $(x_{0},\infty)\cap\mathcal{K}_{f}=\varnothing.$ Indeed, if there exists $r_{1}>r_{0}$ such that $\zeta(z_{0},r_{1})\in\mathcal{K}_{f}$ , then the above argument implies $D(z_{0},r_{1})\subset\mathcal{K}_{f}$ . In particular, $x_{0}\in D(z_{0},r_{1})$ would belong to the interior of $\mathcal{K}_{f}$ , contradicting the assumption that $x_{0}\in\mathcal{J}_{f}$ .

Now let $x_{i}=\zeta(z_{0},r_{i})$ with $r_{0}<r_{1}<r_{2}<\infty$ . For any integer $n\geq 1$ , by (4.1) we have $f^{n}(x_{i})=\zeta(f^{n}(z_{0}),r_{i,n})$ with $r_{1,n}<r_{2,n}.$ Since $z_{0}$ has bounded forward orbit while $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ escape to infinity, there exists $n$ sufficiently large such that $|f^{n}(z_{0})|\leq C_{f}<r_{1,n}<r_{2,n},$ where $C_{f}$ is introduced in (4.2). By Proposition 4.3(2), we obtain

$$ G_{f}(f^{n}(x_{i}))=\frac{\log|a_{d}|}{d-1}+\log r_{i,n}. $$

Therefore, $G_{f}(x_{1})=\frac{1}{d^{n}}G_{f}(f^{n}(x_{1}))<\frac{1}{d^{n}}G_{f}(f^{n}(x_{2}))=G_{f}(x_{2}),$ which proves strict monotonicity. Continuity follows from the continuity of $G_{f}$ , and surjectivity follows from the fact that $\lim_{z\to\infty}G_{f}(z)=+\infty.$

Finally, we prove the last statement. Since $\partial D(z_{0},r)=\zeta(z_{0},r)$ , it suffices to prove $D(z_{0},r)\subset\{G_{f}<G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r))\}.$ Let $p\in D(z_{0},r)$ , by strict monotonicity, one has $G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},|p-z_{0}|))<G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r)).$ Since $p\in D(z_{0},|p-z_{0}|)$ , we have $G_{f}(p)\leq G_{f}\bigl(\zeta(z_{0},|p-z_{0}|)\bigr)<G_{f}\bigl(\zeta(z_{0},r)\bigr),$ which shows that $p\in\{G_{f}<G_{f}(\zeta(z_{0},r))\}.$ ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.5.

Let $x=\zeta(a,r)\in\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ be a point belonging to the convex hull. Then there exists $z_{0}\in\mathcal{J}_{f}$ such that $x$ lies on the segment $I=[z_{0},\infty).$ Write $x=\zeta(z_{0},r)$ . By Lemma 4.6(3), $D(z_{0},r)$ is a connected component of $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(x)\}.$ Hence $x\in\partial\{G_{f}<G_{f}(x)\}.$

To show the converse, it suffices to prove that the closed disk $\bar{D}(a,r)$ contains a point in the Julia set.

Choose an integer $n\geq 1$ such that $G_{f}(f^{n}(x))=d^{n}G_{f}(x)>M_{f},$ where $M_{f}$ is as in (4.4). Then the sublevel set $\{G_{f}<d^{n}G_{f}(x)\}=f^{n}(\{G_{f}<G_{f}(x)\})$ is a disk whose unique boundary point is $f^{n}(x)$ , which is defined by the disk $f^{n}(\bar{D}(a,r)).$ Thus, we obtain $\{G_{f}<d^{n}G_{f}(x)\}\subset f^{n}(\bar{D}(a,r)).$

Since every point in the Julia set satisfies $G_{f}=0$ , we have $\mathcal{J}_{f}\subset f^{n}(\bar{D}(a,r)).$ As the Julia set is backward invariant, it follows that there exists a point of $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ contained in $\bar{D}(a,r)$ . Therefore, $x$ belongs to the convex hull. ∎

#### 4.2.2. Restrict polynomial map to the convex hull

Since $G_{f}\circ f=dG_{f}$ , one has $f^{-1}(\{G_{f}<t\})=\{G_{f}<\frac{t}{d}\}$ and $f(\{G_{f}<t\})=\{G_{f}<td\}$ . It then follows from Proposition 4.5 that $T_{f}$ is totally invariant under $f$ : $f^{-1}(T_{f})=f(T_{f})=T_{f}$ .

Moreover, one can endow $T_{f}$ with additional geometric data. For any $x=\zeta(a,r)\in T_{f}$ , one can associate to it the closed disk $D_{x}\coloneqq\bar{D}(a,r).$ We define the mass of $x$ by

$$ \mu_{f}(x):=\mu_{f}(D_{x}), $$

where $\mu_{f}$ is the equilibrium measure of $f$ .

Given a segment $e=[x_{1},x_{2}]\subset T_{f}$ with $D_{x_{1}}\subset D_{x_{2}}$ , let $r_{i}$ be the radius of $D_{x_{i}}$ for $i=1,2$ . We define the length of $e$ by

$$ l(e)=\log\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}. $$

The following proposition summarizes how the mass and the length behave under $f$ .

#### Proposition 4.7.

Let $x\in T_{f}$ . The following statements hold:

- (1) One has $f(D_{x})=D_{f(x)}$ .

- (2) For all sufficiently large $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , one has $\mu_{f}(f^{m}(x))=1.$

- (3) For every vertex $x\in T_{f}$ , one has

$$ \mu_{f}(f(x))=\frac{d\mu_{f}(x)}{\deg_{x}f}. $$

- (4) Let $e=[x_{1},x_{2}]$ such that $D_{x_{1}}\subset D_{x_{2}}$ . If the interval $(x_{1},x_{2})$ contains no branch points of $T_{f}$ , then:

$$ l\bigl(f(e)\bigr)=\deg_{x_{1}}f\cdot l(e). $$

In particular, $l(e)\leq l\bigl(f(e)\bigr)\leq d\cdot l(e).$

#### Proof.

(1) The first statement follows from §4.1.1.

(2) Note that for a sufficiently large $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , equation (4.4) implies that the set $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(f^{m}(x))\}$ is the disk $D_{f^{m}(x)}$ . Since the measure $\mu_{f}$ is supported on the Julia set, and Proposition 4.3(3) establishes that the filled-in Julia set is the set $\{G_{f}=0\}$ , it follows that the support of $\mu_{f}$ is entirely contained within $D_{f^{m}(x)}$ . Consequently, we have $\mu_{f}(D_{f^{m}(x)})=1$ .

(3) We pick $\epsilon>0$ , and choose a compact subset $K_{\epsilon}\subset D_{f(x)}$ satisfying $\mu_{f}\left(D_{f(x)}\setminus K_{\epsilon}\right)<\epsilon.$ Let $K\coloneqq f^{-1}(K_{\epsilon})\cap D_{x}.$ Since $f_{*}\mu_{f}=\mu_{f}$ , we obtain

$$ \mu_{f}(D_{x}\setminus K)\leq\mu_{f}\left(f^{-1}(D_{f(x)}\setminus K_{\epsilon})\right)=\mu_{f}\left(D_{f(x)}\setminus K_{\epsilon}\right)<\epsilon. $$

Let $0\leq\varphi_{\epsilon}\leq 1$ be a continuous function supported in $D_{x}$ such that $\varphi_{\epsilon}\equiv 1$ on $K$ . Then $f_{*}\varphi_{\epsilon}=\deg_{x}f$ on $K_{\epsilon}$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{f}(D_{x})-\epsilon \displaystyle\leq\int\varphi_{\epsilon}\,d\mu_{f}=\frac{1}{d}\int f_{*}\varphi_{\epsilon}\,d\mu_{f}\leq\frac{\deg_{x}f}{d}\mu_{f}(K_{\epsilon})+\epsilon, \displaystyle\mu_{f}(D_{x}) \displaystyle\geq\int\varphi_{\epsilon}\,d\mu_{f}=\frac{1}{d}\int f_{*}\varphi_{\epsilon}\,d\mu_{f}\geq\frac{\deg_{x}f}{d}\mu_{f}(K_{\epsilon}). $$

Letting $\epsilon\to 0$ , we obtain the desired result.

(4) By construction, there exists a point $x_{0}=\zeta(z_{0},r_{0})$ in the Julia set such that $x_{1}\in[x_{0},x_{2}].$ Write $x_{i}=\zeta(z_{0},r_{i})$ with $r_{0}<r_{1}<r_{2}$ .

Since $(x_{1},x_{2})$ does not contain any branch point of $T_{f}$ , it follows that $x_{1}$ is the unique preimage of $f(x_{1})$ in $D(z_{0},r_{2})$ . Hence $\deg_{x_{1}}f$ equals the Weierstrass degree of $f$ on $D(z_{0},r_{2})$ . It then follows from [13, Theorem 3.33] that $f$ maps the annulus $D(z_{0},r_{2})\setminus\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{1})$ onto $f(D(z_{0},r_{2}))\setminus f(\bar{D}(z_{0},r_{1})),$ and that $l\bigl(f(e)\bigr)=\deg_{x_{1}}f\cdot l(e).$ In particular, since $1\leq\deg_{x_{1}}f\leq d$ , we obtain $l(e)\leq l\bigl(f(e)\bigr)\leq d\cdot l(e).$ ∎

### 4.3. Simplicial tree for tame polynomials

Recall that a simplicial tree $T$ is a nonempty, connected, locally finite, $1$ -dimensional simplicial complex without cycles. We denote by $V$ the set of vertices and by $E$ the set of (unoriented, closed) edges (see e.g., [28, §2]).

In this section, we restrict our attention to tame polynomials. We endow the $\mathbb{R}$ -tree $T_{f}$ with a simplicial tree structure such that the map $f\colon T_{f}\to T_{f}$ is simplicial; that is, $f$ maps each edge $e=[v_{1},v_{2}]$ onto the edge $[f(v_{1}),f(v_{2})]$ .

#### Remark 4.8.

The tameness assumption is imposed to guarantee that the grand orbit of the branch points of $T_{f}$ is discrete, which is necessary for defining the edges. It is not clear whether this property holds for arbitrary polynomials.

#### 4.3.1. Tame polynomials

The notion of a tame polynomial was introduced by Trucco [96] for polynomials for which wild ramification does not occur.

Recall that the ramification locus of a polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ is defined by $\mathcal{R}_{f}\coloneqq\{\,x\in\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}\mid\deg_{x}f\geq 2\}.$ Observe that the set of finite critical points $\mathrm{Crit}(f)\coloneqq\{\,x\in k\mid f^{\prime}(x)=0\}$ is contained in $\mathcal{R}_{f}$ . For a thorough study of the ramification locus, we refer the reader to [39, 40].

Let $\mathbb{H}_{k}=\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,an}\setminus\mathbb{P}^{1}(k)$ be the hyperbolic space over $k$ . If $\mathcal{R}_{f}\cap\mathbb{H}_{k}$ is a locally finite open subtree, then we say that $f$ is a tame polynomial. Let $p$ denote the residue characteristic of $\tilde{k}$ . By [39, Proposition 7.11], the polynomial $f$ is tame if and only if either $p=0$ or $p>0$ and $p\nmid\mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f$ for every disk $D\subseteq\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}.$ In particular, if $p=0$ or $p\geq d+1$ , then $f$ is tame.

Moreover, the following proposition holds; see [96, § 2.6] and [70, § 2.2].

#### Proposition 4.9.

Let $f$ be a tame polynomial. Then for every disk $D$ , the number of critical points in $D$ (counted with multiplicity) is equal to $\mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f-1.$ In particular, $\mathcal{R}_{f}\cup\{\infty\}$ is the convex hull of $\mathrm{Crit}(f)\cup\{\infty\}$ .

#### Proof.

By [13, Proposition 3.9], one has

$$ \mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f=\mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f^{\prime}+1. $$

Moreover, by [13, Theorem 3.13(a)], there are exactly $\mathrm{wdeg}_{D}f-1$ critical points in $D$ , counted with multiplicity. Moreover, $\deg_{x}f\geq 2$ if and only if the associated closed ball contains a critical point. Thus $\cal{R}_{f}\cup\{\infty\}$ is the convex hull of $\mathrm{Crit}(f)\cup\{\infty\}$ . ∎

#### 4.3.2. The simplicial tree structure on $T_{f}$

The construction of the simplicial tree relies on the following characterization of branch points of $T_{f}$ using the values of Green function at critical points.

#### Proposition 4.10.

A point $x$ is a branch point of $T_{f}$ if and only if there exists a point $c^{\prime}\in D_{x}$ lying in the backward orbit of a critical point of $f$ such that $G_{f}(x)=G_{f}(c^{\prime}).$

#### Proof.

Up to replacing $f$ by an iterate, we may assume that $D:=\{G_{f}<d\,G_{f}(x)\}$ is an open disk. Let $D_{i}$ , $1\leq i\leq m$ , be the connected components of $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(x)\}$ whose boundary is equal to $x$ .

Denote by $d_{i}$ the Weierstrass degree of $f$ on $D_{i}$ . By Proposition 4.1(1), we have $\deg_{x}f=\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{i}.$ Moreover, by Proposition 4.9, the number of critical points in $D_{x}\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}D_{i}$ is equal to

$$ (\deg_{x}f-1)-\sum_{i=1}^{m}(d_{i}-1)=m-1. $$

Since $x$ is a branch point if and only if $m\geq 2$ , this is equivalent to the existence of a critical point $c$ in $D_{x}$ such that $G_{f}(x)=G_{f}(c).$ ∎

We define $V_{f}$ to be the set of points $x\in\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1,\mathrm{an}}$ that belong to the grand orbit of a branch point of $T_{f}$ . Since every branch point of $T_{f}$ is of type II and $f$ preserves point types, it follows that every $v\in V_{f}$ is also a type II point.

Since $G_{f}\circ f=dG_{f}$ , Proposition 4.10 implies that

$$ G_{f}(V_{f})\subset\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\mathbb{N}\\
f^{\prime}(c)=0\end{subarray}}d^{n}G_{f}(c), $$

which is a discrete subset of $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ .

It follows that $T_{f}$ admits a decomposition into segments between successive vertices. Denote by $E_{f}$ the collection of closed intervals $[v_{1},v_{2}]$ such that $v_{1},v_{2}\in V_{f}$ and

$$ (v_{1},v_{2})\cap V_{f}=\varnothing. $$

By construction, $V_{f}$ contains all branch points of $T_{f}$ ; thus, the interiors of distinct intervals in $E_{f}$ are disjoint. Furthermore, Proposition 4.4 implies that each sublevel set $\{G_{f}<t\}$ has only finitely many boundary points. It follows that every vertex $v\in V_{f}$ is adjacent to only finitely many intervals in $E_{f}$ . Therefore, the $\mathbb{R}$ -tree $T_{f}$ , equipped with vertex set $V_{f}$ and edge set $E_{f}$ , is a simplicial tree.

Moreover, the induced map $f\colon T_{f}\to T_{f}$ is simplicial by construction.

#### Proposition 4.11.

For any $l\geq 1$ , the polynomial tree $T_{f}$ coincides with $T_{f^{l}}$ as a simplicial tree.

#### Proof.

Since the Julia set is invariant under iteration, the underlying $\mathbb{R}$ -trees $T_{f}$ and $T_{f^{l}}$ coincide. It remains only to prove that their vertex sets $V_{f}$ and $V_{f^{l}}$ are the same. Recall that $G_{f}=G_{f^{l}}$ . Thus $T_{f}$ and $T_{f^{l}}$ have the same set $S$ of branch points. From the definition of the vertex set, the inclusion $V_{f^{l}}\subset V_{f}$ is immediate, since any relation involving iterates of $f^{l}$ is also a relation involving iterates of $f$ . Conversely, let $v\in V_{f}$ . By definition, there exists a branch point $x\in S$ and integers $m,n\geq 1$ such that $f^{m}(v)=f^{n}(x).$ Applying a sufficiently high iterate of $f$ to both sides if necessary, we may assume that $m$ is divisible by $l$ . Thus we may write $m=lk_{1}$ for some $k_{1}\geq 1$ . Similarly, write $n=lk_{2}-r,$ where $k_{2}\geq 1$ and $0\leq r\leq l-1$ . Choose $x^{\prime}\in f^{-r}(x)$ . Since preimages of branch points are again branch points of $T_{f}$ , we have $x^{\prime}\in S$ . Therefore

$$ (f^{l})^{k_{1}}(v)=f^{lk_{1}}(v)=f^{lk_{2}-r}(x)=f^{lk_{2}}(x^{\prime})=(f^{l})^{k_{2}}(x^{\prime}). $$

By the definition of the vertex set for $f^{l}$ , this implies $v\in V_{f^{l}}$ . Hence $V_{f}\subset V_{f^{l}}$ . Combining the two inclusions, we obtain $V_{f}=V_{f^{l}}.$ ∎

## 5. Non-Archimedean Rigidity

In this section, we fix a non-Archimedean field $k$ with residue characteristic $0$ . We will fix two polynomials $f$ and $g$ of degree at least $2$ such that their Julia sets coincide. By [46, §4] and [3, Theorem 10.91], this condition is equivalent to the equality of their equilibrium measures, $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ , and also equivalent to the equality of their Green functions, $G_{f}=G_{g}$ .

### 5.1. Comparison of polynomials with identical trees

Since the residue characteristic of $k$ is $0$ , $f$ and $g$ are automatically tame.

To establish the rigidity of Julia sets, we first assume that $f$ and $g$ have the same degree $d\geq 2.$ Our strategy is to compare the induced actions of $f$ and $g$ on their associated polynomial trees.

The first step is the following proposition, which shows the induced simplicial trees coincide with each other.

#### Proposition 5.1.

Let $f,g$ be two polynomials of degree $d\geq 2$ such that $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}$ . Then the associated polynomial trees $T_{f}$ and $T_{g}$ coincide as simplicial trees.

#### Proof.

By construction, $T_{f}=T_{g}$ as $\mathbb{R}$ -trees. In particular, they have the same branch points. It therefore suffices to show that their vertex sets agree. Let $v\in V_{f}$ , then there exist integers $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and a branch point $v_{\star}$ such that $f^{m}(v)=f^{n}(v_{\star}).$ Choosing $m$ sufficiently large, we may also suppose that $D=\{G_{f}<G_{f}(f^{m}(v))\}$ is a disk. Since $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}$ , one obtains $G_{f}=G_{g}$ . The equality of degrees implies $G_{f}\circ f^{l}=d^{l}G_{f}=d^{l}G_{g}=G_{g}\circ g^{l}.$ Therefore,

$$ G_{g}\bigl(g^{m}(v)\bigr)=G_{f}\bigl(f^{m}(v)\bigr)=G_{f}(f^{n}(v_{\star}))=G_{g}\bigl(g^{n}(v_{\star})\bigr) $$

and $D=\{G_{g}<G_{g}(g^{m}(v))\}.$ Therefore, $g^{m}(v)=g^{n}(v_{\star})=\partial D.$ Hence $v$ belongs to the grand orbit of $v_{\star}$ under $g$ , and therefore $v\in V_{g}$ . By symmetry, one obtains $V_{g}\subset V_{f}$ . Thus $V_{f}=V_{g}.$ ∎

To compare the coefficients of $f$ and $g$ , we study their preimages of a given fixed element in $k$ . This requires comparing the preimages of vertices under $f$ and $g$ . However, $f$ and $g$ may act differently on the tree and hence it is not necessarily true that $f^{-1}(v)=g^{-1}(v).$

To overcome this difficulty, we associate to each vertex $v$ a subset $X_{v}\subset\partial\{G_{f}<G_{f}(v)\}$ containing $v$ , which is minimal with respect to the invariance property

$$ f^{-1}(X_{v})=g^{-1}(X_{v}). $$

The construction of $X_{v}$ is inductive. We begin by setting $X_{0}=\{v\}$ and $Y_{0}=\varnothing$ . Define a sequence of maps $(h_{s})_{s\geq 0}$ by letting $h_{s}=f$ if $s$ is even and $h_{s}=g$ if $s$ is odd. For each $s\geq 1$ , set

$$ X_{s}=X_{s-1}\cup h_{s}(Y_{s-1}),\qquad Y_{s}=Y_{s-1}\cup h_{s}^{-1}(X_{s-1}). $$

Finally, define

$$ \displaystyle X_{v} \displaystyle=\bigcup_{s\geq 0}X_{s}, \displaystyle Y_{v} \displaystyle=\bigcup_{s\geq 0}Y_{s}. $$

The following proposition is a key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.1.

#### Proposition 5.2.

Let $f,g$ be two polynomials of degree $d\geq 2$ such that $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}$ . Then the following statements hold.

- (1) $Y_{v}=f^{-1}(X_{v})=g^{-1}(X_{v})$ ;

- (2) $w\in Y_{v}$ if and only if there exist $s\in\mathbb{N}$ , distinct vertices $v_{0},\dots,v_{s}\in X_{v}$ with $v_{s}=v$ , and points $w_{0},\dots,w_{s}\in Y_{v}$ with $w_{0}=w$ , such that

$$ h_{s}(w_{i})=v_{i}\quad(0\leq i\leq s),\qquad h_{s-1}(w_{i+1})=v_{i}\quad(0\leq i\leq s-1). $$

The diagram below illustrates how the vertices $v_{i}$ and points $w_{i}$ are selected: ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~v_{s}=v}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~v_{s-1}}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~v_{1}}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~v_{0}}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~w_{s}}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~w_{s-1}}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~w_{1}}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\bullet~w_{0}=w}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{s}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{s-1}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{s}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{s}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{s-1}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{s}}$

- (3) Let $\omega\in Y_{v}$ . Let $e_{w}=[w,w^{\prime}]$ and $e_{v}=[v,v^{\prime}]$ be edges such that $D_{w}\subset D_{w^{\prime}}$ and $D_{v}\subset D_{v^{\prime}}$ . Then we have $w^{\prime}\in Y_{v^{\prime}};$

- (4) There exists a non-empty finite set

$$ A\subset\bigcup_{v_{i}\in X_{v}}(D_{v_{i}}\cap k) $$

such that, for every $w\in Y_{v}$ , $A$ has the same number of preimages in $D_{w}$ under $f$ and $g$ , counting multiplicities.

#### Proof of Proposition 5.2.

(1) First, let $w\in Y_{v}$ , and let $s$ be the minimal integer such that $w\in Y_{s}$ . If $s$ is even, then $Y_{s}=Y_{s-1}\cup f^{-1}(X_{s-1})$ . By assumption, $w\in f^{-1}(X_{s-1}).$ Hence $f(w)\in X_{s-1}\subset X_{v}$ . If $s$ is odd, then $X_{s+1}=X_{s}\cup f(Y_{s}).$ Hence $w\in Y_{s}\subset f^{-1}(X_{s+1})\subset f^{-1}(X_{v}).$ The same argument shows that $Y_{v}\subset g^{-1}(X_{v}).$

Conversely, let $w\in f^{-1}(X_{v})$ , and let $s$ be minimal such that $w\in f^{-1}(X_{s})$ . Note that $X_{s}\subset X_{s+1}$ . If $s$ is even, then $w\in f^{-1}(X_{s})\subset Y_{s+1}\cup f^{-1}(X_{s+1})=Y_{s+2}$ . If $s$ is odd, then $w\in Y_{s+1}=Y_{s}\cup f^{-1}(X_{s}).$ In either case, we conclude that $w\in Y_{v}$ . Therefore $f^{-1}(X_{v})\subset Y_{v}$ . The same argument shows that $g^{-1}(X_{v})\subset Y_{v}$ .

Combining both inclusions yields $f^{-1}(X_{v})=g^{-1}(X_{v})=Y_{v},$ as claimed.

(2) The if direction follows directly from (1). To show the only-if direction, let $s$ be the minimal integer such that $w=w_{0}\in Y_{s}$ , where $Y_{s}=Y_{s-1}\cup h_{s}^{-1}(X_{s-1}).$ Then necessarily $w_{0}\in h_{s}^{-1}(X_{s-1})$ .

Set $v_{0}=h_{s}(w_{0})\in X_{s-1}=X_{s-2}\cup h_{s-1}(Y_{s-2}).$ We claim that $v_{0}\notin X_{s-3}$ , otherwise $w_{0}\in h_{s}^{-1}(X_{s-3})=h_{s-2}^{-1}(X_{s-3})\subseteq Y_{s-2}$ , which contradicts the minimality of $s.$ Therefore, $v_{0}\notin X_{s-2}.$

Choose $w_{1}\in Y_{s-2}$ such that $h_{s-1}(w_{1})=v_{0}.$ We claim that $s-2$ is the least integer $t$ such that $w_{1}\in Y_{t}$ . Otherwise, we would have $w_{1}\in Y_{s-3}=Y_{s-4}\cup h_{s-3}^{-1}(X_{s-4}).$ Since $h_{s-3}(w_{1})=v_{0}\notin X_{s-3},$ it follows that $w_{1}\in Y_{s-4}$ . Consequently, $v_{0}=h_{s-3}(w_{1})\in h_{s-3}(Y_{s-4})\subset X_{s-3},$ which contradicts the previous claim.

Iterating this procedure, we successively construct $v_{0},\cdots,v_{s}$ and $w_{0},\cdots,w_{s}$ satisfying the required conditions.

(3) By (2), there exist vertices $v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{s}=v\in X_{v}$ and $w_{0}=w,\dots,w_{s}\in Y_{v}$ such that for all $0\leq i\leq s$ , $h_{s}(w_{i})=v_{i}$ and $h_{s-1}(w_{i+1})=v_{i}.$ Then the corresponding edges $e_{w_{i}}=[w_{i},w_{i}^{\prime}]$ and $e_{v_{i}}=[v_{i},v_{i}^{\prime}]$ satisfy $h_{s}(e_{w_{i}})=e_{v_{i}}$ and $h_{s-1}(e_{w_{i+1}})=e_{v_{i}}.$ In particular, $h_{s}(w_{i}^{\prime})=v_{i}^{\prime}$ and $h_{s-1}(w_{i+1}^{\prime})=v_{i}^{\prime}.$ Applying (2) once again, we conclude that $w^{\prime}\in Y_{v^{\prime}}.$

(4) Let $X_{v}=\{v_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq l},$ and $Y_{v}=\{w_{j}\}_{1\leq j\leq l^{\prime}}.$ By Proposition 4.7(2), there exists $m\in\mathbb{N}$ large enough such that $\mu_{f}(f^{m}(v_{i}))=\mu_{f}(f^{m+1}(w_{j}))=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $1\leq j\leq l^{\prime}$ . Note that $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ . By Proposition 4.7(3), we may define

$$ \displaystyle d_{i} \displaystyle\coloneqq\deg_{v_{i}}f^{m}=\deg_{v_{i}}g^{m}=d^{m}\mu_{f}(v_{i}) \displaystyle\delta_{j} \displaystyle\coloneqq\deg_{w_{j}}f^{m+1}=\deg_{w_{j}}g^{m+1}=d^{m+1}\mu_{f}(w_{j}) $$

For each $j$ , there exist indices $i_{j}$ and $k_{j}$ such that $f$ (resp. $g$ ) maps $D_{w_{j}}$ onto $D_{v_{i_{j}}}$ (resp. $D_{v_{k_{j}}}$ ). We then have $\deg_{w_{j}}f=\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{i_{j}}},$ and $\deg_{w_{j}}g=\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{k_{j}}}.$

Now choose a finite set $A\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{l}(D_{v_{i}}\cap k)$ such that $\#(A\cap D_{v_{i}})=d_{i}$ for each $1\leq i\leq l$ . Then, for every $w_{j}\in Y_{v}$ , the number of preimages of $A$ under $f$ in $D_{w_{j}}$ is $d_{i_{j}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{i_{j}}}=\delta_{j},$ and similarly the number of preimages under $g$ in $D_{w_{j}}$ is $d_{k_{j}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{j}}{d_{k_{j}}}=\delta_{j}.$ ∎

### 5.2. Rigidity of Julia sets for polynomials of the same degree

Recall that for the Julia set $\mathcal{J}$ of a polynomial of degree at least $2$ , $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ denotes the group of affine transformations that preserve $\mathcal{J}$ .

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ , and let $\sigma$ be an affine transformation. Then the following statements are equivalent:

- (1) $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ ;

- (2) $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ ;

- (3) $\mathcal{J}_{\sigma\circ f}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ .

#### Proof.

Assume first that $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ . Since $\sigma(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ , the measures $\mu_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}$ and $\mu_{f}$ are equilibrium measures with the same support. Hence, $\sigma^{*}\mu_{f}=\mu_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}=\mu_{f}.$ Therefore,

$$ (f\circ\sigma)^{*}\mu_{f}=(\sigma\circ f)^{*}\mu_{f}=d\mu_{f}. $$

Applying Theorem 2.1 to $f\circ\sigma$ (or to $\sigma\circ f$ ) and measure $\rho=\mu_{f}$ , we obtain $\mu_{f\circ\sigma}=\mu_{\sigma\circ f}=\mu_{f}.$ Consequently, $\mathcal{\mathcal{J}}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{\mathcal{J}}_{\sigma\circ f}=\mathcal{\mathcal{J}}_{f}.$

Assume that $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{J}_{f}$ . Since $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ is totally invariant under $f$ and $f\circ\sigma$ , we obtain

$$ \mathcal{J}_{f}=(f\circ\sigma)^{-1}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{J}_{f}). $$

Thus $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ , which completes the proof. ∎

We now prove the following rigidity result, which is the core of the proof of Theorem 1.1:

#### Theorem 5.4.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0.$ Let $f$ and $g$ be two polynomials of degree $d\geq 2$ which do not have potential good reduction. Suppose $\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{J}_{f}=\mathcal{J}_{g}$ . Then there exists $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J})$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g.$

#### Remark 5.5.

When both $f$ and $g$ have good reduction, the statement is no longer valid. For example, consider $f(z)=z^{d}$ and $g(z)=z^{d}+z.$ Both maps have good reduction, and therefore their Julia sets reduce to the Gauss point $x_{g}$ . However, there is no affine transformation $\sigma$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g.$

Before beginning the proof of Theorem 5.4, let us explain our argument when $f=z^{2}+c_{1},g=z^{2}+c_{2}$ with $|c_{i}|>1$ . In this case, choose some large $\alpha>0$ so that $\{G_{f}(z)<\alpha\}=\{G_{g}(z)<\alpha\}$ is given by a disk $D(0,R)$ . Taking preimages, we obtain that

$$ f^{-n}(D(0,R))=\left\{G_{f}(z)<\frac{\alpha}{2^{n}}\right\}=\left\{G_{g}(z)<\frac{\alpha}{2^{n}}\right\}=g^{-n}(D(0,R)). $$

Fix an $\varepsilon>0$ . We may then take $n$ large enough so that $f^{-n}(D(0,R))=g^{-n}(D(0,R))$ is a disjoint union of $2^{n}$ disks, each of radius $<\varepsilon$ . Now let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{2^{n}}$ be the roots of $f^{n}(z)=0$ and similarly let $\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{2^{n}}$ be those for $g^{n}(z)=0$ . Then we may arrange them so that $|\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i}|<\varepsilon$ for all $i$ . In particular, we obtain

$$ \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 2^{n}}|\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}-\beta_{i}\beta_{j}|\leq\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 2^{n}}\left|(\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i})\alpha_{j}+(\alpha_{j}-\beta_{j})\beta_{i}\right|\leq\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon. $$

By Viète’s formulas, this implies that the coefficients of $z^{2^{n}-2}$ for $f^{n}(z)$ and $g^{n}(z)$ differ by at most $\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon$ . But this coefficient can easily be computed to be $2^{n-1}c_{1}$ and $2^{n-1}c_{2}$ . Hence

$$ |2^{n-1}||c_{1}-c_{2}|<\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon\implies|c_{1}-c_{2}|<\max\{|c_{1}|,|c_{2}|\}\varepsilon, $$

where we crucially used the fact that $k$ is of residue characteristic $0$ . Letting $\epsilon\to 0$ gives $c_{1}=c_{2}$ , proving rigidity in this case.

For general polynomials, we will use the subset $X_{v}$ for a suitable vertex $v$ , as introduced in Proposition 5.2 as a replacement for $f^{-n}(D(0,R))$ and $g^{-n}(D(0,R))$ . Keeping the notation introduced in §5.1, one has:

#### Lemma 5.6.

Let $v^{0}$ be a vertex such that the sublevel set $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(v^{0})\}$ is a disk. Then for all $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a vertex $v\in f^{-n}(v^{0})$ for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , such that for any $w\in Y_{v}$ , the radius of the associated ball satisfies $\mathrm{diam}(D_{w})<\epsilon.$

#### Proof.

By [50, Theorem 3.1], $f$ admits a repelling type I periodic point $p$ , which necessarily belongs to the Julia set. (Note: Although the original statement is formulated for polynomials over formal Laurent series, the proof remains valid for fields with residue characteristic $0$ . )

Up to iteration, we may assume $p$ is a fixed point. Note that $G_{f}(p)=0$ . Therefore, for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , there exists a unique connected component $D_{n}$ of $\{G_{f}<\frac{1}{d^{n}}G_{f}(v^{0})\}$ containing $p$ .

We claim that there exists $n$ such that $\mathrm{diam}(D_{n})<\epsilon.$ Suppose for contradiction that $\mathrm{diam}(D_{n})\geq\epsilon$ for all $n$ . Then $D(p,\epsilon)$ is contained in the intersection $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}D_{n}$ . Since $f(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}D_{n})=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}D_{n}$ , we conclude that $D(p,\epsilon)$ is contained in the Fatou set of $f$ , which contradicts the fact that $p$ belongs to the Julia set. Let $v=\partial D_{n}$ . Then, $v\in f^{-n}(v^{0})$ and $\mathrm{diam}(D_{v})<\epsilon.$

Let $w\in Y_{v}$ . We claim that $v^{0}=f^{n}(v)=f^{n+1}(w)$ . This follows from the fact that $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(f^{n}(v))\}$ and $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(f^{n+1}(w))\}$ are the same disk with boundary point $v^{0}=f^{n}(v)=f^{n+1}(w)$ .

Let $h_{n}=f$ if $n$ is even and let $h_{n}=g$ if $n$ is odd. By Proposition 5.2(2), for any $w\in Y_{v}$ , there exist $s\in\mathbb{N}$ , distinct vertices $v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{s}=v\in X_{v}$ , and $w_{0}=w,\dots,w_{s}\in Y_{v}$ such that $h_{s}(w_{i})=v_{i}$ and $h_{s-1}(w_{i+1})=v_{i}$ . Let $e_{w_{i}}$ and $e_{v_{i}}$ denote the unique edges with lower vertices $w_{i}$ and $v_{i}$ , respectively. According to Proposition 4.7(4), we have the length relations $l(e_{v_{i}})=\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}\cdot l(e_{w_{i}})$ and $l(e_{w_{i+1}})\leq l(e_{v_{i}})$ . Combining these yields:

$$ l(e_{v})\leq\left(\prod_{i=0}^{s}\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}\right)\cdot l(e_{w}). $$

Note that the disks $D_{w_{i}}$ are disjoint disks. By Proposition 4.9, each disk $D_{w_{i}}$ contains exactly $\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}-1$ critical points (counted with multiplicities). Since the total number of critical points of $h_{s}$ is $d-1$ , there are at most $d-1$ indices $i$ such that $\deg_{w_{i}}h_{s}\geq 2$ . We therefore obtain

$$ l(e_{v})\leq d^{d-1}\,l(e_{w}). $$

Let $v^{0},v^{1},\dots,v^{m}=v$ be the sequence of vertices obtained by descending along the tree to $v$ , and let $v^{0}=w^{0},w^{1},\dots,w^{m+j}=w$ be the sequence descending to $w$ . Since $w\in Y_{v}$ by assumption, it follows from Proposition 5.2(3) that $w^{i+j}\in Y_{v^{i}}$ for each $1\leq i\leq m$ . Therefore, $l(e_{v^{i}})\leq d^{d-1}l(e_{w^{i+j}})$ . Summing these lengths, we obtain:

$$ \log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(D_{v^{0}})}{\mathrm{diam}(D_{v})}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}l(e_{v^{i}})\leq d^{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}l(e_{w^{i+j}})\leq d^{d-1}\log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(D_{v^{0}})}{\mathrm{diam}(D_{w})}. $$

Consequently, as $\epsilon\to 0$ , it follows that $\mathrm{diam}(D_{w})\to 0$ , which completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 5.4.

By Lemma 5.3, it suffices to prove that there exists an affine map $\sigma$ such that $f=\sigma\circ g$ .

Fix a vertex $v^{0}$ such that $\{G_{f}<G_{f}(v^{0})\}$ is a disk. By Lemma 5.6, for all $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a vertex $v\in f^{-n}(v^{0})$ such that for every $w\in Y_{v}$ , one has $\operatorname{diam}(D_{w})<\epsilon.$ Write $Y_{v}=\{w_{j}\}_{1\leq j\leq l}.$ By Proposition 5.2(4), there exists a finite set $A\subset\bigcup_{v_{i}\in X_{v}}D_{v_{i}}\cap k$ such that, for each $1\leq j\leq l$ , the sets $f^{-1}(A)$ and $g^{-1}(A)$ have the same cardinality in $D_{w_{j}}$ , counted with multiplicity. Since $\operatorname{diam}(D_{w_{j}})<\epsilon$ , any $x,y\in D_{w_{j}}\cap k$ satisfy $|x-y|<\epsilon$ .

Let $N=\#A$ , and write $f^{-1}(A)=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{dN}\}$ and $g^{-1}(A)=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{dN}\}$ , counted with multiplicity. After reindexing, we may assume that $|x_{i}-y_{i}|<\epsilon$ for all $1\leq i\leq dN$ . Since $x_{i},y_{i}\in D_{v^{0}}$ by construction, there exists a constant $C>0$ , independent of $\epsilon$ , such that for every $1\leq s\leq d$ , one has

$$ \left|\sum_{i=1}^{dN}x_{i}^{s}-\sum_{i=1}^{dN}y_{i}^{s}\right|\leq C\epsilon. $$

Write $f(z)=a_{d}z^{d}+a_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{0},$ and $g(z)=b_{d}z^{d}+b_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots+b_{0}.$ Assume that $g$ cannot be written as the composition of an affine map with $f$ . Let $i$ be the largest integer such that $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}\neq\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}.$ Then $i\geq 1$ .

Note that for $i\geq 1$ , by Viète’s theorem, the $(d-i)$ -th elementary symmetric function of $f^{-1}(c)$ (resp. $g^{-1}(c)$ ) is independent of the choice of $c\in k$ and is equal to $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}$ (resp. $\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}$ ). Denote by $x_{i}^{c}$ (resp. $y_{i}^{c}$ ) the preimages for $c\in A$ under $f$ (resp. $g$ ). Applying Newton’s identities and Viète’s formulas to preimages of all $c\in A$ under $f$ and $g$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)\left(\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}\right) \displaystyle=(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{s=1}^{d-i}\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}\left(\sum(x_{i}^{c})^{s}\right); \displaystyle(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)\left(\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}\right) \displaystyle=(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{s=1}^{d-i}\frac{b_{i+s}}{b_{d}}\left(\sum(y_{i}^{c})^{s}\right). $$

Since we assume that $\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}=\frac{b_{i+s}}{b_{d}}$ , summing over all $c\in A$ and taking the difference, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)N\left(\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}-\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}\right) \displaystyle=(-1)^{i-1}\sum_{s=1}^{d-i}\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{dN}(x_{j}^{s}-y_{j}^{s})\right). $$

Since the residue characteristic is assumed to be $0$ , we have $|(d-i)N|=1$ . It then follows from the strong triangle inequality that

$$ \left|\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}-\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}\right|\leq C\epsilon\max_{1\leq s\leq d-i}\left|\frac{a_{i+s}}{a_{d}}\right|. $$

Letting $\epsilon\to 0$ , we obtain $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}=\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}$ , which leads to a contradiction.

Therefore, $\frac{a_{i}}{a_{d}}=\frac{b_{i}}{b_{d}}$ for all $i\geq 1$ . Let $\lambda=\frac{a_{d}}{b_{d}}$ and $\mu=a_{0}-\frac{b_{0}a_{d}}{b_{d}}$ , then $f=\lambda g+\mu$ , which proves the claim. ∎

### 5.3. Group of dynamical symmetries

We recall from [42, §3] the notion of the dynamical symmetry group of a polynomial over a field $k$ with characteristic $0$ .

We begin with monic and centered polynomials. A reduced presentation of $f\in k[z]$ is a decomposition

$$ f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m}), $$

where $\mu,m\geq 0$ , $f_{0}(0)\neq 0$ , and $f_{0}$ is not of the form $h(z^{l})$ for any polynomial $h$ with $\deg h\geq 1$ and any $l\geq 2$ . Such a presentation is unique.

The group of dynamical symmetries of $f$ , denoted by $\Sigma_{f}$ , is defined by

$$ \Sigma_{f}=\begin{cases}\mathbb{U}_{m},&\text{if }f_{0}\neq 1,\\
\bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{U}_{m},&\text{if }f_{0}=1,\end{cases} $$

where $\mathbb{U}_{m}$ denotes the cyclic group of $m$ -th roots of unity.

Now let $f$ be an arbitrary polynomial of degree at least $2$ , and let $L$ be an affine transformation such that $L^{-1}\circ f\circ L$ is monic and centered. We define the group of dynamical symmetries of $f$ by

$$ \Sigma_{f}=\bigl\{L^{-1}\circ\sigma\circ L\big|\sigma\in\Sigma_{L^{-1}\circ f\circ L}\bigr\}. $$

This definition is independent of the choice of the affine transformation $M$ .

A priori, the dynamical symmetry group $\Sigma_{f}$ is defined in purely algebraic terms. However, as a consequence of rigidity phenomena for complex Julia sets, Favre–Gauthier [42, Proposition 3.9] proved $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}$ when $f$ is not a monomial.

#### Proposition 5.7.

Let $f$ be a complex polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ . Then:

- (1) The group $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ of affine transformations preserving $\mathcal{J}_{f}$ coincides with the group of all $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aff}(\mathbb{C})$ such that the Green function satisfies $G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{f}(z).$

- (2) If $f$ is not conjugate to the monomial $M_{d}(z)=z^{d}$ , then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}.$ Otherwise, $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{M_{d}})=\mathbb{S}^{1}$ , whereas $\Sigma_{M_{d}}$ is the group of roots of unity.

Following the same philosophy, we establish an analogous comparison between $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ and $\Sigma_{f}$ in the non-Archimedean setting. This will follow from Theorem 5.4.

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let $k$ be a non-Archimedean field with residue characteristic $0$ . Let $f(z)\in k[z]$ be a polynomial of degree at least $2$ .

- (1) The group $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ coincides with the group of $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ such that the Green function satisfies $G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{f}(z)$ ;

- (2) Suppose $f$ has potential good reduction. Let $L\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ such that $L(\mathcal{J}_{f})=x_{g}$ , then

$$ \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\{L^{-1}\circ(az+b)\circ L\mid|a|=1,|b|\leq 1\}. $$

- (3) If $f$ does not have potential good reduction, then

$$ \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}. $$

#### Proof.

(1) Let $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ . Then $\mathcal{J}_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}=\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\mathcal{J}_{f}.$ By [3, Theorem 10.91], we have $G_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}(z)=G_{f}(z).$ It follows from Proposition 4.3(4) that

$$ G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{\sigma^{-1}\circ f\circ\sigma}(z)=G_{f}(z). $$

Conversely, suppose $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aff}(k)$ satisfies $G_{f}(\sigma(z))=G_{f}(z)$ for all $z$ . Then $\sigma$ preserves the filled-in Julia set $\cal{K}_{f}$ , and hence also its boundary, $\mathcal{J}_{f}=\partial\cal{K}_{f}.$ Therefore, $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ .

(2) The second statement follows from the observation that the group of affine transformations fixing $x_{g}$ is precisely $\{az+b\mid|a|=1,|b|\leq 1\}$ .

(3) Up to conjugation, we may assume that $f$ is monic and centered, and write its reduced presentation as $f(z)=z^{\mu}f_{0}(z^{m}).$

By Lemma 5.3, for any $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ we have $\mathcal{J}_{f\circ\sigma}=\mathcal{J}_{f}.$ By Theorem 5.4, there exists an element $\rho(\sigma)\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ such that

$$ f\circ\sigma=\rho(\sigma)\circ f. $$

Moreover, the map $\rho\colon\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is a group homomorphism.

We claim that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite. Assuming this claim, it then follows from [42, Proposition 3.6] that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})\subseteq\Sigma_{f}.$

Conversely, let $\lambda\in\mathbb{U}_{m}=\Sigma_{f}$ . A direct computation shows that

$$ (\lambda f)^{k}(z)=\lambda^{1+\mu+\cdots+\mu^{k-1}}f^{k}(z)\quad\text{for all }k\geq 1. $$

Hence the associated Green functions satisfy $G_{\lambda f}=G_{f},$ which implies $\mathcal{J}_{\lambda f}=\mathcal{J}_{f}.$ By Lemma 5.3, we conclude that $\lambda z\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ . Therefore, $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})=\Sigma_{f}.$

It remains to prove the claim that $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite. By (5.1), each $\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ permutes the critical points of $f$ . Since an affine transformation is uniquely determined by the images of two distinct points, it follows that if $f$ has at least two critical points, then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{J}_{f})$ is finite.

If instead $f$ is unicritical, then, since $f$ is monic, centered, and has bad reduction, it can be written as $f(z)=z^{d}+C$ with $C\in k^{\times}.$ In this case, $\sigma$ fixes the unique critical point $0$ , and hence must be of the form $\sigma(z)=\lambda z$ for some $\lambda\in k^{\times}$ .
